heart tree.meaning: a white weirwood tree with a face, holy to the old gods
heart tree.example: Sansa had prayed to the Seven in their sept and old gods of the heart tree, asking them to bring the old man back, or better still to send another singer, young and handsome.

stand a chance.meaning: to have a possibility of doing well
stand a chance.example: He would have stood a better chance of hatching a real dragon than saving up enough coin to make a golden one.

oft as not.meaning: quite often; as likely as not
oft as not.example: As great a maester as once he’d been, now his robes concealed soiled smallclothes oft as not, and half a year ago some acolytes found him weeping in the Library, unable to find his way back to his chambers.

go to one's head.example: When he pushed back from the bench and got to his feet, the fearsomely strong cider all went to his head at once.

one and ten.meaning: eleven, in the old way of counting (three-and-ten is thirteen)
one and ten.example: She was not quite one-and-ten, her betrothed three-and-ten; even so, she had been winning more oft than not of late.

the gentler sex.meaning: women (an old-fashioned way of saying it)
the gentler sex.example: A true knight must defend the gentler sex.

off hand.meaning: the hand you do not usually write or fight with
off hand.example: “It is no easy thing to fight with your off hand,” observed the Mad Mouse.

murder hole.meaning: a hole in a castle floor or wall through which defenders attack people below
murder hole.example: More arrow slits dotted the insides of those great stone thighs, and when Arya craned her neck around to watch the crow’s nest slip through with a good ten yards to spare, she spied murder holes beneath the Titan’s armored skirts, and pale faces staring down at them from behind the iron bars.

beg leave.example: When the queen reminded him of their meeting later, Ser Kevan gave a weary nod and begged leave to withdraw.

take ship.meaning: to get on a ship in order to travel
take ship.example: He is making his way to Oldtown to take ship.

go ill.example: “Need I say that it will go ill for you if any word of your .

take offense.meaning: to feel hurt or angry about what someone did
take offense.example: Lord Tyrell cannot take offense if you choose one of his own bannermen as Hand.

judge from.meaning: to make a judgment using something as proof
judge from.example: ” Longwaters had not been a tad of a lad for many a year, to judge from his spotted head and the white hairs growing from his chin.

see to it.example: So my brothers and me, we saw to it.

single file.meaning: in a line, one person behind another
single file.example: Through the Mother’s Doors marched white septas from their cloister, seven abreast and singing softly, while the silent sisters came single file down the Stranger’s Steps.

the hour of the wolf.meaning: the darkest part of the night, just before morning

call up.meaning: to bring something into your mind; to remember
call up.example: She seized a chunk of hard lye soap and scrubbed under her arms, trying to call up Renly’s face again.

pick at.meaning: to pull at something with your fingers
pick at.example: The maester hmmmmed and hrrrred, picked at the wax, and finally gave it back.

female parts.meaning: a woman's sex organs (a polite way of saying it)
female parts.example: The Lace Serpent was burned alive, poor woman, though her tongue was torn out first, and her female parts, with which it was said that she had enslaved her lord.

on one's hands.meaning: to have something difficult that you must deal with
on one's hands.example: If it was Ser Shadrich dogging her heels, she might well have a fight on her hands.

of a height.example: The two of them were of a height, but she could not look him in the eye, nor say the simple words her septa had taught her.

all the while.example: I thought it was Ser Dontos, my poor old drunken Florian, but it was Petyr all the while.

in force.meaning: with many soldiers; in large numbers

in one's own right.meaning: because of who you yourself are, not through someone else
in one's own right.example: She knew Lord Nestor dreamed of holding the Gates in his own right, a lord in truth as well as name, but Lysa dreamed of other sons and meant the castle to go to Robert’s little brother.

high seat.meaning: the special chair of a lord; it also means his power
high seat.example: Lord Rodrik’s high seat was vacant.

see to.meaning: to take care of; to deal with
see to.example: “See to my crew, once they’re done unloading Black Wind.

the old way.meaning: the old ironborn way of life: taking what they want by fighting
the old way.example: The Old Way served the isles well when we were one small kingdom amongst many, but Aegon’s Conquest put an end to that.

feed the crabs.meaning: to drown at sea (said as a joke: the dead body feeds the crabs)
feed the crabs.example: “Asha, my two tall sons fed the crabs of Fair Isle.

care to.example: That was not something he would care to hear, however.

call upon.example: Let the wizards call upon their gods.

well and good.example: “You want a woman, well and good.

guard your tongue.meaning: to be careful about what you say

bought and paid for.meaning: secretly paid to serve someone else; bribed
bought and paid for.example: Your maid is bought and paid for.

calm the waters.meaning: to make a tense or angry situation peaceful
calm the waters.example: I had hoped that imprisoning my headstrong nieces would help to calm the waters, but all we’ve done is drive the roaches back beneath the rushes.

cut close to the bone.meaning: to say something too personal or painful
cut close to the bone.example: That cut too close to the bone.

share the rope.meaning: to be hanged, like someone else was
share the rope.example: Podrick had shared the ham and might have shared the rope as well, but his name had saved him.

carry off.example: Two years later he was dead, carried off by the same chill that took Lord and Lady Caron and their daughters.

make a living on one's back.meaning: to earn money as a prostitute
make a living on one's back.example: Last I saw her she was off for King’s Landing t’ make a living on her back.

keep a brave face.meaning: to pretend to be brave when you are afraid
keep a brave face.example: Sam tried to keep a brave face on him, for Gilly’s sake if little else.

bird of prey.meaning: a bird that hunts other animals for food, like a hawk
bird of prey.example: Storm Crow and Talon were faster, Cotter Pyke told Maester Aemon back at Eastwatch-by-the-Sea, but they were fighting ships, lean, swift birds of prey where the rowers sat on open decks.

beg for quarter.meaning: to ask to be spared; to ask for mercy in battle
beg for quarter.example: On the third day Horas Redwyne made him squeal like a pig when he begged for quarter.

a shadow of oneself.meaning: much weaker or worse than before
a shadow of oneself.example: The rumors of his death had not been far wrong, to look at him; wounds and imprisonment had left him a shadow of the man he’d been.

be delivered of.meaning: to give birth to (an old formal way of saying it)
be delivered of.example: Lady Tanda sends word that her daughter Lollys has been delivered of a strong, healthy son.

in the blink of an eye.meaning: very quickly; in a very short time
in the blink of an eye.example: The big man hung his head and grew old, all in the blink of an eye.

take wing.example: The cheeks of the tattooed man were so puffed out they looked about to burst, and the muscles in his chest twitched in a way that it made it seem as if the bird were about to rip free of his flesh and take wing.

stumble on.example: If by some freak’s chance you stumbled onto Sansa Stark, he told me to bring her back to Maidenpool.

flesh and blood.meaning: a close relative, like a son or daughter
flesh and blood.example:
What sort of father uses his own flesh and blood to pay his debts?”

[30] “The princely sort,” Doran Martell had answered.

hit home.example: The bolts hit home so hard they knocked the horse sideways.

through and through.example: It was real silver, solid through and through.

looking glass.example: When Gretchel fetched her Lysa’s silvered looking glass, the color seemed just perfect with Alayne’s mass of dark brown hair.

heart and hand.meaning: completely; with all your feelings and actions
heart and hand.example: My lords, I am with you, heart and hand.

step down.example: if I have not set the Vale to rights, I shall willingly step down as Lord Protector,” Petyr promised them.

taste of blood.meaning: a first experience of killing or battle
taste of blood.example: Well, you’ve had your taste of blood.

put out word.meaning: to spread news so people hear it
put out word.example: They have put out word that they mean to hang him for what he did at Saltpans.

heavy with child.example: One of the women was very old, one was heavy with child, and one was a girl as fresh and pretty as a flower in spring.

have your head.meaning: to have someone killed by cutting off their head
have your head.example: They could have your head for this.

change hands.example: Darry had changed hands several times during the fighting, and its castle had been burned once and sacked at least twice, but Lancel had seemingly wasted little time setting things to rights.

get a bastard by.meaning: to make a woman pregnant with a child born outside marriage
get a bastard by.example: She’ll teach you a few things you’ll find useful on your wedding night, I don’t doubt, and you’re not like to get a bastard by her.

hear tell.meaning: to hear news about something (an old way of saying it)
hear tell.example: He was Prince Joffrey’s sworn shield for many a year, and even here we would hear tell of his deeds, both good and ill.

take out on.meaning: to show your anger toward people who did not cause it
take out on.example: When none was at hand, they took their rage and desperation out upon the townsfolk.

come home on one's shield.example: And if he should come home on his shield, covered in blood and glory, Ser Osney will be there to console his grieving sister.

watch is ended.meaning: said when a man of the Night's Watch dies; his service is over
watch is ended.example: And now his watch is ended.

run down.meaning: to catch someone after chasing them
run down.example: Aboard the Blackbird Gilly could have run him down in hardly any time at all.

dragon's mouth.example: He rode straight into the dragon’s mouth, they say, all in white and swinging his morningstar about his head, slaying left and right.

white as chalk.meaning: very pale, from fear or illness
white as chalk.example: Lady Alla turned white as chalk, and ran from the room.

pleasure with one's mouth.meaning: to give sexual pleasure with the mouth
pleasure with one's mouth.example: One said that the Imp was hiding in an Oldtown brothel, pleasuring men with his mouth.

run off.meaning: to make people go away; to drive away

wager of battle.meaning: a fight to decide whether someone is guilty; trial by battle
wager of battle.example:
“This trial,” she said, in a quiet voice, “what if Margaery demands that her guilt or innocence be determined by wager of battle?”

[50] A smile brushed Cersei’s lips.

a babe in arms.meaning: A baby too young to walk, still carried in someone's arms.
a babe in arms.example: —Rhaegar’s son, {AEGON, a babe in arms, murdered during the Sack of King’s Landing,

daub and wattle.meaning: made of a mix of mud and woven sticks; rough and poor
daub and wattle.example: Pate had never seen King’s Landing, but he knew it was a daub-and-wattle city, a sprawl of mud streets, thatched roofs, and wooden hovels.

six and ten.example: The boy looked to be no more than six-and-ten.

well bred.meaning: well raised and polite; (of horses) born from good parents
well bred.example: A pair of wealthy townsmen sat on well-bred palfreys a dozen places behind her, and farther back she spied a skinny boy on a piebald rounsey.

rough hewn.meaning: cut or shaped roughly, not smooth
rough hewn.example: Above the cairn that marked their resting place, the victors had raised a rough-hewn wooden marker.

grey shot.example: ” Lord Nestor Royce was a bullnecked, barrel-chested, balding man with a grey-shot beard and a stern look.

by blow.meaning: (old, rude) a child born to parents not married to each other; a bastard
by blow.example: ” Her husband’s by-blows had his look as well, though at least Robert had the grace to keep them out of sight.

ill begotten.meaning: born to parents not married to each other; (of plans) badly made
ill begotten.example: Her twisted little brother was too clever to allow Lollys to name her wretched ill-begotten bastard after him, knowing it was sure to draw the queen’s wroth down upon her.

hot tempered.example: In the Reach men said it was the food that made Dornishmen so hot-tempered and their women so wild and wanton.

good daughter.meaning: a polite, kind way to say 'daughter-in-law' — a son's wife
good daughter.example: ” “On the morrow I want you to pay a call on my good-daughter,” Cersei said as Dorcas was dressing her for bed.

paragraphs.context: Rosey was her daughter, fifteen and freshly flowered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pate loves Rosey, but he can never pay her mother's price of a golden dragon; his savings are far too small.
paragraphs.simple: Pate loves a serving girl named Rosey. Her mother Emma says any man who wants Rosey must pay a gold coin called a golden dragon. Pate has saved only a little silver and copper money, which is not nearly enough. He knows he has no real hope of saving enough coin.

paragraphs.context: The alchemist should have come by now. Had it all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pate waits in vain for the alchemist and thinks bitterly about his years serving the senile Archmaester Walgrave.
paragraphs.simple: Pate worries because the stranger who promised him gold has not come. He thinks back over his bad luck. He once thought himself lucky to serve old Archmaester Walgrave with the ravens, but the old man has lost his mind: he forgets where he lives, soils himself, and cannot even give Pate the chain-link he hoped for. The Citadel only keeps Walgrave's high title out of politeness.

paragraphs.context: gold for iron, gold for iron, gold for iron
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pate recalls the alchemist's bargain: a gold dragon for a black iron key, to be paid three days later.
paragraphs.simple: Pate imagines the nightingale singing the words the stranger spoke three days ago. The man called himself an alchemist and said he could change iron into gold. He showed Pate a gold coin with a dragon on it and promised Pate the coin if Pate stole something iron for him. Pate said he was no thief, but the man answered that he would return in three days with his dragon.

paragraphs.context: within a hundred leagues of Qarth is speaking of these dragons
paragraphs.mainIdea: Leo claims sailors everywhere say Daenerys Targaryen has hatched three dragons, and even Archmaester Marwyn believes it.
paragraphs.simple: Leo tells the others that every sailor who has sailed near Qarth is talking about the dragons. Some sailors even say they have seen them. He says Archmaester Marwyn, the Mage, is inclined to believe the stories are true.

paragraphs.context: The night before an acolyte says his vows, he must
paragraphs.mainIdea: Armen explains the glass-candle vigil: an acolyte must spend a night trying to light an unlightable obsidian candle.
paragraphs.simple: Armen tells Roone about the vigil. The night before an acolyte says his vows, he must stand a vigil in the vault. No lantern, torch, lamp, or taper is allowed him, only a candle of obsidian. He must spend the night in darkness unless he can light that candle. Some will try: the foolish and the stubborn, those who study the higher mysteries. They often cut their fingers, for the ridges on the candles are said to be as sharp as razors. Then, with bloody hands, they must wait upon the dawn, brooding on their failure.

paragraphs.context: Am I still a thief if I put it all back
paragraphs.mainIdea: The alchemist never came, and Pate wonders whether returning the stolen things would mean he was never a thief.
paragraphs.simple: The mists are lightening to the east. Dawn has come, and the alchemist has not. Pate does not know whether he should laugh or cry. He asks himself a question he has no answer for: if he puts it all back and no one ever knows, is he still a thief? It is like the questions that Ebrose and Vaellyn once asked him.

paragraphs.context: If I pick that up, I am a thief, he remembered thinking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pate remembers the moment he decided to be a thief: he took the black iron master key, then the silver too.
paragraphs.simple: Pate remembers thinking that picking up the key would make him a thief. The key was old and heavy, made of black iron, and was said to open every door in the Citadel. Only the archmaesters had such keys; the others carried theirs or hid them away, but if Walgrave had hidden his, no one would ever have seen it again. Pate snatched up the key and was halfway to the door before turning back to take the silver too. A thief was a thief, whether he stole a little or a lot. As he left, one of the white ravens called after him, Pate, Pate, Pate.

paragraphs.context: The cobblestones rushed up to kiss him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pate falls dying, unable even to cry for help.
paragraphs.simple: The cobblestones rush up to meet Pate. He tries to cry for help, but his voice is failing too.

paragraphs.context: pushed his head back down as he tried to snatch a breath
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron drowns a struggling boy in the sea as part of the Drowned God's ritual.
paragraphs.simple: It is a bleak, cold morning, and the sea is as grey as lead. The first three men gave their lives to the Drowned God fearlessly, but the fourth is weak in faith and struggles as his lungs cry out for air. Standing waist-deep in the surf, Aeron seizes the naked boy by the shoulders and pushes his head back down as he tries to snatch a breath. Have courage, he says. We came from the sea, and to the sea we must return. Open your mouth and drink deep of god's blessing. Fill your lungs with water, that you may die and be reborn. It does no good to fight.

paragraphs.context: Nine sons had been born from the loins of Quellon Greyjoy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron lists his father's nine sons by three wives and remembers the brothers who died young.
paragraphs.simple: Aeron thinks about his family. His father Quellon Greyjoy had nine sons by three wives. Balon, Euron, Victarion, Urrigon, and Aeron were sons of the second wife; three half-brothers died young, and a sickly youngest half-brother is best forgotten. Aeron dimly remembers Harlon dying slowly of greyscale, a disease that turned his tongue and lips to stone.

paragraphs.context: Balon the eldest and boldest, a fierce and fearless boy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron remembers Balon's brave youth and believes the jealous Storm God murdered him.
paragraphs.simple: Of the four brothers who lived to manhood, Balon was the eldest and the boldest: a fierce, fearless boy who climbed cliffs, sailed, fought, and captained his own ship at seventeen. Though Balon always showed Aeron nothing but scorn, Aeron thinks scorn was more than he deserved. He believes Balon was murdered by a jealous god, and now a storm is coming such as these isles have never known.

paragraphs.context: The wolves have made a weakling of him, as I feared
paragraphs.mainIdea: Balon told Aeron the Starks ruined Theon and hoped Theon was dead so Asha could inherit; Aeron holds that no woman can rule the ironborn.
paragraphs.simple: Aeron remembers his last talk with Balon in the Sea Tower. The king shook his head in despair and said the Starks, the wolves, had made his son Theon weak, and even hoped Theon was dead so nothing would stand in the way of his daughter Asha. Balon saw himself in his wild, headstrong daughter and believed she could succeed him. Aeron tried to tell him he was wrong: no woman will ever rule the ironborn, not even one such as Asha.

paragraphs.context: A flying axe took off half of Urri’s hand when he was ten-and-four
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron remembers how his own axe maimed his brother Urri in a game, and how a maester's treatment killed him.
paragraphs.simple: Aeron remembers his brother Urri. When Urri was fourteen, he and Aeron were playing the finger dance, and Aeron's axe cut off half of Urri's hand. Their stepmother gave Urri to her maester instead of healing him the ironborn way, with fire and seawater. The maester tried to sew the fingers back and used potions and poultices, but the hand rotted and Urri died of fever after his arm was sawn off. This is why Aeron distrusts maesters and their healing.

paragraphs.context: Leave your halls and hovels, your castles and your keeps
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron summons all captains and kings to Old Wyk for a kingsmoot instead of bowing to Euron or Asha.
paragraphs.simple: Aeron tells the lords to look to the sea, not to him or the laws of men. They must raise their sails and sail to Old Wyk, all the captains and the kings. They must not go to Pyke to bow before the godless, nor to Harlaw to consort with scheming women. They must point their prows toward Old Wyk, where stood the Grey King's Hall. In the name of the Drowned God he summons all of them: leave your halls and hovels, your castles and your keeps, and return to Nagga's hill to make a kingsmoot.

paragraphs.context: In Sunspear, on the Broken Arm, along the Greenblood, in the mountains
paragraphs.mainIdea: Obara describes how all of Dorne mourns Oberyn and cries out for vengeance.
paragraphs.simple: Obara tells the captain how Dorne is grieving. Thousands are walking across the desert to help bring Oberyn's body home. The temples are packed to bursting, the red priests have lit their temple fires, and in the pillow houses women are coupling with every man who comes to them and refusing any coin. Everywhere, in Sunspear, on the Broken Arm, along the Greenblood, in the mountains, out in the deep sand, women tear their hair and men cry out in rage. On every tongue is the same question: what will Prince Doran do to avenge his murdered brother?

paragraphs.context: tossed his spear at my feet and gave my mother the back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Obara tells how Oberyn claimed her as his daughter when she chose the spear over her mother's tears.
paragraphs.simple: Obara tells the prince how her father claimed her as a child. Her mother, a whore, did not want to give her up and said Obara might not even be his. Oberyn threw his spear at the girl's feet, struck her mother across the face, and said: girl or boy, we fight our battles, but the gods let us choose our weapons. He pointed at the spear and at her mother's tears. Obara picked up the spear, and Oberyn took her as his own. Her mother drank herself to death within the year.

paragraphs.context: I was the oldest,” the prince said, “and yet I am the last
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran grieves that he, the eldest, has outlived all his siblings.
paragraphs.simple: Prince Doran tells Hotah about his family. He was the eldest child, yet he is the last one alive. Two brothers, Mors and Olyvar, died in their cradles. His sister Elia came when he was nine, and his brother Oberyn a year after that. Doran was already grown when they played in the Water Gardens pools. Now Elia and Oberyn are both dead, and only Doran remains.

paragraphs.context: He could still recall the sounds of the three bells
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sharpening his axe, Hotah remembers Norvos: the bells, the food, and the brand that wed him to his axe.
paragraphs.simple: As Hotah sharpens his longaxe, he thinks of Norvos, the city where he grew up. He remembers the three bells: the deep peals of Noom that set his bones shuddering, the proud strong voice of Narrah, sweet Nyel's silvery laughter. He remembers the taste of wintercake and of nahsa, fermented goat's milk laced with honey. He remembers his mother in her best dress, and the stench of burning hair as the bearded priest touched the brand to the center of his chest. The pain was so fierce he thought his heart might stop, yet he did not flinch, and the hair never grew back over the brand.

paragraphs.context: Only three leagues of coast road divided Sunspear from the Water Gardens
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sunspear and its shadow city are a dusty, crowded town, a different world from the Water Gardens.
paragraphs.simple: Sunspear lies only three leagues from the Water Gardens, but the two places could not be more different. Where the Water Gardens are all pink marble, music, and the smell of lemons, Sunspear smells of dust, sweat, and smoke. The castle is built of mud and straw, brown and dun. Around it sprawls the shadow city: shops, hovels, inns, and pillow houses clinging to the castle walls like barnacles to a ship's hull. It is no more than a town beside great cities, but it is the nearest thing to a true city the Dornish have.

paragraphs.context: Then we need only hail Myrcella as the First of Her Name
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyene proposes crowning Myrcella queen under Dornish law to force a war with the Lannisters.
paragraphs.simple: Tyene lays out her plan. When Dorne joined the realm, it was agreed that Dornish law would always rule in Dorne, and under Dornish law the eldest child inherits regardless of sex. Myrcella is older than her brother Tommen and is in Dorne. So they should wed her to Trystane, crown her Queen of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, and hail her as the lawful heir to the Iron Throne. Then they need only wait for the Lannisters to march on Dorne.

paragraphs.context: You will find my brother’s daughters, take them into custody
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran orders Hotah to arrest all the Sand Snakes and confine them in the Spear Tower.
paragraphs.simple: Prince Doran gives Hotah his command: find his brother's daughters, take them into custody, and confine them in the cells atop the Spear Tower.

paragraphs.context: That is not the way a lion dies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei cannot accept that Tywin died on the privy; she feels a hole in the world where her father stood.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei refuses to believe her father is truly dead. She thinks: that is not the way a lion dies. She feels strangely calm and remembers losing a tooth as a little girl. It did not hurt, but the hole in her mouth felt so strange she could not stop touching it with her tongue. Now there is a hole in the world where her father stood, and holes want filling.

paragraphs.context: When the lion falls the lesser beasts move in
paragraphs.mainIdea: With Tywin dead, Cersei resolves to seize power fast before her enemies push her aside.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks about what Tywin's death means. If Tywin is truly dead, no one is safe, least of all her son Tommen on his throne. When the lion falls, the lesser beasts move in: the jackals and the vultures and the feral dogs. Her enemies will try to push her aside, as they always have. She must move quickly, as she did when Robert died. She tells herself no one will ever force her to marry again or disregard her again: Casterly Rock is hers now, and all the power of House Lannister.

paragraphs.context: The quarrel had taken him in his groin between his navel and his manhood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei sees Tywin's body: killed on the privy by a crossbow quarrel.
paragraphs.simple: For a moment Cersei does not recognize the dead man. He has her father's hair, but he looks smaller and much older. His bedrobe is pushed up around his chest, leaving him naked below the waist. A crossbow quarrel has struck him between his navel and his manhood, sunk so deep that only the feathers show. His hair is stiff with dried blood, and more blood is congealing in his navel.

paragraphs.context: That was how Lord Tywin Lannister dealt with whores
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls how Tywin humiliated his father's mistress and insists the dead girl must have been there for another purpose.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei insists her father had no use for whores; after their mother died he never touched a woman. She remembers what Tywin did when his own father died: he found his father's mistress dressed in his dead mother's jewels and gown, stripped her naked, and had her paraded through the streets of Lannisport for a fortnight, forced to confess to every man she met that she was a thief and a harlot. That was how Tywin dealt with whores, so the dead girl in his bed must have been there for some other purpose.

paragraphs.context: Jon Arryn put Robert Baratheon in her bed, and before he died
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei reviews the past Hands of the King and decides the next one must know his place: her obedient uncle Kevan.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks no Hand ever brought her anything but grief. Jon Arryn put Robert in her bed and began sniffing into her affair with Jaime before he died. Eddard Stark's meddling forced her to kill Robert sooner than she wanted. Tyrion sold Myrcella to the Dornishmen and murdered Joffrey. She decides the next Hand must know his place: it will be her uncle Kevan, tireless, prudent, and unfailingly obedient, as reliable to her as he was to her father.

paragraphs.context: He should be here. He is always here
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei realizes Varys is missing and concludes he must be part of the murder plot.
paragraphs.simple: It suddenly strikes Cersei that Varys is missing. The eunuch always appears whenever anything important happens in the Red Keep, as if from nowhere, yet Jaime is here, Kevan is here, Pycelle has come and gone, but not Varys. A cold finger touches her spine. He must be part of this, she thinks: he feared Tywin meant to take his head, so he struck first. No man knows the Red Keep's secrets better than the master of whisperers, and he once served with Stannis on Robert's council.

paragraphs.context: I will find the girl and keep her safe,” Brienne had promised Ser Jaime
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne recalls her promise to Jaime to find Sansa and keep her safe.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne remembers the promise she made to Jaime back in King's Landing: she will find the girl and keep her safe, for her dead mother's sake, and for Jaime's. Noble words, she thinks, but words are easy and deeds are hard. She lingered too long in the city and learned too little. She should have set out sooner, but to where?

paragraphs.context: She has no home to run to, no father, no mother, no brothers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne reasons that Sansa has no home or family left to flee to and could be anywhere.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne believes Sansa left the city; if she were still in King's Landing, the gold cloaks would have found her. But where would she go? Brienne asks herself what she would do in Sansa's place: she would go home to her father on Tarth. But Sansa's father was beheaded before her eyes, her mother was murdered at the Twins, and Winterfell was sacked and burned. Sansa has no home, no father, no mother, no brothers. She might be in the next town or on a ship to Asshai; one seems as likely as the other.

paragraphs.context: shown her every courtesy, as if she were a proper maid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne remembers Renly's kindness and dancing with him, and how she failed him.
paragraphs.simple: Renly showed Brienne every courtesy, as if she were a proper maid, and pretty. He even danced with her, and in his arms she felt graceful. Because of his example, others later asked her to dance too. From that day she wanted only to be close to Lord Renly, to serve him and protect him. But in the end she failed him: Renly died in her arms, though she did not kill him.

paragraphs.context: If she did poison King Joffrey, the Imp surely forced her hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne thinks about Sansa's suffering at court and believes the dwarf forced her into the poisoning.
paragraphs.simple: Lying awake, Brienne wonders whether Sansa is cold too, wherever she is. Catelyn had said Sansa was a gentle soul who loved lemon cakes and songs of chivalry, yet she watched her father's head cut off and was forced to marry one of his killers. If the tales are true, the dwarf was the cruelest Lannister of all. If Sansa poisoned Joffrey, Brienne thinks, the Imp surely forced her hand. From one of Sansa's maids she learned there was little warmth between Sansa and the dwarf; perhaps she was fleeing him as well as the murder.

paragraphs.context: The sparrow is the humblest and most common of birds
paragraphs.mainIdea: A barefoot septon explains that the sparrows are humble holy men marching to King's Landing with the bones of murdered septons.
paragraphs.simple: The barefoot septon explains who they are. The sparrow is the humblest and most common of birds, and they are the humblest and most common of men. They carry the bones of holy men murdered for their faith: some starved, some tortured. Septs have been robbed, women raped, even silent sisters attacked. Their Mother Above cries out in anguish. It is time, he says, for all anointed knights to forsake their worldly masters and defend the Holy Faith, and to come with them to the city.

paragraphs.context: A certain fool vanished from King’s Landing the night King Joffrey died
paragraphs.mainIdea: Shadrich reveals that the fool Dontos vanished the same night Joffrey died and warns Brienne's 'sister' could be mistaken for Sansa.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Shadrich tells Brienne more: a certain fool disappeared from King's Landing the night King Joffrey died, a stout man with broken veins in his nose, Ser Dontos the Red, once of Duskendale. He warns her that her supposed sister and her drunken fool might be mistaken for the Stark girl and Ser Dontos, which could be most unfortunate. Then he rides ahead.

paragraphs.context: You’ll be defending Ned Stark’s daughter with Ned Stark’s own steel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne draws Oathkeeper, the Valyrian steel sword Jaime gave her, and prays to find Sansa.
paragraphs.simple: In her room Brienne takes out the second longsword hidden in her bedroll. Gold glitters and rubies glow; when she draws it, black and red ripples run deep in the steel. It is Valyrian steel, spell-forged, a sword fit for a hero. As a child her nurse filled her ears with tales of great champions, each bearing a famous sword, and Oathkeeper belongs in their company. You will be defending Ned Stark's daughter with Ned Stark's own steel, Jaime had promised when he gave it to her.

paragraphs.context: We are walking on a bridge of ice with an abyss on either side
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon says the Watch must please both Stannis and the Lannisters, like walking a bridge of ice over an abyss.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Sam how dangerous their position is. Stannis says the Watch has not given him enough; the Lannisters will say it gave too much. Pleasing one king is hard enough, and pleasing two is hardly possible. It is like walking on a bridge of ice with a deep pit on either side: one wrong step and they fall.

paragraphs.context: King’s blood, to wake a dragon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon dismisses the idea that burning Mance would wake a dragon; Mance's blood has no royal power.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Sam what he has heard: Lady Melisandre means to burn Mance Rayder alive to work some sorcery, king's blood to wake a dragon. But Jon calls it nonsense. Where she thinks to find a sleeping dragon, no one knows. Mance's blood is no more royal than Jon's own; he never wore a crown or sat a throne. He is a brigand, nothing more, and there is no power in a brigand's blood.

paragraphs.context: The oldest histories we have were written after the Andals came to Westeros
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam explains that all ancient history was written down thousands of years later, so its truth is doubtful.
paragraphs.simple: Sam tells Jon what his reading has taught him about the histories. The First Men left only runes carved on rocks. The oldest histories were written after the Andals came to Westeros: everything about the Age of Heroes, the Dawn Age, and the Long Night comes from accounts set down by septons thousands of years later. Some archmaesters at the Citadel question all of it, since the old tales are full of kings who ruled for hundreds of years and knights riding a thousand years before knights existed.

paragraphs.context: Fire will dismay them, though, and they are vulnerable to obsidian
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam reports what can kill the Others: fire, obsidian, and perhaps dragonsteel.
paragraphs.simple: Sam tells Jon how the Others can be fought. Their armor turns aside most ordinary blades, and their own swords are so cold they shatter steel. But fire will frighten them, and they are vulnerable to obsidian: Sam himself saw one melt when he stabbed it with the dragonglass dagger Jon gave him. One old account of the Long Night says the last hero slew Others with a blade of dragonsteel, which Sam thinks may mean Valyrian steel.

paragraphs.context: If the red woman requires king’s blood for her spells
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon is sending the elderly Aemon away because Melisandre might burn him for his Targaryen king's blood.
paragraphs.simple: Jon explains the real reason Aemon must leave. The old maester's life will be at risk on a sea voyage at a hundred and two years old, but the risk is greater if he stays. Stannis knows who Aemon is: a Targaryen, with a king's blood in his veins. If the red woman needs king's blood for her spells, Aemon would be in deadly danger here.

paragraphs.context: I need you to become my new maester
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon orders Sam to go to the Citadel and train as a maester, since the Watch has swordsmen enough but almost no readers.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Sam why he must go to Oldtown. The Night's Watch has hundreds of men who can loose an arrow, but only a handful who can read and write. Sam must become Jon's new maester. There are parchment and ink at the Citadel, as well as longbows, and Jon expects Sam to continue his archery practice.

paragraphs.context: From this day forth, you will not call yourself a craven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon commands Sam to stop calling himself a craven and to obey; he leaves before sunrise.
paragraphs.simple: Sam protests that he cannot disobey his father, but Jon, now Lord Snow with eyes hard as ice, cuts him off. Sam has no father anymore, only brothers; his life belongs to the Night's Watch. Jon gives him his orders: pack for Oldtown, leaving an hour before sunrise, and from this day forth never call himself a craven again. He has faced more in the past year than most men face in a lifetime. Jon cannot command Sam to be brave, but he can command him to hide his fears.

paragraphs.context: Arya never seemed to find the places she set out to reach
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya recalls how every attempt to reach safety failed: Winterfell, Riverrun, the Twins, Saltpans.
paragraphs.simple: Arya thinks about how she never reaches the places she sets out for. Yoren swore to take her to Winterfell, but she ended up in Harrenhal and Yoren died. When she escaped Harrenhal for Riverrun, outlaws captured her and dragged her to the hollow hill instead. Then the Hound dragged her to the Twins. She left him dying by the river and went to Saltpans hoping for a ship to Eastwatch, but even the iron coin could not sway the captain to take her toward the Wall, where Jon Snow is.

paragraphs.context: whenever Braavos stood in danger he would wake with fire in his eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Old Nan's tale says the Titan wakes to smash Braavos's enemies, and eats little highborn girls.
paragraphs.simple: Old Nan told the Stark children stories of the Titan of Braavos back in Winterfell. He was a giant as tall as a mountain, and whenever Braavos stood in danger he would wake with fire in his eyes, his rocky limbs grinding as he waded into the sea to smash the city's enemies. Nan always ended by saying the Braavosi feed him on the juicy pink flesh of little highborn girls, which made Sansa squeak. Maester Luwin said the Titan was only a statue, and Nan's stories only stories.

paragraphs.context: The Moonsingers led us to this place of refuge
paragraphs.mainIdea: Denyo explains Braavos's gods: the Moonsingers' temple is greatest, and the Many-Faced God dwells with the rest on one isle.
paragraphs.simple: Denyo tells Arya about the gods of Braavos. The Moonsingers led his people to this hidden refuge where Valyria's dragons could not find them, so theirs is the greatest temple. The Father of Waters is honored too, though his temple must be rebuilt each time he takes a new bride. All the other gods dwell together on one island in the middle of the city, and that is where she will find the Many-Faced God.

paragraphs.context: Real tears were trickling from her eyes, to fill the bowl she cradled
paragraphs.mainIdea: Inside the temple Arya sees statues of many strange gods in the gloom.
paragraphs.simple: As Arya's eyes adjust, she sees the temple is far larger inside than it looked outside. Unlike a Westerosi sept with seven altars, here there are more gods than seven. Statues line the walls, huge and frightening, with red candles burning at their feet like distant stars. The nearest is a twelve-foot marble woman with real tears trickling from her eyes into the bowl she holds. Beyond her are a man with a lion's head on a throne, a huge rearing horse of bronze and iron, a great stone face, a pale infant with a sword, a shaggy black goat, and a hooded man with a staff. The rest are only looming shapes in the dark.

paragraphs.context: He drank deep, and dropped the cup into the pool with a soft plop
paragraphs.mainIdea: The weeping man drinks, and Arya sees the spreading bloodstain: he has been stabbed.
paragraphs.simple: The young man drinks deep and drops the cup into the pool with a soft plop. Then he pushes himself to his feet, swaying and holding his belly, and for a moment Arya thinks he is going to fall. Then she sees the dark stain spreading below his belt: he has been stabbed. He pays her no mind and lurches unsteadily toward the wall, crawling into a shadowed alcove onto a hard stone bed. When Arya peers around, she sees other alcoves too, with old people lying on them.

paragraphs.context: This is the House of Black and White, my child
paragraphs.mainIdea: The priest names the temple and tells Arya she is young to seek the Many-Faced God.
paragraphs.simple: A hooded priest in a black-and-white robe speaks to Arya in the Common Tongue. His voice is gentle. He tells her this is the House of Black and White, a place of peace where she is safe, though she is young to seek the favor of the Many-Faced God.

paragraphs.context: at the end of every road stands Him of Many Faces, waiting
paragraphs.mainIdea: The priest explains the Many-Faced God: countless faces, waiting at the end of every road.
paragraphs.simple: Arya asks if the Many-Faced God is like the southern god with seven faces. The priest says no: he has faces beyond count, as many faces as there are stars in the sky. In Braavos men worship as they will, but at the end of every road stands Him of Many Faces, waiting. He will be there for Arya one day, but she need not rush to his embrace.

paragraphs.context: “No one has ever tried to eat my worm before,” he said
paragraphs.mainIdea: The skull-faced priest melts into a kindly old man after Arya eats the grave worm.
paragraphs.simple: The yellow skull melts too, and the kindliest old man Arya has ever seen is smiling down at her. No one has ever tried to eat his worm before, he says. Are you hungry, child?

paragraphs.context: a golden lioness crouched upon each shoulder
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei studies her father's richly armored body and is troubled by the faint smile on his dead face.
paragraphs.simple: The silent sisters dressed Lord Tywin as if for one last battle. He wore his finest armor, heavy steel colored deep crimson, with gold worked into his gloves, leg guards, and chest plate. Golden sun shapes covered his shoulders, a golden lioness crouched on each one, and a lion with a mane crowned the great helmet beside his head. On his chest lay a long sword in a gold-covered case set with red stones, his hands folded over it in gloves of gold mail. Even in death his face looked noble, except for his mouth: the corners of his lips curved up slightly, giving him a look of mild amusement. That should not be. She blamed Pycelle; he should have told the sisters that Tywin Lannister never smiled. The half smile made him seem less fearful, and so did the fact that his eyes were closed. Her father's eyes had always been unsettling: pale green, almost glowing, flecked with gold. His eyes could see inside you, could see how weak and worthless and ugly you were deep down.

paragraphs.context: If we need gold, His Grace should sit Lord Tywin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei remembers how her father once silenced a joking lord with only a long cold stare.
paragraphs.simple: Unbidden, a memory came to her of the feast King Aerys had thrown when Cersei first came to court, a girl as green as summer grass. Old Merryweather had been chattering about raising the tax on wine when Lord Rykker said, 'If we need gold, His Grace should sit Lord Tywin on his chamber pot.' It was a crude joke: put Tywin on the toilet and gold will come out. Aerys and his flatterers laughed loudly, whilst Father stared at Rykker over his wine cup. Long after the laughter had died that gaze lingered. Rykker turned away, turned back, met Father's eyes, then ignored them, drank a tankard of ale, and stalked off red-faced, defeated by a pair of unflinching eyes.

paragraphs.context: Atonement is best achieved through prayer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei warns Lancel to keep silent about their past, hiding the threat inside pious words.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei wondered how Lancel meant to atone for her. Knighting him was a mistake, and bedding him a bigger one. Lancel was a weak reed, and she liked his newfound piety not at all; he had been much more amusing when he was trying to be Jaime. What has this mewling fool told the High Septon? And what will he tell his little Frey wife when they lie together in the dark? If he confessed to bedding Cersei, she could weather that; men were always lying about women, and she would call it the bragging of a callow boy smitten by her beauty. If he sings of Robert and the strongwine, though — the plot to kill the king — that would be deadly. 'Atonement is best achieved through prayer,' Cersei told him. 'Silent prayer.' She left him to think about that: confess nothing aloud.

paragraphs.context: My uncle Garth has agreed to serve as master of coin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mace Tyrell tells Cersei his uncle Garth is coming to join the small council, claiming her father had agreed to it.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrell went on: his son Willas is an able lad — his leg may be twisted but he has no want of wits — and Garlan will soon take Brightwater, so the Reach will be in good hands if Mace is needed elsewhere. The governance of the realm must come first, Lord Tywin often said. And he was pleased to bring good tidings: 'My uncle Garth has agreed to serve as master of coin, as your lord father wished. He is making his way to Oldtown to take ship. His sons will accompany him. Lord Tywin mentioned something about finding places for the two of them as well. Perhaps in the City Watch.' Cersei had never agreed to any of this; Tyrell was trying to pack the council with his own kin.

paragraphs.context: I caught a whiff of something unpleasant in the holy sept
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Olenna mocks Garth's flatulence and slyly hints that she too smelled Lord Tywin's rotting corpse.
paragraphs.simple: Olenna slid her arm through her son's. 'It would seem that Lord Tywin did not share his plans with our regent, I can't imagine why. Still, there it is, no use hectoring Her Grace. She is quite right, you must write Lord Leyton before Garth boards a ship. You know the sea will sicken him and make his farting worse.' She gave Cersei a toothless smile. 'Your council chambers will smell sweeter with Lord Gyles, though I daresay that coughing would drive me to distraction. We all adore dear old uncle Garth, but the man is flatulent, that cannot be gainsaid. I do abhor foul smells.' Her wrinkled face wrinkled up even more. 'I caught a whiff of something unpleasant in the holy sept, in truth. Mayhaps you smelled it too?' She was hinting that she had smelled the stink of Tywin's corpse — and daring Cersei to deny it.

paragraphs.context: The king is Garth the Twelfth, and the hand is
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn identifies the strange coin as a pre-Conquest coin of House Gardener of the Reach.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn agreed it was no dragon. “It dates from before the Conquest, Your Grace. The king is Garth the Twelfth, and the hand is the sigil of House Gardener.” The coin was struck before Aegon’s Conquest: the king’s face was Garth the Twelfth, and the hand marked it as a coin of House Gardener — of Highgarden, of the Reach.

paragraphs.context: I wished to understand the nature of death, so I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn explains that the Citadel stripped him of his chain for cutting open living people to study death.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei asked why the Citadel had taken his chain. 'The archmaesters are all craven at heart. The grey sheep, Marwyn calls them. I was as skilled a healer as Ebrose, but aspired to surpass him. For hundreds of years the men of the Citadel have opened the bodies of the dead, to study the nature of life. I wished to understand the nature of death, so I opened the bodies of the living. For that crime the grey sheep shamed me and forced me into exile... but I understand the nature of life and death better than any man in Oldtown.' That intrigued her. She gave him the dying Mountain to study, confined to the black cells.

paragraphs.context: so long as you name me regent as well as Hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kevan agrees to serve only if Cersei gives up the regency to him and returns to Casterly Rock.
paragraphs.simple: 'Very well. I will remain and serve His Grace...' Kevan said. 'Very good,' Cersei started to say, but Ser Kevan raised his voice and bulled right over her. '...so long as you name me regent as well as Hand and take yourself back to Casterly Rock.' For half a heartbeat Cersei could only stare at him. 'I am the regent,' she reminded him. 'You were. Tywin did not intend that you continue in that role. He told me of his plans to send you back to the Rock and find a new husband for you.' Cersei's anger rose: she would not wed again, and she would not give up power.

paragraphs.context: and his father too, I think
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kevan's parting words imply he knows Jaime — not Robert — is Tommen's true father.
paragraphs.simple: 'You would abandon your king when he needs you most,' Cersei told him. 'You would abandon Tommen.' 'Tommen has his mother.' Ser Kevan's green eyes met her own, unblinking. A last drop of wine trembled wet and red beneath his chin, and finally fell. 'Aye,' he added softly, after a pause, 'and his father too, I think.' He was saying, gently but plainly, that he knew the truth: Jaime, not Robert, fathered Cersei's children — and Tommen has his real father in Jaime.

paragraphs.context: Tyrion may have loosed the crossbow bolt that slew him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime tells Loras and Swann that he, not Tyrion alone, killed their father: Tyrion loosed the bolt, but Jaime loosed Tyrion.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime dismissed the two knights: “He was not your father.” Then, to the corpse: “You did not kill him. I did. Tyrion may have loosed the crossbow bolt that slew him, but I loosed Tyrion.” The word “loosed” does double work — Tyrion shot the bolt, but Jaime set Tyrion free — so the guilt is Jaime’s. “Leave me.”

paragraphs.context: a Lannister pays his debts.” The words had come so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime recalls telling Varys that a Lannister always repays what he owes — the family words he used to justify freeing Tyrion.
paragraphs.simple: Varys had asked whether Jaime believed Tyrion innocent of the king’s murder. “Innocent or guilty,” Jaime had said, like the fool he was, “a Lannister pays his debts.” The words had come so easy. A Lannister always repays what is owed — and Jaime used the proud family saying to justify the treason of freeing his brother.

paragraphs.context: You poor stupid blind crippled fool
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime remembers Tyrion's parting words: Cersei has been unfaithful, and Tyrion confessed to killing Joffrey.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime could see his brother now, the way the dwarf had grinned beneath the stub of his nose as the torchlight licked his face. 'You poor stupid blind crippled fool,' Tyrion had snarled, in a voice thick with malice. 'Cersei is a lying whore, she's been fucking Lancel and Osmund Kettleblack and probably Moon Boy for all I know. And I am the monster they all say I am. Yes, I killed your vile son.' These words — that Cersei betrayed him, that Tyrion murdered Joffrey — poisoned Jaime's mind and haunt him through the whole vigil.

paragraphs.context: When this battle’s done I mean to call a council
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rhaegar's last words to Jaime promised a council and changes after the battle — words Jaime never forgot.
paragraphs.simple: Rhaegar had put his hand on Jaime’s shoulder. “When this battle’s done I mean to call a council. Changes will be made. I meant to do it long ago, but... well, it does no good to speak of roads not taken. We shall talk when I return.” Those were the last words Rhaegar Targaryen ever spoke to him — promises of change that died with the prince.

paragraphs.context: Lord Hightower burned every ship in port, closed the gates
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pycelle tells how Quenton Hightower did cruel but necessary things during a plague — and compares him to Tywin.
paragraphs.simple: Pycelle said: 'I was a boy in Oldtown when the grey plague took half the city and three-quarters of the Citadel. Lord Hightower burned every ship in port, closed the gates, and commanded his guards to slay all those who tried to flee, be they men, women, or babes in arms. They killed him when the plague had run its course. On the very day he reopened the port, they dragged him from his horse and slit his throat, and his young son's as well. To this day the ignorant in Oldtown will spit at the sound of his name, but Quenton Hightower did what was needed. Your father was that sort of man as well. A man who did what was needed.' The praise is double-edged: necessary, but monstrous.

paragraphs.context: Six prisoners, Jaime thought sourly, while we pay wages for
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime realizes the dungeons are corrupt: the crown pays for twenty turnkeys but only a dozen exist.
paragraphs.simple: Longwaters explained the staffing: 'The crown pays wages for twenty turnkeys, my lord, a full score, but during my time we have never had more than twelve. We are supposed to have six undergaolers as well, two on each level, but there are only the three.' At present there were four prisoners on the first level and one on the second, besides the fled Tyrion. 'Six prisoners,' Jaime thought sourly, 'while we pay wages for twenty turnkeys, six undergaolers, a chief undergaoler, a gaoler, and a King's Justice.' Someone has been pocketing the wages of men who do not exist.

paragraphs.context: If I had a suspicious nature I might wonder why
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime suspects Osmund Kettleblack had the two turnkeys killed to silence them about his own part in Tyrion's escape.
paragraphs.simple: Kettleblack shrugged: 'They won't be missed. I'll wager they was part of it, along with the one who's gone missing.' No, Jaime could have told him — Varys had only drugged their wine to make them sleep. 'If so, we might have coaxed the truth from them.' Then, with Tyrion's words about Cersei and Kettleblack ringing in his head: 'If I had a suspicious nature I might wonder why you were in such haste to make certain these two were never put to the question. Did you need to silence them to conceal your own part in this?' Kettleblack choked: 'All we done was what the queen commanded.'

paragraphs.context: How much can a crown be worth, when a crow
paragraphs.mainIdea: Watching crows feast on the dead, Jaime reflects that crowns are worthless when even crows can dine on kings.
paragraphs.simple: The stench of death reminded Jaime of the pass below the Golden Tooth, where he had won a victory early in the war. On the morning after the battle, the crows had feasted on victors and vanquished alike, as once they had feasted on Rhaegar Targaryen after the Trident. “How much can a crown be worth, when a crow can dine upon a king?” The wordplay — crown and crow sound alike — mocks all ambition: kings and commoners alike end as meat for birds.

paragraphs.context: A boy knelt; a knight rose
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime remembers his own vigil at fifteen, when Ser Arthur Dayne knighted him at dawn.
paragraphs.simple: It had been years since his last vigil, when he was a boy of fifteen. He had worn no armor then, only a plain white tunic, in a sept not a third as large as any of the Great Sept's transepts. Jaime had laid his sword across the Warrior's knees, piled his armor at his feet, and knelt upon the rough stone floor before the altar. When dawn came his knees were raw and bloody. 'All knights must bleed, Jaime,' Ser Arthur Dayne had said. With dawn he tapped Jaime on the shoulder; the pale blade was so sharp that even that light touch cut through his tunic, so he bled anew. He never felt it. A boy knelt; a knight rose. But that was long ago, and the boy was dead.

paragraphs.context: A man can bear most anything, if he must
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime comforts the frightened Tommen, telling him people can endure horrors by fighting them, laughing at them, or hiding inside themselves.
paragraphs.simple: 'I wasn't scared,' the boy insisted. 'The smell made me sick. Didn't it make you sick? How could you bear it, Uncle, ser?' Jaime answered: 'I have smelled my own hand rotting, when Vargo Hoat made me wear it for a pendant. A man can bear most anything, if he must. I have smelled a man roasting, as King Aerys cooked him in his own armor. The world is full of horrors, Tommen. You can fight them, or laugh at them, or look without seeing... go away inside.' Tommen confessed: 'I... I used to go away inside sometimes, when Joffy...' — when Joffrey frightened him, he hid inside his own mind.

paragraphs.context: Even sieges have their dangers,” she murmured
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei hints she hopes Mace Tyrell might die at Storm's End — and Jaime understands her meaning.
paragraphs.simple: A wary smile crept across Cersei’s face. “Even sieges have their dangers,” she murmured. “Why, our Lord of Highgarden might even lose his life in such a venture.” Beneath the sweet tone was a hope: send Mace Tyrell to war at Storm’s End, and the war might kill him.

paragraphs.context: The looters come with the carrion crows after every battle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne rides through a market where scavengers sell armor and clothes stripped from the dead of a recent battle.
paragraphs.simple: The gatehouse opened on a market square where people were selling arms and armor very cheaply — looted from the dead. 'The looters come with the carrion crows after every battle.' Brienne walked her horse past mail shirts still caked with brown blood, dinted helms, notched longswords, leather boots, fur cloaks, stained surcoats with suspicious rents. She knew many of the badges: the mailed fist, the moose, the white sun, the double-bladed axe — northern sigils. Tarly men had died here too, and men of the stormlands: red and green apples, the thunderbolts of Leygood, the ants of Ambrose, Tarly's striding huntsman on many a badge. Friend or foe, the crows care not.

paragraphs.context: Lord Denys rose against his king and took him captive
paragraphs.mainIdea: The maester recounts the Defiance of Duskendale: Lord Denys seized King Aerys, and Barristan the Bold later rescued him.
paragraphs.simple: 'In Duskendale they love Lord Denys still, despite the woe he brought them. 'Tis Lady Serala that they blame, his Myrish wife. The Lace Serpent, she is called.' The smallfolk say she filled her husband's ear with poison until Lord Denys rose against his king and took him captive. In the taking, his master-at-arms Ser Symon Hollard cut down Ser Gwayne Gaunt of the Kingsguard. For half a year Aerys was held within the town walls, whilst the King's Hand — Tywin — sat outside with a mighty host. Tywin had strength enough to storm the town any time, but Lord Denys sent word that at the first sign of assault he'd kill the king. This defiance is what drove Aerys mad.

paragraphs.context: She’s gone back north, she has
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa's former maid tells Brienne the girl always prayed in the godswood, and guesses she has gone back north.
paragraphs.simple: In King's Landing, Brienne had found Brella, one of Sansa's former maids, doing washing in a brothel. 'I served with Lord Renly before m'lady Sansa, and both turned traitor,' Brella complained. But when Brienne asked about Sansa, she said: 'I'll tell you what I told Lord Tywin. That girl was always praying. She'd go to sept and light her candles like a proper lady, but near every night she went off to the godswood. She's gone back north, she has. That's where her gods are.' Brienne took the hint seriously: Sansa's true gods are the old northern gods.

paragraphs.context: Or would she seek her own blood instead?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne reasons through where Sansa might have fled: the Wall, Riverrun, or the Vale.
paragraphs.simple: The north was huge, and Brienne had no notion which of her father's bannermen Sansa might trust. Or would she seek her own blood instead? Though all her siblings were slain, Sansa still had an uncle and a bastard half brother on the Wall in the Night's Watch. Another uncle, Edmure Tully, was a captive at the Twins, but his uncle Ser Brynden still held Riverrun. And Lady Catelyn's younger sister ruled the Vale. Blood calls to blood. Sansa might well have run to one of them. Which one, though? The Wall was too far and bleak; Riverrun meant crossing war-torn lands and siege lines; the Eyrie would be simpler, and Lady Lysa would surely welcome her sister's daughter.

paragraphs.context: There was a fool at Maidenpool, now that I think
paragraphs.mainIdea: The holy brother recalls a ragged fool at Maidenpool who was seeking passage across the narrow sea.
paragraphs.simple: “Gold?” The brother gave her a red smile. “A bowl of that crab stew would be enough reward for me, but I fear I cannot help you. Fools I’ve met, and plenty, but not so many pretty maids. ”“There was a fool at Maidenpool, now that I think of it. He was clad in rags and dirt, as near as I could tell, but under the dirt was motley.” A ragged fool in a jester’s motley — it might be Dontos Hollard, or it might not.

paragraphs.context: Seeking passage for three? Not two?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne is startled: the fool sought passage for three people, not two.
paragraphs.simple: The brother had said the fool was seeking passage for three across the narrow sea. Brienne repeated it back, disbelieving: “Seeking passage for three? Not two?” If the fool was Dontos and one of the three was Sansa, then a third person was traveling with them — but who?

paragraphs.context: I heard another man boasting that he’d fooled a fool
paragraphs.mainIdea: The brother heard that a man called Nimble Dick boasted of having 'fooled a fool' — a possible lead.
paragraphs.simple: 'That I could not say,' the dwarf told her, 'but one night some of Lord Tarly's soldiers visited the Goose looking for him, and a few days later I heard another man boasting that he'd fooled a fool and had the gold to prove it. He was drunk, and buying ale for everyone.' 'Fooled a fool,' Brienne said. 'What did he mean by that?' 'I could not tell you. His name was Nimble Dick, though, that I do recall.' The little man spread his hands. 'I fear that's all that I can offer you, aside from a small man's prayers.' Brienne bought him his crab stew, and bread and wine as well, and began to plan her road to Maidenpool.

paragraphs.context: always courteous and eager to please. She loved tales of knightly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne recalls Lady Catelyn describing Sansa — and renews her vow to find the girl.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne remembered the night Lady Catelyn learned her sons were dead. 'I have no sons but Robb,' Catelyn had said, as if a knife were twisting her belly. She turned over her hands to show Brienne the scars where a knife once bit deep, then talked about her daughters. 'Sansa was a little lady, always courteous and eager to please. She loved tales of knightly valor. She will grow into a woman far more beautiful than I, you can see that. I would often brush her hair myself. She had auburn hair, thick and soft... the red in it would shine like copper in the light of the torches.' Brienne swore to Catelyn's restless shade: 'I will find her, my lady. I will never stop looking. I will give up my life if need be, give up my honor, give up all my dreams, but I will find her.'

paragraphs.context: She broke Ser Humfrey’s collarbone, two ribs, and their betrothal
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne recalls how she ended her last betrothal by defeating the old knight who demanded she obey him.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne thought of her own betrothal as she considered the boy facing her. She was sixteen when she was promised to Ser Humfrey Wagstaff, a proud old man of five-and-sixty. 'I will not have my lady wife cavorting about in man's mail,' he warned. 'On this you shall obey me, lest I be forced to chastise you.' Yet somehow she found the courage to tell him she would accept chastisement only from a man who could outfight her. The old knight purpled but agreed to don his armor to teach her a woman's proper place. They fought with blunted tourney weapons, so her mace had no spikes. She broke Ser Humfrey's collarbone, two ribs, and their betrothal. He was her third prospective husband, and her last.

paragraphs.context: His lady. You’re looking for her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The stuttering boy reveals he is Podrick Payne, Tyrion Lannister's abandoned squire, hoping Brienne will lead him to Sansa.
paragraphs.simple: “To find her.” The boy got to his feet. “His lady. You’re looking for her. Brella told me. She’s his wife. Not Brella, Lady Sansa. So I thought, if you found her...” His face twisted in sudden anguish. “I’m his squire,” he repeated, as the rain ran down his face, “but he left me.” The stuttering boy was Podrick Payne — Tyrion Lannister’s abandoned squire — and he had been following Brienne in hopes she would lead him to Sansa, Tyrion’s wife.

paragraphs.context: But the sky cells had a wall of empty air
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Eyrie's sky cells are open to the air, so the imprisoned singer's mournful songs echo across the whole castle.
paragraphs.simple: If the Eyrie had been made like other castles, only rats and gaolers would have heard the dead man singing; dungeon walls are thick enough to swallow songs and screams alike. But the sky cells had a wall of empty air, so every chord the dead man played flew free to echo off the stony shoulders of the Giant's Lance. And the songs he chose: he sang of the Dance of the Dragons, of fair Jonquil and her fool, of Jenny of Oldstones and the Prince of Dragonflies. He sang of betrayals, and murders most foul, of hanged men and bloody vengeance. He sang of grief and sadness. No matter where Sansa went in the castle, she could not escape the music; it chilled her like the cold thin air.

paragraphs.context: We have come to an agreement, Marillion and I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr assures Sansa the tortured singer will say whatever they need — Mord the gaoler has 'persuaded' him.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa feared Lord Nestor would see Marillion and hear the truth about Lysa's death. But Petyr put down his quill. 'On the contrary. I shall insist on it. We have come to an agreement, Marillion and I. Mord can be most persuasive. And if our singer disappoints us and sings a song we do not care to hear, why, you and I need only say he lies. Whom do you imagine Lord Nestor will believe?' 'Us?' Sansa wished she could be certain. 'Of course. Our lies will profit him.' Petyr was confident: Mord's tortures had broken Marillion, and Nestor would believe whatever served his own interests.

paragraphs.context: Littlefinger never lifted so much as his little finger for her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa realizes Petyr is two people — kind protector and sly Littlefinger — and that Littlefinger never once helped her in King's Landing.
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes it seemed to her that the Lord Protector was two people as well. He was Petyr, her protector, warm and funny and gentle... but he was also Littlefinger, the lord she'd known at King's Landing, smiling slyly and stroking his beard as he whispered in Queen Cersei's ear. And Littlefinger was no friend of hers. When Joff had her beaten, the Imp defended her, not Littlefinger. When the mob sought to rape her, the Hound carried her to safety, not Littlefinger. When the Lannisters wed her to Tyrion against her will, Ser Garlan the Gallant gave her comfort, not Littlefinger. Littlefinger never lifted so much as his little finger for her — except to get her out of the city, which she first thought was Ser Dontos's doing.

paragraphs.context: I have no place but here, Sansa thought miserably
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa lists all she has lost and concludes she has nowhere to go and no true friend but Petyr.
paragraphs.simple: She would have fled them both, perhaps, but there was nowhere for her to go. Winterfell was burned and desolate, Bran and Rickon dead and cold. Robb had been betrayed and murdered at the Twins, along with their lady mother. Tyrion had been put to death for killing Joffrey, and if she ever returned to King's Landing the queen would have her head as well. The aunt she'd hoped would keep her safe had tried to murder her instead. Her uncle Edmure was a captive of the Freys, while her great-uncle the Blackfish was under siege at Riverrun. 'I have no place but here,' Sansa thought miserably, 'and no true friend but Petyr.'

paragraphs.context: but Marillion grieves for his fingers, for his eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa reflects that the singer's sad song about a grieving mother really expresses his own grief for his ruined hands and eyes.
paragraphs.simple: After 'Alysanne' the singer stopped, but at dawn Sansa heard 'On a Misty Morn' drifting up from below. That was more properly a woman's song, a lament sung by a mother on the dawn after some terrible battle, as she searches amongst the dead for the body of her only son. 'The mother sings her grief for her dead son,' Sansa thought, 'but Marillion grieves for his fingers, for his eyes.' Mord had cut off the singer's fingers and blinded him. The words rose like arrows and pierced her in the darkness. 'Oh, have you seen my boy, good ser? His hair is chestnut brown. He promised he'd come back to me. Our home's in Wendish Town.'

paragraphs.context: The only woman Petyr ever loved was Sansa’s murdered mother
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa comforts Robert with a kindly meant lie, while recalling that Petyr truly loved only her mother Catelyn.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa smoothed Robert's hair. 'You miss her, I know. Lord Petyr misses her too. He loved her just as you do.' That was a lie, though kindly meant. The only woman Petyr ever loved was Sansa's murdered mother. He had confessed as much to Lady Lysa just before he pushed her out the Moon Door. She was mad and dangerous. She murdered her own lord husband, and would have murdered Sansa if Petyr had not come along to save her. Robert did not need to know that, though. He was only a sick little boy who'd loved his mother.

paragraphs.context: the boy twitched and flailed and wet himself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robert suffers a violent shaking fit in front of the visitors, and no one can do anything but watch.
paragraphs.simple: Helpless as the rest, Sansa could only stand and watch as the shaking spell ran its course. One of Robert’s legs kicked Ser Lothor in the face. Brune cursed, but still held on as the boy twitched and flailed and wet himself. Their visitors said not a word; Lord Nestor at least had seen these fits before. It was long moments before Robert’s spasms began to subside, and seemed even longer. By the end, the little lordling was so weak he could not stand, and Brune carried him from the hall.

paragraphs.context: it was I who killed her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr falsely takes blame for Lysa's death, knowing the lords will refuse to believe him and blame Marillion instead.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr Baelish sighed. 'It was unseemly, and I put an end to it. Lysa agreed to send him away. That was why she met him here, that day. I should have been with her, but I never dreamt... if I had not insisted... it was I who killed her.' 'No,' Sansa thought, 'you mustn't say that, you mustn't tell them, you mustn't.' But Albar Royce was shaking his head. 'No, my lord, you must not blame yourself,' he said. 'This was the singer's work. Bring him up, Lord Petyr. Let us write an end to this sorry business.' Petyr's false confession worked perfectly: by blaming himself, he made the lords rush to blame Marillion instead.

paragraphs.context: No man lingers long in the sky cells
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Nestor remarks that no one survives long in the sky cells — sooner or later the prisoner throws himself out.
paragraphs.simple: 'The man must die,' Ser Marwyn Belmore declared when the singer was taken away. 'He should have followed Lady Lysa out the Moon Door.' 'Without his tongue,' Ser Albar Royce added. 'Without that lying, mocking tongue.' 'I have been too gentle with him, I know,' Petyr said apologetically. 'If truth be told, I pity him. He killed for love.' 'For love or hate,' said Belmore, 'he must die.' 'Soon enough,' Lord Nestor said gruffly. 'No man lingers long in the sky cells. The blue will call to him.' He meant the open blue sky beyond the cell's missing wall would tempt the prisoner to throw himself out — or drive him mad.

paragraphs.context: Men of honor will do things for their children that they
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr explains his scheme: Nestor accepted the bribe because it benefits his son, and honorable men will compromise for their children.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa puzzled out the scheme: 'You gave Lord Nestor the Gates of the Moon to be certain of his support.' 'I did,' Petyr admitted, 'but our rock is a Royce, which is to say he is overproud and prickly. Had I asked him his price, he would have swelled up like an angry toad at the slight upon his honor. But this way... the man is not utterly stupid, but the lies I served him were sweeter than the truth. He wants to believe that Lysa valued him above her other bannermen. One of those others is Bronze Yohn, after all, and Nestor is very much aware that he was born of the lesser branch of House Royce. He wants more for his son. Men of honor will do things for their children that they would never consider doing for themselves.'

paragraphs.context: Lord Nestor’s claim to the Gates will suddenly be called into
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa realizes Petyr signed the grant himself so that Nestor's claim depends on Petyr staying in power.
paragraphs.simple: 'The signature... you might have had Lord Robert put his hand and seal to it, but instead...' '...I signed myself, as Lord Protector. Why?' 'So... if you are removed, or... or killed...' '...Lord Nestor's claim to the Gates will suddenly be called into question. I promise you, that is not lost on him. It was clever of you to see it. Though no more than I'd expect of mine own daughter.' The trick: if the Vale lords remove Petyr, Nestor loses the Gates too — so Nestor must now protect Petyr to protect his own prize.

paragraphs.context: Can you be my daughter in your heart?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr orders Sansa to become Alayne completely, even in her heart.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr warned her that Oswell and Ser Lothor knew her secret — but Oswell was long in his service, Brune was close-mouthed by nature, and Kettleblack and Brune watched each other. “Trust no one,” he said. “You are Alayne, and you must be Alayne all the time.” He put two fingers on her breast. “Even here. In your heart. Can you do that? Can you be my daughter in your heart?”

paragraphs.context: If a lie was kindly meant, there was no harm in it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa comforts herself with the thought that kindly meant lies do no harm, as Robert climbs into her bed.
paragraphs.simple: “I suppose I am,” Sansa said, when Robert asked if she was his mother now. “If a lie was kindly meant, there was no harm in it.” The line echoes through the whole chapter: every lie Sansa tells is kindly meant — and each one binds her tighter to Petyr’s game.

paragraphs.context: A sudden storm and a broken rope had sent Balon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha doubts the official story that her father Balon died by accident in a storm.
paragraphs.simple: Even now, it was hard to credit that frail, sickly Lady Alannys had outlived her husband Lord Balon, who had seemed so hard and strong. When Asha had sailed away to war, she had done so with a heavy heart, fearing that her mother might well die before she could return. Not once had she thought that her father might perish instead. 'A sudden storm and a broken rope had sent Balon Greyjoy to his death. Or so they claim.' The Drowned God plays savage japes upon us all, but men are crueler still. Asha suspected her uncle Euron — the Crow's Eye — had returned just in time to arrange it.

paragraphs.context: he would always be ten years old, it seemed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha recalls her sick mother's confusion: Lady Alannys still thinks of Theon as the ten-year-old boy taken hostage.
paragraphs.simple: On her last visit Asha had found Lady Alannys in a window seat huddled beneath a pile of furs, staring out across the sea. Her mother's skin had been parchment thin, her long hair white. Some pride remained in the way she held her head, but her eyes were dim and cloudy, and her mouth had trembled when she asked after Theon. 'Did you bring my baby boy?' she had asked. Theon had been ten years old when he was carried off to Winterfell a hostage, and so far as Lady Alannys was concerned he would always be ten years old, it seemed. 'Theon could not come,' Asha had to tell her. 'Father sent him reaving along the Stony Shore.' Her mother only nodded slowly, yet it was plain how deep the words had cut her.

paragraphs.context: On the blades were writ the words Rodrik and Maron
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha dreads telling her mother that Theon is dead, picturing her grief as knives already buried in her heart.
paragraphs.simple: 'And now I must tell her that Theon is dead, and drive yet another dagger through her heart. There were two knives buried there already. On the blades were writ the words Rodrik and Maron, and many a time they twisted cruelly in the night.' Rodrik and Maron were Asha's brothers, dead long ago; her mother never stopped grieving them. 'I will see her on the morrow,' Asha vowed to herself. Her journey had been long and wearisome, she could not face her mother now.

paragraphs.context: Aeron Damphair has called a kingsmoot
