paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik reveals that Aeron Damphair has called a kingsmoot — an ancient gathering to choose a new king.
paragraphs.simple: Asha had feared the other lords had all gone to Pyke to do homage to the Crow's Eye. 'Old Wyk?' she asked. 'Why Old Wyk?' 'I thought you would have heard. Aeron Damphair has called a kingsmoot.' Asha threw back her head and laughed. 'The Drowned God must have shoved a pricklefish up Uncle Aeron's arse. A kingsmoot? Is this some jape, or does he mean it truly?' 'The Damphair has not japed since he was drowned. And the other priests have taken up the call. Blind Beron Blacktyde, Tarle the Thrice-Drowned... even the Old Grey Gull has left that rock he lives on to preach this kingsmoot all across Harlaw. The captains are gathering on Old Wyk as we speak.'

paragraphs.context: Urron of Orkmont let his axemen loose among them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik recalls the last kingsmoot, where Urron Greyiron murdered all the other candidates and ruled unchosen for a thousand years.
paragraphs.simple: 'On Old Wyk,' confirmed Lord Rodrik. 'Though I pray it is not bloody. I have been consulting Haereg's History of the Ironborn. When last the salt kings and the rock kings met in kingsmoot, Urron of Orkmont let his axemen loose among them, and Nagga's ribs turned red with gore. House Greyiron ruled unchosen for a thousand years from that dark day, until the Andals came.' Nagga was the great sea dragon whose bones form the holy hall on Old Wyk. Rodrik feared Euron might repeat Urron's crime: 'Euron Greyjoy sounds queerly like Urron Greyiron to these old ears.'

paragraphs.context: It’s land we need, not crowns
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik argues the ironborn should seek land and alliance with a mainland king, not chase crowns.
paragraphs.simple: 'Going to Old Wyk serves no purpose. This dream of kingship is a madness in our blood. I told your father so the first time he rose, and it is more true now than it was then. It's land we need, not crowns. With Stannis Baratheon and Tywin Lannister contending for the Iron Throne, we have a rare chance to improve our lot. Let us take one side or the other, help them to victory with our fleets, and claim the lands we need from a grateful king.' 'That might be worth some thought,' said Asha, 'once I sit the Seastone Chair.' She agreed with the plan — but only after she herself was queen.

paragraphs.context: No woman has ever ruled the ironborn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik warns Asha she cannot win: no woman has ever ruled the ironborn, and she has three uncles against her.
paragraphs.simple: Her uncle sighed. 'You will not want to hear this, Asha, but you will not be chosen. No woman has ever ruled the ironborn. Gwynesse is seven years my elder, but when our father died the Ten Towers came to me. It will be the same for you. You are Balon's daughter, not his son. And you have three uncles.' 'Four.' 'Three kraken uncles. I do not count.' Rodrik counted only the Greyjoy uncles who could claim the throne: Euron, Victarion, and Aeron. His message was plain: the ironborn will never choose a woman, and Asha's fight is hopeless.

paragraphs.context: Dead history is writ in ink, the living sort in blood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik prefers reading about the past to living through it: dead history is written in ink, living history in blood.
paragraphs.simple: Asha urged him to come: 'Nuncle, how can you even think of not attending? This will be history, alive...' 'I prefer my history dead. Dead history is writ in ink, the living sort in blood.' 'Do you want to die old and craven in your bed?' 'How else? Though not till I'm done reading.' Lord Rodrik went to the window. 'You have not asked about your lady mother.' 'I was afraid,' Asha admitted. 'How is she?' 'Stronger. She may yet outlive us all. She will certainly outlive you, if you persist in this folly.'

paragraphs.context: Now all I see are crows, squabbling over the corpse of Westeros
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rodrik says Westeros has gone from one king to five, and now only crows squabble over its corpse.
paragraphs.simple: Asha told him what she had found in the north: parts of many bodies, wolves — the four-legged sort — showing scant reverence for their two-legged kin, bones scattered and cracked open for their marrow. 'Crows will fight over a dead man's flesh and kill each other for his eyes.' Lord Rodrik stared across the sea, watching the play of moonlight on the waves. 'We had one king, then five. Now all I see are crows, squabbling over the corpse of Westeros.' He fastened the shutters. 'Do not go to Old Wyk, Asha. Stay with your mother. We shall not have her long, I fear.'

paragraphs.context: who showed her how to brew moon tea to keep
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha explains she lost her virtue young and has used moon tea ever since to avoid pregnancy.
paragraphs.simple: “Go touch one... or two, or ten. I have touched more men than I can count. Some with my lips, more with my axe.” She had surrendered her virtue at six-and-ten, to a beautiful blond-haired sailor on a trading galley up from Lys. He only knew six words of the Common Tongue, but “fuck” was one of them — the very word she’d hoped to hear. Afterward, Asha had the sense to find a woods witch, who showed her how to brew moon tea to keep her belly flat. Moon tea is the drink women use to prevent pregnancy.

paragraphs.context: I am your queen, not your wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha rejects Tris's marriage proposal at knifepoint: she will be his queen, not his wife.
paragraphs.simple: Tris seized her upper arm. In a blink her dirk was at his throat. 'Take your hand away or you won't live long enough to breed a son. Now.' When he did, she lowered the blade. 'You want a woman, well and good. I'll put one in your bed tonight. Pretend she's me, if that will give you pleasure, but do not presume to grab at me again. I am your queen, not your wife. Remember that.' Asha sheathed her dirk and left him standing there, with a fat drop of blood slowly creeping down his neck, black in the pale light of the moon. She would take the Seastone Chair — but she would never be any man's wife.

paragraphs.context: Tommen’s hold upon the Iron Throne was not secure enough
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei explains why she must endure the hated wedding: Tommen's throne is not secure enough to risk offending Highgarden.
paragraphs.simple: It was the wedding that enraged her, though the slow-witted Swyft girl made a safer target. Tommen's hold upon the Iron Throne was not secure enough for her to risk offending Highgarden. Not so long as Stannis Baratheon held Dragonstone and Storm's End, so long as Riverrun continued in defiance, so long as ironmen prowled the seas like wolves. So Jocelyn must needs eat the meal Cersei would sooner have served to Margaery Tyrell and her hideous wrinkled grandmother. Cersei hated every moment of the wedding, but she needed the Tyrells' swords and gold too badly to refuse it.

paragraphs.context: He could be under the floor even now, listening to every
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei is convinced Tyrion is still hiding in the castle, listening and plotting to kill Tommen.
paragraphs.simple: 'Safe.' The word tasted bitter on her tongue. Jaime did not understand. No one understood. 'Tyrion will not kill the same way twice. He is too cunning for that. He could be under the floor even now, listening to every word we say and making plans to open Tommen's throat.' 'Suppose he was,' said Jaime. 'Whatever plans he makes, he will still be small and stunted. Tommen will be surrounded by the finest knights in Westeros. The Kingsguard will protect him.' Cersei glanced at Jaime's pinned-up sleeve: 'I remember how well they guarded Joffrey, these splendid knights of yours.' Her fear of Tyrion had become an obsession no guard could soothe.

paragraphs.context: She is the boy’s own mother, after all, of that
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olenna slyly insinuates doubt about Tommen's parentage while pretending to agree with Cersei.
paragraphs.simple: 'I am sure Her Grace knows best,' Lady Olenna had said to Lady Alerie. 'She is the boy's own mother, after all, of that we are all sure. And surely we can agree about the wedding night? A man should not sleep apart from his wife on the night of their wedding. It is ill luck for their marriage if they do.' The heavy stress on 'of that we are all sure' was a knife wrapped in courtesy: everyone had read Stannis's letter claiming Cersei's children were Jaime's, not Robert's. Olenna was reminding Cersei, sweetly, that she knew.

paragraphs.context: If the gods are good, the fire may smoke a few rats
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei plans to burn the Tower of the Hand after the feast, hoping the fire will flush out Tyrion and his helpers.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime asked if she still meant to burn the Tower of the Hand. 'After the feast.' It was the only part of the day's festivities that Cersei thought she might enjoy. 'Our lord father was murdered in that tower. I cannot bear to look at it. If the gods are good, the fire may smoke a few rats from the rubble.' 'Tyrion, you mean.' 'Him, and Lord Varys, and this gaoler.' She half-believed Tyrion was still hiding somewhere in the castle's secret passages, and hoped wildfire would smoke him out like a rat from a hole.

paragraphs.context: And two guardsmen vanished exploring a side tunnel
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime describes the dangerous search of the tower: secret passages, a room of skulls, lost men — but no Tyrion.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime protested that the tower had been searched thoroughly: 'I've had a small army going at it with picks and hammers. We've knocked through walls and ripped up floors and uncovered half a hundred secret passages.' Some of the secret crawlways were so small that Jaime needed pages and stableboys to explore them. A passage to the black cells was found, and a stone well that seemed to have no bottom. They found a chamber full of skulls and yellowed bones, and four sacks of tarnished silver coins from the reign of the first King Viserys. They found a thousand rats as well. One boy got stuck in a narrow passage and had to be pulled out by his feet, shrieking. Another fell down a shaft and broke his legs. And two guardsmen vanished exploring a side tunnel. But neither Tyrion nor Varys was amongst them.

paragraphs.context: And wouldn’t a stag be more fitting for King Robert’s trueborn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olenna blocks Cersei's wish to use the Lannister cloak, insisting the bride wear Baratheon colors — a dig at the parentage rumors.
paragraphs.simple: When it was time for the changing of the cloaks, Tommen covered Margaery with the heavy cloth-of-gold monstrosity that Robert had cloaked Cersei in on their own wedding day, with the crowned stag of Baratheon worked upon its back in beads of onyx. Cersei had wanted to use the fine red silk cloak Joffrey had used — 'It was the cloak my lord father used when he wed my lady mother' — but the Queen of Thorns had balked her. 'That old thing? It looks a bit threadbare to me... and dare I say, unlucky? And wouldn't a stag be more fitting for King Robert's trueborn son? In my day a bride donned her husband's colors, not his lady mother's.' The 'trueborn son' was another needle: Olenna knew the rumors.

paragraphs.context: there were already too many rumors concerning Tommen’s parentage
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei yields on the cloak because Stannis's letter has already spread rumors that Tommen is not Robert's son.
paragraphs.simple: 'Thanks to Stannis and his filthy letter, there were already too many rumors concerning Tommen's parentage. Cersei dared not fan the fires by insisting that he drape his bride in Lannister crimson, so she yielded as gracefully as she could. But the sight of all that gold and onyx still filled her with resentment. The more we give these Tyrells, the more they demand of us.' Stannis had declared to the realm that Cersei's children were born of incest with Jaime; every public choice Cersei made now had to avoid feeding that fire.

paragraphs.context: When a dog goes bad, the fault lies with his master
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kevan answers Cersei's demand for Sandor's head with a pointed remark about masters and their dogs.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei told Kevan to bring her Sandor Clegane's head: 'Joff may have liked the man, but Tommen was always afraid of him... with good reason, it would seem.' 'When a dog goes bad, the fault lies with his master,' Ser Kevan said. Then he turned and walked away. The Hound had been Joffrey's sworn shield — the 'dog' went bad under a bad master. Kevan's cool reply laid the blame for Sandor's savagery at the Lannisters' own door, and Cersei had no answer for it.

paragraphs.context: until there comes another, younger and more beautiful, to cast
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls Maggy the Frog's prophecy: she will be queen until a younger, more beautiful queen casts her down.
paragraphs.simple: Whenever Cersei looked at Olenna, the face of Maggy the Frog seemed to float before her eyes. In truth the bent-back sorceress had looked nothing like the Queen of Thorns, yet Olenna's nasty little smile put Cersei back in Maggy's tent again. She could still remember the smell of it, redolent with queer eastern spices, and the softness of Maggy's gums as she sucked the blood from Cersei's finger. 'Queen you shall be,' the old woman had promised, with her lips still wet and red and glistening, 'until there comes another, younger and more beautiful, to cast you down and take all that you hold dear.' Cersei glanced past Tommen to where Margaery sat laughing: the younger queen had arrived.

paragraphs.context: every time she looked at Tommen, she saw Joffrey clawing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei is haunted by Joffrey's death: every glance at Tommen shows her Joffrey clawing at his poisoned throat.
paragraphs.simple: 'My son is safe,' Cersei told herself. 'No harm can come to him, not here, not now. Yet every time she looked at Tommen, she saw Joffrey clawing at his throat.' And when the boy began to cough the queen's heart stopped beating for a moment. She knocked aside a serving girl in her haste to reach him. 'Only a little wine that went down the wrong way,' Margaery assured her, smiling, taking Tommen's hand and kissing his fingers. 'My little love needs to take smaller sips. See, you scared your lady mother half to death.' 'I'm sorry, Mother,' Tommen said, abashed. Cersei fled to weep where no one could see: 'A woman may weep, but not a queen.'

paragraphs.context: Your maid is bought and paid for
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Merryweather warns Cersei that her maid Senelle is spying for Margaery.
paragraphs.simple: Alone in the back passage, Cersei met Lady Merryweather, who lowered her voice: 'There is something you must know. Your maid is bought and paid for. She tells Lady Margaery everything you do.' 'Senelle?' Sudden fury twisted in the queen's belly. Was there no one she could trust? 'You are certain of this?' Taena told her how it worked: 'Have her followed. Margaery never meets with her directly. Her cousins are her ravens, they bring her messages. Sometimes Elinor, sometimes Alla, sometimes Megga. All of them are as close to Margaery as sisters. They meet in the sept and pretend to pray. Put your own man in the gallery on the morrow, and he will see Senelle whispering to Megga beneath the altar of the Maiden.'

paragraphs.context: They are dead and burning, every one, with all their
paragraphs.mainIdea: Watching the tower burn, Cersei savors the thought that all the King's Hands she has known are dead and burning.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thought of all the King's Hands that she had known through the years: Owen Merryweather, Jon Connington, Qarlton Chelsted, Jon Arryn, Eddard Stark, her brother Tyrion. And her father, Lord Tywin Lannister, her father most of all. 'All of them are burning now,' she told herself, savoring the thought. 'They are dead and burning, every one, with all their plots and schemes and betrayals. It is my day now. It is my castle and my kingdom.' The burning tower became, in her mind, a funeral pyre for every man who had ever stood between her and power.

paragraphs.context: The wildfire was cleansing her, burning away all her rage and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei feels the wildfire cleansing her, burning away rage and fear and filling her with resolve.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime urged her to come inside, but Cersei refused: 'No need. I feel too alive for sleep. The flames are so pretty. I want to watch them for a while.' 'You should not stay alone.' 'I will not be alone. Ser Osmund can remain with me and keep me safe. Your Sworn Brother.' 'If it please Your Grace,' said Kettleblack. 'It does.' Cersei slid her arm through his, and side by side they watched the fire rage. 'The wildfire was cleansing her, burning away all her rage and fear, filling her with resolve.' Jaime watched her with disquiet: she looked the way Aerys used to look at burnings.

paragraphs.context: only madmen fight wars they cannot win
paragraphs.mainIdea: Prince Doran tells Arys his mother taught him that only madmen fight wars they cannot win.
paragraphs.simple: Arys dared to ask: 'And you, my prince?' 'My mother taught me long ago that only madmen fight wars they cannot win.' If the bluntness of the question had offended him, Prince Doran hid it well. 'Yet this peace is fragile... as fragile as your princess.' 'Only a beast would harm a little girl,' Arys said. Doran's answer was a warning and an excuse at once: he would not fight a war he could not win, even to avenge his brother Oberyn — and Myrcella's safety was the fragile thing holding the peace together.

paragraphs.context: Her name was Rhaenys. She was a princess too
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran reminds Arys that his own sister's little daughter Rhaenys was murdered too — princesses are not safe.
paragraphs.simple: 'My sister Elia had a little girl as well. Her name was Rhaenys. She was a princess too.' The prince sighed. 'Those who would plunge a knife into Princess Myrcella do not bear her any malice, no more than Ser Amory Lorch did when he killed Rhaenys, if indeed he did. They seek only to force my hand. For if Myrcella should be slain in Dorne whilst under my protection, who would believe my denials?' Doran's point: killers would not hate Myrcella herself; they would kill her to start a war between Dorne and the Iron Throne, exactly as Elia's children were killed to destroy House Targaryen.

paragraphs.context: Autumn is a lovely season there
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran describes the Water Gardens as his haven and promises Myrcella will be safe and happy there.
paragraphs.simple: Doran apologized for his frailty and said Sunspear wearied him. 'As soon as my duty allows, I mean to return to the Water Gardens. When I do I shall take Princess Myrcella with me.' Before Arys could protest, the prince raised a swollen-knuckled hand: 'You shall go as well. And her septa, her maids, her guards. Sunspear's walls are strong, but beneath them is the shadow city. Even within the castle hundreds come and go each day. The Gardens are my haven. Prince Maron raised them as a gift for his Targaryen bride, to mark Dorne's marriage to the Iron Throne. Autumn is a lovely season there... hot days, cool nights, the salt breeze off the sea, the fountains and the pools. And there are other children, boys and girls of high and gentle birth. Myrcella will have friends of her own age to play with. She will not be lonely.'

paragraphs.context: I could die now, happy, the knight thought
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arys gives in to Arianne, and for a dozen heartbeats he is at peace.
paragraphs.simple: Arys stopped resisting and went to Arianne’s bed. For a dozen heartbeats at least he was at peace: “I could die now, happy, the knight thought.” He did not die.

paragraphs.context: My father is very good at doing nothing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne says her father excels at doing nothing — he calls it thinking.
paragraphs.simple: Arys worried: 'What if someone were to go to your father and tell him how I'd dishonored you?' 'My father is many things, but no one has ever said he was a fool. The Bastard of Godsgrace had my maidenhead when we were both fourteen. Do you know what my father did when he learned of it?' She gathered the bedclothes in her fist and pulled them up under her chin. 'Nothing. My father is very good at doing nothing. He calls it thinking.' Arianne's contempt for Doran is complete: she sees his caution not as wisdom but as cowardice dressed up in fine words.

paragraphs.context: the princess was braver than her brother, and brighter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arys reflects that Myrcella is braver, brighter, and more confident than Tommen — the women are the strong ones.
paragraphs.simple: 'Nor is he his sister.' It was true. Tommen was a good-hearted little man who always tried his best, but the last time Ser Arys saw him he had been weeping on the quay. Myrcella never shed a tear, though it was she who was leaving hearth and home to seal an alliance with her maidenhood. The truth was, the princess was braver than her brother, and brighter and more confident as well. Her wits were quicker, her courtesies more polished. Nothing ever daunted her, not even Joffrey. 'The women are the strong ones, truly.' He was thinking not only of Myrcella, but of her mother and his own, of the Queen of Thorns, of the Sand Snakes — and of Princess Arianne, her most of all.

paragraphs.context: I am my father’s heir. Should I give up my rights
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne argues Dornish law makes her her father's heir, and asks why a daughter should yield to sons.
paragraphs.simple: 'A son comes before a daughter,' Arys said. 'Why? What god has made it so? I am my father's heir. Should I give up my rights to my brothers?' 'You twist my words. I never said... Dorne is different. The Seven Kingdoms have never had a ruling queen.' In Dorne the eldest child inherits regardless of sex — so Arianne is Doran's heir by law, and by the same Dornish law Myrcella, being older than Tommen, should inherit the Iron Throne before him. Arianne was building her case: crowning Myrcella is not treason in Dorne, it is justice.

paragraphs.context: bringing on the terrible war the singers named the Dance of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arys recalls how Ser Criston Cole set brother against sister and caused the Dance of the Dragons.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne pressed him: 'The first Viserys intended his daughter Rhaenyra to follow him, do you deny it? But as the king lay dying the Lord Commander of his Kingsguard decided that it should be otherwise.' Arys knew the history: 'Ser Criston Cole. Criston the Kingmaker had set brother against sister and divided the Kingsguard against itself, bringing on the terrible war the singers named the Dance of the Dragons. Some claimed he acted from ambition, for Prince Aegon was more tractable than his willful older sister. Others allowed him nobler motives, and argued that he was defending ancient Andal custom. A few whispered that Ser Criston had been Princess Rhaenyra's lover before he took the white and wanted vengeance on the woman who had spurned him.' Arianne's point: one white knight caused that disaster — another could repair it.

paragraphs.context: Set a crown upon her head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne asks Arys to do no more than his oath requires: protect Myrcella — and crown her queen.
paragraphs.simple: “What would you have me do?” “No more than you have sworn. Protect Myrcella with your life. Defend her... and her rights. Set a crown upon her head.” “I swore an oath!” “To Joffrey, not to Tommen.” “Aye, but Tommen is a good-hearted boy. He will be a better king than Joffrey.” “But not better than Myrcella.” Arianne was asking Arys to commit treason — and dressing it as duty.

paragraphs.context: what one king does another can undo, or change
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne argues that since one king made the Kingsguard's vows, another — a queen — can change them and let Arys marry her.
paragraphs.simple: 'Aegon the Dragon made the Kingsguard and its vows, but what one king does another can undo, or change. Formerly the Kingsguard served for life, yet Joffrey dismissed Ser Barristan so his dog could have a cloak. Myrcella would want you to be happy, and she is fond of me as well. She will give us leave to marry if we ask.' Arianne put her arms around him and laid her face against his chest. 'You can have me and your white cloak both, if that is what you want.' She was offering him everything his vows forbade — love, marriage, honor — if he would only help her crown Myrcella.

paragraphs.context: one day you will sit where I sit and rule all Dorne
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne reveals she once found a letter proving her father meant Quentyn — not her — to rule Dorne.
paragraphs.simple: 'Not Trys. Quentyn.' Her eyes were bold and black as sin, unflinching. 'I have known the truth since I was four-and-ten, since the day that I went to my father's solar to give him a good night kiss, and found him gone. My mother had sent for him, I learned later. He'd left a candle burning. When I went to blow it out, I found a letter lying incomplete beside it, a letter to my brother Quentyn, off at Yronwood. My father told Quentyn that he must do all that his maester and his master-at-arms required of him, because 'one day you will sit where I sit and rule all Dorne, and a ruler must be strong of mind and body.' My father's words, written in his own hand. They burned themselves into my memory. I cried myself to sleep that night, and many nights thereafter.' This old wound explained everything: Arianne had never felt like her father's true heir.

paragraphs.context: The Golden Company is different. A brotherhood of exiles and the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne argues the Golden Company never breaks contracts — unless they are sailing home, which means Quentyn is treating with them.
paragraphs.simple: “No,” Arianne said. “I would believe it of any of the other free companies, yes. Most of them would change sides for half a groat. The Golden Company is different. A brotherhood of exiles and the sons of exiles, united by the dream of Bittersteel. It’s home they want, as much as gold. Lord Yronwood knows that as well as I do. His forebears rode with Bittersteel during three of the Blackfyre Rebellions.” Her reasoning: the Company broke its Myrish contract because someone offered them what they truly want — a return to Westeros. That someone, she believed, was Quentyn.

paragraphs.context: I swear, no man will steal your birthright whilst I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Won over, Arys kneels and swears his sword, life, and honor to Arianne and Myrcella's cause.
paragraphs.simple: 'I will.' Ser Arys sank to one knee. 'Myrcella is the elder, and better suited to the crown. Who will defend her rights if not her Kingsguard? My sword, my life, my honor, all belong to her... and to you, my heart's delight. I swear, no man will steal your birthright whilst I still have the strength to lift a sword. I am yours. What would you have of me?' 'All.' She knelt to kiss his lips. 'All, my love, my true love, my sweet love, and forever. But first...' 'Ask, and it is yours.' '...Myrcella.' The seduction was complete: guilt, love, and flattery had turned the Kingsguard knight into Arianne's sworn conspirator.

paragraphs.context: Tywin Lannister chose to hang him as a lesson to other
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne learns Podrick's history: his knight master was hanged by Tywin for stealing, and the boy was spared only by his name.
paragraphs.simple: Far from home, alone, and penniless, the boy attached himself to a fat hedge knight named Ser Lorimer the Belly, part of Lord Lefford’s contingent guarding the baggage train. “The boys who guard the foodstuffs always eat the best,” Lorimer liked to say — until he was caught with a stolen ham from Tywin’s own stores. “Tywin Lannister chose to hang him as a lesson to other looters.” Podrick had shared the ham and might have shared the rope, but his name saved him: Ser Kevan took charge of him and later sent him to squire for Tyrion.

paragraphs.context: I’ve seen pages half your age who could have beat you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne tests Podrick with wooden swords and finds him brave but weak and untrained.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne cut two wooden swords from fallen branches to get a sense of Podrick's skills. The boy was slow of speech but not of hand, she was pleased to learn. Though fearless and attentive, he was also underfed and skinny, and not near strong enough. If he had survived the Battle of the Blackwater as he claimed, it could only be because no one thought him worth the killing. 'You may call yourself a squire,' she told him, 'but I've seen pages half your age who could have beat you bloody. If you stay with me, you'll go to sleep with blisters on your hands and bruises on your arms most every night, and you'll be so stiff and sore you'll hardly sleep. You don't want that.' 'I do,' the boy insisted. 'I want that. The bruises and the blisters.'

paragraphs.context: cutting off their teats for trophies
paragraphs.mainIdea: A patrol captain warns Brienne that the Hound is raiding across the Trident with a hundred outlaws.
paragraphs.simple: On the road they had met one of Lord Randyll's patrols, bristling with longbows and lances. The horsemen surrounded them while their captain questioned Brienne, but in the end he let them continue. 'Be wary, woman. The next men you meet may not be as honest as my lads. The Hound has crossed the Trident with a hundred outlaws, and it's said they're raping every wench they come upon and cutting off their teats for trophies.' Brienne felt obligated to pass the warning to the farmer and his wife. The man only spat: 'Dogs and wolves and lions, may the Others take them all. These outlaws won't dare come too near to Maidenpool. Not so long as Lord Tarly has the rule there.'

paragraphs.context: She would not be here now, dressed in man’s mail and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hearing of a wedding, Brienne reflects on her own broken betrothal and the different life she might have had.
paragraphs.simple: The farmer said the eggs were for Lord Mooton's daughter's wedding to Tarly's son. Brienne had been betrothed at seven, to a boy three years her senior, Lord Caron's younger son, a shy boy with a mole above his lip. They had only met the once, on the occasion of their betrothal. Two years later he was dead, carried off by the same chill that took Lord and Lady Caron and their daughters. Had he lived, they would have been wed within a year of her first flowering, and her whole life would have been different. She would not be here now, dressed in man's mail and carrying a sword, hunting for a dead woman's child. More like she'd be at Nightsong, swaddling a child of her own and nursing another. It was not a new thought. It always made her feel a little sad, but a little relieved as well.

paragraphs.context: She’s as mean as she is ugly, and there’s no one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Hyle Hunt greets Brienne with cruel mockery, repeating the lie that she slew King Renly.
paragraphs.simple: When the guards threatened Brienne, a languid young knight stepped from the gatehouse wearing a surcoat with a brown deer, dead and bound and slung beneath a pole. 'Best let her by, lads,' warned Ser Hyle Hunt. 'This is Brienne the Beauty, the Maid of Tarth, who slew King Renly and half his Rainbow Guard. She's as mean as she is ugly, and there's no one uglier... except perhaps for you, Pisspot, but your father was the rear end of an aurochs, so you have a good excuse. Her father is the Evenstar of Tarth.' The guards laughed, but the halberds parted. Brienne knew Hyle of old: he had been one of the knights who played the cruel game with her at Highgarden.

paragraphs.context: A crow was pulling strips of flesh from the ripe ruins
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne watches Lord Tarly dispense justice in the fishmarket, beneath a gallows with four corpses.
paragraphs.simple: They found Lord Tarly in the fishmarket, doing justice. A platform had been thrown up beside the water, from which his lordship could look down upon the men accused of crimes. To his left stood a long gallows, with ropes enough for twenty men. Four corpses swung beneath it. One looked fresh, but the other three had plainly been there for some time. A crow was pulling strips of flesh from the ripe ruins of one of the dead men. The other crows had scattered, wary of the crowd of townsfolk who'd gathered in hopes of someone's being hanged. Lord Randyll shared the platform with Lord Mooton; Tarly wore mail and boiled leather and a grey steel breastplate, the greatsword Heartsbane at his shoulder.

paragraphs.context: but a man who steals from a sept is stealing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tarly orders seven fingers cut off a thief who stole from a sept — stealing from the gods is worse.
paragraphs.simple: A stripling in a roughspun cloak was being heard: 'I never hurt no one, m'lord. I only took what the septons left when they run off. If you got to take my finger for that, do it.' 'It is customary to take a finger from a thief,' Lord Tarly replied in a hard voice, 'but a man who steals from a sept is stealing from the gods.' He turned to his captain of guards. 'Seven fingers. Leave his thumbs.' 'Seven?' The thief paled. When the guards seized him he tried to fight, but feebly, as if he were already maimed. Watching him, Brienne could not help think of Ser Jaime, and the way he'd screamed when Zollo's arakh came flashing down.

paragraphs.context: This is a war, not a harvest ball
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Tarly scorns Brienne for wearing armor, saying war is no place for a woman.
paragraphs.simple: Tarly's voice became a whip. 'You never should have donned mail, nor buckled on a sword. You never should have left your father's hall. This is a war, not a harvest ball. By all the gods, I ought to ship you back to Tarth.' 'Do that and answer to the throne.' Her voice sounded high and girlish, when she wanted to sound fearless. She had Podrick bring the king's letter. Tarly took it and unrolled it, scowling, his lips moving as he read. 'The king's business. What sort of business?' 'Lie to me and I will hang you.' 'S-sansa Stark.' He handed back the letter: 'Go where you want and do as you will... but when you're raped don't look to me for justice. You will have earned it with your folly.'

paragraphs.context: Lady Lysa is dead. Some singer pushed her off a mountain
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tarly tells Brienne that Lysa Arryn is dead and Littlefinger now holds the Eyrie — bad news for her search.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne blurted out: 'She might have gone to the Vale instead, to her mother's sister.' Lord Randyll gave her a contemptuous look. 'Lady Lysa is dead. Some singer pushed her off a mountain. Littlefinger holds the Eyrie now... though not for long. The lords of the Vale are not the sort to bend their knees to some upjumped jackanapes whose only skill is counting coppers.' He handed her back her letter and strode away. 'Lysa Tully is dead.' Brienne stood beneath the gallows, the precious parchment in her hand. With Lady Lysa dead, the Vale no longer seemed a likely refuge — and Brienne had to wonder who else the crows had dined on.

paragraphs.context: now it was autumn and they were falling like leaves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne learns Hyle's fellow knights are dead, and mourns them as fallen 'knights of summer.'
paragraphs.simple: Hyle tried to explain himself: 'It was only a game to pass the time. We meant no harm.' He hesitated. 'Ben died, you know. Cut down on the Blackwater. Farrow too, and Will the Stork. And Mark Mullendore took a wound that cost him half his arm.' 'Good,' Brienne wanted to say. 'Good, he deserved it.' But she remembered Mullendore sitting outside his pavilion with his monkey on his shoulder in a little suit of chain mail, the two of them making faces at each other. What was it Catelyn Stark had called them, that night at Bitterbridge? The knights of summer. And now it was autumn and they were falling like leaves. Even the men who had wronged her deserved a moment of grief.

paragraphs.context: the whole sum to go to whoever claimed her maidenhead
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne learns the knights' kindness was a wager: each paid a gold dragon to whoever could take her maidenhead.
paragraphs.simple: Randyll Tarly solved the mystery. His young son Dickon had overheard four knights laughing as they saddled their horses, and told his lord father what they said. 'They had a wager. Three of the younger knights had started it, he told her: Ambrose, Bushy, and Hyle Hunt, of his own household. As word spread through the camp, however, others had joined the game. Each man was required to buy into the contest with a golden dragon, the whole sum to go to whoever claimed her maidenhead.' 'I have put an end to their sport,' Tarly told her. 'Some of these... challengers... are less honorable than others, and the stakes were growing larger every day. It was only a matter of time before one of them decided to claim the prize by force.' Every gift, every compliment at Highgarden had been part of the game.

paragraphs.context: A woman’s war is in the birthing bed.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tarly tells Brienne the gods made women to bear children, and a woman's war is in the birthing bed.
paragraphs.simple: 'They were knights,' Brienne said, stunned, 'anointed knights.' 'And honorable men. The blame is yours.' The accusation made her flinch. 'I would never... my lord, I did nought to encourage them.' 'Your being here encouraged them. If a woman will behave like a camp follower, she cannot object to being treated like one. A war host is no place for a maiden. If you have any regard for your virtue or the honor of your House, you will take off that mail, return home, and beg your father to find a husband for you.' 'I came to fight,' she insisted. 'To be a knight.' 'The gods made men to fight, and women to bear children,' said Randyll Tarly. 'A woman's war is in the birthing bed.'

paragraphs.context: been no ships there for a while. Thirty years, say
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nimble Dick admits the 'smugglers' cove' he sent the fool to has seen no ships in thirty years — he tricked him.
paragraphs.simple: 'A smugglers' cove. You sent the fool to smugglers.' 'Him and them two girls.' He chuckled. 'Only thing, well, the place I sent them, been no ships there for a while. Thirty years, say.' That was how Nimble Dick had 'fooled a fool': he took the frightened fool's gold and sent him and the two girls to a lonely ruin where no ship would ever come. 'What's this fool to you?' 'Those two girls are my sisters.' Brienne offered gold for the truth: one golden dragon for the place, six if they found her sister. 'Sweet. Puts me in mind o' Crackclaw Point,' said Dick Crabb, biting the coin.

paragraphs.context: he could uproot pine trees with one hand and chuck
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nimble Dick tells the legend of Ser Clarence Crabb, whose wife brought the heads of his victims back to life as whispering counselors.
paragraphs.simple: 'The Whispers. You heard o' Clarence Crabb, o' course.' 'No.' That surprised him. 'Ser Clarence Crabb, I said. I got his blood in me. He was eight foot tall, and so strong he could uproot pine trees with one hand and chuck them half a mile. No horse could bear his weight, so he rode an aurochs.' 'What does he have to do with this smugglers' cove?' 'His wife was a woods witch. Whenever Ser Clarence killed a man, he'd fetch his head back home and his wife would kiss it on the lips and bring it back t' life. Lords, they were, and wizards, and famous knights and pirates. One was king o' Duskendale. They gave old Crabb good counsel. Being they was just heads, they couldn't talk real loud, but they never shut up neither. When you're a head, talking's all you got to pass the day. So Crabb's keep got named the Whispers. Still is, though it's been a ruin for a thousand years.'

paragraphs.context: his lord father had tried to teach him how to swim
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam recalls his father trying to teach him to swim by throwing him into a pond — after which he feared deep water.
paragraphs.simple: Looking at the water only made Sam think of drowning. When he was small his lord father had tried to teach him how to swim by throwing him into the pond beneath Horn Hill. The water had gotten in his nose and in his mouth and in his lungs, and he coughed and wheezed for hours after Ser Hyle pulled him out. After that he never dared go in any deeper than his waist. The Bay of Seals was a lot deeper than his waist, and not so friendly as that little fishpond. Its waters were grey and green and choppy, and the wooded shore was a snarl of rocks and whirlpools. Even if he could swim that far, the waves were like to smash him against some stone and break his head to pieces.

paragraphs.context: He did not want to be a maester, with a heavy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam dreads becoming a maester and facing his father, and does not want to leave his brothers of the Watch.
paragraphs.simple: Sam did not know what he was doing on the boat. 'Going to the Citadel to forge a chain and be a maester, to be of better service to the Watch,' he told himself, but the thought just made him weary. He did not want to be a maester, with a heavy chain wrapped around his neck, cold against his skin. He did not want to leave his brothers, the only friends he'd ever had. And he certainly did not want to face the father who had sent him to the Wall to die. It was different for the others: for them the voyage would have a happy ending — Gilly safe at Horn Hill, Aemon resting in Oldtown, Dareon singing at some lord's court. 'I am going for them,' he told himself, 'for the Night's Watch, and for the happy ending.'

paragraphs.context: The whole city is built in a lagoon on a hundred
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam cheers Gilly up with his book knowledge of Braavos: a city on islands, a giant titan, boats instead of horses.
paragraphs.simple: Sam tried to take his mind off his sickness by talking with Gilly as she nursed her son. 'This ship will take us as far as Braavos. We'll find another ship to carry us to Oldtown. I read a book about Braavos when I was small. The whole city is built in a lagoon on a hundred little islands, and they have a titan there, a stone man hundreds of feet high. They have boats instead of horses, and their mummers play out written stories instead of just making up the usual stupid farces. The food is very good too, especially the fish. They have all kinds of clams and eels and oysters, fresh from their lagoon. We ought to have a few days between ships. If we do, we can go and see a mummer show, and have some oysters.' He thought that would excite her. He could not have been more wrong. 'If you want, m'lord,' Gilly said dully.

paragraphs.context: Egg wanted me to help him rule, but I knew my
paragraphs.mainIdea: Old Maester Aemon recalls sailing to the Wall with great pomp, escorted by Ser Duncan and even Bloodraven.
paragraphs.simple: 'What is he looking at?' Dareon wondered, watching blind old Aemon gaze at the sea. 'For him it's as dark up here as it is down in the cabin.' The old man heard him. 'I was not born blind,' he reminded them. 'When last I passed this way, I saw every rock and tree and whitecap, and watched the grey gulls flying in our wake. I was five-and-thirty and had been a maester of the chain for sixteen years. Egg wanted me to help him rule, but I knew my place was here. He sent me north aboard the Golden Dragon, and insisted that his friend Ser Duncan see me safe to Eastwatch. No recruit had arrived at the Wall with so much pomp since Nymeria sent the Watch six kings in golden fetters. Egg emptied out the dungeons too, so I would not need to say my vows alone. My honor guard, he called them. One was no less a man than Brynden Rivers. Later he was chosen lord commander.'

paragraphs.context: she washed the tears off his face with a bit of lace
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam remembers being shamed on the Arbor, and learning his father never meant to bring him home.
paragraphs.simple: On the Arbor, things went from bad to worse. Lord Redwyne's twin sons despised Sam on first sight. Every morn they found some fresh way to shame him in the practice yard. On the third day Horas Redwyne made him squeal like a pig when he begged for quarter. On the fifth his brother Hobber clad a kitchen girl in his own armor and let her beat Sam with a wooden sword until he began to cry. When she revealed herself, all the squires and pages and stableboys howled with laughter. 'The boy needs a bit of seasoning, that's all,' his father told Lord Redwyne that night. It was not until they were back at Horn Hill that his mother told Sam the truth: his father had never meant for him to return. Horas was to come home in Sam's place, whilst Sam remained on the Arbor as Lord Paxter's page and cupbearer — and might have been betrothed to Redwyne's daughter. 'My poor Sam,' she murmured, washing his tears with lace dampened with her spit. 'My poor poor Sam.'

paragraphs.context: supposedly their warriors ate the hearts and livers of the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam recalls what he has read about Skagos: savage stoneborn, unicorns, and rumors of cannibalism.
paragraphs.simple: The island sat at the mouth of the Bay of Seals, massive and mountainous, a stark and forbidding land peopled by savages. They lived in caves and grim mountain fastnesses, Sam had read, and rode great shaggy unicorns to war. Skagos meant 'stone' in the Old Tongue. The Skagosi named themselves the stoneborn, but their fellow northmen called them Skaggs and liked them little. Only a hundred years ago Skagos had risen in rebellion. Their revolt had taken years to quell and claimed the life of the Lord of Winterfell and hundreds of his sworn swords. Some songs said the Skaggs were cannibals; supposedly their warriors ate the hearts and livers of the men they slew. In ancient days, the Skagosi had sailed to the nearby isle of Skane, seized its women, slaughtered its men, and ate them on a pebbled beach in a feast that lasted for a fortnight. Skane remained unpeopled to this day.

paragraphs.context: Egg, I dreamed that I was old
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the rain, the ancient Maester Aemon mistakes Sam for his long-dead brother Egg and says he dreamed he was old.
paragraphs.simple: Sam had kept old Aemon company in the rain until the ancient maester fell asleep. When Sam woke him, Aemon’s blind white eyes came open. “Egg?” he said, as the rain streamed down his cheeks. “Egg, I dreamed that I was old.” Egg was Aemon’s little brother, dead for many years; lost in a dream, the old man thought he was young again and his brother was beside him.

paragraphs.context: That is the sound of grief, and there is no potion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon tells Sam that Gilly's weeping is not fear but grief — and no potion can cure grief.
paragraphs.simple: Sam was at his wit's end: between the storms and Gilly's sobbing he had not slept for days. 'Isn't there something you can give her?' he asked Maester Aemon very softly. 'Some herb or potion, so she won't be so afraid?' 'It is not fear you hear,' the old man told him. 'That is the sound of grief, and there is no potion for that. Let her tears run their course, Sam. You cannot stem the flow.' Sam had not understood. 'She's going to a safe place. A warm place. Why should she be grieving?' 'Sam,' the old man whispered, 'you have two good eyes, and yet you do not see. She is a mother grieving for her child.'

paragraphs.context: the babe will still be Dalla’s son, and not the child
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon reveals the truth: the baby Gilly nurses is Dalla’s son — Jon switched the babes at the Wall.
paragraphs.simple: “... the babe will still be Dalla’s son, and not the child of her body.” Aemon spoke the truth Sam had not seen: the baby Gilly nursed was not her own son. Jon had switched the babes at the Wall — this child was Dalla’s, Mance Rayder’s son, while Gilly’s own boy remained behind.

paragraphs.context: Gilly did not leave the child willingly, I am certain
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon explains that Gilly did not give up her child willingly — Jon must have used threats and promises.
paragraphs.simple: “She nursed them both and loved them both,” said Aemon, “but not alike. No mother loves all her children the same, not even the Mother Above. Gilly did not leave the child willingly, I am certain. What threats the Lord Commander made, what promises, I can only guess... but threats and promises there surely were.” “No. No, that’s wrong. Jon would never...” “Jon would never. Lord Snow did.”

paragraphs.context: Sometimes there is no happy choice, Sam, only one less
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon explains that Jon switched the babies to protect Mance's son from Melisandre's fires — choosing the less grievous evil.
paragraphs.simple: “Jon would never. Lord Snow did. Sometimes there is no happy choice, Sam, only one less grievous than the others.” Aemon’s point: Jon the man would never do such a thing, but Jon the Lord Commander had to choose — and chose the evil that grieved him least.

paragraphs.context: The worst isn’t done. The worst is just beginning, and there
paragraphs.mainIdea: As new storms gather, Sam despairs: the worst is just beginning, and there are no happy endings.
paragraphs.simple: Wordless, Sam staggered up onto the deck to retch, but there was nothing in his belly to bring up. Night had come upon them, a strange still night such as they had not seen for many days. The sea was black as glass. At the oars, the rowers rested. The wind was in the sails, and to the north Sam could even see a scattering of stars, and the red wanderer the free folk called the Thief. 'That ought to be my star,' Sam thought miserably. 'Slayer.' Dareon appeared beside him, oblivious to Sam's pain. 'A sweet night, for once. Look, the stars are coming out. We might even get a bit of moon. Might be the worst is done.' 'No.' Sam wiped his nose, and pointed south with a fat finger, toward the gathering darkness. 'There.' Lightning flashed, and distant clouds glowed like mountains heaped on mountains, purple and red and yellow, taller than the world. 'The worst isn't done. The worst is just beginning, and there are no happy endings.' 'Gods be good,' said Dareon, laughing. 'Slayer, you are such a craven.'

paragraphs.context: Once that went without saying when men spoke of those
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kevan pointedly remarks that 'good and valiant knight' once went without saying for men of the Kingsguard.
paragraphs.simple: “Once that went without saying when men spoke of those who wore the white cloak.” Kevan’s cool reply to Jaime’s praise of Balon Swann: there was a time when no one needed to say a white knight was good and valiant — it went without saying. The Kingsguard’s honor had fallen that far.

paragraphs.context: Sandor Clegane is raiding along the Trident, it would seem
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kevan reports that Sandor Clegane is raiding along the Trident, and Cersei wants his head.
paragraphs.simple: “For a while, mayhaps. Sandor Clegane is raiding along the Trident, it would seem. Your sister wants his head. It may be that he has joined Dondarrion.” Kevan’s news: the Hound was raiding the riverlands, and Cersei wanted him dead.

paragraphs.context: what was there to stop a niece from ordering an uncle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime fears Cersei might have Kevan killed — or let the Hound do it for her.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime let Kevan go, his missing sword hand twitching. He had hoped against hope that Cersei had somehow misunderstood, but plainly that was wrong. 'He knows about the two of us. About Tommen and Myrcella. And Cersei knows he knows.' Ser Kevan was a Lannister of Casterly Rock. Jaime could not believe that she would ever do him harm, but... 'I was wrong about Tyrion, why not about Cersei? When sons were killing fathers, what was there to stop a niece from ordering an uncle slain? An inconvenient uncle, who knows too much.' Though perhaps Cersei was hoping that the Hound might do her work for her. If Sandor Clegane cut down Ser Kevan, she would not need to bloody her own hands. And he will, if they should meet: Kevan was no longer young, and the Hound...

paragraphs.context: I told Falyse that I would not have our father’s noble
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei learns that Bronn named Lollys's bastard 'Tyrion' — after she forbade the name Tywin.
paragraphs.simple: Pycelle brought the tidings, desperately uncomfortable: 'There has been a bird. From Stokeworth. Lady Tanda sends word that her daughter Lollys has been delivered of a strong, healthy son.' 'And you will never guess what they have named the little bastard, brother.' 'They wanted to name him Tywin, I recall.' 'Yes, but I forbade it. I told Falyse that I would not have our father's noble name bestowed upon the ill-gotten spawn of some pig boy and a feeble-witted sow.' 'Lady Stokeworth insists the child's name was not her doing,' Pycelle put in, mopping his brow. 'Lollys's husband made the choice. This man Bronn, he... it would seem that he...' 'Tyrion,' ventured Jaime. 'He named the child Tyrion.' The old man gave a tremulous nod.

paragraphs.context: all the time he’s been hiding in Lollys’s womb
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime jokes that Cersei has been hunting Tyrion everywhere while he was hiding in Lollys's womb.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime had to laugh. “There you are, sweet sister. You have been looking everywhere for Tyrion, and all the time he’s been hiding in Lollys’s womb.”

paragraphs.context: We are sworn to protect her as well,” Jaime had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime recalls how Aerys would visit Queen Rhaella after burnings, and the Kingsguard could not protect her from her own husband.
paragraphs.simple: The sight of Cersei enraptured by the wildfire filled Jaime with disquiet, reminding him of Aerys Targaryen and the way a burning would arouse him. A king has no secrets from his Kingsguard. Relations between Aerys and his queen had been strained during the last years of his reign. But whenever Aerys gave a man to the flames, Queen Rhaella would have a visitor in the night. The day he burned his mace-and-dagger Hand, Jaime and Jon Darry had stood at guard outside her bedchamber whilst the king took his pleasure. “You’re hurting me,” they had heard Rhaella cry through the oaken door. “You’re hurting me.” “We are sworn to protect her as well,” Jaime had finally been driven to say. “We are,” Darry allowed, “but not from him.”

paragraphs.context: I use Taena to feed the little queen what I want
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei reveals she knows Taena spies for Margaery — and uses her to feed the little queen chosen information.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime warned her: 'She is one of Margaery Tyrell's companions. She's informing on you to the little queen.' 'Of course she is.' Cersei went to fill her cup anew. 'Margaery was thrilled when I asked her leave to take Taena on as my companion. You should have heard her. She will be a sister to you, as she's been to me. Of course you must have her! I have my cousins and my other ladies. Our little queen does not want me to be lonely.' 'If you know she is a spy, why take her on?' 'Margaery is not half so clever as she thinks. She has no notion what a sweet serpent she has in that Myrish slut. I use Taena to feed the little queen what I want her to know. Some of it is even true.' Cersei's eyes were bright with mischief. 'And Taena tells me everything Maid Margaery is doing.'

paragraphs.context: she pays him with hands from Highgarden, each half the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei shares Taena's gossip: Olenna cheats merchants by paying with underweight old Gardener coins.
paragraphs.simple: “Did you know that the Queen of Thorns keeps a chest of coins in her wheelhouse? Old gold from before the Conquest. Should any tradesman be so unwise as to name a price in golden coins, she pays him with hands from Highgarden, each half the weight of one of our dragons. What merchant would dare complain of being cheated by Mace Tyrell’s lady mother?” A “hand” was the old Gardener coin — the same kind Qyburn found beneath the gaoler’s chamber pot.

paragraphs.context: she was wrong. Their father had been as relentless and implacable
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime judges that Cersei is nothing like Tywin: he was a glacier, she is wildfire.
paragraphs.simple: His sister liked to think of herself as Lord Tywin with teats, but she was wrong. Their father had been as relentless and implacable as a glacier, where Cersei was all wildfire, especially when thwarted. She had been giddy as a maiden when she learned that Stannis had abandoned Dragonstone, certain that he had finally given up the fight and sailed away to exile. When word came down from the north that he had turned up again at the Wall, her fury had been fearful to behold. She does not lack for wits, but she has no judgment, and no patience. Jaime saw it clearly: Cersei had Tywin's pride and cruelty, but none of his cold patience.

paragraphs.context: You are seeing dwarfs in every shadow and making foes of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime warns Cersei she sees enemies everywhere and is turning friends into foes.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime warned her: “The crows will feast upon us all if you go on this way, sweet sister. Cersei, listen to yourself. You are seeing dwarfs in every shadow and making foes of friends. Uncle Kevan is not your enemy. I am not your enemy.”

paragraphs.context: You could have had me, but you chose a cloak instead
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei casts Jaime out, saying he chose his white cloak over her.
paragraphs.simple: “My vows...” “...did not stop you slaying Aerys. Words are wind. You could have had me, but you chose a cloak instead. Get out.”

paragraphs.context: They belonged to Criston Cole, who served the first Viserys
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime ends his talk with Loras on Criston Cole, the Kingmaker — a Kingsguard knight remembered as both great and terrible.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime had been quizzing Loras on forgotten Kingsguard knights: Long Tom Costayne, who served sixty years; Ser Donnel of Duskendale; Addison Hill; the White Owl; Jeffory Norcross, called Neveryield; Red Robert Flowers. 'A lot of brave men have worn the white cloak. Most have been forgotten.' 'Most deserve to be forgotten. The heroes will always be remembered. The best.' 'The best and the worst.' So one of us is like to live in song. 'And a few who were a bit of both. Like him.' He tapped the page he had been reading. 'Who?' Loras craned his head around to see. 'Ten black pellets on a scarlet field. I do not know those arms.' 'They belonged to Criston Cole, who served the first Viserys and the second Aegon.' Jaime closed the White Book. 'They called him Kingmaker.'

paragraphs.context: smell of decay filled her audience chamber like some rank rose
paragraphs.mainIdea: The men open the sack and show Cersei a rotting head crawling with maggots. She thinks it smells like her father.
paragraphs.simple: Three ragged, dirty men kneel before Cersei with a leather sack. When the chief one opens it, a terrible smell of rot fills the room. The head he pulls out is grey-green and covered in maggots. Cersei thinks the smell is like her dead father. Her ladies gasp and feel sick.

paragraphs.context: too dim to realize that he was more hostage than Hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei thinks Ser Harys Swyft is too stupid to see he is really a hostage, not the true Hand. Keeping him near forces his goodson Kevan Lannister to think twice before opposing her.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Harys Swyft is soft, bald, and always flattering. He wears a yellow coat with his house's rooster sewn in blue stones, and a blue cloak with a hundred golden hands. He was happy to be named Hand, too stupid to understand he is more a hostage than a real Hand. His daughter married Cersei's uncle Kevan, who loves his wife. As long as Cersei holds Swyft, Kevan must think twice before going against her. A flimsy shield is better than none.

paragraphs.context: his eyes were grey-green where Prince Rhaegar’s had been purple
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aurane Waters reminds Cersei of Prince Rhaegar. Though ten years younger, he clearly desires her, and she wonders if he would shave his beard for her.
paragraphs.simple: Aurane Waters looks bored by the talk about septons. Up close his hair is more silver than gold, and his eyes are grey-green where Prince Rhaegar's were purple, but the likeness is still there. Cersei wonders if he would shave his beard for her. He wants her; she can see it in how he looks at her. Men have looked at her that way since she was a girl. When she was small she sometimes wore her brother Jaime's clothes as a joke, and she was always surprised how differently men treated her when they thought she was a boy.

paragraphs.context: we have too many gold cloaks and too little gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei tells the council she will put off paying the crown's debts to the Faith and the Iron Bank until the war ends, and use the saved money to build a new fleet.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says the treasurer means they have too many gold cloaks and too little gold. Though the crown's income is large, it cannot keep up with King Robert's old debts. So she has decided to delay paying what is owed to the Holy Faith and the Iron Bank of Braavos until the war is over. The new High Septon will wring his holy hands and the Braavosi will complain, but she does not care. The saved money will build their new fleet.

paragraphs.context: Only a blind man could fail to see our war is all but won
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei claims the war is almost won: Lord Tyrell has Storm's End surrounded, Riverrun is besieged, and Redwyne's fleet is moving on Dragonstone. Only Stannis remains to trouble them.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei agrees the war is all but won. Lord Tyrell has Storm's End invested, meaning surrounded. Riverrun is besieged by the Freys and her cousin Daven. Lord Redwyne's ships have passed the Straits of Tarth and are sailing up the coast. Only a few fishing boats are left on Dragonstone to fight Redwyne's landing. The castle may hold for a while, but once they have the port they can cut the garrison off from the sea. Then only Stannis himself will remain to vex them.

paragraphs.context: Roose Bolton should have no trouble winning them to our cause
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei says the northmen hate the wildlings, so Roose Bolton should win them over easily. Some have already joined his bastard son to clear the ironmen from Moat Cailin, and White Harbor is close to joining too.
paragraphs.simple: The northmen hate the wildlings, Cersei agrees, so Roose Bolton should have no trouble winning them to their cause. A few northmen have already joined with Bolton's bastard son to help drive the wretched ironmen out of Moat Cailin and clear the way for Lord Bolton's return. She forgets some of the house names, but even White Harbor is about to join them. Its lord has agreed to marry both his granddaughters to their Frey friends and open his port to their ships.

paragraphs.context: Manderly has clapped the wretch inside a cell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Manderly has put Stannis's envoy, the onion smuggler Davos, in a cell, and asks Cersei what to do with him. Cersei wishes Stannis dead and is glad Renly died instead of the other way round.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Manderly has sent Stannis's letters on to Cersei and answered Stannis with evasions. Stannis demands White Harbor's swords and silver but offers nothing in return. Just this morning another bird came: Stannis sent his onion smuggler to treat with White Harbor, and Manderly has clapped the wretch inside a cell. He asks Cersei what to do with him. She thinks she must one day light a candle to the Stranger for carrying Renly off and leaving Stannis. If it had been the other way round, her life would have been harder.

paragraphs.context: singing to the Stranger, begging for his kiss
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei rages about Sansa Stark: she took the girl into her household and Sansa repaid her by helping murder Joffrey. When they find the Imp, they will find Sansa too, and Cersei promises she will die.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei bristles and says she has not forgotten the little she-wolf, refusing to say the girl's name. She should have thrown Sansa into the black cells as a traitor's daughter, but instead she made her part of her own household. Sansa shared her hearth and hall and played with her children. Cersei fed her, dressed her, and tried to make her less ignorant, and in return Sansa helped murder her son. When they find the Imp, they will find Lady Sansa too. She is not dead, but before Cersei is done with her, she promises the girl will be singing to the Stranger, begging for his kiss, meaning she will die.

paragraphs.context: will be wed to his son Ramsay as soon as Moat Cailin has fallen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei says Eddard Stark's younger daughter (really a fake) will marry Ramsay Bolton to secure their claim to Winterfell, and the Night's Watch has madly chosen Ned Stark's bastard Jon Snow as Lord Commander.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei goes on: Lord Eddard's younger daughter is with Lord Bolton and will be wed to his son Ramsay as soon as Moat Cailin has fallen. As long as the girl plays her part well enough to cement their claim to Winterfell, neither Bolton will care that she is really some steward's girl dressed up by Littlefinger. If the north must have a Stark, they will give them one. Then another problem: the brothers of the Night's Watch have taken leave of their wits and chosen Ned Stark's bastard son to be their Lord Commander.

paragraphs.context: the city is not a healthy place for a growing girl
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls threatening Robert when he wanted to bring a bastard daughter to court. She calls Jon Snow a traitor's son like his father, who would have handed the realm to Stannis.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says she glimpsed Jon Snow once at Winterfell, where the Starks tried to hide him. He looks very like his father. Robert's own bastards had his look too, though at least Robert kept them out of sight. Once, after the business with the cat, Robert talked of bringing some baseborn daughter of his to court. Cersei told him to do as he pleased, but the city might not be a healthy place for a growing girl. The bruise those words won her was hard to hide from Jaime, but they heard no more about the bastard girl. Cersei calls Jon Snow a traitor like his father: the father would have handed the realm to Stannis, and the son has given Stannis lands and castles.

paragraphs.context: should be dealt with: with a dagger, not a declaration
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei agrees to have Jon Snow removed from command by secret murder. If the bastard boy is truly his father's son, he will suspect nothing and may even thank her before the blade slides between his ribs.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei is delighted to finish the plan: to remove Jon Snow from the command. That is just what they shall do. She laughs. If this bastard boy is truly his father's son, he will not suspect a thing. Perhaps he will even thank her, before the blade slides between his ribs. It must be done carefully, and she will handle the rest herself. This is how an enemy should be dealt with: with a dagger, not a declaration. They have done good work today, she tells her lords, and asks if there is anything else.

paragraphs.context: It was the sheer elegance of it that pleased her most
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei plans to frame Queen Margaery by having Osney Kettleblack caught with her, with his own brother Osmund discovering them so the other Kettleblacks stay trusted. She thinks her dead father would admire the plan.
paragraphs.simple: After the council, Cersei tells herself she was made for this. What pleases her most is the sheer elegance of the plan. Even Mace Tyrell would not dare defend his darling daughter if she was caught in the act with the likes of Osney Kettleblack, and neither Stannis nor Jon Snow would wonder why Osney was being sent to the Wall. She will make sure Ser Osmund is the one to discover his brother with the little queen, so the loyalty of the other two Kettleblacks need not be questioned. If her father could only see her now, he would not be so quick to talk of marrying her off again. A pity he is so dead, her and Robert, Jon Arryn, Ned Stark, Renly, all dead. Only Tyrion remains, and not for long.

paragraphs.context: you must pick up the sword that he let fall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion's captains urge him to claim the Seastone Chair now that Balon's sons are dead, but he answers that Balon commanded him to hold Moat Cailin against the northmen.
paragraphs.simple: Victarion remembers what he told his captains at Moat Cailin when they first urged him to claim the Seastone Chair. Red Ralf Stonehouse had argued that Balon's sons were dead and Asha was a woman, so Victarion, who was his brother's strong right arm, must pick up the sword that Balon let fall. When Victarion reminded them that Balon had commanded him to hold the Moat against the northmen, Ralf Kenning said the wolves were broken and asked what good it was to win this swamp and lose the isles. Ralf the Limper added that the Crow's Eye had been too long away and did not know them.

paragraphs.context: Aeron speaks with the Drowned God’s voice
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the Damphair calls a kingsmoot, Victarion gives command of Moat Cailin to Ralf Kenning and sails home to the Iron Islands, believing the Drowned God may will him to sit the Seastone Chair.
paragraphs.simple: But when the Damphair's summons came, the call to kingsmoot, everything changed. Victarion reminds himself that Aeron speaks with the Drowned God's voice, and if the Drowned God wills that he should sit the Seastone Chair, then so be it. The next day he gave command of Moat Cailin to Ralf Kenning and set off overland for the Fever River, where the Iron Fleet lay among the reeds and willows. Rough seas and fickle winds had delayed him, but only one ship was lost, and he was home.

paragraphs.context: Sore shoulders and an aching back were easier to bear than bloody bowels
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion arms himself to go ashore: a nine-layer cloth-of-gold kraken cloak over mail and leather. He has worn mail day and night because the poisoned arrows of the bog devils kill slowly and horribly.
paragraphs.simple: They drop anchor twenty yards from Silence, Euron's ship. Victarion orders a boat lowered and buckles on his swordbelt as the rowers take their places: his longsword on one hip, a dirk on the other. Nute the Barber fastens his cloak about his shoulders. It is made of nine layers of cloth-of-gold, sewn in the shape of the kraken of House Greyjoy, with arms dangling to his boots. Beneath he wears heavy grey chain mail over boiled black leather. At Moat Cailin he had taken to wearing mail day and night. Sore shoulders and an aching back were easier to bear than bloody bowels. The poisoned arrows of the bog devils need only scratch a man, and a few hours later he would be squirting and screaming as his life ran down his legs in gouts of red and brown. Whoever wins the Seastone Chair, he will deal with the bog devils.

paragraphs.context: I have no luck with wives
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the feast, many captains promise Victarion their voices for the kingsmoot. When Hotho Harlaw offers him a daughter for a queen, Victarion thinks of his three dead wives.
paragraphs.simple: That night the men of the Iron Fleet raise a huge sailcloth tent above the tideline so Victarion can feast fifty famous captains on roast kid, salted cod, and lobster. Aeron comes too. He eats fish and drinks water while the captains drink enough ale to float the Iron Fleet. Many promise Victarion their voices: Fralegg the Strong, clever Alvyn Sharp, humpbacked Hotho Harlaw. Hotho offers him a daughter for his queen. Victarion tells him he has no luck with wives. His first wife died in childbed, giving him a stillborn daughter. His second had been stricken by a pox. And his third, he does not finish saying.

paragraphs.context: Balon was mad, Aeron is madder, and Euron is maddest of them all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Baelor Blacktyde, who returned from eight years as a hostage in Oldtown worshipping the Seven, calls Balon, Aeron and Euron all mad, and asks Victarion if he will end this mad war if made king.
paragraphs.simple: Baelor Blacktyde is harder to please. He sits by Victarion's elbow in a black-and-green patterned lambswool tunic, smooth-faced and handsome, with a sable cloak pinned by a silver seven-pointed star. He had been eight years a hostage in Oldtown and came back worshipping the seven green land gods. He says Balon was mad, Aeron is madder, and Euron is maddest of them all. Then he asks Victarion: if he shouts Victarion's name at the kingsmoot, will Victarion make an end of this mad war?

paragraphs.context: You serve one god, Damphair, but I have served ten thousand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Euron mocks his brother Aeron, boasting he has seen and served ten thousand gods across the world, from Ib to Asshai, and that men pray when they see his sails. He calls himself the godliest man ever to raise sail.
paragraphs.simple: Euron says he has often sat upon the Seastone Chair of late, and it raises no objections. He asks who knows more of gods than he does: horse gods and fire gods, gods of gold with gemstone eyes, gods carved of wood or chiseled into mountains, gods of empty air. He knows them all. He has seen people garland them with flowers and shed the blood of goats, bulls, and children in their names. He has heard prayers in half a hundred tongues: cure my leg, make the maiden love me, save me, make me wealthy, protect me from my enemies and from the Silence. He laughs and says Aeron calls him godless, but he is the godliest man ever to raise sail. Aeron serves one god, but Euron has served ten thousand. From Ib to Asshai, when men see his sails, they pray.

paragraphs.context: They looked a bit like galleys, stroking hard to ram
paragraphs.mainIdea: Outside the tent Victarion watches the night: clouds like warships, stars few and faint, longships resting on the sand, and larger ships anchored in the misty bay.
paragraphs.simple: Outside the tent the wind is rising. Clouds race across the moon's pale face. They look a bit like galleys, warships rowing hard to ram an enemy. The stars are few and faint. All along the strand, the beach, the longships rest with their tall masts rising like a forest from the surf. Victarion can hear their hulls creaking as they settle on the sand. He hears the keening of their lines, the sound of banners flapping. Beyond, in the deeper waters of the bay, larger ships bob at anchor, grim shadows wreathed in mist.

paragraphs.context: it grieves me to say so, but you may be right
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha tells Victarion she has drunk with the captains for four days and has the Harlaws and some others, but not enough support. She is thinking of shouting her uncle Victarion's name at the kingsmoot.
paragraphs.simple: Asha laughs and asks if that is why she always loses the pissing contests. She tells her uncle, it grieves her to say so, but he may be right. For four days and four nights she has been drinking with the captains and the kings, listening to what they say and what they will not say. Her own men are with her, and many Harlaws. She has Tris Botley too, and a few others. Not enough. She kicks a rock into the water between two longships and says she is of a mind to shout her uncle's name at the kingsmoot.

paragraphs.context: To end this war before this war ends us
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha proposes making peace with the north: return Deepwood Motte, Torrhen's Square and Moat Cailin in exchange for Sea Dragon Point and the Stony Shore, sealed with an exchange of hostages.
paragraphs.simple: Asha says her plan is to end this war before this war ends them. They have won all they are likely to win, and stand to lose it all just as quickly unless they make a peace. She has shown Lady Glover every courtesy, and the lady swears her lord will treat with Asha. If they hand back Deepwood Motte, Torrhen's Square, and Moat Cailin, she says, the northmen will cede them Sea Dragon Point and all the Stony Shore. Those lands are thinly peopled, yet ten times larger than all the isles put together. An exchange of hostages will seal the pact, and each side will agree to make common cause with the other should the Iron Throne come against them.

paragraphs.context: been the first sea dragon, the mightiest ever to rise from the waves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron recalls the legend of Nagga, the first sea dragon, whose stone bones now form the Grey King's hall where the kingsmoot will be held.
paragraphs.simple: On the top of the hill, forty-four huge stone ribs rise from the earth like pale tree trunks. They are the bones of Nagga, the first sea dragon, the mightiest ever to rise from the waves. She fed on krakens and drowned whole islands in her anger, but the Grey King killed her, and the Drowned God turned her bones to stone so men would never stop wondering at the courage of the first king. Her ribs became the beams and pillars of his longhall, and her jaws became his throne. He ruled here for a thousand years and seven, Aeron remembers. Here he took his mermaid wife and planned his wars against the Storm God, ruling stone and salt in robes of woven seaweed and a tall pale crown made from Nagga's teeth.

paragraphs.context: Men were smaller now. Their lives had grown short.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron thinks of the hall's lost glory in the dawn of days: all the wonder is gone, and only Nagga's bones remain to remind the ironborn.
paragraphs.simple: But that was in the dawn of days, when mighty men still lived. The hall was warmed by Nagga's living fire, which the Grey King had made his servant. Tapestries woven from silver seaweed hung on its walls. The Grey King's warriors feasted on the bounty of the sea at a table shaped like a great starfish, sitting on thrones carved from mother-of-pearl. Gone, all the glory gone. Men were smaller now, and their lives had grown short. The Storm God drowned Nagga's fire after the Grey King's death, the chairs and tapestries were stolen, the roof and walls rotted away, and the sea swallowed the great throne of fangs. Only Nagga's bones endured to remind the ironborn of all the wonder that had been.

paragraphs.context: to them the wisdom to know the true king when he stands before them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron prays all night at Nagga's bones, asking the Drowned God to give his people the wisdom to know the true king and the strength to shun the false.
paragraphs.simple: Nine wide steps had been cut from the stony hilltop. Behind rose the howling hills of Old Wyk, with black cruel mountains in the distance. Aeron stopped where the doors once stood, pulled the cork from his waterskin, drank salt water, and turned to face the sea. We were born from the sea, and to the sea we must return. He could hear the endless rumble of the waves and feel the power of the god below the waters. Aeron went to his knees and prayed: you have sent your people to me. They have left their halls and hovels, their castles and keeps, and come here to Nagga's bones from every fishing village and hidden valley. Now grant them the wisdom to know the true king when he stands before them, and the strength to shun the false.
