He prayed all night, for when the god was in him, Aeron Greyjoy needed no sleep, no more than the waves or the fishes of the sea.

paragraphs.context: The vision he spoke of was doubtless a snare set by the Storm God
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aeron thinks Gylbert Farwynd's eyes are mad and his vision a trap of the Storm God. The captains reject Gylbert's gifts and his claim fades to silence.
paragraphs.simple: Aeron saw that Gylbert's eyes were now grey, now blue, as changeable as the seas. Mad eyes, fool's eyes, he thought. The vision Gylbert spoke of was doubtless a snare set by the Storm God to lure the ironborn to destruction. The offerings his men spilled out before the kingsmoot included sealskins and walrus tusks, arm rings of whalebone, warhorns banded in bronze. The captains looked and turned away, leaving lesser men to take the gifts. When the fool finished talking and his champions began shouting his name, only the Farwynds took up the cry, and not even all of them. Soon the cries of Gylbert King faded away to silence. A gull screamed above them and landed on one of Nagga's ribs as the Lord of the Lonely Light walked back down the hill.

paragraphs.context: If old is wise, no one is wiser than me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Erik Ironmaker, eighty-eight years old, claims the kingship, boasting of his hammer, his battle deeds, and his many heirs.
paragraphs.simple: A huge man roared from where he sat: why not him, who better? He is Erik Ironmaker, Erik the Just, Erik Anvil-Breaker. One of his champions lifted his hammer for all to see, a monstrous thing with its handle wrapped in old leather and a head like a brick of steel as large as a loaf of bread. Erik said he cannot count how many hands he has smashed to pulp with that hammer, but some thief could tell them, nor how many heads he has crushed on his anvil, but some widows could. He could tell all his battle deeds, but he is eighty-eight and would not live long enough to finish. If old is wise, no one is wiser than him. If big is strong, no one is stronger. If they want a king with heirs, he has more than he can count. He likes the sound of King Erik and shouts for them to say it with him.

paragraphs.context: You all know me. If you want sweet words, look elsewhere.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion speaks plainly to the kingsmoot: he has no singer's tongue, only an axe. He was Balon's loyal brother in every war, and promises only more of the same.
paragraphs.simple: When Victarion rose, his champions stood beneath him: Ralf the Limper, Red Ralf Stonehouse, and Nute the Barber, all noted warriors. Stonehouse carried the Greyjoy banner, the golden kraken on black. As soon as it unfurled, the captains began shouting Victarion's name. He waited for quiet, then said they all knew him. If they wanted sweet words, they should look elsewhere. He had no singer's tongue. He had an axe, and his huge mailed hands, which he raised to show them. He was a loyal brother: when Balon wed, he sent Victarion to bring back his bride. He led Balon's longships into many battles and lost only one. The first time Balon took a crown, Victarion sailed into Lannisport to singe the lion's tail. The second time, Balon sent him to skin the Young Wolf. All they would get from him was more of what they got from Balon. That was all he had to say.

paragraphs.context: a sharp shrill sound that cut through the tumult like a knife through curds
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha stops Victarion's cheering with a piercing whistle, snatches up a driftwood crown, and pushes past his champions to speak.
paragraphs.simple: It was not Euron who ended the shouting, but the woman. She put two fingers in her mouth and whistled, a sharp shrill sound that cut through the tumult like a knife through curds. Shouting for her uncle, she bent, snatched up a twisted golden collar, and bounded up the steps. Nute seized her arm, and for half a heartbeat Aeron hoped his brother's champions would keep her silent, but Asha wrenched free and said something to Red Ralf that made him step aside. As she pushed past, the cheering died away. She was Balon Greyjoy's daughter, and the crowd was curious to hear her speak.

paragraphs.context: Teats on a king are a terrible thing, is that the song?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha mocks the men who say a woman cannot be king, draws a dirk she calls her suckling babe, and names her three champions.
paragraphs.simple: When a man calls her daughter, Asha slips a hand beneath her jerkin and jokes about showing them what a woman looks like, saying some of them have not seen one since they were weaned. They laugh. Teats on a king are a terrible thing, is that the song? she asks. She admits she is a woman, though not an old woman, and teases Ralf the Limper about his name. Then she draws a dirk from between her breasts and holds it up: she is a mother too, and this is her suckling babe. She names her champions, who push past Victarion's three to stand below her: Qarl the Maid, Tristifer Botley, and Ser Harras Harlaw, whose sword Nightfall is as storied as Dunstan Drumm's Red Rain.

paragraphs.context: I give you the wealth of the Stony Shore
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha upends three chests to show the kingsmoot the true wealth of the north: pebbles, pinecones, and turnips. She shames them for trading their sons' lives for turnips.
paragraphs.simple: Asha asks what they have grasped: the north, leagues of land far from the sea. They have taken Moat Cailin, Deepwood Motte, Torrhen's Square, even Winterfell, but what do they have to show for it? At her signal her men bring forward chests of oak and iron. She upends the first: I give you the wealth of the Stony Shore. An avalanche of pebbles clatters down the steps, grey and black and white, worn smooth by the sea. The second chest holds the riches of Deepwood: pinecones pouring out to roll into the crowd. From the third chest comes the gold of Winterfell: yellow turnips, round and hard and big as a man's head. Asha stabs one with her dirk and shouts to Harmund Sharp that his son Harrag died at Winterfell for this. She tosses him the turnip: if he would trade his other sons' lives for turnips, let him shout her uncle's name.

paragraphs.context: a thousand ants in a boil at his feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: The crowd splits between Asha and Victarion, shoving and shouting, until it seems a savage storm of fury is about to engulf them all.
paragraphs.simple: Others hold their tongues or mutter to their neighbors. No craven's peace, roars Ralf the Limper. Red Ralf Stonehouse waves the Greyjoy banner and bellows Victarion's name. Men begin to shove one another. Someone flings a pinecone at Asha's head. When she ducks, her makeshift crown falls off. For a moment it seems to the priest as if he stands atop a giant anthill, with a thousand ants in a boil at his feet. Shouts of Asha and Victarion surge back and forth, and it seems some savage storm is about to engulf them all. Aeron thinks the Storm God is among them, sowing fury and discord.

paragraphs.context: It is the horn of hell, he wanted to scream
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man blows a hellish horn whose shriek burns the ears; its glyphs burn with white fire and the sound fills the whole wet world.
paragraphs.simple: It is a terrible sound, a wail of pain and fury that seems to burn the ears. Aeron covers his and prays for the Drowned God to raise a mighty wave and smash the horn to silence, but the shriek goes on and on. It is the horn of hell, he wants to scream, though no man would hear him. The tattooed man's cheeks are so puffed out they look about to burst, and the muscles in his chest twitch so that the bird tattoo seems about to rip free of his flesh and take wing. The glyphs on the horn burn brightly, every line and letter shimmering with white fire. On and on the sound goes, echoing among the howling hills and across the waters to ring against the mountains of Great Wyk, until it fills the whole wet world.

paragraphs.context: You won’t find any dragons in my saddlebags
paragraphs.mainIdea: Crabb is caught stealing from Brienne's saddlebag. She tells him her gold is on her person; the fat purse in the bag is only coppers and flour to make it look fatter.
paragraphs.simple: Nimble Dick Crabb shows his true colors the next day when they stop to water the horses. Brienne steps behind some bushes to empty her bladder. As she is squatting, she hears Podrick cry out at Crabb to get away from there. She finishes, hikes up her breeches, and returns to find Dick wiping flour off his fingers. She tells him he will find no dragons, meaning gold coins, in her saddlebags. She keeps her gold on her person: some in the pouch at her belt, the rest hidden in pockets sewn inside her clothing. The fat purse in her saddlebag holds only coppers large and small, pennies and halfpennies, groats and stars, plus fine white flour to make it fatter still. She had bought the flour from the cook at the Seven Swords the morning she rode out from Duskendale.

paragraphs.context: Their blood feuds were as deep and dark as the bogs between their hills
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nimble Dick tells the history of Crackclaw Point: its people always resisted outside kings, fought each other in deep blood feuds, and held the Crabbs mightiest of all.
paragraphs.simple: The Darklyn kings of Duskendale had tried to impose their rule on Crackclaw Point, and the Mootons of Maidenpool had tried too, and later the haughty Celtigars of Crab Isle. But the Crackclaws knew their bogs and forests as no outsider could, and if hard pressed would vanish into the caverns that honeycombed their hills. When not fighting would-be conquerors, they fought each other. Their blood feuds were as deep and dark as the bogs between their hills. From time to time some champion would bring peace to the Point, but it never lasted longer than his lifetime. Lord Lucifer Hardy was a great one, and the Brothers Brune as well, and Old Crackbones even more so, but the Crabbs were the mightiest of all. Dick still refuses to believe Brienne has never heard of Ser Clarence Crabb and his exploits.

paragraphs.context: We’re all good dragon men, up Crackclaw way
paragraphs.mainIdea: Crabb tells how Crackclaw bent the knee to Aegon's sister Visenya, owes fealty to no lesser lord, and sent men with Prince Rhaegar to the Trident.
paragraphs.simple: Crabb gives Brienne a sideways look and tells the old story. When Aegon sent his sister Visenya up to Crackclaw, the lords had heard of Harren's end. Being no fools, they laid their swords at her feet. The queen took them as her own men and said they would owe no fealty to Maidenpool, Crab Isle, or Duskendale. The Celtigars may send men to collect taxes on the eastern shore, but the Crackclaws bow only to their own lords and the true king, not Robert and his ilk. Crabb spits. There were Crabbs and Brunes and Boggses with Prince Rhaegar on the Trident, and in the Kingsguard too: a Hardy, a Cave, a Pyne, and three Crabbs. They are all good dragon men, up Crackclaw way.

paragraphs.context: You’ll find truth in your looking glass, not on the tongues of men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne remembers how Septa Roelle taught her that men's flattery was only to win her father's favor, a harsh lesson that made her wary and mistrustful.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne curls up beneath her cloak with Podrick yawning beside her. She thinks she was not always wary. When she was a little girl she believed all men were as noble as her father, even the men who called her pretty and tall and bright and clever and graceful when she danced. It was Septa Roelle who lifted the scales from her eyes. They only say those things to win your lord father's favor, the woman had said. You will find truth in your looking glass, not on the tongues of men. It was a harsh lesson, one that left her weeping, but it stood her in good stead at Harrenhal when Ser Hyle and his friends played their game. A maid has to be mistrustful in this world, or she will not be a maid for long, she thinks as the rain begins to fall.

paragraphs.context: heads is too big, and they got scales where a proper man’s got hair
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nimble Dick gleefully describes the squishers: fish-white monsters with big heads, scales, webbed fingers, and green needle teeth who steal children.
paragraphs.simple: Monsters, Nimble Dick says with relish. They look like men till you get close, but their heads is too big, and they got scales where a proper man's got hair. Fish-belly white they are, with webs between their fingers. They are always damp and fishy-smelling, but behind their blubbery lips they have rows of green teeth sharp as needles. Some say the First Men killed them all, but Dick says not to believe it. They come by night and steal bad little children, padding along on webbed feet with a little squish-squish sound. The girls they keep to breed with, but the boys they eat, tearing at them with those sharp green teeth. He grins at Podrick: they would eat him, boy, eat him raw.

paragraphs.context: she was convinced it would happen here, on ground that he knew well
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne is weary and suspects Nimble Dick may be leading them into a trap on ground he knows, or in circles while a rider hunts them.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne thinks the fool Dick promised her may be like her own reflection in a pond, but it seems pointless to turn back when she has come so far. She is weary, though; her thighs are hard as iron from the saddle, and of late she has slept only four hours a night while Podrick watched over her. If Nimble Dick meant to try to murder them, she is convinced it would happen here, on ground that he knew well. He could be taking them to some robbers' den where he has kin as treacherous as he is. Or perhaps he is just leading them in circles, waiting for that rider to catch up. They have seen no sign of the man since leaving Lord Brune's castle, but that does not mean he has given up the hunt.

paragraphs.context: In battle half a heartbeat is a lifetime
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne recalls Ser Goodwin's warning: training is one thing, but killing a man is another. He told of a champion squire who flinched from the killing blow and died for it.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne tells herself she may need to kill Nimble Dick, and the thought makes her queasy. Her old master-at-arms always doubted she was hard enough for battle. She had a man's strength in her arms, Ser Goodwin had said, but a heart as soft as any maid's. It is one thing to train in the yard with a blunted sword, and another to drive a foot of sharpened steel into a man's gut and see the light go out of his eyes. To toughen her, Goodwin sent her to her father's butcher to slaughter lambs and suckling pigs. The piglets squealed and the lambs screamed like frightened children, and she wept blindly, her clothes so bloody she gave them to her maid to burn. But Goodwin still had doubts. A piglet is a piglet; a man is different. When he was a squire, he had a friend strong and quick and agile, a champion in the yard. Then war came to the Stepstones. He saw his friend drive his foeman to his knees and knock the axe from his hand, but when he might have finished, he held back for half a heartbeat. In battle half a heartbeat is a lifetime. The man slipped out his dirk and found a chink in his friend's armor. All his strength, speed, valor, and hard-won skill were worth less than a mummer's fart, because he flinched from killing. Remember that, girl.

paragraphs.context: Mounds of poisonous red ivy grew over the heap of broken stones
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne reaches the ruined castle of the Whispers: unmortared stones, a collapsed curtain wall, and waves swirling below over a shattered tower and a cavern mouth.
paragraphs.simple: The castle is built of old, unmortared stones, no two the same. Moss grows thick in the clefts between the rocks, and trees grow up from the foundations. Most old castles have a godswood; by the look of it, the Whispers has little else. Brienne walks her mare to the cliff's edge, where the curtain wall has collapsed. Mounds of poisonous red ivy grow over the heap of broken stones. She ties the horse to a tree and edges as close to the precipice as she dares. Fifty feet below, the waves swirl in and over the remnants of a shattered tower. Behind it, she glimpses the mouth of a large cavern.

paragraphs.context: a slender young weirwood with a trunk as white as a cloistered maid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne crosses the overgrown bailey past a ruined stable and collapsed keep to a pale young weirwood with dark red leaves, standing where the wall has fallen into sky and sea.
paragraphs.simple: The bailey opens up before her, overgrown. To her left is the main gate and the collapsed shell of what might have been a stable. Saplings poke out of half the stalls and grow up through the dry brown thatch of its roof. To her right she sees rotted wooden steps going down into the darkness of a dungeon or root cellar. Where the keep had been is a pile of collapsed stones, overgrown with green and purple moss. The yard is all weeds and pine needles. Soldier pines stand everywhere, drawn up in solemn ranks. In their midst is a pale stranger: a slender young weirwood with a trunk as white as a cloistered maid. Dark red leaves sprout from its reaching branches. Beyond is the emptiness of sky and sea where the wall has collapsed.

paragraphs.context: one of Crabb’s knees exploded in a spray of blood and bone
paragraphs.mainIdea: The fool Shagwell drops from the weirwood with a triple morningstar and shatters Crabb's knee, revealing Dick made the map that led the Bloody Mummers here.
paragraphs.simple: Shagwell drops from the weirwood, braying laughter. He wears motley, but so faded and stained it shows more brown than grey or pink. Instead of a jester's flail he carries a triple morningstar, three spiked balls chained to a wooden haft. He swings it hard and low, and one of Crabb's knees explodes in a spray of blood and bone. That is funny, Shagwell crows as Dick falls. The sword Brienne gave Dick flies from his hand and vanishes in the weeds. He writhes on the ground, screaming and clutching at the ruins of his knee. Oh look, says Shagwell, it is Smuggler Dick, the one who made the map for them. Did he come all this way to give them back their gold?

paragraphs.context: We heard the Mountain killed him piece by piece
paragraphs.mainIdea: Timeon tells how the Bloody Mummers scattered after Harrenhal, and how the Mountain killed Vargo Hoat slowly, cutting him piece by piece.
paragraphs.simple: Timeon shrugs and says they all went their own ways after leaving Harrenhal. Urswyck and his men rode south for Oldtown. Rorge thought he might slip out at Saltpans. Timeon and his lads made for Maidenpool but could not get near a ship. The Dornishman hefts his spear. Brienne did for Vargo with that bite, he says; Vargo's ear turned black and started leaking pus. Rorge and Urswyck wanted to leave, but the Goat said they had to hold his castle. He called himself Lord of Harrenhal and said no one would take it from him, speaking slobbery as he always talked. They heard the Mountain killed him piece by piece: a hand one day, a foot the next, lopped off neat and clean. They bandaged the stumps so Hoat would not die. He was saving his cock for last, but some bird called him to King's Landing, so he finished it and rode off.

paragraphs.context: his thick hair fell to his collar like a silver glacier
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne studies Ser Gerold Dayne, the Darkstar: handsome with silver hair and purple eyes, but with a cruel mouth and a crueler tongue.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne watches Darkstar warily. He is highborn enough to make a worthy husband, she thinks. Her father would question her good sense, but their children would be as beautiful as dragonlords. If there was a handsomer man in Dorne, she did not know him. Ser Gerold Dayne has an aquiline nose, high cheekbones, a strong jaw. He keeps his face clean-shaven, but his thick hair falls to his collar like a silver glacier, divided by a streak of midnight black. He has a cruel mouth, though, and a crueler tongue. His eyes seem black as he sits against the dying sun sharpening his steel, but she has looked at them from closer and knows they are purple. Dark purple. Dark and angry.

paragraphs.context: a slave revolt in Astapor, dragons in Qarth, grey plague in Yi Ti
paragraphs.mainIdea: By the campfire the company trades sailors' tales from the east: slave revolts, dragons, plagues, a new corsair king, and the Golden Company breaking its contract with Myr.
paragraphs.simple: Once the kindling catches, they sit around the flames and pass a skin of summerwine from hand to hand, all but Darkstar, who prefers unsweetened lemonwater. Garin is lively and entertains them with the latest tales from the Planky Town at the mouth of the Greenblood, where the orphans of the river trade with the carracks, cogs, and galleys from across the narrow sea. If the sailors can be believed, the east is seething with wonders and terrors: a slave revolt in Astapor, dragons in Qarth, grey plague in Yi Ti. A new corsair king has risen in the Basilisk Isles and raided Tall Trees Town, and in Qohor followers of the red priests have rioted and tried to burn down the Black Goat. And the Golden Company broke its contract with Myr, just as the Myrmen were about to go to war with Lys.

paragraphs.context: That is Nymeria’s star, burning bright, and that milky band behind her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Under the stars Arianne thinks of Nymeria's star and the ten thousand ships, and vows to be as bright as Nymeria and not let Quentyn rob her of her birthright.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne leaves them to their banter. Drey and Spotted Sylva are her dearest friends besides her cousin Tyene, and Garin has teased her since they were babies, but just now she is in no mood for jokes. The sun is gone and the sky is full of stars, so many. She leans her back against a fluted pillar and wonders if her brother is looking at the same stars tonight, wherever he might be. Do you see the white one, Quentyn? That is Nymeria's star, burning bright, and that milky band behind her, those are ten thousand ships. She burned as bright as any man, and so shall I. You will not rob me of my birthright.

paragraphs.context: crept through a window of a night, tickled the lock on Quentyn’s little strongbox
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne has learned her brother Quentyn is secretly sailing east under a false name with Yronwood's son and a maester, and her friends found scrolls in his strongbox.
paragraphs.simple: Prince Doran still pretends her brother is with Lord Yronwood, but Garin's mother saw Quentyn at the Planky Town, posing as a merchant. One of his companions has a lazy eye, the same as Cletus Yronwood, Lord Anders's randy son. A maester travels with them too, a maester skilled in tongues. Her brother is not as clever as he thinks. A clever man would have left from Oldtown, even if it meant a longer voyage; there he might have gone unrecognized. Arianne has friends among the orphans of the Planky Town, and some grew curious why a prince and a lord's son might travel under false names and seek passage across the narrow sea. One of them crept through a window of a night, tickled the lock on Quentyn's little strongbox, and found the scrolls within.

paragraphs.context: Dressed in Myrcella’s bedrobe with the maester’s salve smeared across her face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arys explains the decoy plan: a Lannister lookalike girl dressed as Myrcella, and a shorter man in his armor with the visor down, will fool anyone watching.
paragraphs.simple: Arys says they saw the decoy only from a distance. The Imp picked her for this purpose over many girls of nobler birth. Myrcella helped curl her hair and painted the dots on her face herself. They are distant kin. Lannisport teems with Lannys, Lannetts, Lantells, and lesser Lannisters, and half of them have that yellow hair. Dressed in Myrcella's bedrobe with the maester's salve smeared across her face, she might even have fooled Arys in a dim light. It was harder to find a man to take his place. Dake is closest to his height but too fat, so he put Rolder in his armor and told him to keep his visor down. The man is three inches shorter, but perhaps no one will notice if Arys is not there to stand beside him. He will keep to Myrcella's chambers in any case.

paragraphs.context: We are seven, Arianne realized as they rode
paragraphs.mainIdea: As the seven riders set out, Arianne takes it as a good omen. She plans to crown Myrcella, free the Sand Snakes, and send her father back to the Water Gardens.
paragraphs.simple: The moon has crowned the Moonmaid as they set out from the ruins of Shandystone, riding south and west. Arianne and Ser Arys lead, with Myrcella on a frisky mare between them. Garin follows with Spotted Sylva, and her two Dornish knights take the rear. We are seven, Arianne realizes as they ride. She had not thought of that before, but it seems a good omen for their cause. Seven riders on their way to glory. One day the singers will make all of them immortal. Drey wanted a larger party, but that might attract attention, and every extra man doubled the risk of betrayal. That much her father taught her. Even young, Doran Martell was cautious, much given to silences and secrets. It is time he put his burdens down, but she will suffer no slights to his honor. She will return him to his Water Gardens to live out his years among laughing children and the smell of limes and oranges, with Quentyn for company. Once she crowns Myrcella and frees the Sand Snakes, all Dorne will rally to her banners.

paragraphs.context: so her people would understand that there could be no going back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arys tells Myrcella how Nymeria burned her ships on marrying Mors Martell so there could be no going back, and how some Rhoynar became the orphans of the Greenblood.
paragraphs.simple: We are Rhoynar in part, Arys tells Myrcella. Nymeria's blood is in them, along with that of Mors Martell, the Dornish lord she married. On the day they wed, Nymeria fired her ships, so her people would understand that there could be no going back. Most were glad to see those flames, for their voyagings had been long and terrible before they came to Dorne, and many had been lost to storm, disease, and slavery. A few mourned, however. They did not love this dry red land or its seven-faced god, so they clung to their old ways, hammered boats together from the hulks of the burned ships, and became the orphans of the Greenblood. The Mother in their songs is not the Dornish Mother, but Mother Rhoyne, whose waters nourished them from the dawn of days.

paragraphs.context: but of the two, the sun is the more deadly
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the brutal Dornish heat Ser Arys refuses to veil his face and nearly cooks in his heavy clothes, recalling the Young Dragon's words that the Dornish sun is deadlier than the spear.
paragraphs.simple: The Dornish cover their faces as Arianne does, and Spotted Sylva helps veil the little princess from the sun, but Ser Arys stays stubborn. Before long sweat runs down his face and his cheeks take on a rosy blush. Much longer and he will cook in those heavy clothes, she thinks. He would not be the first. In centuries past, many a host came down from the Prince's Pass with banners streaming, only to wither and broil on the hot red Dornish sands. The arms of House Martell display the sun and spear, the Dornishman's two favored weapons, the Young Dragon once wrote in his boastful Conquest of Dorne, but of the two, the sun is the more deadly.

paragraphs.context: yet it remained the life of Dorne
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greenblood is a small murky river but the life of Dorne. Arianne plans to sail up it and the Vaith, then cross the deep sands to crown Myrcella at the Hellholt.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne once crossed the Mander with three Sand Snakes to visit Tyene's mother. Compared to that mighty waterway, the Greenblood is scarce worthy of the name of river, yet it remains the life of Dorne. It takes its name from the murky green of its sluggish waters, but as they approach, the sunlight seems to turn those waters gold. She has seldom seen a sweeter sight. The next part should be slow and simple, she thinks: up the Greenblood and onto the Vaith, as far as a poleboat can go. That will give her time to prepare Myrcella for all that is to come. Beyond Vaith the deep sands wait. They will need help from Sandstone and the Hellholt to make that crossing, but she does not doubt it will be forthcoming. The Red Viper was fostered at Sandstone, and Prince Oberyn's paramour Ellaria Sand is Lord Uller's natural daughter; four of the Sand Snakes are his granddaughters. She will crown Myrcella at the Hellholt and raise her banners there.

paragraphs.context: the white knight’s armor had as well been made of parchment
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Arys charges gallantly and stupidly at the poleboat; crossbow bolts pierce his shield and shoulder, and his horse is speared, yet he rides on.
paragraphs.simple: He rode headlong for the poleboat, his white cloak streaming behind him. Arianne had never seen anything half so gallant, or half so stupid. No, she shrieked, but she found her tongue too late. A crossbow thrummed, then another. Hotah bellowed a command. At such close range, the white knight's armor had as well been made of parchment. The first bolt punched right through his heavy oaken shield, pinning it to his shoulder. The second grazed his temple. A thrown spear took his mount in the flank, yet still the horse came on, staggering as it hit the gangplank. No, some foolish little girl was shouting, no, please, this was not supposed to happen. She could hear Myrcella shrieking too, her voice shrill with fear.

paragraphs.context: her pale face in her hands, blood streaming through her fingers
paragraphs.mainIdea: The plan collapses: Myrcella lies on the ground with blood streaming through her fingers, and Arianne, shaking and sobbing, feels she has fallen into a terrible red nightmare.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne does not remember climbing from her horse; perhaps she fell. Yet she finds herself on her hands and feet in the sand, shaking and sobbing and retching up her supper. No, is all she can think, no, no one was to be hurt, it was all planned, she was so careful. She hears Areo Hotah roar for them to go after Arys, that he must not escape. Myrcella is on the ground, wailing, shaking, her pale face in her hands, blood streaming through her fingers. Arianne does not understand. Men scramble onto horses while others swarm over her and her companions, but none of it makes sense. She has fallen into a dream, some terrible red nightmare. This cannot be real. She will wake soon and laugh at her night terrors.

paragraphs.context: the waif, the little girl with the big eyes and hollow face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya meets the other servants of the temple: the nameless kindly man, the waif, the acolytes in black-and-white robes, and the mute serving men. She is given servant's garb.
paragraphs.simple: The kindly man never told Arya his name. Neither did the waif, the little girl with the big eyes and hollow face who reminded her of another little girl named Weasel. Like Arya, the waif lived below the temple, along with three acolytes, two serving men, and a cook called Umma. Umma liked to talk as she worked, but Arya could not understand a word she said. The others had no names, or did not choose to share them. One serving man was very old, his back bent like a bow. The second was red-faced, with hair growing from his ears. She took them both for mutes until she heard them praying. The acolytes were younger. The eldest was her father's age; the other two could not have been much older than Sansa, who had been her sister. The acolytes wore black and white too, but their robes had no cowls and were black on the left side and white on the right. With the kindly man and the waif it was the opposite. Arya was given servant's garb: a tunic of undyed wool, baggy breeches, linen smallclothes, cloth slippers for her feet.

paragraphs.context: stop was the first Braavosi word she learned
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya works in the kitchens with Umma, chopping, kneading, and filleting fish from the brackish waters around Braavos, and learns her first Braavosi word.
paragraphs.simple: She got along well enough with the cook. Umma would slap a knife into her hand and point at an onion, and Arya would chop it. Umma would shove her toward a mound of dough, and Arya would knead it until the cook said stop, and stop was the first Braavosi word she learned. Umma would hand her a fish, and Arya would bone it and fillet it and roll it in the nuts the cook was crushing. The brackish waters around Braavos teemed with fish and shellfish of every sort, the kindly man explained. A slow brown river entered the lagoon from the south, wandering through a wide expanse of reeds, tidal pools, and mudflats. Clams and cockles abounded here, mussels and muskfish, frogs and turtles, mud crabs and leopard crabs and climber crabs, red eels, black eels, striped eels, lampreys, and oysters, all appearing often on the table where the servants of the Many-Faced God ate. Some nights Umma spiced the fish with sea salt and cracked peppercorns, or cooked the eels with chopped garlic. Once in a great while the cook would even use some saffron. Hot Pie would have liked it here, Arya thought.

paragraphs.context: back home, people were scared to die
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya asks why the people who come to the temple seem so peaceful, remembering how people back home wept and begged and screamed when death came for them.
paragraphs.simple: Supper was her favorite time. It had been a long while since Arya had gone to sleep every night with a full belly. Some nights the kindly man would let her ask him questions. Once she asked why the people who came to the temple always seemed so peaceful; back home, people were scared to die. She remembered how that pimply squire had wept when she stabbed him in the belly, and the way Ser Amory Lorch had begged when the Goat had him thrown in the bear pit. She remembered the village by the God's Eye, and the way the villagers shrieked and screamed and whimpered whenever the Tickler started asking after gold.

paragraphs.context: It is pork, child,” he told her, “only pork.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dead come to the temple to drink sweet dark water and sleep forever; their bodies are washed and carried below, where only priests may go. Arya fears the meat is human flesh.
paragraphs.simple: The dead were never hard to find. They came to the House of Black and White, prayed for an hour or a day or a year, drank sweet dark water from the pool, and stretched out on a stone bed behind one god or another. They closed their eyes, and slept, and never woke. The gift of the Many-Faced God takes myriad forms, the kindly man told her, but here it is always gentle. When they found a body he would say a prayer and make certain life had fled, and Arya would fetch the serving men to carry the dead down to the vaults. There acolytes would strip and wash the bodies. The dead men's clothes and coins and valuables went into a bin for sorting. Their cold flesh was taken to the lower sanctum where only the priests could go; what happened there Arya was not allowed to know. Once, eating her supper, a terrible suspicion seized her, and she put down her knife and stared suspiciously at a slice of pale white meat. The kindly man saw the horror on her face. It is pork, child, he told her, only pork.

paragraphs.context: sleep on rose petals and wear silken skirts that rustle when you walk
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man tells Arya she is wrong that the temple is her only place: he offers to send her to be a courtesan, or to find her a husband, whatever she desires.
paragraphs.simple: You believe this is the only place for you, the kindly man says, as if he had heard her thoughts. You are wrong in that. You would find softer service in the household of some merchant. Or would you sooner be a courtesan, and have songs sung of your beauty? Speak the word, and they will send you to the Black Pearl or the Daughter of the Dusk. You will sleep on rose petals and wear silken skirts that rustle when you walk, and great lords will beggar themselves for your maiden's blood. Or if it is marriage and children you desire, tell them, and they will find a husband for you: some honest apprentice boy, a rich old man, a seafarer, whatever you desire.

paragraphs.context: the lone wolf dies, but the pack survives
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya steals out at night thinking there is no place here for Arya Stark. She remembers her father's words about the pack, but her pack is dead or scattered.
paragraphs.simple: In the black of night she rose again, donned the clothes she had worn from Westeros, and buckled on her swordbelt. Needle hung from one hip, her dagger from the other. With her floppy hat on her head, her fingerless gloves tucked into her belt, and her silver fork in one hand, she went stealing up the steps. There is no place here for Arya of House Stark, she was thinking. Arya's place was Winterfell, only Winterfell was gone. When the snows fall and the white winds blow, the lone wolf dies, but the pack survives. She had no pack, though. They had killed her pack, Ser Ilyn and Ser Meryn and the queen, and when she tried to make a new one all of them ran off: Hot Pie and Gendry and Yoren and Lommy Greenhands, even Harwin, who had been her father's man. She shoved through the doors, out into the night.

paragraphs.context: amongst the wretched slaves who toiled in the deep mines beneath the Fourteen Flames
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man tells the tale of their beginnings: the Faceless Men first took root among the wretched slaves toiling in the burning mines of old Valyria.
paragraphs.simple: The kindly man tells the tale of their beginnings. If Arya would be one of them, she had best know who they are and how they came to be. Men may whisper of the Faceless Men of Braavos, but they are older than the Secret City. Before the Titan rose, before the Unmasking of Uthero, before the Founding, they were. They have flowered in Braavos among the northern fogs, but they first took root in Valyria, amongst the wretched slaves who toiled in the deep mines beneath the Fourteen Flames that lit the Freehold's nights of old. Most mines are dank and chilly places cut from cold dead stone, but the Fourteen Flames were living mountains with veins of molten rock and hearts of fire. So the mines of old Valyria were always hot, and grew hotter as the shafts were driven deeper, ever deeper. The slaves toiled in an oven. The rocks were too hot to touch. The air stank of brimstone and would sear their lungs as they breathed it. The soles of their feet would burn and blister, even through the thickest sandals. Sometimes, breaking through a wall in search of gold, they found steam instead, or boiling water, or molten rock. Certain shafts were cut so low the slaves could not stand upright, but had to crawl or bend. And there were wyrms in that red darkness too.

paragraphs.context: Are their gods all deaf? he wondered
paragraphs.mainIdea: No one knows who the first Faceless Man was, but he heard the slaves of a hundred nations all praying for the same thing, release, and wondered if all their gods were deaf.
paragraphs.simple: No one knows who he was, the kindly man answers. Some say he was a slave himself. Others insist he was a freeholder's son, born of noble stock. Some will even tell you he was an overseer who took pity on his charges. The truth is, no one knows. Whoever he was, he moved amongst the slaves and would hear them at their prayers. Men of a hundred different nations labored in the mines, and each prayed to his own god in his own tongue, yet all were praying for the same thing. It was release they asked for, an end to pain. A small thing, and simple. Yet their gods made no answer, and their suffering went on. Are their gods all deaf? he wondered, until a realization came upon him, one night in the red darkness.

paragraphs.context: You need only learn to read a face
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man teaches Arya to tell truth from lies by reading faces: eyes, mouth, jaw muscles, blinks, stares, lip-licking, hidden mouths, false smiles.
paragraphs.simple: A man does not need to be a wizard to know truth from falsehood, not if he has eyes, the kindly man says. You need only learn to read a face. Look at the eyes. The mouth. The muscles here, at the corners of the jaw, and here, where the neck joins the shoulders. He touches her lightly with two fingers. Some liars blink. Some stare. Some look away. Some lick their lips. Many cover their mouths just before they tell a lie, as if to hide their deceit. Other signs may be more subtle, but they are always there. A false smile and a true one may look alike, but they are as different as dusk from dawn. Can you tell dusk from dawn?

paragraphs.context: men who’d lived beyond their years would announce that they were going hunting
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya washes corpses and wonders what brings the old to the black pool, remembering Old Nan's tale of old men in long winters who announce they are going hunting and never return.
paragraphs.simple: Soon after, the kindly man commands her to help the other acolytes prepare the corpses. The work is not nearly as hard as scrubbing steps for Weese. Sometimes if the corpse is big or fat she struggles with the weight, but most of the dead are old dry bones in wrinkled skins. Arya looks at them as she washes them, wondering what brought them to the black pool. She remembers a tale she heard from Old Nan, about how sometimes during a long winter men who had lived beyond their years would announce that they were going hunting. And their daughters would weep and their sons would turn their faces to the fire, she can hear Old Nan saying, but no one would stop them, or ask what game they meant to hunt, with the snows so deep and the cold wind howling. She wonders what the old Braavosi tell their sons and daughters, before they set off for the House of Black and White.

paragraphs.context: the view made her forget all that for half a heartbeat
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne enjoys her new, larger apartments in the Maiden's Tower and the golden morning view over the Vale from her balcony.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne's apartments in the Maiden's Tower are larger and more lavish than the little bedchamber where she was kept when Lady Lysa was alive. She has a dressing room and a privy of her own now, and a balcony of carved white stone that looks off across the Vale. While Gretchel tends the fire, Alayne pads barefoot across the room and slips outside. The stone is cold beneath her feet, and the wind blows fiercely, as it always does up here, but the view makes her forget all that for half a heartbeat. Maiden's is the easternmost of the Eyrie's seven slender towers, so she has the Vale before her, its forests and rivers and fields all hazy in the morning light. The way the sun hits the mountains makes them look like solid gold.

paragraphs.context: vowing to defend Lord Robert, the Vale, and one another
paragraphs.mainIdea: The six Lords Declarant have gathered a thousand men each against Petyr, vowing to defend Lord Robert and the Vale and to end his misrule.
paragraphs.simple: Young Lord Hunter and his levies joined the others two days past. Nestor Royce has closed the Gates against them, but he has fewer than three hundred men in his garrison. Each of the Lords Declarant brought a thousand, and there are six of them. Alayne knows their names as well as her own: Benedar Belmore, Symond Templeton, Horton Redfort, Anya Waynwood, Gilwood Hunter, and Yohn Royce, mightiest of them all, the redoubtable Bronze Yohn. The six gathered at Runestone after Lysa Arryn's fall and made a pact together, vowing to defend Lord Robert, the Vale, and one another. Their declaration made no mention of the Lord Protector, but spoke of misrule that must be ended, and of false friends and evil counselors as well.

paragraphs.context: Lyn Corbray was more dangerous than all six of the Lords Declarant put together
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne fears Lyn Corbray, a deadly duelist who slew Prince Lewyn of the Kingsguard on the Trident, and wonders why he is coming.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr's words do little to soothe her fears. Lyn Corbray has slain almost as many men in duels as in battle. He won his spurs during Robert's Rebellion, fighting first against Lord Jon Arryn at the gates of Gulltown, and later beneath his banners on the Trident, where he cut down Prince Lewyn of Dorne, a white knight of the Kingsguard. Petyr says Prince Lewyn was sorely wounded by the time the tide of battle swept him to his final dance with Lady Forlorn, Corbray's sword, but adds that is not a point to raise with Corbray, since those who do are soon given the chance to ask Martell himself the truth of it, down in the halls of hell. If even half of what she heard from Lord Robert's guards is true, Lyn Corbray is more dangerous than all six of the Lords Declarant put together. Why is he coming, she asks; she thought the Corbrays were for Petyr.

paragraphs.context: he bestowed the Lady upon his younger son
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr explains the Corbray brothers: Lyn won their father's Valyrian sword Lady Forlorn on the Trident, while Lyonel got lands and title but feels cheated, and Lyn hates Petyr too.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Lyonel Corbray is well disposed toward Petyr's rule, Petyr says, but his brother goes his own way. On the Trident, when their father fell wounded, it was Lyn who snatched up Lady Forlorn and slew the man who had cut his father down. Whilst Lyonel carried the old man back to the maesters in the rear, Lyn led his charge against the Dornishmen threatening Robert's left, broke their lines to pieces, and slew Lewyn Martell. So when old Lord Corbray died, he bestowed the Lady upon his younger son. Lyonel got his lands, his title, his castle, and all his coin, yet still feels he was cheated of his birthright, whilst Ser Lyn loves Lyonel as much as he loves Petyr. Lyn had wanted Lysa's hand for himself.

paragraphs.context: A pitcher of milk went flying as his hand caught it, flailing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Little Robert throws a violent fit at breakfast, hurling porridge and milk, knocking his chair over and kicking Alayne in the belly.
paragraphs.simple: Robert shouts about his porridge and this time flings the bowl, porridge and honey and all. Petyr Baelish ducks aside nimbly, but Maester Colemon is not so quick. The wooden bowl catches him square in the chest, and its contents explode upward over his face and shoulders. He yelps in a most unmaesterlike fashion, while Alayne turns to soothe the little lordling, but too late. The fit is on him. A pitcher of milk goes flying as his hand catches it, flailing. When he tries to rise he knocks his chair backwards and falls on top of it. One foot catches Alayne in the belly, so hard it knocks the wind from her. Oh, gods be good, she hears Petyr say, disgusted.

paragraphs.context: His doublet displayed nine black stars within a golden saltire
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne studies the Lords Declarant by their heraldry at the feast, and makes sure to keep the hard-drinking Young Lord Hunter's cup full.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr gave Alayne a roll of arms to study, so she knows their heraldry if not their faces. The red castle is Redfort, plainly: a short man with a neat grey beard and mild eyes. Lady Anya is the only woman amongst the Lords Declarant, wearing a deep green mantle with the broken wheel of Waynwood picked out in beads of jet. Six silver bells on purple, that is Belmore, pear-bellied and round of shoulder, his ginger-grey beard a horror sprouting from a multiplicity of chins. Symond Templeton's beard, by contrast, is black and sharply pointed. A beak of a nose and icy blue eyes make the Knight of Ninestars look like some elegant bird of prey. His doublet displays nine black stars within a golden saltire. Young Lord Hunter's ermine cloak confuses her till she spies the brooch pinning it, five silver arrows fanned. She would put his age closer to fifty than forty. His father ruled Longbow Hall for nigh on sixty years, only to die so abruptly that some whisper the new lord hastened his inheritance. Hunter's cheeks and nose are red as apples, which bespeaks a fondness for wine. She makes certain to fill his cup as often as he empties it.

paragraphs.context: He will know me. How could he not?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bronze Yohn's face brings back Sansa's memories of Winterfell, and she fears he will recognize her, yet dares not beg him for protection.
paragraphs.simple: Last of all come the Royces, Lord Nestor and Bronze Yohn. The Lord of Runestone stands as tall as the Hound. Though his hair is grey and his face lined, Lord Yohn still looks as though he could break most younger men like twigs in those huge gnarled hands. His seamed and solemn face brings back all of Sansa's memories of his time at Winterfell. She remembers him at table, speaking quietly with her mother. She hears his voice booming off the walls when he rode back from a hunt with a buck behind his saddle. She can see him in the yard, a practice sword in hand, hammering her father to the ground and turning to defeat Ser Rodrik as well. He will know me. How could he not? She considers throwing herself at his feet to beg for his protection. He never fought for Robb, why should he fight for her? The war is finished and Winterfell is fallen. Lord Royce, she asks timidly, will he have a cup of wine, to take the chill off?

paragraphs.context: but I do not like the way he smiles
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the solar, Nestor Royce sits beside Petyr while Lyn Corbray stands by the hearth smiling at Ser Lothor Brune, and Alayne dislikes his smile.
paragraphs.simple: As you say, Father, Alayne says. The candles are lighted, and the solar smells of nutmeg and other costly spices. She goes to fetch the flagon whilst the visitors arrange themselves side by side, all save Nestor Royce, who hesitates before walking around the table to take the empty chair beside Lord Petyr, and Lyn Corbray, who goes to stand beside the hearth instead. The heart-shaped ruby in the pommel of his sword shines redly as he warms his hands. Alayne sees him smile at Ser Lothor Brune. Ser Lyn is very handsome, for an older man, she thinks, but I do not like the way he smiles.

paragraphs.context: We speak with one voice here. Runestone suits us all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Waynwood speaks for all the Lords Declarant: they want Robert fostered at Runestone with better maester, master-at-arms, and companions his own age.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Waynwood sighs. Lord Petyr, if you think to set us one against the other, you may spare yourself the effort. We speak with one voice here. Runestone suits us all. Lord Yohn raised three fine sons of his own; there is no man more fit to foster his young lordship. Maester Helliweg is a good deal older and more experienced than their own Maester Colemon, and better suited to treat Lord Robert's frailties. In Runestone the boy will learn the arts of war from Strong Sam Stone. No man could hope for a finer master-at-arms. Septon Lucos will instruct him in matters of the spirit. At Runestone he will also find other boys his own age, more suitable companions than the old women and sellswords that presently surround him.

paragraphs.context: If Margaery Tyrell thinks to cheat me of my hour in the sun
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei vows not to give up her rule until Tommen comes of age, after a lifetime of playing the dutiful daughter and suffering wife, and she will not let Margaery cheat her of her hour.
paragraphs.simple: That's my good boy, Cersei thinks. The rule is hers; she does not mean to give it up until Tommen comes of age. She waited, so he can wait. She waited half her life. She played the dutiful daughter, the blushing bride, the pliant wife. She suffered Robert's drunken groping, Jaime's jealousy, Renly's mockery, Varys with his titters, Stannis endlessly grinding his teeth. She contended with Jon Arryn, Ned Stark, and her vile, treacherous, murderous dwarf brother, all the while promising herself that one day it would be her turn. If Margaery Tyrell thinks to cheat her of her hour in the sun, she had bloody well think again.

paragraphs.context: need to use the gold cloaks to chase these sparrows from the city
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei's morning is full of ruling: Gyles's ledgers, Waters's new warships, merchants complaining of sparrows in the streets, and then Pycelle intrudes.
paragraphs.simple: Still, it is an ill way to break her fast, and Cersei's day does not soon improve. She spends the rest of the morning with Lord Gyles and his ledger books, listening to him cough about stars and stags and dragons, meaning coins. After him Lord Waters arrives to report that the first three dromonds are nearing completion and beg for more gold to finish them in the splendor they deserve. The queen is pleased to grant his request. Moon Boy capers as she takes her midday meal with members of the merchant guilds and listens to them complain about sparrows wandering the streets and sleeping in the squares. She thinks she may need to use the gold cloaks to chase these sparrows from the city, when Pycelle intrudes.

paragraphs.context: No mother should outlive her children, and no captain should outlive his ship
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pycelle wants experienced Blackwater captains for the new ships, but Cersei sides with Waters's younger men, saying the old captains only proved they know how to swim.
paragraphs.simple: The Grand Maester has been especially querulous in council of late. At the last session he complained bitterly about the men Aurane Waters chose to captain her new dromonds. Waters means to give the ships to younger men, whilst Pycelle argues for experience, insisting the commands should go to those captains who survived the fires of the Blackwater. Seasoned men of proven loyalty, he calls them. Cersei calls them old, and sides with Lord Waters. The only thing these captains proved was that they know how to swim, she said. No mother should outlive her children, and no captain should outlive his ship. Pycelle took the rebuke with ill grace.

paragraphs.context: She never goes riding but she takes a tail
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei's spy reports Margaery is never alone: always surrounded by ladies, cousins, companions, guards, and men, even in the Maidenvault.
paragraphs.simple: Margaery's people say she is never alone. The king is with her most all the time, and when he is not, there is someone else. Two of her ladies share her bed, different ones every night. Two others bring her breakfast and help her dress. She prays with her septa, reads with her cousin Elinor, sings with her cousin Alla, sews with her cousin Megga. When she is not off hawking with Janna Fossoway and Merry Crane, she is playing come-into-my-castle with that little Bulwer girl. She never goes riding but she takes a tail, four or five companions and a dozen guards at least. And there are always men about her, even in the Maidenvault.

paragraphs.context: It had been Jaime she had been thinking of when she spoke
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery catches Cersei out: Robert was an indifferent jouster who preferred the melee, and it was Jaime Cersei was really thinking of.
paragraphs.simple: A flush creeps up Cersei's neck. The girl has caught her out. Robert Baratheon was an indifferent jouster, in truth. During tourneys he much preferred the melee, where he could beat men bloody with blunted axe or hammer. It had been Jaime she had been thinking of when she spoke. It is not like her to forget herself. Robert won the tourney of the Trident, she has to say. He overthrew Prince Rhaegar and named me his queen of love and beauty. She is surprised Margaery does not know that story, good-daughter. She gives Margaery no time to frame a reply, and sends her son off with Ser Osmund while she takes Ser Loras aside for a word.

paragraphs.context: When her brother returned he asked her if she wanted Robert dead
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls Robert's affair with a widowed cousin at Greenstone; when Jaime confirmed it and offered to kill Robert, she said she wanted him horned, not dead.
paragraphs.simple: There was a female cousin too, a chunky little widow with breasts as big as melons, whose husband and father both died at Storm's End during the siege. Her father was good to me, Robert told Cersei, and she and I would play together when we were small. It did not take him long to start playing with her again. As soon as Cersei closed her eyes, the king would steal off to console the poor lonely creature. One night she had Jaime follow him, to confirm her suspicions. When her brother returned he asked her if she wanted Robert dead. No, she replied, I want him horned. She likes to think that was the night Joffrey was conceived.

paragraphs.context: It is all because I am a woman
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei rages that men counsel, contradict, and refuse her only because she is a woman who cannot fight them with a sword, and decides she must rid herself of Jaime.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei tells Jaime he was better before he lost his hand, and lists greater knights: Barristan, Arthur Dayne, and Prince Rhaegar a match for even Dayne. She tells him not to prate about how fierce Loras is; he is just a boy. She is tired of Jaime balking her. No one ever balked her lord father. When Tywin Lannister spoke, men obeyed. When Cersei speaks, they feel free to counsel her, to contradict her, even refuse her. It is all because she is a woman. Because she cannot fight them with a sword. They gave Robert more respect than they give her, and Robert was a witless sot. She will not suffer it, especially not from Jaime. She needs to rid herself of him, and soon. Once she dreamt the two of them might rule the Seven Kingdoms side by side, but Jaime has become more of a hindrance than a help.

paragraphs.context: As a catspaw he leaves much to be desired
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei sizes up the aging Ser Balman as her catspaw for murder, and speaks honeyed words about restoring the name Tyrion to honor.
paragraphs.simple: The queen sips her wine and studies him. Ser Balman was a noted jouster once, and one of the handsomest knights in the Seven Kingdoms. He could still boast a handsome mustache; elsewise, he has not aged well. His wavy blond hair has retreated, whilst his belly advances inexorably against his doublet. As a catspaw he leaves much to be desired, she reflects. Still, he should serve. Tyrion was a king's name before the dragons came. The Imp has despoiled it, but perhaps this child can restore the name to honor. If the bastard lives so long. She tells him he is not to blame, that Lady Tanda is the sister she never had, and her voice breaks. Forgive me. She lives in fear.

paragraphs.context: as Rhaegar’s little girl had discovered in this very castle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei muses that black cats bring ill luck, as Rhaegar's little girl discovered in this castle, and remembers Aerys's cruel refusal of her as Rhaegar's bride.
paragraphs.simple: Better than cutting them out of their mother with a dagger, Cersei thinks. Margaery's clumsy attempts at seduction are so obvious as to be laughable. Tommen is too young for kisses, so she gives him kittens. Cersei rather wishes they were not black, though. Black cats brought ill luck, as Rhaegar's little girl had discovered in this very castle. She would have been Cersei's daughter, if the Mad King had not played his cruel jape on her father. It had to have been madness that led Aerys to refuse Lord Tywin's daughter and take his son instead, whilst marrying his own son to a feeble Dornish princess with black eyes and a flat chest.

paragraphs.context: her father had promised her that she would marry Rhaegar
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei remembers watching Rhaegar play his harp as a girl, and her father's secret promise that she would marry him, which she once drew as flying behind him on a dragon.
paragraphs.simple: The memory of the rejection still rankles, even after all these years. Many a night she watched Prince Rhaegar in the hall, playing his silver-stringed harp with those long, elegant fingers of his. Had any man ever been so beautiful? He was more than a man, though. His blood was the blood of old Valyria, the blood of dragons and gods. When she was just a little girl, her father had promised her that she would marry Rhaegar. She could not have been more than six or seven. Never speak of it, child, he told her, smiling his secret smile that only Cersei ever saw. Not until His Grace agrees to the betrothal. It must remain their secret for now. And so it had, though once she drew a picture of herself flying behind Rhaegar on a dragon, her arms wrapped tight about his chest. When Jaime discovered it she told him it was Queen Alysanne and King Jaehaerys.

paragraphs.context: but I will mend his hurt when we are wed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls the tourney where the young Rhaegar unhorsed her uncles, and how she drowned in his sad purple eyes and thought she would mend his hurt when they wed.
paragraphs.simple: Seventeen and new to knighthood, Rhaegar Targaryen wore black plate over golden ringmail when he cantered onto the lists. Long streamers of red and gold and orange silk floated behind his helm, like flames. Two of her uncles fell before his lance, along with a dozen of her father's finest jousters, the flower of the west. By night the prince played his silver harp and made her weep. When she was presented to him, Cersei almost drowned in the depths of his sad purple eyes. He has been wounded, she recalled thinking, but I will mend his hurt when we are wed. Next to Rhaegar, even her beautiful Jaime seemed no more than a callow boy. The prince is going to be her husband, she thought, giddy with excitement, and when the old king dies she will be the queen. Her aunt confided the truth before the tourney: she must be especially beautiful, for at the final feast it would be announced that she and Prince Rhaegar were betrothed.

paragraphs.context: The memory of that foretelling still made her flesh crawl a lifetime later
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei remembers daring to visit Maggy the Frog's tent with Jeyne and Melara, letting the old woman taste their blood and laughing at her prophecies.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei had been so happy that day. Elsewise she would never have dared visit the tent of Maggy the Frog. She had only done it to show Jeyne and Melara that the lioness fears nothing. She was going to be a queen. Why should a queen be afraid of some hideous old woman? The memory of that foretelling still made her flesh crawl a lifetime later. Jeyne ran shrieking from the tent in fear, the queen remembers, but Melara stayed and so did she. They let Maggy taste their blood, and laughed at her stupid prophecies. None of them made the least bit of sense. She was going to be Prince Rhaegar's wife, no matter what the woman said. Her father had promised it, and Tywin Lannister's word was gold.

paragraphs.context: but a man does not marry his heir to his servant’s daughter
paragraphs.mainIdea: There was no betrothal feast; Aerys coldly refused Tywin's proposal, saying a man does not marry his heir to his servant's daughter.
paragraphs.simple: Her laughter died at tourney's end. There was no final feast, no toasts to celebrate her betrothal to Prince Rhaegar. Only cold silences and chilly looks between the king and her father. Later, when Aerys and his son and all his gallant knights departed for King's Landing, the girl went to her aunt in tears, not understanding. Your father proposed the match, Lady Genna told her, but Aerys refused to hear of it. You are my most able servant, Tywin, the king said, but a man does not marry his heir to his servant's daughter. Dry those tears, little one. Have you ever seen a lion weep? Your father will find another man for you, a better man than Rhaegar.

paragraphs.context: we’ll have fresh eggs and new-churned butter aboard. Is m’lady seeking passage north?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne searches the Maidenpool docks for a ship north; a captain of the Seastrider offers her clean passage to Gulltown and on to White Harbor.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Randyll's men still prowl the docks, but their serjeant knows Brienne by sight and lets her pass. The fisherfolk are tying up for the night and crying the day's catch, but she is interested in the larger ships that ply the narrow sea. Half a dozen are in port, though one, a galleas called the Titan's Daughter, is casting off to ride out on the evening tide. She and Podrick make the rounds of the ships that remain. The master of the Gulltown Girl takes Brienne for a whore and says his ship is not a bawdy house, and a harpooner on the Ibbenese whaler offers to buy her boy, but they have better fortune elsewhere. She buys Podrick an orange on the Seastrider, a cog just in from Oldtown by way of Tyrosh, Pentos, and Duskendale. Gulltown next, her captain tells her, thence around the Fingers to Sisterton and White Harbor, if the storms allow. She is a clean ship, the Strider, not so many rats as most, and they will have fresh eggs and new-churned butter aboard. Is m'lady seeking passage north?

paragraphs.context: mocking her, pinching at her as she slashed at them with her sword
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne has a restless night and dreams of the men she killed dancing around her and mocking her, even as she cuts them to ribbons.
paragraphs.simple: They have a restless night. Three times Brienne wakes: once when the rain begins, and once at a creak that makes her think Nimble Dick is creeping in to kill her. The second time she wakes with knife in hand, but it is nothing. In the darkness of the cramped little cabin, it takes her a moment to remember that Nimble Dick is dead. When she finally drifts back to sleep, she dreams about the men she has killed. They dance around her, mocking her, pinching at her as she slashes at them with her sword. She cuts them all to bloody ribbons, yet still they swarm around her: Shagwell, Timeon, and Pyg, aye, but Randyll Tarly too, and Vargo Hoat, and Red Ronnet Connington. Ronnet has a rose between his fingers. When he holds it out to her, she cuts his hand off.

paragraphs.context: even if he could get past the mountain clans. Where’s a dog to go?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Hyle shows on his map that the Hound is trapped: Freys at the Twins, Blackwoods and Brackens west, Randyll at Maidenpool, and the Vale road closed by snow.
paragraphs.simple: Aye, Ser Hyle says, but he does not think their dog will have wandered too far from the mouth of the Trident. Westeros has lost its charm for him, it seems. At Saltpans he was looking for a ship. Hyle draws a roll of sheepskin from his boot, pushes the sausages aside, and unrolls it. It proves to be a map. The Hound butchered three of his brother's men at the old inn by the crossroads, here. He led the raid on Saltpans, here. He taps Saltpans with his finger. He may be trapped. The Freys are up here at the Twins, Darry and Harrenhal are south across the Trident, west he has the Blackwoods and the Brackens fighting, and Lord Randyll is here at Maidenpool. The high road to the Vale is closed by snow, even if he could get past the mountain clans. Where's a dog to go?

paragraphs.context: Dondarrion kissed her and brought her back to life, and now she cannot die
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hyle tells of Lady Stoneheart, supposedly hanged by the Freys and kissed back to life by Beric Dondarrion, now leading a band that cannot die.
paragraphs.simple: He is not dead, Hyle says; Alyn is certain of that. Dondarrion's men are looking for the Hound too. They have put out word that they mean to hang him for what he did at Saltpans. They had no part of that. Lord Randyll is putting it about that they did, in hopes of turning the commons against Beric and his brotherhood. He will never take the lightning lord so long as the smallfolk protect him. And there is this other band, led by this woman Stoneheart. Lord Beric's lover, according to one tale. Supposedly she was hanged by the Freys, but Dondarrion kissed her and brought her back to life, and now she cannot die, no more than he can. Brienne considers the map. If Clegane was last seen at Saltpans, that would be the place to find his trail.

paragraphs.context: it was to trudge from one flyspeck of a village to the next
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald is a wandering septon without a sept, trudging from village to village to marry, bury, and forgive sins, sleeping in kitchens, stables, or hedges.
paragraphs.simple: Meribald is a septon without a sept, only one step up from a begging brother in the hierarchy of the Faith. There are hundreds like him, a ragged band whose humble task it is to trudge from one flyspeck of a village to the next, conducting holy services, performing marriages, and forgiving sins. Those he visits are expected to feed and shelter him, but most are as poor as he is, so he cannot linger in one place too long without causing hardship to his hosts. Kindly innkeeps sometimes let him sleep in their kitchens or stables, and there are septries and holdfasts and even a few castles where he knows he will be given hospitality. Where no such places are at hand, he sleeps beneath the trees or under hedges. There are many fine hedges in the riverlands, Meribald says. The old ones are the best. There is nothing beats a hundred-year-old hedge. Inside one of those a man can sleep as snug as at an inn, and with less fear of fleas.

paragraphs.context: What he works at makes no matter. What matters is, he works.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald preaches that he loves the Smith above all: the Smith labors, and what matters is that a man works, whether as smith, farmer, or cobbler.
paragraphs.simple: One god with seven aspects, Meribald says to Podrick. That is so, and Brienne is right to point it out, but the mystery of the Seven Who Are One is not easy for simple folk to grasp, and he is nothing if not simple, so he speaks of seven gods. He has never known a boy who did not love the Warrior. He is old, though, and being old, he loves the Smith. Without his labor, what would the Warrior defend? Every town has a smith, and every castle. They make the plows they need to plant crops, the nails they use to build ships, iron shoes to save the hooves of faithful horses, the bright swords of lords. No one could doubt the value of a smith, and so they name one of the Seven in his honor, but they might as easily have called him the Farmer or the Fisherman, the Carpenter or the Cobbler. What he works at makes no matter. What matters is, he works. The Father rules, the Warrior fights, the Smith labors, and together they perform all that is rightful for a man. Just as the Smith is one aspect of the godhead, the Cobbler is one aspect of the Smith. It was he who heard Meribald's prayer and healed his feet.

paragraphs.context: the crooked muddy tracks that do not appear on parchment maps
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald says his forty-year circuit has taught him every smallfolk track, market town, and nameless village, though he only glimpses great lords' castles from afar.
paragraphs.simple: It will be forty years soon, the septon says, and his dog barks. From Maidenpool to Maidenpool, his circuit takes him half a year and oftentimes more, but he will not say he knows the Trident. He glimpses the castles of the great lords only at a distance, but he knows the market towns and holdfasts, the villages too small to have a name, the hedges and the hills, the rills where a thirsty man can drink and the caves where he can shelter. And the roads the smallfolk use, the crooked muddy tracks that do not appear on parchment maps, he knows them too. He chuckles. He should. His feet have trod every mile of them, ten times over.

paragraphs.context: they are demons. They say the pack is led by a monstrous she-wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald tells of a monstrous she-wolf leading a wolf pack that fears neither steel nor fire, brings down aurochs alone, and eats no flesh but man.
paragraphs.simple: Meribald says he has been spared that, Seven save him, but he has heard them in the night, more than once. So many voices, a sound to curdle a man's blood. It even set Dog to shivering, and Dog has killed a dozen wolves. He ruffles the dog's head. Some will tell you that they are demons. They say the pack is led by a monstrous she-wolf, a stalking shadow grim and grey and huge. They will tell you that she has been known to bring aurochs down all by herself, that no trap nor snare can hold her, that she fears neither steel nor fire, slays any wolf that tries to mount her, and devours no other flesh but man.

paragraphs.context: War seems a fine adventure, the greatest most of them will ever know
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald says most outlaws are evil men driven by greed, but broken men deserve pity: common folk marched off to war with sickles and hoes, dreaming of glory.
paragraphs.simple: Septon Meribald disagrees that outlaws are like singers' heroes. There are many sorts of outlaws, just as there are many sorts of birds. A sandpiper and a sea eagle both have wings, but they are not the same. The singers love to sing of good men forced outside the law to fight some wicked lord, but most outlaws are more like the ravening Hound than the lightning lord. They are evil men, driven by greed, soured by malice, despising the gods and caring only for themselves. Broken men are more deserving of pity, though they may be just as dangerous. Almost all are common-born, simple folk who had never been more than a mile from the house where they were born until some lord came to take them off to war. Poorly shod and poorly clad, they march away beneath his banners, oftentimes with no better arms than a sickle or a sharpened hoe, or a maul they made themselves by lashing a stone to a stick with strips of hide. Brothers march with brothers, sons with fathers, friends with friends. They have heard the songs and stories, so they go off with eager hearts, dreaming of the wonders they will see, of the wealth and glory they will win. War seems a fine adventure, the greatest most of them will ever know.

paragraphs.context: the iron thunder of their charge seems to fill the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meribald describes how broken men steal from corpses, then from the living, until they fight beside strangers under a banner they hardly know as armored knights charge down.
paragraphs.simple: If they want new boots or a warmer cloak or maybe a rusted iron halfhelm, they need to take them from a corpse, and before long they are stealing from the living too, from the smallfolk whose lands they are fighting in, men very like the men they used to be. They slaughter their sheep and steal their chickens, and from there it is just a short step to carrying off their daughters too. And one day they look around and realize all their friends and kin are gone, that they are fighting beside strangers beneath a banner that they hardly recognize. They don't know where they are or how to get back home, and the lord they are fighting for does not know their names, yet here he comes, shouting for them to form up, to make a line with their spears and scythes and sharpened hoes, to stand their ground. And the knights come down on them, faceless men clad all in steel, and the iron thunder of their charge seems to fill the world.

paragraphs.context: Some kisses are worth more than yellow gold, Slayer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam waits in vain for Dareon, who spends his nights with Braavosi courtesans and bravos instead of singing for the silver they desperately need.
paragraphs.simple: Sam looks out the window once more, hoping against hope to see the singer hurrying home. Darkness falls across the secret city, creeping through the alleys and down the canals. The good folk of Braavos will soon be shuttering their windows and sliding bars across their doors. Night belongs to the bravos and the courtesans. Dareon's new friends, Sam thinks bitterly. They are all the singer can talk about of late. He is trying to write a song about one courtesan, a woman called the Moonshadow who heard him singing beside the Moon Pool and rewarded him with a kiss. You should have asked her for silver, Sam said. It is coin they need, not kisses. But the singer only smiles. Some kisses are worth more than yellow gold, Slayer.

paragraphs.context: No leech can make him young again
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam squanders their last silver on a healer, but all the silver buys is dreamwine: Aemon is old, death is in his lungs, and no leech can make him young again.
paragraphs.simple: Instead Sam squandered the last of their silver on a healer from the House of the Red Hands, a tall pale man in robes embroidered with swirling stripes of red and white. All that the silver bought him was half a flask of dreamwine. This may help gentle his passing, the Braavosi said, not unkindly. When Sam asked if there wasn't any more he could do, he shook his head. Ointments he has, potions and infusions, tinctures and venoms and poultices. He might bleed him, purge him, leech him, but why? No leech can make him young again. This is an old man, and death is in his lungs. Give him this and let him sleep.

paragraphs.context: frightened her so badly that she lost the map and soon herself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gilly, sent for sweet water, is terrified by the stony maze of Braavos and loses the map and herself; Sam finds her weeping at a dead sealord's feet.
paragraphs.simple: They have no wine. Dareon promised to buy some with the coin from his singing. We'll have wine later, Sam has to say. There's water, but it's not the good water. The good water comes over the arches of the great brick aqueduct the Braavosi call the sweetwater river. Rich men have it piped into their homes; the poor fill their pails and buckets at public fountains. Sam sent Gilly out to get some, forgetting that the wildling girl has lived her whole life in sight of Craster's Keep and never seen so much as a market town. The stony maze of islands and canals that is Braavos, devoid of grass and trees and teeming with strangers who speak words she cannot understand, frightened her so badly that she lost the map and soon herself. Sam found her weeping at the stony feet of some long-dead sealord. All we have is canal water, he tells Maester Aemon, but the cook gave it a boil. There's dreamwine too, if he needs more of that.

paragraphs.context: did not grow on Braavos, save in the courts and gardens of the mighty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Firewood is dear in Braavos because no trees grow there save in the mighty men's gardens; it comes by barge, and they cannot sail for Oldtown with Aemon so weak.
paragraphs.simple: There's no more wood. Dareon paid the innkeep double for a room with a hearth, but none of them realized wood would be so costly here. Trees did not grow on Braavos, save in the courts and gardens of the mighty. Nor would the Braavosi cut the pines that cover the outlying islands around their great lagoon and act as windbreaks to shield them from storms.
