Instead, firewood is brought in by barge, up the rivers and across the lagoon. Even dung is dear here; the Braavosi use boats in place of horses. None of that would have mattered if they had departed as planned for Oldtown, but that proved impossible with Maester Aemon so weak. Another voyage on the open sea would kill him.

paragraphs.context: only cold and dark and pain beyond the wall called death?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon tells Sam he will not see Oldtown again and wonders fearfully what if there is no sweet afterlife, only cold and dark and pain beyond death.
paragraphs.simple: I shall not see Oldtown again. I know that now, the old man says, tightening his grip on Sam's arm. I will be with my brothers soon. Some were bound to me by vows and some by blood, but they were all my brothers. And my father, he never thought the throne would pass to him, and yet it did. He used to say that was his punishment for the blow that slew his brother. I pray he found the peace in death that he never knew in life. The septons sing of sweet surcease, of laying down our burdens and voyaging to a far sweet land where we may laugh and love and feast until the end of days, but what if there is no land of light and honey, only cold and dark and pain beyond the wall called death?

paragraphs.context: the sour eye that he reserved for guests who had overstayed their welcome
paragraphs.mainIdea: Overwhelmed by Gilly's weeping, Sam buckles on his swordbelt and storms out to find Dareon, avoiding the innkeep's sour eye.
paragraphs.simple: Gilly nods, cradling the babe against her breast, her eyes welling full of tears. She is going to weep again, Sam realizes. It is more than he can take. His swordbelt hangs from a peg on the wall, beside the old cracked horn that Jon gave him. He rips it down and buckles it about him, then sweeps his black wool cloak about his rounded shoulders, slumps through the door, and clatters down a wooden stair whose steps creak beneath his weight. The inn has two front doors, one opening on a street and one on a canal. Sam goes out through the former, to avoid the common room where the innkeep is sure to give him the sour eye that he reserved for guests who had overstayed their welcome.

paragraphs.context: a man can sing about battles doesn’t mean he’s fit to fight one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam hurries through Braavos to find Dareon, fearing the singer's loose tongue and quick temper will get him killed by the bravos who duel in the streets at night.
paragraphs.simple: With his hood up and his cloak flapping, Sam makes his way along the cobblestones toward the Ragman's Harbor. His swordbelt keeps threatening to fall down about his ankles, so he has to keep tugging it back up as he goes. He stays to the smaller, darker streets, where he is less likely to meet anyone, yet every passing cat still makes his heart thump, and Braavos crawls with cats. He needs to find Dareon, he thinks. Dareon is a man of the Night's Watch, his Sworn Brother; they will puzzle out what to do together. Maester Aemon's strength is gone, and Gilly would be lost here even if she were not grief-stricken, but Dareon. He should not think ill of him. Dareon could be hurt, perhaps that is why he did not come back. He could be dead, lying in some alley in a pool of blood, or floating facedown in one of the canals. At night the bravos swagger through the city in their parti-colored finery, spoiling to prove their skill with those slender swords they wear. Some would fight for any cause, some for none at all, and Dareon has a loose tongue and quick temper, especially when he's been drinking. Just because a man can sing about battles doesn't mean he's fit to fight one.

paragraphs.context: With you or without, my Lady leaves on the tide
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam remembers the captain refusing to wait: with them or without, his ship leaves on the tide, and Dareon had done all the talking with his honeyed tongue.
paragraphs.simple: Sam remembers standing on the dock with Dareon, watching the ship's oars rise and fall as she beat for the Titan and the open sea. Well, that's done, the singer said. If Sam had been a braver man, he would have shoved Dareon into the water. When it came to talking girls out of their clothes Dareon had a honeyed tongue, yet in the captain's cabin somehow Sam had done all the talking, trying to persuade the Braavosi to wait for them. Three days I have waited for this old man, the captain said. My holds are full, and my men have fucked their wives farewell. With you or without, my Lady leaves on the tide.

paragraphs.context: sat Dareon, nuzzling at the neck of the woman in his lap
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam finds Dareon at last in a dockside den, drunk among dancers and sailors, nuzzling a woman in his lap while wearing his black cloak on her.
paragraphs.simple: The one-eyed woman peels away, though she keeps one hand on Sam's arm. One of the dancers calls out that he can slay her if he likes, and the other asks if he'd let her touch his sword. Behind them a purple galleas is painted on the wall, crewed by women clad in thigh-high boots and nothing else. A Tyroshi sailor is passed out in a corner, snoring into his huge scarlet beard. Elsewhere an older woman with huge breasts is turning tiles with a massive Summer Islander in black-and-scarlet feathers. In the center of it all sits Dareon, nuzzling at the neck of the woman in his lap. She is wearing his black cloak.

paragraphs.context: for once he was too angry to be afraid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam snaps and beats Dareon bloody with his fists, too angry to be afraid, until someone drags him off and something hard crashes into his head.
paragraphs.simple: Sam does not think about it. His hand comes up, curled into a fist, and crashes into the singer's mouth. Dareon curses and his naked wife gives a shriek, and Sam throws himself onto the singer and knocks him backwards over a low table. They are almost of a height, but Sam weighs twice as much, and for once he is too angry to be afraid. He punches the singer in the face and in the belly, then begins to pummel him about the shoulders with both hands. When Dareon grabs his wrists, Sam butts him with his head and breaks his lip. The singer lets go and Sam smashes him in the nose. Somewhere a man is laughing, a woman cursing. The fight seems to slow, as if they are two black flies struggling in amber. Then someone drags Sam off the singer's chest. He hits that person too, and something hard crashes into his head.

paragraphs.context: They like the smell of roses but have no love for lions
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime sees that the smallfolk cheer the Tyrells (roses) but hate the Lannisters (lions), and thinks Cersei should take note.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime's column rides through King's Landing, but no one cheers for them the way crowds cheered Mace Tyrell earlier. A few whores call out, a pie man cries his wares, and in Cobbler's Square two ragged sparrows — poor wandering holy men — preach doom to several hundred commoners. The crowd only watches with dull, cold eyes. Jaime remarks that the people love the smell of Tyrell roses but have no love for Lannister lions, and thinks his sister would be wise to notice that. Ser Ilyn, who cannot speak, makes no reply.

paragraphs.context: They come round sniffing after you, my lord, but we saw them off
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Roger Hogg tells Jaime how Amory Lorch's lion soldiers and then real wolves ravaged his lands, and asks what he should do.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Roger, a big rough old knight, tells Jaime his troubles. First came a band of Lannister soldiers — the men of Ser Amory Lorch, whose shield bore a manticore, a monster with a man's face and a lion's body. Lorch killed half Roger's sheep and three good milk goats and tried to burn him out of his tower, but the walls were solid stone eight feet thick, so Lorch rode off bored. Then came wolves on four legs, which ate the sheep the soldiers had left. Roger got some good pelts in return, but fur does not fill bellies. He asks Jaime what he should do.

paragraphs.context: so Ser said to give him roast goat. The Qohorik didn’t
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rafford admits the Mountain's men cut up Vargo Hoat's corpse and fed it to the starving captives as roast meat.
paragraphs.simple: Rafford explains what became of the rest of Vargo Hoat's body. One of the captives kept begging for food, so Ser Gregor ordered the men to give him roast goat. The Qohorik had little meat on him, but the Mountain took his hands and feet first, then his arms and legs, and had the flesh roasted.

paragraphs.context: When Merryweather failed so dismally to contain Robert’s Rebellion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime recalls the Conningtons' history: Jon Connington, Rhaegar's friend, was made Hand and then stripped and exiled by the Mad King.
paragraphs.simple: It all comes back to Jaime. Jon Connington was Prince Rhaegar's close friend. When Lord Merryweather failed miserably to stop Robert's rebellion and Rhaegar could not be found, the Mad King Aerys made Jon his Hand instead. But Aerys was always cutting off his Hands: after Jon lost the Battle of the Bells, Aerys stripped him of his honors, lands, and wealth and packed him off across the sea to die in exile, where he soon drank himself to death. Red Ronnet's father was Jon's cousin. He joined the rebellion and was rewarded with Griffin's Roost after the Trident — though Robert kept the gold and gave most of the Connington lands to more loyal supporters.

paragraphs.context: You are speaking of a highborn lady, ser. Call her by her name
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Red Ronnet keeps mocking Brienne, Jaime strikes him across the mouth with his golden hand and orders him to say her name.
paragraphs.simple: Red Ronnet keeps insulting Brienne, joking that the sight of her naked would have made the bear flee in terror. Jaime's golden hand cracks across Ronnet's mouth so hard that the knight goes stumbling down the steps. His lantern falls and smashes, and the spilled oil spreads out burning. Jaime tells him he is speaking of a highborn lady and must call her by her name. Ronnet edges away from the flames on his hands and knees, spits a glob of blood at Jaime's foot, and obeys: Brienne the Beauty.

paragraphs.context: the absence of a bloody sheet meant little, by itself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei reasons that a missing bloodstained wedding sheet proves nothing about Margaery, since horse-riding highborn girls often lose their maidenhead that way.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks about whether Margaery is still a maiden. In Westeros people look for blood on the wedding-night sheet as proof, and no sheet was shown after Margaery's wedding to Renly. But Cersei remembers hearing that common peasant girls bleed heavily on their wedding nights, while highborn maids like Margaery are different: a lord's daughter is more likely to give her maidenhead to a horse than to a husband, it is said — and Margaery has been riding since she was old enough to walk. So the absence of a bloody sheet means little by itself. She moves on to asking Taena about Margaery's many admirers among the household knights.

paragraphs.context: During the reign of King Baelor the Blessed a simple stonemason
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls how Baelor the Blessed had an illiterate stonemason — then an eight-year-old boy — made High Septon, and how badly both turned out.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks about the history of High Septons. Long ago, during the reign of King Baelor the Blessed, a simple stonemason was chosen as High Septon. He worked stone so beautifully that Baelor decided he must be the Smith — the god of craftsmen — reborn in mortal flesh. But the man could neither read nor write, nor even remember the words of the simplest prayers. Some still say Baelor's Hand had him poisoned, to spare the realm embarrassment. After he died, Baelor had an eight-year-old boy raised to High Septon instead. The boy was said to work miracles, but even his little healing hands could not save Baelor during the king's final fast, when Baelor starved himself to death.

paragraphs.context: Your Grace, these are the bones of holy men and women
paragraphs.mainIdea: A one-legged sparrow explains the bone-heap at Baelor's statue: murdered holy folk brought from across the realm as witness to the Faith's suffering.
paragraphs.simple: A one-legged man leaning on a wooden crutch steps forward to answer Cersei's angry question. The bones and skulls heaped waist-deep around the great marble statue of Baelor are the remains of holy men and women murdered for their faith: septons, septas, and brothers and sisters of the Faith's orders — brown and dun and green, white and blue and grey. Some were hanged, some cut open. Septs have been robbed, maidens and mothers raped by godless men and demon-worshipers, and even the silent sisters attacked. The sparrows carried these bones from all over the realm to bear witness to the agony of the Holy Faith.

paragraphs.context: That crown has been sold. So have the others in our vaults
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow explains that he sold the crystal crown and all the Faith's riches to feed the poor.
paragraphs.simple: The High Sparrow answers Cersei about the beautiful crown of crystal and spun gold her father gave his predecessor. That crown has been sold, he says — and so have the other crowns in their vaults, and all their rings, and their robes of cloth-of-gold and cloth-of-silver. The poor need food in their bellies more than priests need gold and crystal on their heads. Wool will keep a man just as warm, he says; that is why the Seven gave men sheep. Cersei thinks he is utterly mad — or that the Most Devout were terrified of the beggars at their doors when they chose him.

paragraphs.context: At Saltpans he slew an aged septon and despoiled a girl
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow accuses the Hound of raping a twelve-year-old girl at Saltpans, then giving her to his men who mutilated her.
paragraphs.simple: The High Sparrow throws Cersei's own former sworn man in her face. At Saltpans, he says, the Hound slew an aged septon and despoiled a girl of twelve — an innocent child promised to the Faith. He wore his armor as he raped her, and her tender flesh was torn and crushed by his iron mail. When he was done he gave her to his men, who cut off her nose and nipples. Cersei answers that the king cannot be blamed for every man who ever served House Lannister: Sandor Clegane is a traitor and a brute, which is why she dismissed him. He fights for the outlaw Beric Dondarrion now, not for King Tommen.

paragraphs.context: Three hundred years ago, when Aegon the Dragon landed beneath this
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow explains he must pray and fast like the High Septon who anointed Aegon the Conqueror before he will bless Tommen.
paragraphs.simple: The High Sparrow tells Cersei why the blessing must wait: he must do as the High Septon did three hundred years ago. When Aegon the Dragon landed beneath this very hill, the High Septon locked himself inside the Starry Sept of Oldtown and prayed for seven days and seven nights, taking no food but bread and water. When he came out, he announced the Faith would not oppose Aegon and his sisters: the Crone — the goddess of wisdom — had lifted her lamp and shown him what lay ahead. If Oldtown fought the Dragon, Oldtown would burn, and the Hightower, the Citadel, and the Starry Sept would be cast down. Lord Hightower was a godly man; hearing the prophecy, he kept his soldiers home and opened the city gates to Aegon. Then His High Holiness anointed the Conqueror with the seven holy oils. The new High Septon says he must pray and fast likewise, for as long as need be.

paragraphs.context: The Faith Militant reborn . . . that would be the answer to three
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow eagerly accepts Cersei's offer to undo Maegor's laws and restore the Faith's ancient military orders.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei has pointed at the Warrior's statue and suggested that Maegor's old laws — which forced the Faith to lay down its swords three hundred years ago — could be undone. The High Sparrow rises to the bait at once. The Faith Militant reborn, he says, would be the answer to three hundred years of prayer. The Warrior would lift his shining sword again and cleanse this sinful realm of all its evil. If the king allows him to restore the ancient blessed orders of the Sword and the Star, every godly man in the Seven Kingdoms will know Tommen to be their true and rightful lord.

paragraphs.context: The Warrior’s Sons were an order of knights who gave up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei explains to Taena the history of the Faith's two ancient military orders: the Warrior's Sons and the Poor Fellows.
paragraphs.simple: Riding home triumphant, Cersei explains the old orders to Lady Merryweather, who has never heard of them. The Warrior's Sons were an order of knights who gave up their lands and gold and swore their swords to the High Septon. The Poor Fellows were humbler but far more numerous: wandering begging brothers who carried axes instead of begging bowls, escorting travelers from sept to sept and town to town. Their badge was the seven-pointed star, red on white, so the smallfolk named them Stars. The Warrior's Sons wore rainbow cloaks and inlaid silver armor over hair shirts, with star-shaped crystals in the pommels of their longswords. They were the Swords. Holy men, ascetics, fanatics, sorcerers, dragonslayers, demon-hunters — there were many tales. But all agreed they were implacable, merciless, in their hatred of every enemy of the Holy Faith.

paragraphs.context: For House Tyrell to hope to rule, he had to be removed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei convinces herself the Tyrells poisoned Joffrey and smuggled Tyrion to Highgarden.
paragraphs.simple: Watching Margaery, Cersei's thoughts spiral into suspicion. The girl is forever trying to steal Tommen from her, she thinks. Joffrey would have seen through that schemer's smile — Joff was too strong for her. So for House Tyrell to hope to rule, he had to be removed. Then it comes back to her: Margaery and her grandmother once plotted to marry Sansa Stark to Margaery's crippled brother Willas. Lord Tywin forestalled that by stealing a march on them — wedding Sansa to Tyrion first. The link was there all along, she realizes with a start. The Tyrells bribed the gaolers to free Tyrion and whisked him down the roseroad to join his vile bride. By now both are safe in Highgarden, hidden behind a wall of roses.

paragraphs.context: Two thousand years had passed, but in the watchtowers along their
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion recalls the ancient defense of the Shield Islands: beacon fires summon fisherfolk-turned-warriors and the four lords' longships.
paragraphs.simple: Two thousand years have passed, but the old watch still holds. On the rocky shores of the four Shield Islands, greybeards keep the ancient vigil in watchtowers. At the first glimpse of enemy longships the old men light their beacon fires, and the call leaps from hill to hill and island to island: fear, foes, raiders. When the fisherfolk see the fires burning on the high places, they put aside their nets and plows and take up swords and axes. Their lords rush from their castles with knights and men-at-arms. Warhorns echo across the waters from Greenshield, Greyshield, Oakenshield, and Southshield, and their longships slide out from moss-covered stone pens along the shores, oars flashing, to seal the Mander's mouth and hound and harry the raiders upriver to their doom.

paragraphs.context: Euron’s mutes and mongrels had cut him into seven parts, to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion remembers how Lord Baelor Blacktyde was seized and cut into seven pieces for refusing Euron as king.
paragraphs.simple: Drinking in the dark, Victarion remembers Baelor Blacktyde's words — Balon was mad, Aeron madder, Euron maddest of all. After the kingsmoot the young lord tried to sail home rather than accept Euron as his liege. But the Iron Fleet closed the bay, the habit of obedience was rooted deep in Victarion, and Euron wore the driftwood crown. Blacktyde's ship Nightflyer was seized and he was delivered to the king in chains. Euron's mutes and mongrels cut him into seven parts, to feed the seven green-land gods that Euron worships.

paragraphs.context: “Sold?” There were no slaves in the Iron Islands, only thralls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion is disgusted that Euron sells captives as slaves; the ironborn keep thralls, who are never bought or sold.
paragraphs.simple: Told that the captive women and children are to be sold as slaves, Victarion objects. There are no slaves in the Iron Islands, he says — only thralls. A thrall is bound to serve, but he is not chattel, not property: his children are born free, so long as they are given to the Drowned God. And thralls are never bought or sold for gold. A man pays the iron price for thralls — takes them by force in war — or else has none. It is by the king's decree, the man tells him. Nute the Barber shrugs: thralls or slaves, it makes no matter; their men could not defend them, so now they are the victors', to do with as they will.

paragraphs.context: The women had no choice but to obey. The youngest one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Euron forces Lord Hewett's ladies to strip and serve the feast naked, shaming their captive lord.
paragraphs.simple: Euron commands it as a jape: since he has promised his bastard girl Falia first choice of the ladies' clothes after the feast, the women had best disrobe now, so their fine gowns will not be stained with grease and wine. A roar of laughter washes over the hall. The women have no choice but to obey. The youngest one cries a little, but her mother comforts her and helps undo the laces down her back. Afterward they keep serving as before, moving along the tables with flagons of wine to fill each empty cup — only now they do so naked.

paragraphs.context: Rise, Andrik the Unsmiling, Lord of Southshield.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Euron names four new lords of the Shield Islands — and pointedly not Victarion.
paragraphs.simple: Standing on the table amid the cheering captains, Euron names the new lords of the four Shield Islands, saying the isles need strong men to hold them. He raises Ser Harras Harlaw as Lord of Greyshield — the Knight stands, one hand on the moonstone pommel of his Valyrian steel sword Nightfall. He raises Andrik the Unsmiling as Lord of Southshield — Andrik shoves his women away and lurches to his feet like a mountain rising from the sea. He raises Maron Volmark, a beardless boy of sixteen, as Lord of Greenshield. And he raises Nute the Barber as Lord of Oakenshield. Victarion's own name is not called.

paragraphs.context: Galleys guard the Redwyne Straits. The Dornish coast is dry and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Reader lists the perils of Euron's planned voyage to Slaver's Bay: straits, pirates, storms, and no welcome at the end.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Rodrik the Reader steps forward and questions the king's plan, sounding all its hazards. When shall they return, he asks — a year, three years, five? War galleys guard the Redwyne Straits. The Dornish coast is dry and bleak: four hundred leagues of whirlpools, cliffs, and hidden shoals with hardly a safe landing anywhere. Beyond wait the Stepstones, with their storms and their nests of Lysene and Myrish pirates. If a thousand ships set sail, three hundred may reach the far side of the narrow sea — and then what? Lys will not welcome them, nor Volantis. Where will they find fresh water and food? The first storm will scatter them across half the earth.

paragraphs.context: I once held a dragon’s egg in this hand, brother. This Myrish
paragraphs.mainIdea: Euron tells of the dragon's egg he once held and the wizard he killed when it would not hatch.
paragraphs.simple: Euron answers Victarion's scorn — what do dragons make? Woe, he says — with a story. He once held a real dragon's egg in his hand. A wizard from Myr swore he could hatch it if given a year and all the gold he required. When Euron grew bored with the man's excuses, he slew him, cutting him open. As the wizard watched his own entrails sliding through his fingers, he protested: But it has not been a year. Euron laughs at the memory. He adds, almost in passing, that Cragorn — the man who blew his dragon horn — is dead: when the maester cut him open, his lungs were charred as black as soot.

paragraphs.context: Shade-of-the-evening, the wine of the warlocks. I came upon a cask
paragraphs.mainIdea: Euron describes capturing Qartheen warlocks, killing one and feeding him to the others, and offers Victarion the warlocks' wine.
paragraphs.simple: Euron explains the strange drink he pours: shade-of-the-evening, the wine of the warlocks. He came upon a cask of it when he captured a trading galleas out of Qarth, along with cloves and nutmeg, forty bolts of green silk, and four warlocks who told a curious tale. One warlock presumed to threaten him, so Euron killed him and fed him to the other three. At first they refused to eat of their friend's flesh, but when they grew hungry enough they had a change of heart. Men are meat, Euron says. He drinks deep and smiles; Victarion tastes it, spits it out, and demands to know if Euron means to poison him.

paragraphs.context: They spoke of a one-eyed man and another who wore a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Mariya reports the outlaws who killed her husband: a one-eyed man, a yellow-cloaked man, and a scarred hooded woman who leads them — while Beric and his priest were not seen.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Mariya tells Jaime what is known of the outlaws who hanged her husband Merrett. At first they thought it was Lord Beric's band. The killers scattered after leaving Oldstones. Lord Vypren tracked one group to Fairmarket and lost them there. Black Walder led hounds and hunters into Hag's Mire after the others, but the peasants denied seeing them — until questioned sharply, they sang a different song. They spoke of a one-eyed man, another who wore a yellow cloak, and a woman cloaked and hooded. The peasants would have it that her face was torn and scarred, her eyes terrible to look upon — and they claim she led the outlaws. Beric Dondarrion and the red priest, Lady Mariya says with certainty, were not seen.

paragraphs.context: He paid the smallfolk for the food we ate, brought their grievances
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime explains how Ser Arthur Dayne broke the Kingswood Brotherhood: by winning the smallfolk's love instead of terrorizing them.
paragraphs.simple: Strongboar urges cutting out the smallfolk's tongues for lying, and Jaime answers him. If you want their help, he says, you need to make them love you. That was how Ser Arthur Dayne — the Sword of the Morning — did it, when Jaime rode with him against the Kingswood Brotherhood as a squire. Arthur paid the smallfolk for the food the knights ate, brought their grievances to King Aerys, got them more grazing land around their villages, and even won them the right to fell a set number of trees each year and take a few of the king's deer in autumn. The forest folk had looked to the outlaw Toyne to defend them, but Arthur did more for them than the Brotherhood ever could — and won them to his side. After that, the rest was easy.

paragraphs.context: All that remains of Saltpans is the castle, and old Ser Quincy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Arwood describes the utter destruction of Saltpans by the Hound: a whole town burned, its people slaughtered.
paragraphs.simple: Young Ser Arwood insists Strongboar has not seen what the Hound did at Saltpans. When the reports reached the Twins, Arwood rode there with Harys Haigh, his brother Donnel, and fifty men — archers and men-at-arms. They had thought it was Lord Beric's work and hoped to find his trail. All that remains of Saltpans is the castle, and old Ser Quincy was so frightened he would not open his gates, only shouting down at them from his battlements. The rest is bones and ashes. A whole town. The Hound put the buildings to the torch and the people to the sword, and rode off laughing. As for the women — Arwood will not speak of it at table. It made him sick to see.

paragraphs.context: The brave man slays with a sword, the craven with a wineskin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lancel confesses that he poisoned King Robert with strongwine — making them both kingslayers.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime puts a hand on his weeping cousin's shoulder. What do you know of sin, he asks — I killed my king. Lancel answers with a terrible line: the brave man slays with a sword, the craven with a wineskin. They are both kingslayers, ser, he says. Jaime tries to brush it off: Robert was no true king, and some might even say a stag is a lion's natural prey. But as he speaks he can feel the bones beneath Lancel's skin — and something else as well. Lancel is wearing a hair shirt under his tunic, a shirt of rough cloth worn against the skin as penance.

paragraphs.context: she was afraid of him, and with good reason. He made me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lancel confesses he lay with Cersei after Robert's death — never finishing inside her — and says Tyrion made him betray her.
paragraphs.simple: Pressed by Jaime, Lancel finishes his confession in a whisper. He never spilled his seed in her womb, he says — it is not treason unless you finish inside. After the king died, with Jaime a captive, Lord Tywin in the field, and Tyrion frightening her, Cersei was afraid, and Lancel gave her comfort. It was Tyrion, he says, who made him betray her. Jaime's mind races: Lancel, and Ser Osmund, and how many more? Was the part about Moon Boy just a gibe?

paragraphs.context: I am renouncing this lordship and this wife. Hardstone is welcome to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lancel announces he will give up Darry and his wife to join the newly restored Warrior's Sons.
paragraphs.simple: Lancel tells Jaime his decision, calmly. He is renouncing his lordship and his wife — Hardstone, Ser Harwyn Plumm, is welcome to both of them, if he likes. On the morrow Lancel will return to King's Landing and swear his sword to the new High Septon and the Seven. He means to take holy vows and join the Warrior's Sons. Jaime is baffled: those orders were proscribed — outlawed — three hundred years ago. Lancel says the new High Septon has revived them and sent out a call for worthy knights to pledge their lives and swords to the Seven; the Poor Fellows are to be restored as well.

paragraphs.context: I took her on Raymun Darry’s bed after stepping over Robert
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the godswood, Jaime confesses to the silent Ilyn Payne how he once took Cersei in this very castle while Robert lay drunk beside them.
paragraphs.simple: To escape the eyes and ears of the castle yard, Jaime leads Ser Ilyn to Darry's godswood. He points with his sword at a window: that was Raymun Darry's bedchamber, where King Robert slept on their return from Winterfell, after Ned Stark's daughter ran off. Robert and Cersei fought half the night — well, Cersei fought, and Robert drank — over whether the Stark girl should lose a hand. Past midnight the queen summoned Jaime inside. The king lay passed out snoring on the Myrish carpet. Jaime asked if she wanted him to carry Robert to bed. Instead she told him to carry her to bed, and shrugged out of her robe. He took her on Raymun Darry's bed after stepping over Robert. If the king had woken, Jaime would have killed him there and then.

paragraphs.context: He cut poor Clement’s tongue out when he would not speak
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brother Narbert tells how a raider cut out Brother Clement's tongue at Saltpans — mocking his vow of silence — and that some wounds do not show.
paragraphs.simple: Narbert explains the grave they passed on the hill. It is for Brother Clement, dead at forty-eight — not of years, but of wounds taken at Saltpans. Clement had carried some of the septry's mead to market there on the day the outlaws descended on the town. One raider cut poor Clement's tongue out when he would not speak: since Clement had taken a vow of silence, the raider said he had no need of it. Narbert adds that the Elder Brother keeps the worst tidings from outside to himself, so as not to disturb the peace of the septry — many brothers came here to escape the horrors of the world, not to dwell on them. Clement was not the only wounded man among them. Some wounds do not show.

paragraphs.context: We bury them side by side, Stark and Lannister, Blackwood and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother describes the septry's sad duty: burying the war's dead — friend and foe alike — that wash up on their shores.
paragraphs.simple: The Elder Brother sighs over the river's gifts. Their gravedigger knows no rest. The river washes up too many corpses these days — rivermen, westermen, northmen, knights and common knaves alike — and the brothers bury them side by side: Stark and Lannister, Blackwood and Bracken, Frey and Darry. That is the duty the river asks of them in return for all its gifts, and they do it as best they can. Sometimes they find a woman, though — or worse, a little child. Those are the cruelest gifts. He turns the talk to confession: since the raiders slew old Septon Bennet, the septry has had no one to hear their confessions, and he hopes Meribald has time to absolve them.

paragraphs.context: her breasts had been torn and chewed and eaten, as if by
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother describes treating a dying rape victim of Saltpans, whose curses were for Ser Quincy Cox, who barred his gates.
paragraphs.simple: The Elder Brother's smile vanishes as he tells of Saltpans. The raiders burned everything save the castle — only that was made of stone, though it had as well been made of suet for all the good it did the town. It fell to him to treat some of the survivors the fisherfolk brought across the bay after the flames died. One poor woman had been raped a dozen times, and her breasts had been torn and chewed and eaten, as if by some cruel beast. He did what little he could. As she lay dying, her worst curses were not for the men who raped her, nor the monster who devoured her living flesh — but for Ser Quincy Cox, who barred his gates when the outlaws entered the town and sat safe behind stone walls as his people screamed and died.

paragraphs.context: I am certain that the child was with Sandor Clegane at
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother tells Brienne the Hound is dead — and that he never had Sansa; it was Arya who was with him.
paragraphs.simple: The Elder Brother gives Brienne two shocks. First: her Dornish informer did not lie, but she did not understand him. Eddard Stark had two daughters — it was the younger one, Arya, that Sandor Clegane made off with, not Sansa. Second: the man she hunts is dead. He is certain the child was with Sandor at the inn by the crossroads, the one old Masha Heddle used to keep before the lions hanged her. He is certain they were on their way to Saltpans. Beyond that he does not know where the girl is, or even if she lives. She may have been among the children slain at Saltpans.

paragraphs.context: this was a bitter, tormented soul, a sinner who mocked both gods
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother sketches Sandor Clegane's life: a hate-driven man whose only dream was killing his brother — a dream Oberyn's spear took from him.
paragraphs.simple: The Elder Brother says he knew a little of Sandor Clegane. Sandor was Prince Joffrey's sworn shield for many a year, and even on the Quiet Isle they heard tell of his deeds, both good and ill. If even half of what they heard was true, this was a bitter, tormented soul, a sinner who mocked both gods and men. He served but found no pride in service. He fought but took no joy in victory. He drank to drown his pain in a sea of wine. He did not love, nor was he loved himself. It was hate that drove him. Though he committed many sins, he never sought forgiveness. Where other men dream of love, wealth, or glory, Sandor Clegane dreamed of slaying his own brother — a sin so terrible the Elder Brother shudders just to speak of it. Yet that hope was all this sad and angry creature lived for — and even that was taken from him when Prince Oberyn of Dorne stabbed Ser Gregor with a poisoned spear.

paragraphs.context: I had women too, and there I did disgrace myself, for some
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother confesses his own past: a violent knight who took women by force, drank, and lived a life writ in red.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne asks why he would give up knighthood. He answers: he never chose it. His father was a knight, and his father's father before him, and so were all his brothers. He was trained for battle since the day they deemed him old enough to hold a wooden sword. He saw his share of battles and did not disgrace himself in them. But he had women too, and there he did disgrace himself — for some he took by force. There was a girl he wished to marry, the younger daughter of a petty lord, but he was his father's thirdborn son and had neither land nor wealth to offer her, only a sword, a horse, a shield. When he was not fighting, he was drunk. All in all, he was a sad man. His life was writ in red — in blood and wine.

paragraphs.context: I took an arrow through the thigh and another through the foot
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Elder Brother recounts his death at the Battle of the Trident — fighting for Rhaegar, struck down, and washed up on the Quiet Isle.
paragraphs.simple: He tells Brienne when it changed: when he died in the Battle of the Trident. He fought for Prince Rhaegar, though Rhaegar never knew his name — he cannot say why, save that the lord he served served a lord who served a lord who had decided to support the dragon rather than the stag. Had that lord decided otherwise, he might have fought on the other side of the river. The singers would have us believe it was all Rhaegar and Robert struggling in the stream for a woman both claimed to love, but other men were fighting too, and he was one. He took an arrow through the thigh and another through the foot, and his horse was killed from under him, yet he fought on — desperate only to find another horse, for without one he would no longer be a knight. He never saw the blow that felled him. He heard hooves behind his back and thought, a horse! — but before he could turn, something slammed into his head and knocked him back into the river, where by rights he should have drowned.

paragraphs.context: the bitter tears she shed the night her king wed Margaery Tyrell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne pours out her whole life story — betrayals, betrothals, Renly, Catelyn, Jaime — and vows she must find the Stark girl or die trying.
paragraphs.simple: All of it comes pouring out of Brienne then, like black blood from a wound: the betrayals and the broken betrothals, Red Ronnet and his rose, Lord Renly dancing with her, the cruel wager for her maidenhead, the bitter tears she shed the night her king wed Margaery Tyrell, the mêlée at Bitterbridge, the rainbow cloak she had been so proud of, the shadow in the king's pavilion, Renly dying in her arms, Riverrun and Lady Catelyn, the voyage down the Trident, dueling Jaime in the woods, the Bloody Mummers, the bear pit, Jaime leaping down onto the sand, the long ride to King's Landing, Sansa Stark, the vow she swore to Jaime and the vow she swore to Lady Catelyn, Oathkeeper, Duskendale, Maidenpool, the men she killed. I have to find her, she finishes. There are others looking, all wanting to capture her and sell her to the queen. She has to find her first. She promised Jaime. Oathkeeper, he named the sword. She has to try to save her — or die in the attempt.

paragraphs.context: Give me the command, Your Grace. The castle will be yours within
paragraphs.mainIdea: Loras begs for command of the Dragonstone assault, promising the castle within a fortnight — and Cersei grants it, delighted.
paragraphs.simple: Before the old maester can finish objecting, Loras Tyrell strides forward and sinks to one knee. He begs Cersei: give him the command. It will take half a year or more to starve Dragonstone into submission, as Lord Redwyne means to do — but give him the assault, and the castle will be Tommen's within a fortnight, if he has to tear it down with his bare hands. No one has given Cersei such a lovely gift since Sansa Stark ran to her to betray Lord Eddard's plans. She is pleased to see Margaery go pale.

paragraphs.context: No matter what befell the boy on Dragonstone, however, the queen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei calculates that she wins whatever happens to Loras: victory hurts Stannis, failure disgraces him, death removes him.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks it through: no matter what befell the boy on Dragonstone, she will be the winner. If Loras takes the castle, Stannis suffers a grievous blow and the Redwyne fleet can sail off to meet the ironmen. If he fails, she will see that he has the lion's share of the blame — nothing tarnishes a hero as much as failure. And if he comes home on his shield, covered in blood and glory, she has Ser Osney ready to console his grieving sister Margaery.

paragraphs.context: What he lacks in gallantry he will give you tenfold in devotion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn offers Cersei a different kind of champion: a devoted, unstoppable warrior.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn tells Cersei he had another sort of champion in mind for the Kingsguard — not the gallant young knight she described. What he lacks in gallantry he will give her tenfold in devotion. He will protect her son, kill her enemies, and keep her secrets, and no living man will be able to withstand him.

paragraphs.context: Usually he rolled off and went to sleep as soon as it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei remembers Robert's drunken assaults in their marriage bed — the pain, the shame, and the one wedding night he made her want him.
paragraphs.simple: Lying with Taena, Cersei remembers the worst nights with Robert: lying helpless underneath him as he took his pleasure, stinking of wine and grunting like a boar. Usually he rolled off and went to sleep as soon as it was done, snoring before his seed could dry upon her thighs. She was always sore afterward — raw between the legs, her breasts painful from the mauling he would give them. The only time he ever made her wet was on their wedding night. In the first years, when he mounted her more often, she would close her eyes and pretend he was Rhaegar. She could not pretend he was Jaime: he was too different, too unfamiliar — even the smell of him was wrong.

paragraphs.context: “B-Bronn drove his lance through the chest of Balman’s poor h-h-h-horse.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Falyse tearfully reports that Bronn killed her husband Balman in single combat — lancing the horse, then a dagger through Balman's eye.
paragraphs.simple: Falyse stammers through the tale: Bronn drove his lance through the chest of Balman's poor horse. When the beast fell, Balman's legs were crushed. He screamed piteously for the maester.

paragraphs.context: Take her and do with her as you will, then. But
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei hands the broken Lady Falyse over to Qyburn for his experiments, on condition she never leaves the black cells.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei takes Qyburn aside and tells him of Balman's folly. She cannot have Falyse spreading tales about the city — her grief has made her witless. Does he still need women for his work? He does: his puppeteers — the subjects of his cruel experiments — are quite used up. Take her and do with her as you will, then, Cersei says. But once she goes down into the black cells — need she say more? Qyburn understands: Falyse will never come out alive. Cersei puts her smile back on and returns to her guest: Sweet Falyse, Maester Qyburn's here. He'll help you rest. Oh, good, says Falyse vaguely. Oh, good.

paragraphs.context: The siege drags on. The Blackfish sits inside the castle, we sit
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daven briefs Jaime: the siege is stalled and boring; the Freys squabble while the Blackfish waits them out.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Daven gives Jaime the picture at Riverrun. The siege drags on — bloody boring, if you want the truth. The Blackfish sits inside the castle, the besiegers sit outside in their camps. Daven wishes the Blackfish would make a sortie, to remind them all they are still at war — and it would be nice if he culled some Freys too, starting with Ryman, who is drunk more often than not, and Edwyn, who is as full of hate as a boil is full of pus. Meanwhile their supposed ally Lord Emmon Frey does nothing but try to tell Daven how to run the siege — demanding the castle be taken without damaging it, since it is now his lordly seat.

paragraphs.context: Every day at dawn he brings forth Edmure Tully, drapes a noose
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daven describes Ryman Frey's daily theater: hanging a noose on Edmure Tully each dawn and taking it off each night.
paragraphs.simple: Asked where to begin with the Freys, Daven starts here. While he has been building rams and siege towers, Ryman Frey has raised a gibbet. Every day at dawn he brings forth Edmure Tully, drapes a noose around his neck, and threatens to hang him unless the castle yields. The Blackfish pays this mummer's show no mind at all — so come evening, Lord Edmure is taken down again, unharmed. Daven adds, almost in passing: Edmure's wife is with child, did Jaime know? He had not.

paragraphs.context: He was bedding her during the Red Wedding. Roslin’s a pretty little
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daven reveals Edmure bedded Roslin during the Red Wedding and she is pregnant — and once the child is born, the Freys will have no more use for Edmure.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime is surprised: Edmure bedded his bride after the Red Wedding? Daven corrects him — during it. Roslin is a pretty little thing, hardly like a Frey at all, and strangely fond of Edmure. Perwyn says she is praying for a girl. Jaime thinks it through: once Edmure's son is born, Lord Walder will have no more need of Edmure himself. Daven agrees.

paragraphs.context: We have the castle well encircled. Ser Ryman and the Freys are
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daven lays out the siege dispositions: three camps ring the castle, with a boom across the Red Fork to stop escapes by boat.
paragraphs.simple: Daven describes the dispositions of the siege. They have the castle well encircled. Ser Ryman and the Freys hold the ground north of the Tumblestone. South of the Red Fork sits Lord Emmon, with Ser Forley Prester and what remains of Jaime's old army, plus the river lords who came over to the king's side after the Red Wedding — a sullen lot, Daven says, good for sulking in their tents and not much more. Daven's own camp lies between the rivers, facing the moat and Riverrun's main gates. They have thrown a boom — a floating barrier — across the Red Fork downstream of the castle, guarded by Manfryd Yew and Raynard Ruttiger with nets as well, so no one can escape by boat. The nets also catch fish, which helps keep the army fed.

paragraphs.context: Addam Marbrand’s scouts had found them, hanging black-faced beneath a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime tells of foragers found hanged with crabapples in their mouths — and Daven suspects outlaws, deserters, or vengeful river lords.
paragraphs.simple: Daven says half the men he sends out to forage for food never return: some desert, others are found hanging under trees with ropes about their necks. Jaime says they came on some two days past. Addam Marbrand's scouts had found them hanging black-faced beneath a crabapple tree. The corpses had been stripped naked, and each man had a crabapple shoved between his teeth. None bore any wounds — plainly, they had surrendered. Strongboar grew furious at that, vowing bloody vengeance on men who would truss up warriors to die like suckling pigs. It might have been outlaws, Daven says — or bands of northmen, or the river lords who bent their knees but whose hearts are still wolfish.

paragraphs.context: He paid a dragon for the head of any unrepentant Warrior’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Genna warns Jaime about the history of the Faith Militant: Maegor's bounty, thousands slain, and Jaehaerys's pardon.
paragraphs.simple: Genna warns Jaime that Cersei's reasons for re-arming the Faith had better be good, and recites the history. Even the Conqueror trod carefully with the Faith, so they would not oppose him. When Aegon died and the lords rose up against his sons, both military orders were in the thick of that rebellion — backed by the more pious lords and many of the smallfolk. King Maegor finally put a bounty on them: he paid a gold dragon for the head of any unrepentant Warrior's Son, and a silver stag for the scalp of a Poor Fellow. Thousands were slain — but nearly as many still roamed the realm, defiant, until the Iron Throne slew Maegor and King Jaehaerys agreed to pardon all those who would set aside their swords.

paragraphs.context: but Tyrion is Tywin’s son, not you. I said so once
paragraphs.mainIdea: Genna tells Jaime the devastating truth she once told Tywin: Tyrion — not Jaime — is truly Tywin's son.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime asks why Genna should fear Tywin having left a son. She answers: she has known Jaime since he was a babe at Joanna's breast. He smiles like Gerion and fights like Tygett, and there is some of Kevan in him — else he would not wear the white cloak. But Tyrion is Tywin's son, not Jaime. She once said so to Tywin's face, and he would not speak to her for half a year. Men are such thundering great fools, she says — even the sort who come along once in a thousand years.

paragraphs.context: In that one she was always looking for her mother, stumbling through
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cat describes the dream she hates: searching for her mother through mud, blood, and fire while a dog-headed monster holds her back.
paragraphs.simple: Cat says the wolf dreams are the good ones: in them she is swift and strong, running down her prey with her pack at her heels. The dream she hates is the other one — the one where she has two feet instead of four. In that one she is always looking for her mother, stumbling through a wasted land of mud and blood and fire. It is always raining in that dream, and she can hear her mother screaming — but a monster with a dog's head will not let her go to save her. In that dream she is always weeping, like a frightened little girl. Cats never weep, she tells herself, no more than wolves do. It's just a stupid dream.

paragraphs.context: but Braavos is the bastard child who ran away from home. We
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man teaches Cat Braavos's secret history: a hidden city founded by escaped slaves, and their one shared god — death.
paragraphs.simple: The kindly man teaches Cat the history of Braavos. The Nine Free Cities are the daughters of Valyria that was, he says, but Braavos is the bastard child who ran away from home. The Braavosi are a mongrel folk — the sons of slaves and whores and thieves. Their forebears came from fifty different lands to this place of refuge, to escape the dragonlords who had enslaved them. The city's very existence was a secret for a century, and its location was hidden three times as long. Fifty gods came with the refugees — but there is one god all of them shared in common: Him of Many Faces.

paragraphs.context: Singers sang of them, goldsmiths and jewelers showered them with gifts, craftsmen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cat describes the famed courtesans of Braavos — their barges, their splendor, and the adoration of the whole city.
paragraphs.simple: The courtesans of Braavos are famed across the world, Cat tells the sailors. Singers sing of them, goldsmiths and jewelers shower them with gifts, craftsmen beg for the honor of their custom, merchant princes pay royal ransoms to have them on their arms at balls and feasts, and bravos — Braavosi swordsmen — slay each other in their names. As she pushes her barrow along the canals, Cat sometimes glimpses one floating by on her way to a lover. Every courtesan has her own barge, and servants to pole her to her trysts. The Poetess always has a book to hand, the Moonshadow wears only white and silver, and the Merling Queen is never seen without her Mermaids. Each is more beautiful than the last — even the Veiled Lady, though only those she takes as lovers ever see her face.

paragraphs.context: With the coin his singing brought him, the crow had transformed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cat recognizes Dareon as a Night's Watch deserter living in luxury and seducing the brothel girls.
paragraphs.simple: It makes Cat angry to see Dareon sitting there so brazen, making eyes at the young whore Lanna as his fingers dance across the harp strings. The whores call him the black singer, but there is hardly any black about him now. With the coin his singing brought him, the crow has transformed himself into a peacock: a plush purple cloak lined with vair, a striped white-and-lilac tunic, a bravo's parti-colored breeches, even a silken cloak and a burgundy velvet one lined with cloth-of-gold. The only black about him is his boots — he threw all the rest in a canal, announcing he is done with darkness.

paragraphs.context: Sweetsleep is the gentlest of poisons,” the waif told her, as she was
paragraphs.mainIdea: The waif teaches Arya three poisons: sweetsleep, the tears of Lys, and basilisk blood.
paragraphs.simple: Helping the waif prepare her potions, Arya gets a lesson in poisons. Sweetsleep is the gentlest of them, the waif says as she grinds it with a mortar and pestle: a few grains will slow a pounding heart and stop a shaking hand, making a man feel calm and strong; a pinch will grant a night of deep and dreamless sleep; three pinches will produce the sleep that does not end. The taste is very sweet, so it is best used in cakes and pies and honeyed wines. Then the waif shows her a crueler poison — tasteless and odorless, and so easier to hide: the tears of Lys. Dissolved in wine or water, it eats at a man's bowels and belly, killing him like a sickness of those parts. Last is a paste spiced with basilisk blood: it gives cooked flesh a savory smell, but eaten it produces violent madness in beasts as well as men — a mouse will attack a lion after a taste of it.

paragraphs.context: She should have sought the favor of the Many-Faced God, but she
paragraphs.mainIdea: The waif tells her life story: poisoned by her stepmother, saved by her father's sacrifice to the Many-Faced God.
paragraphs.simple: The waif answers Arya's challenge with her own story. She was born the only child of an ancient House, her noble father's heir. Her mother died when she was little. When she was six, her father wed again. His new wife treated her kindly — until she gave birth to a daughter of her own. Then it was her wish that the waif should die, so her own blood might inherit the father's wealth. She should have sought the favor of the Many-Faced God, the waif says, but she could not bear the sacrifice he would ask of her. Instead she thought to poison the girl herself. It left her as Arya sees her now — small and scarred — but she did not die. When the healers told her father what his wife had done, he came to the temple and made sacrifice, offering up all his wealth — and her. The Many-Faced God heard his prayer: she was brought to serve, and her father's wife received the gift.

paragraphs.context: Dareon is dead. The black singer who was sleeping at the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya confesses to the kindly man that she killed Dareon — and admits she is Arya of House Stark.
paragraphs.simple: For her third new thing, Arya does not hesitate: Dareon is dead. The black singer who was sleeping at the Happy Port — really a deserter from the Night's Watch. Someone slit his throat and pushed him into a canal, but kept his boots. Good boots are hard to find, the kindly man says. Just so, says Arya, trying to keep her face still. He wonders aloud who could have done this thing. Arya of House Stark, she answers, watching his eyes, his mouth, the muscles of his jaw. That girl? he says. I thought she had left Braavos. Who are you? No one, she says. You lie, he tells her.

paragraphs.context: When the milk came, Arya drank it down. It smelled a little
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man gives Arya drugged warm milk; she wakes blind.
paragraphs.simple: The kindly man does not rage at Arya's confession. He only asks the waif to bring him wine — and warm milk for their friend Arya, who has returned so unexpectedly. On her way across the city Arya had wondered what he would say about Dareon; she had played the talk out in her head fifty times, like a mummer in a show. But she had never thought warm milk. When the milk comes, Arya drinks it down. It smells a little burnt and has a bitter aftertaste. Go to bed now, child, he says. On the morrow you must serve. That night she dreams she is a wolf again — but alone this time, with no pack, prowling over rooftops and along canal banks, stalking shadows through the fog. When she wakes the next morning, she is blind.

paragraphs.context: He was the blood of the dragon, but now his fire has
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam delivers a eulogy for Maester Aemon over his body aboard the Cinnamon Wind.
paragraphs.simple: Sam puts on his black Night's Watch clothes to speak the funeral words for Maester Aemon, somewhere off the sun-scorched southern coast of Dorne. He begins, He was a good man — but at once he knows the words are wrong. No: he was a great man. A maester of the Citadel, chained and sworn, and a Sworn Brother of the Night's Watch, ever faithful. When he was born they named him for a hero who died too young, but though he lived a very long time, his own life was no less heroic. No man was wiser, gentler, or kinder. At the Wall, a dozen Lords Commander came and went during his years of service, but he was always there to counsel them — and he counseled kings as well. He could have been a king himself, but when they offered him the crown he told them to give it to his younger brother. How many men would do that? He was the blood of the dragon, but now his fire has gone out. He was Aemon Targaryen. And now his watch is ended.

paragraphs.context: It was a prince that was promised, not a princess. Rhaegar, I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aemon explains the prophecy error: the promised prince was Daenerys all along — dragons are neither male nor female.
paragraphs.simple: Sam remembers Aemon's last strong night, on Braavos. Talk of dragons had almost restored the old man to himself, and he spoke of the prophecy. No one ever looked for a girl, he said. It was a prince that was promised, not a princess. He had thought it was Rhaegar: the smoke was from the fire that devoured Summerhall on the day of Rhaegar's birth, the salt from the tears shed for those who died. Rhaegar shared the belief when young, but later became persuaded it was his own son Aegon who fulfilled the prophecy — for a comet had been seen above King's Landing on the night Aegon was conceived, and Rhaegar was certain the bleeding star had to be a comet. What fools we were, who thought ourselves so wise! The error crept in from the translation. Dragons are neither male nor female — now one, now the other, as changeable as flame. The language misled them all for a thousand years. Daenerys is the one, born amidst salt and smoke. The dragons prove it.

paragraphs.context: Will I feast forever in the Father’s golden hall as the septons
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dying, Aemon confesses his fear of death and charges Sam to convince the Citadel that Daenerys is their hope.
paragraphs.simple: Aemon makes Sam promise to carry his message to the Citadel. Melisandre has misread the signs, he says: Stannis has some dragon blood, yes, but her sword is wrong — light without heat, an empty glamor — and the false light can only lead them deeper into darkness. Daenerys is their hope. The Citadel must send her a maester: she must be counseled, taught, protected. Then tears run from his blind white eyes as he admits the truth: I am dying, Sam. Death should hold no fear for a man as old as me, but it does. It is always dark where I am — so why should I fear the darkness? Yet he cannot help wondering what follows when the last warmth leaves his body. Will he feast forever in the Father's golden hall, as the septons say? Talk with Egg again, find Dareon whole and happy, hear his sisters singing to their children? Or do the horselords have the truth of it — will he ride the night sky forever on a stallion made of flame? Or must he return again to this vale of sorrow? Who has been beyond the wall of death to see? Only the wights — and they know what those are like.

paragraphs.context: He spoke of dreams and never named the dreamer, of a glass
paragraphs.mainIdea: In his final days Aemon raves of glass candles, unhatchable eggs, and the sphinx as riddle.
paragraphs.simple: After his last good day, the old man spends more time sleeping than awake, curled under furs in the captain's cabin. When he wakes he calls for Sam, insisting he must tell him something — but often he has forgotten what by the time Sam arrives. Even when he remembers, his talk is all a jumble. He speaks of dreams and never names the dreamer, of a glass candle that could not be lit and eggs that would not hatch. He says the sphinx is the riddle, not the riddler — whatever that means. Once he wakes weeping: The dragon must have three heads, he wails, but I am too old and frail to be one of them. I should be with her, showing her the way, but my body has betrayed me.

paragraphs.context: She wanted king’s blood for her fires. Val knew she did. Lord
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gilly explains why the babies were swapped: Melisandre wanted king's blood to burn, so Dalla's son was hidden and Gilly's left in his place.
paragraphs.simple: Sam blames Jon for sending the hundred-and-two-year-old Aemon to sea — he should never have been sent, and might have lived ten more years at Castle Black. Gilly answers quietly: if he had stayed, the red woman would have burned him. Even here, far from the Wall, she will not say Melisandre's name aloud. She wanted king's blood for her fires. Val knew she did. Lord Snow too. That was why they made Gilly take Dalla's babe away and leave her own behind in his place. Aemon at least went to sleep and never woke — but if he had stayed, she would have burned him.

paragraphs.context: What mad cruel god would give a man eyes and tell him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kojja Mo tells Sam there is no shame in loving: the gods gave men their bodies for pleasure, and only a monster god would forbid their use.
paragraphs.simple: Cornered by Kojja Mo, Sam stammers about his vow: no wife, no children — he said the words. Kojja answers with her people's wisdom. All you Westerosi make a shame of loving, she says, but there is no shame in loving. If your septons say there is, your seven gods must be demons. In the isles they know better. Their gods gave men legs to run with, noses to smell with, hands to touch and feel. What mad, cruel god would give a man eyes and tell him he must forever keep them shut, and never look at all the beauty in the world? Only a monster god, a demon of the darkness. She puts her hand between his legs: the gods gave him that too — for the giving of pleasure and the making of children. There is no shame in that.

paragraphs.context: The trees watch over us,” Gilly whispered, brushing the tears from his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam yields: he goes to Gilly, and she comforts him — where there are no trees, the old gods cannot see.
paragraphs.simple: Sam looks despairingly at the distant haze of the Dornish shore — he could never swim so far, he knows. So he goes to Gilly. What they did, he says — if he could take a wife, he would sooner have her than any princess or highborn maiden, but he can't. He is still a crow. He said the words, Gilly. He went with Jon into the woods and said the words before a heart tree. Gilly whispers, brushing the tears from his cheeks: The trees watch over us. In the forest, they see all — but there are no trees here. Only water, Sam. Only water.

paragraphs.context: but he turned what could have been a bloodless victory into a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aurane reports that Loras turned a near-bloodless win into a slaughter: a thousand dead, and Loras himself dying.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Waters gives Cersei the true cost of Dragonstone. He never saw a braver knight than Loras, he says — but Loras turned what could have been a bloodless victory into a slaughter. A thousand men are dead, or near enough to make no matter. Most of them Cersei's own — and not just common men, but knights and young lords, the best and the bravest. And Loras himself will make a thousand and one: they carried him inside the castle after the battle, but his wounds are grievous. He has lost so much blood that the maesters will not even leech him — the bleeding doctors dare not take more.

paragraphs.context: Loras was the first one through the breach when the ram broke
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei tells Margaery a heroic tale of Loras's assault — first through the breach, wounded again and again, fighting on.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei goes to the Maidenvault to give Margaery the news herself, and tells it as high heroism. Redwyne had miners digging a tunnel under the castle walls, but that was too slow for the Knight of Flowers — no doubt he was thinking of her father's people suffering on the Shields. Half a day after taking command, when Stannis's castellan refused his offer to settle the siege in single combat, Loras ordered the assault. He was the first one through the breach when the ram broke the castle gates — rode straight into the dragon's mouth, they say, all in white, swinging his morningstar about his head, slaying left and right. A crossbow quarrel through the thigh, another through the shoulder — still he fought on, blood streaming from him. Then a mace blow broke some ribs.

paragraphs.context: Margaery wrenched free of her embrace, so violently that Cersei almost
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery violently rejects Cersei's comfort, insisting her brother is not dead yet.
paragraphs.simple: When Cersei takes Margaery in her arms to comfort her, the younger queen wrenches free of the embrace so violently that Cersei almost falls. Dying is not dead, Margaery says. Cersei starts — no, but the maesters say — and Margaery screams it again: Dying is not dead! Cersei tries, I only want to spare you — and Margaery cuts her off: I know what you want. Get out. Cersei bows, her face a mask of cool courtesy: Sweet daughter. I am so sad for you. I will leave you with your grief. And thinks: now you know how I felt, the night my Joffrey died.

paragraphs.context: Within, the head of a dwarf reposed upon a bed of soft
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tyroshi opens his chest to reveal a dwarf's head — which Cersei at once declares is not Tyrion's.
paragraphs.simple: The Tyroshi throws open the cedar chest with a flourish and steps back smiling. Within, the head of a dwarf reposes upon a bed of soft blue velvet, staring up at her. Cersei takes a long look. That is not my brother, she says — and there is a sour taste in her mouth. This man has brown eyes; Tyrion had one black eye and one green. The Tyroshi claims the eyes had decayed and he replaced them with glass — but of the wrong color, as she says. Cersei is not fooled: this creature is bald, twice her brother's age, and missing his teeth — and he has no nose, she adds, because the Tyroshi cut it off.

paragraphs.context: They carried kite shields of a style not common since the Conquest
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei observes the Warrior's Sons escorting Septon Raynard — their arms, numbers, and Lancel among them.
paragraphs.simple: The Faith's delegation is led by Cersei's old friend Septon Raynard, escorted across the city by six of the Warrior's Sons — seven in all, a holy and propitious number, for the new High Septon does everything by sevens. The knights wear swordbelts striped in the seven colors of the Faith. Crystals adorn the pommels of their longswords and the crests of their greathelms. They carry kite shields of a style not common since the Conquest, bearing a device not seen in the Seven Kingdoms for centuries: a rainbow sword shining bright upon a field of darkness. Qyburn claims close to a hundred knights have already pledged their lives and swords to the Warrior's Sons, with more turning up every day — household knights, hedge knights, younger sons, old men wanting to atone for old sins. And then there is Lancel, Cersei's mooncalf cousin, who has forsaken castle, lands, and wife to join them.

paragraphs.context: If he is dying now, it can only be because someone wants
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei suspects Lord Gyles is being murdered and orders Pycelle to keep him alive.
paragraphs.simple: Pycelle comes grey-faced and apologetic: Lord Gyles Rosby is too weak to leave his bed and may soon join his forebears. Cersei complains: Gyles has had that cough for years — he coughed through half of Robert's reign and all of Joffrey's — and it never killed him before. If he is dying now, it can only be because someone wants him dead. Pycelle blinks in disbelief: who would want Lord Gyles dead? His heir, perhaps, Cersei says. Or the little queen. Some woman he once scorned. An old enemy. A new one. You. The old man blanches. Whatever the treatment — purging, bleeding, poultices, sweetsleep for the coughing — she orders him back to Gyles with one command: tell him he does not have her leave to die.

paragraphs.context: This time I want Tommen to whip the boy himself. He is
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Tommen defies her, Cersei orders him to whip his whipping boy Pate until he bleeds.
paragraphs.simple: Tommen shouts at his mother, his round face turning red: she is not to touch Margaery — he is the king, not her — he forbids it. Cersei stares, incredulous, then takes him by the ear and drags him squealing to the door. She orders Ser Boros Blount to escort him to his bedchamber and bring up Pate, Tommen's whipping boy. This time Tommen must whip the boy himself, and continue until the boy is bleeding from both cheeks. If His Grace refuses, or says one word of protest, Qyburn is to remove Pate's tongue — so His Grace can learn the cost of insolence.

paragraphs.context: Queen you shall be . . . until there comes another, younger and more
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maggy's prophecy: Cersei will be queen until a younger, more beautiful queen casts her down.
paragraphs.simple: The dream replays the fateful night in the crone's tent. Young Cersei asks when she will wed the prince. Never, Maggy says. You will wed the king. The girl is puzzled — for years after, she took those words to mean she would not marry Rhaegar until old Aerys died. I will be queen, though? she asks. Aye, says Maggy, malice gleaming in her yellow eyes. Queen you shall be — until there comes another, younger and more beautiful, to cast you down and take all that you hold dear. Anger flashes across the child's face. If she tries, she says, I will have my brother kill her.

paragraphs.context: And when your tears have drowned you, the valonqar shall wrap his
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maggy's final prophecy: Cersei's children will die crowned in gold, and the little brother will strangle her.
paragraphs.simple: The old woman is not done with young Cersei. Gold shall be their crowns and gold their shrouds, she says of the children to come — they will be crowned in gold and buried in gold. And when your tears have drowned you, the valonqar shall wrap his hands about your pale white throat and choke the life from you. What is a valonqar, the golden girl demands — some monster? She calls Maggy a liar and a warty frog and a smelly old savage, says she does not believe a word, and drags Melara away.

paragraphs.context: Walk with me a bit,” she said, “and tell me true. I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei begins her plot against Margaery: testing whether Osney Kettleblack could kill Ser Boros — the first step toward framing the little queen.
paragraphs.simple: The next day Cersei comes upon Osmund Kettleblack sparring in the yard and calls him aside. Walk with me a bit, she says, and tell me true. She wants no empty boasting, no talk of how a Kettleblack is thrice as good as any other knight — much may ride upon his answer. His brother Osney: how good a sword is he? Osmund says Osney is good — not as strong as his brothers, but quick to the kill. If it came to it, could he defeat Ser Boros Blount? Osmund chortles: Boros the Belly, forty or fifty, half-drunk half the time, fat even when sober — if Boros wants killing, Osney could do it easily enough. Why, has Boros done some treason? No, Cersei says. But Osney has. She is laying the first stone of her plan to bring Margaery down.

paragraphs.context: dregs from a dozen armies, the leavings of the lords
paragraphs.mainIdea: Every hundred yards they pass another hanged corpse. Brienne sees badges from many armies and realizes these dead are broken men, the leftover soldiers of many lords.
paragraphs.simple: As Brienne and her friends ride on, they keep finding dead men hanging from trees. Each dead man has a rope around his neck, and his mouth is full of salt. Some wear old cloaks of different colors, and some have small pictures sewn on their clothes. Brienne sees axes, arrows, fish, trees, leaves, and other signs. She understands that these men were soldiers from many different armies who lost everything in the war and turned to stealing. Now someone has hanged them all.

paragraphs.context: On the gallows tree, all men are brothers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Death has made all the hanged men look the same. Brienne remembers a line from a book: on the gallows tree, all men are brothers.
paragraphs.simple: The dead men had been different in life. Some had no hair and some had beards. Some were young and some were old. Some were short and some were tall. But now their bodies are swollen and their faces are rotten, so they all look the same. Brienne remembers a line she once read in a book: when men hang from the same tree, they are all brothers. She cannot remember which book it was.

paragraphs.context: The innkeep never hung another sign, so men forgot the dragon
paragraphs.mainIdea: Septon Meribald tells the inn's history: a rebel's black dragon sign angered the loyal Lord Darry, who destroyed it, so the inn lost its name and became the River Inn.
paragraphs.simple: Septon Meribald tells a story about the inn. Long ago, a son born outside marriage rose up against his trueborn brother the king. He used a black dragon as his sign. The lord of these lands was loyal to the true king, and the black dragon sign made him angry. He cut the sign post down, broke the sign into pieces, and threw them into the river. Years later, one dragon head was found on the Quiet Isle, red with rust. The innkeeper never hung a new sign. People forgot about the dragon and started calling the place the River Inn. In those days the river ran right past the inn, and guests could catch fish from their windows.

paragraphs.context: Renly had been lean and lithe, whereas this boy had the heavy shoulders
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne studies the smith boy and knows he is not Renly: he is younger, stockier, and full of anger, though he shares Renly's black hair and blue eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne looks hard at the boy and knows he is not Renly. Renly is dead; he died in her arms at one-and-twenty. This is only a boy, younger than Renly was when she first saw him. His jaw is squarer and his brows are thicker. Renly had been slim and graceful, but this boy has the big shoulders and strong right arm of a smith. He wears a leather apron with nothing under it. Dark hair covers his cheeks and chin, and his black hair is thick and hangs past his ears. Renly's hair had been the same black, but his was always clean and combed, sometimes cut short, sometimes tied back with a gold ribbon, never dirty and tangled. And Renly's blue eyes had been warm and full of laughter, but this boy's eyes are full of anger and distrust.

paragraphs.context: I have the virtue of being still amongst the living
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Hyle half-jokes that he wants to marry Brienne: he would gain Tarth, and she would get the children he waves at. He claims he is able, having fathered a bastard.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Hyle tells Brienne what he really wants to win: her. She is Lord Selwyn's only living child, and men have married far less promising brides for far smaller prizes than Tarth. He admits he is no Renly Baratheon, but he is alive, and some would say that is his only good quality. Marriage would help them both. He would get her lands, and she would get a castle full of children. He waves at the inn's children. He says he can father children; he knows of at least one child of his born outside marriage. He promises he would not bring that girl into Brienne's home. The last time he visited her, her mother threw hot soup at him.

paragraphs.context: Stannis told it true, that day he met with Renly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne accepts that Joffrey and Tommen were never Robert's sons, but the black-haired smith boy might be. Dog's frantic barking cuts her off.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne thinks about what Stannis told Renly: Joffrey and Tommen are not truly King Robert's sons. She believes it now. But this boy with the black hair could be Robert's son. She starts to speak to him, telling him to listen, but then she hears Dog barking loudly. Someone is coming.

paragraphs.context: His face was broad and hairless, maggot white
paragraphs.mainIdea: Seven riders splash into the yard, armed, some wounded; the last is a huge pale man with weeping sores on his cheeks.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne thinks she may not want to meet these riders. They ride into the yard through the rain puddles. Under the sound of rain and the dog's barking, she hears swords and armor clinking under their torn cloaks. She counts them: two, four, six, seven. Some ride like wounded men. The last rider is huge, as big as two of the others. His horse is tired and bloody and stumbles under his weight. All the riders have their hoods up against the driving rain except him. His face is wide and hairless, white like a maggot, and his round cheeks are covered with sores that leak fluid.

paragraphs.context: All she could do was slide back away from him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne has no shield and can only back away from the outlaw's whirling axe as lightning flashes; the mud nearly trips her and the axe grazes her shoulder.
paragraphs.simple: The outlaw keeps coming at Brienne, bleeding and roaring with anger. He shouts cruel names at her and says he will give her to his dog. His axe swings in deadly circles, a dark shape that turns silver each time lightning flashes. Brienne has no shield to block the blows. All she can do is move back, dodging left and right as the axe flies at her. Once her heel slips in the mud and she almost falls, but she catches herself. The axe cuts her left shoulder and leaves burning pain behind it. One of the watching outlaws shouts that he hit her, and another tells her to try dodging that blow.

paragraphs.context: like an avalanche of wet wool and milk-white flesh
paragraphs.mainIdea: The giant outlaw hurls Brienne into the mud, tears Oathkeeper from her hand, and gropes for her throat; punching him is like hitting wet dough.
paragraphs.simple: The huge man throws himself on Brienne like a falling mountain of wet cloth and pale flesh. He knocks her off her feet and slams her into the ground.
