She lands in a puddle, and water goes up her nose and into her eyes. The air is knocked out of her, and her head hits a half-buried stone with a crack. All she can say is no before he lands on top of her, pushing her deeper into the mud with his weight. One hand pulls her head back by her hair. The other feels for her throat. Oathkeeper has been torn from her hand. She has only her hands to fight with, but when she hits his face with her fist, it feels like punching a ball of wet white dough. He hisses at her.

paragraphs.context: He is eating me, she realized, but she had no strength
paragraphs.mainIdea: Biter tears his mouth free, chews and swallows her flesh; Brienne drifts toward unconsciousness, struck by his foot-long pointed tongue, which looks like a sword.
paragraphs.simple: Biter pulls his mouth free, full of Brienne's blood and flesh. He spits, grins, and bites into her again with his pointed teeth. This time he chews and swallows. Brienne understands that he is eating her, but she has no strength left to fight. She feels as if she is floating above her own body, watching the horror happen to some other woman, to some foolish girl who thought she could be a knight. She tells herself it will be over soon, and then it will not matter. Biter throws his head back, opens his mouth, howls, and sticks out his tongue at her. The tongue is pointed and sharp, dripping blood, longer than any tongue should be. It slides out of his mouth, red and wet and shining, a terrible and disgusting sight. Brienne thinks his tongue is a foot long, just before darkness takes her. It looks almost like a sword.

paragraphs.context: the great knight who had once enthralled a squire with tales
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Blackfish clearly hates Jaime. Jaime remembers the great knight who once thrilled him as a squire with tales of the Ninepenny Kings, and notes he chose plain dress for this meeting.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime can see that Ser Brynden Tully does not love him. The Blackfish has a rough, deeply lined face burned by wind, under stiff grey hair. But Jaime can still see the great knight who once filled a young squire with wonder by telling stories of the Ninepenny Kings. The horses' feet clatter on the wooden boards of the drawbridge. Jaime had thought hard about what to wear to this meeting, gold armor or white. In the end he chose a leather jacket and a red cloak.

paragraphs.context: the way that Eddard Stark had looked at him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime wants to defend himself over Catelyn's death, but the Blackfish's contempt, like Ned Stark's long ago, silences him. He says he came to speak of the living.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime wants to say that he had nothing to do with Lady Catelyn's death, and that her daughters were gone before he reached King's Landing. He wants to speak of Brienne and the sword he gave her. But the Blackfish is looking at him the way Eddard Stark had looked at him when he found him on the Iron Throne with the Mad King's blood on his blade. So Jaime only says that he came to speak of the living, not the dead, of those who need not die but will.

paragraphs.context: Strike your banners and open your gates
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime offers terms: strike the banners, open the gates, and the garrison lives. Men may stay to serve Lord Emmon or leave, but must give up their arms.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime tells the Blackfish what he wants. Pull down your flags and open your gates, and he will let the men of Riverrun live. Those who wish to stay at Riverrun and serve Lord Emmon may do so. The rest may go where they please, but Jaime will require them to hand over their weapons and armor.

paragraphs.context: I would have slain Robb Stark in the Whispering Wood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime answers the Blackfish's scorn: he would have killed Robb Stark himself if he could have reached him. The boy is dead regardless.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks this is a terrible thing to hear. He says he would have killed Robb Stark in the Whispering Wood if he could have reached him, but some fools got in his way. He asks whether it matters how the boy died. Robb is no less dead, and his kingdom died with him.

paragraphs.context: a cripple and an old man are well matched
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime offers single combat: free him from his vow to Lady Catelyn and he will fight the Blackfish sword to sword, winner taking Riverrun.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime reminds the Blackfish that he once had two hands. A voice inside him asks whether he would throw his life away for pride. He says some might call a cripple and an old man well matched. He asks the Blackfish to free him from his promise to Lady Catelyn, and then he will meet him sword to sword. If Jaime wins, Riverrun belongs to the Lannisters. If the Blackfish kills him, the siege will be lifted.

paragraphs.context: Lord Piper and both Lords Vance came to speak for the repentant lords
paragraphs.mainIdea: The war council gathers: river lords seeking pardon, westermen, Lady Genna daring anyone to question her, and Edwyn Frey speaking for his indisposed father.
paragraphs.simple: The lords gather quickly. Lord Piper and both Lords Vance come to speak for the river lords who now regret rebelling; their loyalty will soon be tested. The west is represented by Ser Daven, Strongboar, Addam Marbrand, and Forley Prester. Lord Emmon Frey joins them with his wife. Lady Genna takes her seat with a look that dares any man to question why she is there. No one does. The Freys send Ser Walder Rivers, called Bastard Walder, and Ryman's firstborn Edwyn, a pale thin man with a pinched nose and limp dark hair. Under a blue wool cloak, Edwyn wears a jacket of finely worked grey leather with fancy patterns cut into it. He announces that he speaks for House Frey because his father is unwell this morning.

paragraphs.context: the twin towers of House Frey displayed on shield and banners
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime walks through the Frey camp, mud and dung underfoot, Frey banners everywhere, past men who once fought for Robb Stark, his golden hand heavy at his side.
paragraphs.simple: The paths between the cookfires are raw brown mud mixed with horse dung, torn up by hooves and boots. Everywhere Jaime sees the twin towers of House Frey on shields and flags, blue on grey, along with the signs of lesser houses sworn to the Twins: the heron of Erenford, the pitchfork of Haigh, Lord Charlton's three sprigs of mistletoe. The arrival of the Kingslayer does not go unnoticed. An old woman selling piglets stops to stare, a knight with a half-familiar face kneels, and two soldiers pissing in a ditch turn and spray each other. Someone calls out to Ser Jaime, but he walks on without turning. Around him he sees the faces of men he had tried his best to kill in the Whispering Wood, where the Freys had fought under Robb Stark's direwolf banners. His golden hand hangs heavy at his side.

paragraphs.context: Better a sword than a rope. Do it, Payne
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmure, filthy with a noose around his neck atop the gallows, takes Jaime for his executioner and begs for a quick death by sword.
paragraphs.simple: On top of the gallows stands the Lord of Riverrun, staring at the trapdoor beneath him. His feet are black and caked with mud, and his legs are bare. Edmure wears a dirty silk tunic striped in Tully red and blue, and a noose of hemp rope around his neck. At the sound of Jaime's footsteps, he raises his head and licks his dry, cracked lips. He says the word Kingslayer. The sight of Ser Ilyn widens his eyes. He says a sword is better than a rope, and tells Payne to do it.

paragraphs.context: a backhand blow delivered with his golden hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime backhands Ryman with his golden hand, mocks his fat head and thick neck, and asks Ilyn how many strokes would cut through it.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime hits Ryman with the back of his hand, using his golden hand. The blow sends Ryman stumbling backward into the arms of his whore. Jaime tells Ryman he has a fat head and a thick neck too. Then he asks Ser Ilyn how many strokes of the sword it would take to cut through that neck.

paragraphs.context: Strongboar grabbed the end of it and pulled him to his feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ilyn shears the noose; Edmure collapses, and Strongboar hauls him upright by the rope, laughing at him as a fish on a leash.
paragraphs.simple: Edmure Tully has fallen face down on the scaffold when Ser Ilyn's blade cuts the rope in two. A foot of hemp rope still hangs from the noose around his neck. Strongboar grabs the end of the rope and pulls Edmure to his feet. He calls him a fish on a leash and laughs, saying it is a sight he never saw before.

paragraphs.context: that’s your death she has growing in her belly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime thinks coldly that Roslin's unborn child is Edmure's death, his leverage. Then he politely orders bathwater, clean clothes, and wine for his guest.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks to himself that the child growing in Roslin's belly is Edmure's death. Back at his pavilion, he sends away Strongboar and Ser Ilyn but keeps the singer, telling the man he may need a song soon. He orders Lew to heat bathwater for his guest, Pia to find Edmure clean clothes with no lions on them, and Peck to bring wine for Lord Tully. Then he asks Edmure if he is hungry.

paragraphs.context: Yield the castle and no one dies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime lays out generous terms: the smallfolk go free, the Blackfish may take the black, Edmure an honored hostage, Roslin's child provided for. All for yielding.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime tells Edmure to yield the castle and no one will die. The smallfolk may leave in peace or stay to serve Lord Emmon. Ser Brynden will be allowed to take the black, along with as many of the garrison as choose to join him. Edmure may do the same if the Wall appeals to him, or he may go to Casterly Rock as Jaime's captive and enjoy all the comforts and courtesy due a hostage of his rank. Jaime will send Edmure's wife to join him if he likes. If her child is a boy, he will serve House Lannister as a page and a squire, and when he earns his knighthood they will give him lands. If Roslin gives Edmure a daughter, Jaime will see her well provided with a dowry when she is old enough to marry. Edmure himself may even be given parole once the war is over. All he must do is yield the castle.

paragraphs.context: I’ll send him to you when he’s born
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime threatens total ruin if Edmure refuses: the castle razed, the river diverted, and Edmure's newborn flung back inside by trebuchet.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime asks Edmure if he must make him say the words. Pia stands by the tent flap with her arms full of clothes, and his squires and the singer are listening too. Jaime thinks: let them hear, let the world hear, it makes no difference. He forces a smile and tells Edmure he has seen their numbers, their ladders, towers, trebuchets, and rams. If Jaime gives the command, his cousin will bridge the moat and break the gate. Hundreds will die, most of them Edmure's own people. Edmure's former bannermen will form the first wave of attackers, so he will begin his day by killing the fathers and brothers of men who died for him at the Twins. The second wave will be Freys, and Jaime has no shortage of those. His westermen will follow when Edmure's archers run low on arrows and his knights are too tired to lift their blades. When the castle falls, everyone inside will be put to the sword. The herds will be slaughtered, the godswood cut down, the keeps and towers burned. Jaime will pull the walls down and turn the Tumblestone over the ruins, until no man can tell a castle ever stood there. He stands up and adds that Edmure's wife may give birth before that. Edmure will want his child, Jaime supposes. He will send the baby to Edmure when it is born, with a trebuchet.

paragraphs.context: yet you lost him to a boar
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei blames Pycelle for the deaths of Joffrey, Robert, and Jon Arryn, mocking his hand-wringing excuses.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei asks Pycelle if he served Joffrey the way he served her husband Robert, who was as strong as any man in the Seven Kingdoms, yet died from a boar's wound. She reminds him of Jon Arryn too. She says he would surely have killed Ned Stark as well if she had let him keep Ned longer. She asks whether it was at the Citadel that he learned to wring his hands and make excuses.

paragraphs.context: Time to squeeze the fruit and taste the juice
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei reads Pycelle's fear and accuses him of haunting the Maidenvault to spy on her for Margaery.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei sees that Pycelle's fear is plain to see. She thinks he is ripe enough, and it is time to squeeze the fruit and taste the juice. She asks why he is lying to her if he claims to be loyal. She says he began visiting Margaery before Loras left for Dragonstone, so he should stop telling stories about only wanting to comfort their good-daughter in her grief. She asks what brings him to the Maidenvault so often. It cannot be Margaery's empty conversation. She asks if he is courting Margaery's pox-faced septa, or playing with little Lady Bulwer, or spying for Margaery and telling her Cersei's secrets.

paragraphs.context: Get off those saggy knees and try to remember
paragraphs.mainIdea: Pycelle's moon-tea admission confirms Margaery's guilt to Cersei; she pivots at once to seizing Rosby's wealth.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says she knows what moon tea is for, and that this proves it. She tells Pycelle to get off his saggy knees and try to remember what it was like to be a man. Pycelle struggles to rise, and takes so long that she has to tell Osmund Kettleblack to pull him up again. As for Lord Gyles, she says their Father Above will surely judge him fairly. She asks whether he left any children.

paragraphs.context: Gyles knew of our dire need for gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei plans to take Rosby's gold and lands for Tommen and her own men, with Aurane Waters in mind for the seat.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei waves away the annoyance that Gyles was not of Tommen's blood. She says Gyles knew how badly they needed gold, and surely told Pycelle of his wish to leave all his lands and wealth to Tommen. Rosby's gold would fill their empty coffers again, and Rosby's lands and castle could be given to one of her own men as a reward for loyal service. Perhaps Lord Waters. Aurane has been hinting that he needs a seat of his own; his lordship is an empty honor without one. He has his eye on Dragonstone, Cersei knows, but there he aims too high. Rosby would suit his birth and station better.

paragraphs.context: Margaery has a lover. That is high treason
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei decides the moon tea proves Margaery's adultery, high treason punishable by death, and already pictures the headsman.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks the little queen has desires that Tommen is still too young to satisfy. That is always a danger when a grown woman marries a child, even more so with a widow. Margaery may claim Renly never touched her, but Cersei will not believe it. Women drink moon tea for only one reason; maidens have no need of it at all. Cersei decides her son has been betrayed. Margaery has a lover, and that is high treason, punishable by death. She can only hope that Mace Tyrell's prune-faced mother lives long enough to see the trial. By insisting Tommen and Margaery marry at once, Lady Olenna condemned her precious rose to the headsman's sword. Jaime has taken Ser Ilyn Payne away, so Cersei supposes she must find a new King's Justice to cut Margaery's head off.

paragraphs.context: we must have proof, something more substantial than moon tea
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei needs proof of treason beyond moon tea, proof strong enough to force even Mace Tyrell to condemn his own daughter.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei feels surrounded by roses, which angers her. She still needs Mace Tyrell, if not his daughter, at least until Stannis is defeated. Then she will need none of them. But how can she get rid of the daughter without losing the father? She says treason is treason, but they must have proof, something more solid than moon tea. If Margaery is proved unfaithful, even her own father must condemn her, or her shame becomes his.

paragraphs.context: That only makes their sins more shocking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei plans a supper with the Merryweathers to spring the trap, with roast boar and music to help it along.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei calls Margaery's ladies shameless women dressed in a maiden's white, which only makes their sins more shocking. She says their names will live in shame. Suddenly she can almost taste her victory. She tells Taena that her husband is Cersei's justiciar, and the two of them must dine with her this very night. She wants it done quickly, before Margaery decides to return to Highgarden or sail to Dragonstone to be with her wounded brother near death. Cersei will order the cooks to roast a boar, and of course they must have music, to help with digestion.

paragraphs.context: akin to replacing a destrier with a donkey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei offers Orton Merryweather the Handship, valuing him mostly because his strong wife Taena can rule through him.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei tells Lord Orton that the office is in his blood. His grandfather took her own father's place as Hand to Aerys. Replacing Tywin Lannister with Owen Merryweather had been like replacing a warhorse with a donkey, to be sure, but Owen had been an old, finished man when Aerys raised him, pleasant if useless. His grandson is younger. Well, he has a strong wife. It is a pity Taena cannot serve as Hand herself. She is three times the man her husband is, and far more amusing. But she is Myrish-born and female, so Orton must do. Cersei says she has no doubt he is more able than Ser Harys. Her chamber pot is more able than Ser Harys, she thinks. She asks if he will consent to serve.

paragraphs.context: the painted wood exploded into shards and splinters
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei smashes the lute across the Blue Bard's face and orders him dragged to the dungeons.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei calls the singer a liar. She smashes the lute across his face so hard that the painted wood bursts into shards and splinters. She tells Lord Orton to summon her guards and take this creature to the dungeons.

paragraphs.context: blood was streaming down his chin from all his broken teeth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Even under torture in the black cells the Bard gives only denials, and Cersei wonders if they seized the wrong singer.
paragraphs.simple: Even in the black cells, all they get from the singer are denials, prayers, and pleas for mercy. Soon blood is streaming down his chin from his broken teeth, and he wets his dark blue breeches three times over, yet he keeps to his lies. Cersei asks whether it is possible they have the wrong singer.

paragraphs.context: Qyburn had a razor in his hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn strips the Bard naked at razor's edge while Cersei commands him to describe pleasuring the little queen.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn says they know better. He has a razor in his hand, its edge gleaming faintly in the torchlight. He cuts away the Blue Bard's clothing until the man is naked except for his high blue boots. Cersei is amused to see that the hair between his legs is brown. She commands him to tell them how he pleasured the little queen.

paragraphs.context: he had more skill at making lutes than barrels
paragraphs.mainIdea: Under torture the Bard tells his whole life: a chandler's son who ran off at twelve to become a wandering musician.
paragraphs.simple: In the end the Blue Bard tells them his whole life, back to his first name day. His father had been a candle-maker, and Wat was raised to that trade, but as a boy he found he was better at making lutes than barrels. When he was twelve he ran off to join a troupe of musicians he had heard playing at a fair. He had wandered half the Reach before coming to King's Landing, hoping to find favor at court.

paragraphs.context: he had told them how Margaery would fondle herself
paragraphs.mainIdea: By dawn, tortured into a false confession, the Bard names Margaery's supposed lovers, ending with the Knight of Flowers.
paragraphs.simple: By dawn the singer's high blue boots are full of blood, and he has told them how Margaery would touch herself while watching her cousins pleasure him with their mouths. At other times he would sing for her while she satisfied her lusts with other lovers. The queen demands to know who they were, and the wretched Wat names Ser Tallad the Tall, Lambert Turnberry, Jalabhar Xho, the Redwyne twins, Osney Kettleblack, Hugh Clifton, and the Knight of Flowers.

paragraphs.context: And Osney is the plum that makes the pudding
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei edits the confession, dropping the great lords, keeping Osney as the prize witness, and warns the Bard to repeat it at trial.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says she prefers this song to the other one. Leaving the great lords out of it is for the best. The others are lesser men: Ser Tallad had been a hedge knight, Jalabhar Xho is an exile and a beggar, Clifton is the only one of the little queen's guardsmen. And Osney is the plum that makes the pudding. She tells the Bard she knows he feels better for having told the truth, and he will want to remember that when Margaery comes to trial. If he starts lying again, there will be consequences.

paragraphs.context: this time it was her chained to the wall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei dreams she is the tortured prisoner and Tyrion, naked and hairy, vows she will see her children crowned and die.
paragraphs.simple: Praying proves a waste of breath; as ever, the gods are deaf. Cersei dreams she is down in the black cells again, only this time it is her chained to the wall instead of the singer. She is naked, and blood drips from the tips of her breasts where the Imp tore off her nipples with his teeth. She begs him not to harm her children. Tyrion only leers at her. He is naked too, covered with coarse hair that makes him look more like a monkey than a man. He tells her she shall see her children crowned, and she shall see them die. Then he takes her bleeding breast into his mouth and begins to suck, and pain cuts through her like a hot knife.

paragraphs.context: It was foreseen when I was ten
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei confesses her deepest terror: a prophecy heard at ten foretold that Tyrion will kill her.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei tells Taena that he is going to kill her. It was foreseen when she was ten. She had only wanted to know who she would marry, but the woman said something else.

paragraphs.context: if they never spoke about the prophecies, they would not come true
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei recalls the maegi Maggy: Melara believed silence would stop the prophecies, and valonqar means little brother.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei speaks of the maegi, and the words tumble out of her. She can still hear Melara Hetherspoon insisting that if they never spoke about the prophecies, the prophecies would not come true. But Melara was not silent in the well. She screamed and shouted. Cersei says Tyrion is the valonqar, and asks Taena if they use that word in Myr. It is High Valyrian, and it means little brother. Cersei had asked Septa Saranella about the word after Melara drowned.

paragraphs.context: had been required to observe that particular holy day
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei notes that Margaery will lead her maidens to Baelor's Sept on Maiden's Day, the perfect stage for the trap.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks of fasting and purifying herself for Maiden's Day. It has been years since she was required to keep that holy day. Thrice married, yet Margaery would still have them believe she is a maid. Modest in white, the little queen will lead her hens to Baelor's Sept to light tall white candles at the Maiden's feet and hang paper garlands about her holy neck. At least a few of her hens. On Maiden's Day, widows, mothers, and whores are all barred from the septs, along with men, lest they spoil the sacred songs of innocence. Only virgin maids may take part.

paragraphs.context: First you must confess your treason
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei tells Osney he must first confess his treason, so his soul is cleansed of its festering shame.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says that was the right answer. First he must confess his treason. A man's sins can poison his soul if left to fester. She knows it must be hard for him to live with what he has done. It is past time he rid himself of his shame.

paragraphs.context: After you cut her head off, I want to take that kiss
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei lays out the whole plot; Osney agrees, asking only for the kiss Margaery never gave him once she is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei tells Osney all she has in mind. As he listens, fear slowly spreads across his face. When she finishes, he says that after they cut Margaery's head off, he wants to take the kiss she never gave him.

paragraphs.context: He cannot mean to kill me, she told herself a hundred times
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne comforts herself that her father cannot mean to kill her, and plans to throw herself at his feet, weeping, to beg his pardon.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne takes comfort from one thought. Why would her father go to such trouble to make her comfortable in prison if he meant to have her killed as a traitor? He cannot mean to kill her, she tells herself a hundred times. He does not have it in him to be so cruel. She is his blood and seed, his heir, his only daughter. If she must, she will throw herself under the wheels of his chair, admit her fault, and beg him for pardon. And she will weep. When he sees tears rolling down her face, he will forgive her.

paragraphs.context: It is for my prince to command, for Hotah to obey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hotah tells Arianne that only her deeds matter, not her intentions, and that he must obey his prince.
paragraphs.simple: Areo Hotah tells the little princess that what she meant does not matter. Only what she did matters. His face is like stone. He says he is sorry. It is for his prince to command, and for Hotah to obey.

paragraphs.context: a drear and dreadful prison where the vilest of criminals were sent
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne learns her friends are held at Ghaston Grey, a dreadful rock prison, and offers her own blood instead of theirs.
paragraphs.simple: Ghaston Grey is a crumbling old castle on a rock in the Sea of Dorne, a drear and dreadful prison where the worst criminals are sent to rot and die. Arianne asks if her father means to kill her friends. She cannot believe it. All they did, they did out of love for her. If her father must have blood, she says, it should be hers.

paragraphs.context: Someone told. Could it have been Ser Arys
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne torments herself wondering who betrayed the plot: did Arys's guilt, or his love for Myrcella, turn him?
paragraphs.simple: Someone told. Arianne wonders if it could have been Ser Arys. Had the white knight's guilt won out over his lust? Had he loved Myrcella more than her, and betrayed his new princess to make up for betraying the old one? Was he so ashamed of what he had done that he threw his life away at the Greenblood rather than live to face dishonor?

paragraphs.context: Not hot irons or the rack, but simple silence
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne laughs at her father's idea of torment: no torture, only silence, which she calls feebleness disguised as subtlety.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne wonders if this is her father's idea of torment. Not hot irons or the rack, but simple silence? That is so like Doran Martell that she has to laugh. He thinks he is being subtle when he is only being weak. She decides to enjoy the quiet, and use the time to heal and make herself strong for what must come.

paragraphs.context: It must be someone with real power
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne plots to smuggle a letter to a powerful lord, one great enough to cow Doran into releasing her.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne thinks triumphantly that she has a raven, but who should she send it to? The only one of her fellow plotters to escape her father's net is Darkstar. By now Ser Gerold may well have been caught; if not, he has surely fled Dorne. Her next thought is of Garin's mother and the orphans of the Greenblood. No, not them. It must be someone with real power, someone who took no part in their plot but might feel sympathy for them. She thinks of asking her own mother, but Lady Mellario is far away in Norvos, and Prince Doran has not listened to his wife for many years. Not her either. She needs a lord, one great enough to frighten her father into setting her free.

paragraphs.context: Arianne finally decided that she had but two real hopes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne rules out Yronwood, Dalt, and Sylva's father, settling on Harmen Uller and Franklyn Fowler as her only real hopes.
paragraphs.simple: The most powerful of the Dornish lords is Anders Yronwood, the Bloodroyal, Lord of Yronwood and Warden of the Stone Way, but Arianne knows better than to ask help from the man who raised her brother Quentyn. No. Drey's brother Ser Deziel Dalt once hoped to marry her, but he is far too dutiful to go against his prince. Besides, though the Knight of Lemonwood might frighten a petty lord, he is not strong enough to sway the Prince of Dorne. No. The same is true of Spotted Sylva's father. No. Arianne finally decides she has but two real hopes: Harmen Uller, Lord of Hellholt, and Franklyn Fowler, Lord of Skyreach and Warden of the Prince's Pass.

paragraphs.context: he shall not be forgotten when I wed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne writes her secret letter, offering marriage and a share in ruling Dorne to whoever rescues her.
paragraphs.simple: For days Arianne wavers as she writes her secret letter. She begins by promising a hundred silver stags to the man who brings the letter, to make sure it is delivered. She writes where she is, and begs for rescue. She promises that whoever frees her from this cell shall not be forgotten when she marries. That should bring the heroes running. Unless Prince Doran has stripped her of her rights, she remains the lawful heir to Sunspear, and the man who marries her will one day rule Dorne beside her. Arianne can only pray her rescuer proves younger than the greybeards her father has offered her over the years. She had told him she wants a husband with teeth when she refused the last one.

paragraphs.context: She has been caught was all that she could think
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cedra never returns; Arianne fears the girl was caught with the letter and lies awake dreading what comes next.
paragraphs.simple: The girl does not return the next day, however. Nor the day after that. When it is time for Arianne to bathe, Morra and Mellei fill her tub instead, and stay to wash her back and brush her hair. The princess asks them if Cedra has taken ill, but neither will answer. The only thing she can think is that Cedra has been caught. What else could it be? That night she hardly sleeps, for fear of what might come next.

paragraphs.context: If you saddle yourself with a fool or a brute
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne recalls Oberyn's teaching to his daughters: wed or take pleasure as you choose, but choose well.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne Martell had grown up expecting that one day she would marry some great lord of her father's choosing. That was what princesses were for, she had been taught, though her uncle Oberyn had seen things differently. The Red Viper had told his own daughters that if they wished to wed, they should wed, and if not, they should take their pleasure where they found it, for there is little enough pleasure in this world. But they should choose well. If they tied themselves to a fool or a brute, they should not look to him to free them. He had given them the tools to do that for themselves.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes it is best to study a game before you attempt to play it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran tells Arianne to study cyvasse before playing it, his quiet lesson on her reckless plotting.
paragraphs.simple: Doran tells her to play against herself. Sometimes it is best to study a game before you attempt to play it. He asks how well she knows the game, Arianne.

paragraphs.context: the slash opened her cheek down to the bone
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran tells Arianne that Darkstar nearly killed Myrcella: her cheek slashed to the bone, her ear cut off, her face ruined forever.
paragraphs.simple: Doran asks if she thought Myrcella was dead. No, though Darkstar did his best. All eyes were on her white knight, so no one is quite certain what happened, but it seems her horse shied away from his at the last instant, or he would have taken off the top of the girl's skull. As it is, the slash opened her cheek down to the bone and cut off her right ear. Maester Caleotte was able to save her life, but no medicine will ever restore her face. She was Doran's ward, Arianne, betrothed to her own brother and under his protection. She has dishonored all of them.

paragraphs.context: Valor is a poor substitute for numbers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran warns that Dorne cannot win a war alone against the Iron Throne, and Arianne's folly may have started one.
paragraphs.simple: Doran says the word is not if, but when. Dorne has the fewest people of the Seven Kingdoms. The Young Dragon made all their armies larger in his book, to make his conquest seem more glorious, and it has pleased the Dornish to water the seed he planted and let their foes think them stronger than they are. But a princess ought to know the truth. Courage is a poor substitute for numbers. Dorne cannot hope to win a war against the Iron Throne alone. And yet that may well be what Arianne has given them. He asks if she is proud, and gives her no time to answer. Then he asks what he is to do with her.

paragraphs.context: I found it hard to believe that you would conspire against me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran admits his mistake: he could not believe his daughter would plot against him, and had to learn the painful truth.
paragraphs.simple: Doran says that was his mistake, and it has proved a grievous one. Arianne is his daughter. She is the little girl who used to run to him when she skinned her knee. He found it hard to believe that she would conspire against him. He had to learn the truth.

paragraphs.context: this was no harmless game of cyvasse
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran pardons the young plotters as foolish children, except Darkstar, but warns their treason could have cost their heads.
paragraphs.simple: Doran says that as it happens, he agrees. Aside from Darkstar, her fellow plotters were no more than foolish children. Still, this was no harmless game of cyvasse. She and her friends were playing at treason. He might have had their heads off.

paragraphs.context: I have worked at the downfall of Tywin Lannister
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran reveals he has plotted Tywin's ruin since Elia's murder, and warns that Arianne's folly may drag thousands to hell with him.
paragraphs.simple: Doran tells her she mistakes patience for forgiveness. He has worked at the downfall of Tywin Lannister since the day they told him of Elia and her children. It had been his hope to strip Tywin of all that he held most dear before killing him, but it seems his dwarf son has robbed Doran of that pleasure. He takes some small comfort in knowing Tywin died a cruel death at the hands of the monster he himself fathered. Be that as it may, Lord Tywin is howling down in hell, where thousands more will soon join him if Arianne's folly turns to war. Her father grimaces, as if the very word is painful to him. He asks if that is what she wants.

paragraphs.context: when did you decide to disinherit me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arianne accuses Doran of favoring Quentyn and disinheriting her, quoting his letter back at him through furious tears.
paragraphs.simple: Arianne asks why not. He favors Quentyn and always has. Quentyn looks like him and thinks like him, and Doran means to give him Dorne; he should not trouble to deny it. She read his letter, and the words still burn as bright as fire in her memory. He wrote to Quentyn that one day he would sit where Doran sits and rule all Dorne. She asks him when he decided to disinherit her. Was it the day Quentyn was born, or the day she was born? What did she ever do to make him hate her so? To her fury, there are tears in her eyes.

paragraphs.context: The pact was sealed in secret
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran reveals a secret pact: Arianne was promised in marriage long ago, something he meant to tell her when she came of age.
paragraphs.simple: Doran says the pact was sealed in secret. He meant to tell her when she was old enough, when she came of age, he thought, but things did not go as planned.

paragraphs.context: Obara, Nym, and Tyene lack for nothing but their freedom
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran shows Oberyn's daughters are well treated, then drifts into tender memory of Arianne's childhood at the Water Gardens.
paragraphs.simple: Doran asks if she truly believes he would harm his brother's children. Obara, Nym, and Tyene lack nothing but their freedom, and Ellaria and her daughters are happily settled at the Water Gardens. Dorea stalks about knocking oranges off the trees with her morningstar, and Elia and Obella have become the terror of the pools. He sighs. It has not been so long since Arianne was playing in those pools. She used to ride the shoulders of an older girl, a tall girl with wispy yellow hair.

paragraphs.context: Prince Doran pressed the onyx dragon into her palm
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran whispers Vengeance, Justice, Fire and blood, pressing a black dragon cyvasse piece into Arianne's hand.
paragraphs.simple: Doran says the word vengeance. His voice is soft, as if he fears someone might be listening. Then he says justice. Prince Doran presses the onyx dragon into her palm with his swollen, gouty fingers, and whispers the words fire and blood.

paragraphs.context: he was apt to go into a shaking fit
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne must handle Robert gently, since rough handling brings shaking fits, and she coaxes him out of bed with the promise of food.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne tells herself they cannot have that. When Robert is handled roughly, he is likely to go into a shaking fit. She asks the little lord if he is hungry, and whether she should send Maddy down for berries and cream or warm bread and butter. Too late she remembers there is no warm bread; the kitchens are closed and the ovens are cold. She tells herself that if it gets Robert out of bed, it will be worth the trouble of lighting a fire.

paragraphs.context: The Winged Knight was Ser Artys Arryn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne promises Robert tales of the Winged Knight, the legendary falcon-rider who founded Arryn glory, once they reach the Gates of the Moon.
paragraphs.simple: The Winged Knight was Ser Artys Arryn. Legend says he drove the First Men from the Vale and flew to the top of the Giant's Lance on a huge falcon to kill the Griffin King. There are a hundred tales of his adventures. Little Robert knows them all so well he could say them from memory, but he likes to have them read to him anyway. Alayne tells the boy they have to go, but she promises to read him two tales of the Winged Knight when they reach the Gates of the Moon.

paragraphs.context: she had been born on the wrong side of the blanket
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sweetrobin's clumsy kiss makes Sansa dream of Loras, then remember bitterly that no Tyrell would ever kiss a bastard.
paragraphs.simple: Before she can call the servants, Sweetrobin throws his skinny arms around her and kisses her. It is a little boy's kiss, and clumsy. Everything Robert Arryn does is clumsy. Sansa thinks that if she closes her eyes she can pretend he is the Knight of Flowers. Ser Loras once gave Sansa Stark a red rose, but he never kissed her, and no Tyrell would ever kiss Alayne Stone. Pretty as she is, she was born on the wrong side of the blanket, a bastard.

paragraphs.context: tied up like a sack of barleycorn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne knows Robert must not be seen tied up like baggage on the descent; the full extent of his frailty must stay hidden.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne is certain of one thing: the Lord of the Eyrie cannot come down from his mountain tied up like a sack of grain. Her father had warned her that they must not let people see how weak and cowardly Robert truly is. She wishes Petyr were here. He would know what to do.

paragraphs.context: Time will not matter if his lordship has a shaking fit
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne warns the maester that a shaking fit on the mountain would be fatal: Robert must be kept calm at all costs.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne tells Maester Colemon that time will not matter if his lordship has a shaking fit and falls off the mountain. If her father were here, she knows he would tell the maester to keep Lord Robert calm at all costs.

paragraphs.context: She could hear the wind whistling round the bucket
paragraphs.mainIdea: The winch bucket lurches downward with Robert's hands blessedly still, the Eyrie shrinking above them like a honeycomb of ice.
paragraphs.simple: Ser Lothor shouts for them to go. Someone shoves the bucket hard. It sways and tips, scrapes against the floor, then swings free. Alayne hears the crack of Mord's whip and the rattle of the chain. They begin to descend, in jerks and starts at first, then more smoothly. Robert's face is pale and his eyes are puffy, but his hands are still. The Eyrie shrinks above them. The sky cells on the lower levels make the castle look like a honeycomb from below. A honeycomb made of ice, Alayne thinks, a castle made of snow. She can hear the wind whistling round the bucket.

paragraphs.context: The Lords Declarant were down from six to three, it would seem
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne learns the Lords Declarant have shrunk from six to three, and that Petyr failed to win Lady Waynwood.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne is surprised to hear about Anya Waynwood. The Lords Declarant seem to be down from six to three. Petyr Baelish had been confident of winning Symond Templeton to his side on the day he left the mountain, but not Lady Waynwood. Alayne asks if there was more news. The Eyrie is such a lonely place that she is eager for any bit of news from the world beyond, however small.

paragraphs.context: She did not want to look stupid, though
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne is baffled why Waynwood's ward should be her heir when she has sons, but she hides her confusion politely.
paragraphs.simple: Alayne is confused. Why should Lady Waynwood's ward be her heir? Lady Waynwood has sons of her own blood. One is the Knight of the Bloody Gate, Ser Donnel. Alayne does not want to look stupid, though, so all she says is that she prays he proves a worthy knight.

paragraphs.context: It is water now, Alayne thought, but come dark
paragraphs.mainIdea: The descent turns perilous: worn-smooth steps hold water that will freeze by dark, with wind skirling around her.
paragraphs.simple: They pass under a wind-carved arch where long icicles cling to the pale stone, dripping down on them. On the far side the path narrows and plunges down sharply for a hundred feet or more. Myranda has to drop back. Alayne gives the mule his head. The steepness makes her cling tightly to her saddle. The steps here have been worn smooth by the iron-shod hooves of countless mules, until they look like a series of shallow stone bowls. Water fills the bottoms of the bowls, shining golden in the afternoon sun. It is water now, Alayne thinks, but come dark all of it will turn to ice. She realizes she has been holding her breath, and lets it out. Mya Stone and Lord Robert have almost reached the rock spire where the slope levels off again. She tries to look only at them. She tells herself she will not fall, that Mya's mule will see her through. The wind skirls around her as she bumps and scrapes her way down step by step. It seems to take a lifetime.

paragraphs.context: their cloaks snapping and flapping behind them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne leads Robert across the bare stone saddle: ice underfoot, broken stones, and wind howling like a ghost wolf.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Robert calls himself Ser Sweetrobin, and Alayne knows she dare not wait for Mya to return. She helps the boy dismount, and hand in hand they walk out onto the bare stone saddle, their cloaks snapping and flapping behind them. All around is empty air and sky, with the ground falling away sharply on either side. There is ice underfoot, and broken stones just waiting to turn an ankle, and the wind is howling fiercely. It sounds like a wolf, Sansa thinks. A ghost wolf, big as mountains.

paragraphs.context: I knew that he would always be there to catch me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mya remembers a laughing giant who threw her into the sky and always caught her, her father Robert Baratheon, until one day he was gone.
paragraphs.simple: Mya shakes her head and says she remembers a man throwing her in the air when she was very little. He stands as tall as the sky, and he throws her so high it feels like flying. They both laugh so much she can hardly catch her breath, and finally she laughs so hard she wets herself, which only makes him laugh louder. She was never afraid when he threw her. She knew he would always be there to catch her. She pushes her hair back. Then one day he was not there. Men come and go. They lie, or die, or leave you. But a mountain is not a man, and a stone is a mountain's daughter. She trusts her father, and she trusts her mules. She will not fall. She puts her hand on a jagged spur of rock and gets to her feet, saying they had best finish: they have a long way to go, and she can smell a storm.

paragraphs.context: when the times are interesting you can never have too many swords
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr has hired hungry knights as extra swords, since interesting times demand as many blades as possible.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr calls them hungry knights. He thought it best to have a few more swords about them. The times grow ever more interesting, and when the times are interesting you can never have too many swords. The Merling King has returned to Gulltown, and old Oswell had some tales to tell.

paragraphs.context: I always anticipated that she would beggar the realm and destroy herself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr reports that Cersei is ruining herself fast with a council of fools; he thrives on chaos but had hoped for quiet years.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr does not hold her kiss against her. He says she would not believe half of what is happening in King's Landing. Cersei stumbles from one idiocy to the next, helped along by her council of the deaf, the dim, and the blind. He always expected she would beggar the realm and destroy herself, but he never thought she would do it so fast. It is quite vexing. He had hoped for four or five quiet years to plant seeds and let fruits ripen, but now that hope is gone. It is a good thing he thrives on chaos. What little peace and order the five kings left will not long survive the three queens, he fears.

paragraphs.context: She did not want to wed again, not now, perhaps not ever
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alayne panics at the marriage plan and whispers that she is already married, to Tyrion.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr speaks of a marriage, and Alayne's throat tightens. She does not want to wed again, not now, perhaps not ever. She stammers that she cannot marry. She looks at the door to make sure it is closed. Then she whispers that she is married. He knows.

paragraphs.context: The marriage must needs wait until Cersei is done
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr's scheme: a betrothal now, the wedding after Cersei falls and Sansa is widowed, and she must win Harry's approval.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr puts a finger to her lips to silence her. He says the dwarf married Ned Stark's daughter, not his. Be that as it may, this is only a betrothal. The marriage must wait until Cersei is done and Sansa is safely widowed. And Alayne must meet the boy and win his approval. Lady Waynwood will not make him marry against his will; she was quite firm on that.

paragraphs.context: You are promised to Harrold Hardyng, sweetling
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr explains the deal: he bought up Waynwood debt and offered a huge dowry to betroth Alayne to Harry the Heir.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr asks if she thinks the Waynwoods would sell a son for gold. For a start, she is the Lord Protector's bastard, and must never forget it. The Waynwoods are very old and very proud, but not as rich as one might think, as he discovered when he began buying up their debt. Lady Anya would never sell a son for gold, but a ward is different. Young Harry is only a cousin, and the dowry Petyr offered her ladyship was even larger than the one Lyonel Corbray just collected. It had to be, for her to risk Bronze Yohn's anger. This will put all of Bronze Yohn's plans awry. Alayne is promised to Harrold Hardyng, provided she can win his boyish heart, which should not be hard for her.

paragraphs.context: He begot three children, two sons and a daughter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr begins the Arryn genealogy: Jasper Arryn's three children, and how the lordship passed to Jon.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr tells her she will understand, and to listen. He takes her hand and brushes his finger lightly down the inside of her palm. He begins with Lord Jasper Arryn, Jon Arryn's father. Jasper fathered three children, two sons and a daughter. Jon was the eldest, so the Eyrie and the lordship passed to him. His sister Alys married Ser Elys Waynwood, uncle to the present Lady Waynwood. Petyr makes a wry face at the pairing of Elys and Alys. Jasper's younger son, Ser Ronnel Arryn, married a Belmore girl, but only lay with her once or twice before dying of a bad belly. Their son Elbert was being born in one bed even as poor Ronnel was dying in another down the hall. He asks if she is paying close attention.

paragraphs.context: she was whelping once a year
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr traces the Waynwood line: Alys's nine children, the deaths that thinned them, and Denys Arryn's marriage making his children heirs after Elbert.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr goes on. Jon Arryn married three times, but his first two wives gave him no children, so for long years his nephew Elbert was his heir. Meanwhile Elys was dutifully getting Alys with child, and she was giving birth once a year. She gave him nine children, eight girls and one precious little boy, another Jasper, after which she died exhausted. Boy Jasper, careless of the heroic efforts that went into begetting him, got himself kicked in the head by a horse at three years old. A pox took two of his sisters soon after, leaving six. The eldest married Ser Denys Arryn, a distant cousin of the Lords of the Eyrie. There are several branches of House Arryn scattered across the Vale, all as proud as they are poor, except the Gulltown Arryns, who had the rare good sense to marry merchants. They are rich but ill-mannered, so no one talks about them. Ser Denys came from one of the poor, proud branches, but he was a famed jouster, handsome and gallant and full of courtesy. And he had that magic Arryn name, which made him ideal for the eldest Waynwood girl. Their children would be Arryns, and the next heirs to the Vale if any ill befell Elbert. Well, as it happened, Mad King Aerys befell Elbert. Petyr asks if she knows that story.

paragraphs.context: When Robert dies, Harry the Heir becomes Lord Harrold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Petyr lays out the endgame: when Sweetrobin dies, Harry becomes Lord of the Eyrie, and Sansa revealed at his wedding will win the Vale's swords for Winterfell.
paragraphs.simple: Petyr raises an eyebrow. He says not if Robert dies, but when. Their poor brave Sweetrobin is such a sickly boy that it is only a matter of time. When Robert dies, Harry the Heir becomes Lord Harrold, Defender of the Vale and Lord of the Eyrie. Jon Arryn's bannermen will never love Petyr, nor their silly shaking Robert, but they will love their Young Falcon. And when they gather for his wedding, and Alayne comes out with her long auburn hair, wearing a maiden's cloak of white and grey with a direwolf on the back, every knight in the Vale will pledge his sword to win back her birthright. So those are his gifts to her, his sweet Sansa: Harry, the Eyrie, and Winterfell. He asks if that is worth another kiss.

paragraphs.context: with weeping sores upon his cheeks
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne dreams of Harrenhal's bear pit, but it is Biter who faces her; she screams for Jaime as he tears her face.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne dreams she is at Harrenhal, down in the bear pit again. This time it is Biter facing her, huge and bald and maggot-white, with weeping sores on his cheeks. He comes at her naked, touching himself and grinding his filed teeth together. Brienne runs from him, calling for her sword, for Oathkeeper. The watchers do not answer. Renly is there, with Nimble Dick and Catelyn Stark. Shagwell, Pyg, and Timeon have come too, and the corpses from the trees with their sunken cheeks, swollen tongues, and empty eye sockets. Brienne wails in horror at the sight of them, and Biter grabs her arm, yanks her close, and tears a chunk from her face. She hears herself scream the name Jaime.

paragraphs.context: She remembered his teeth tearing into the flesh of her face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Waking bound, Brienne relives the fight in the mud and is seized by fear that Biter may still be alive.
paragraphs.simple: It all comes back to her: lightning above and mud below, the rain pinging softly against the dark steel of the Hound's helm, the terrible strength in Biter's hands. Suddenly she cannot stand being bound. She tries to wrench free of her ropes, but that only chafes her worse. Her wrists are tied too tightly. There is dried blood on the hemp. She asks if he is dead, trembling. Biter. Is he dead? She remembers his teeth tearing into the flesh of her face. The thought that he might still be out there somewhere, breathing, makes her want to scream.

paragraphs.context: When Brienne closed her eyes, she saw the corpses swaying
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne pictures the Hangwoman's swaying corpses and panics, demanding news of Podrick, Hyle, Meribald, and Dog.
paragraphs.simple: The Hangwoman. When Brienne closes her eyes, she sees the corpses swaying under the bare brown limbs, their faces black and swollen. Suddenly she is desperately afraid. She asks about Podrick, her squire. Where is Podrick? And the others: Ser Hyle, Septon Meribald. Dog. She demands to know what they did with Dog.

paragraphs.context: She could not fight without her magic sword
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne dreams of facing Clarence Crabb at the Whispers with an empty scabbard, terrified of failing Jaime as she failed Renly.
paragraphs.simple: Then she is back at the Whispers, standing among the ruins and facing Clarence Crabb. He is huge and fierce, mounted on an aurochs shaggier than he is. The beast paws the ground in fury, tearing deep furrows in the earth. Crabb's teeth have been filed into points. When Brienne goes to draw her sword, she finds her scabbard empty. She cries no as Ser Clarence charges. It is not fair. She cannot fight without her magic sword. Ser Jaime gave it to her. The thought of failing him as she failed Lord Renly makes her want to weep. She begs for her sword; she has to find it.

paragraphs.context: Guest right don’t mean so much as it used to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girl says guest right means little since m'lady came back from the wedding; even the hanged men by the river thought they were guests.
paragraphs.simple: The girl says guest right does not mean so much as it used to, not since m'lady came back from the wedding. Some of the men swinging down by the river figured they were guests too.

paragraphs.context: It was a sword she wanted
paragraphs.mainIdea: Twelve-year-old Brienne, ungainly in silk brocade, dreads her betrothed's arrival; she wants a sword, not a rose.
paragraphs.simple: In the dream she is dressed in silk brocade, a quartered gown of blue and red decorated with golden suns and silver crescent moons. On another girl it might be a pretty gown, but not on her. She is twelve, ungainly and uncomfortable, waiting to meet the young knight her father has arranged for her to marry, a boy six years older, sure to be a famous champion one day. She dreads his arrival. Her bosom is too small, her hands and feet too big. Her hair keeps sticking up, and there is a pimple nestled in the fold beside her nose. Her father promised he will bring a rose for her, but a rose is no good; a rose cannot keep her safe. It is a sword she wants. Oathkeeper. She has to find the girl. She has to find his honor.

paragraphs.context: I have seen sows more beautiful than you
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the dream her betrothed mocks her, throws the rose in her face, and his griffins turn to lions as she cries for Jaime.
paragraphs.simple: Finally the doors open, and her betrothed strides into her father's hall. She tries to greet him as she was taught, only to have blood pour from her mouth. She has bitten her tongue off as she waited. She spits it at the young knight's feet and sees the disgust on his face. He calls her Brienne the Beauty in a mocking tone, and says he has seen sows more beautiful than her. He tosses the rose in her face. As he walks away, the griffins on his cloak ripple and blur and change to lions. She wants to cry out for Jaime to come back for her, but her tongue lies on the floor by the rose, drowned in blood.

paragraphs.context: Like rats, we must run back to our holes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros explains they hide in caves like rats with enemies multiplying daily, and offers her milk, bread, and honey.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros calls their cave a hole, saying that like rats they must run back to their holes when the dogs come sniffing after them, and there are more dogs every day. He wears the ragged remains of an old robe, pink and white. His hair is long and grey and tangled, and the loose skin of his cheeks and chin is covered with coarse stubble. He asks if she is hungry, and whether she could keep down a cup of milk, or perhaps some bread and honey.

paragraphs.context: She felt naked without her mail
paragraphs.mainIdea: Waking stripped in the cave, Brienne demands her clothes, her sword, and the way out.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne says she wants her clothes and her sword. She feels naked without her mail, and she wants Oathkeeper at her side. She demands the way out. The floor of the cave is dirt and stone, rough under her bare feet. Even now she feels light-headed, as if floating. The flickering light casts strange shadows. She thinks of them as spirits of the slain, dancing all about her, hiding when she turns to look. Everywhere she sees holes and cracks and crevices, but there is no way to know which passages lead out, which go deeper into the cave, and which go nowhere. All are black as pitch.

paragraphs.context: We have been hunting that lot for so long
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros explains Lem disobeyed orders chasing the Mad Dog; Brienne's wounds were won honorably, which is why Jeyne treated them.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros asks why indeed Brienne fought so bravely, then looks away from her. He says Lem should not have left the crossroads. Lem was told to stay close and hidden, and to come at once if he saw smoke rising from the chimney. But when word reached him that the Mad Dog of Saltpans had been seen heading north along the Green Fork, he took the bait. They have been hunting that lot for so long. Still, Lem ought to have known better. As it was, half a day passed before he realized the mummers had used a stream to hide their tracks and doubled back behind him, and then he lost more time circling a column of Frey knights. If not for Brienne, only corpses might have remained at the inn by the time Lem and his men got back. That is why Jeyne dressed her wounds, perhaps. Whatever else she may have done, she won those wounds honorably, in the best of causes.

paragraphs.context: I only know the road is dark
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros confesses the brotherhood is broken and lost: no king, no brotherhood, only a dark road with no end in sight.
paragraphs.simple: The man tells her they were king's men when they began, but king's men must have a king, and they have none. They were brothers too, but now their brotherhood is broken. He does not know who they are, if truth be told, nor where they might be going. He only knows the road is dark. The fires have not shown him what lies at its end.

paragraphs.context: War makes monsters of us all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros remembers justice fondly, then admits that war makes monsters of them all.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros speaks of justice with a wan smile. He remembers justice; it had a pleasant taste. Justice was what they were about when Beric led them, or so they told themselves. They were king's men, knights, and heroes. But some knights are dark and full of terror, my lady. War makes monsters of us all.

paragraphs.context: and you stole it off his corpse
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne insists she killed Rorge, who had stolen the Hound's helm from Clegane's grave.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne remembers lightning flashing and the mud beneath her feet. She says it was Rorge she killed. He took the helm from Clegane's grave, and the outlaws stole it off his corpse.

paragraphs.context: Rorge a beast in human skin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros condemns the helm and its wearers: Clegane a tormented man, Rorge a beast in human skin.
paragraphs.simple: The red priest says there is nothing good about that helm, nor the men who wore it. Sandor Clegane was a man in torment, and Rorge a beast in human skin.

paragraphs.context: the red and black ripples in the blade almost seem to move
paragraphs.mainIdea: The outlaws present Oathkeeper as evidence; Stoneheart stares only at the golden lion pommel with ruby eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Another outlaw steps forward, a younger man in a greasy sheepskin jerkin, holding Oathkeeper. He says the sword proves the charge. His voice carries the accents of the north. He slides the sword from its scabbard and lays it before Lady Stoneheart. In the firelight the red and black ripples in the blade almost seem to move, but the woman in grey has eyes only for the pommel: a golden lion's head, with ruby eyes that shine like two red stars.

paragraphs.context: Thoros of Myr drew a parchment from his sleeve
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros produces the writ bearing the boy king's seal, damning proof of Lannister backing.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros of Myr says there is this as well. He draws a parchment from his sleeve and puts it down next to the sword. It bears the boy king's seal and names the bearer as one going lawfully about his business.

paragraphs.context: The sword was given me for a good purpose
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne pleads that Jaime gave her the sword for a good purpose, bound by his oath to Catelyn Stark.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne says the sword was given to her for a good purpose. Ser Jaime swore an oath to Catelyn Stark, and the sword is part of keeping it.

paragraphs.context: We all know about the Kingslayer and his oaths
paragraphs.mainIdea: The outlaws sneer that Jaime's oaths are worthless, sworn before his friends cut Catelyn's throat.
paragraphs.simple: The big man in the yellow cloak answers that Jaime must have sworn it before his friends cut Catelyn's throat for her. They all know about the Kingslayer and his oaths.

paragraphs.context: Are we supposed to believe the Lannisters are handing out gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: The outlaws call her a liar: no Lannister gives jeweled swords to foes, and her companions are the Imp's squire and Tarly's knight.
paragraphs.simple: The big man tells her to deny it all she wants, but the sword says she is a liar. Are they supposed to believe the Lannisters hand out gold and ruby swords to their foes? That the Kingslayer meant for her to hide the girl from his own twin? He supposes the paper with the boy king's seal was just in case she needed to wipe herself with it. And then there is the company she keeps. He beckons, the outlaws part, and two more captives are brought forth. He tells Lady Stoneheart the boy was the Imp's own squire, and the other is one of Randyll Tarly's household knights.

paragraphs.context: “They’re lions,” said the one-eyed man
paragraphs.mainIdea: The one-eyed man votes to hang them all as lions, since Tarly has hanged scores of theirs.
paragraphs.simple: The one-eyed man says they are lions, and that is enough. He votes that they hang. Tarly has hanged a score of theirs, and it is past time they strung up some of his.

paragraphs.context: It was made for treachery and murder
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stoneheart hisses through her fingers: the sword is Oathbreaker, False Friend, like Brienne herself.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Stoneheart hisses through her fingers. No, she says. They should call the sword Oathbreaker, she says. It was made for treachery and murder. She names it False Friend. Like Brienne.

paragraphs.context: you once swore her your service
paragraphs.mainIdea: The northman reminds Brienne that she once swore her service to Catelyn Stark herself.
paragraphs.simple: The northman says the oath was to her, to Catelyn. He asks if Brienne has forgotten that she once swore her service to that lady.

paragraphs.context: Her hair was dry and brittle, white as bone
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stoneheart unveils: a rotting corpse-face, flesh hanging in strips, dried blood, skull showing through.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Stoneheart lowers her hood and unwinds the grey wool scarf from her face. Her hair is dry and brittle, white as bone. Her brow is mottled green and grey, spotted with the brown blooms of decay. The flesh of her face clings in ragged strips from her eyes down to her jaw. Some of the rips are crusted with dried blood, but others gape open to reveal the skull beneath.

paragraphs.context: she rose. May the Lord of Light protect us. She rose
paragraphs.mainIdea: Thoros explains: throat slashed, three days dead, Beric gave her the kiss of life and the flame passed to her.
paragraphs.simple: Thoros of Myr confirms that she is Catelyn Stark. The Freys slashed her throat from ear to ear. When they found her by the river she had been dead three days. Harwin begged Thoros to give her the kiss of life, but it had been too long, and Thoros would not do it. So Lord Beric put his lips to hers instead, and the flame of life passed from him to her. And she rose. Thoros prays the Lord of Light protect them. She rose.

paragraphs.context: All she asks from you is Jaime Lannister
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stoneheart's price: her son alive, or his killers dead, and from Brienne only Jaime Lannister.
paragraphs.simple: The big man says she wants her son alive, or the men who killed him dead. She wants to feed the crows, like they did at the Red Wedding. Freys and Boltons, yes. They will give her those, as many as she likes. All she asks from Brienne is Jaime Lannister.

paragraphs.context: he leapt into the bear pit empty-handed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne pleads that Jaime saved her from rape, came back for her, and sent her after Sansa; he is not the man he was.
paragraphs.simple: The name Jaime is like a knife twisting in her belly. Brienne stammers to Lady Catelyn that she does not understand. Jaime saved her from being raped when the Bloody Mummers took them, and later he came back for her; he leapt into the bear pit empty-handed. She swears he is not the man he was. He sent her after Sansa to keep her safe. He could not have had a part in the Red Wedding.

paragraphs.context: I will not make that choice
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brienne refuses the choice between Jaime and the noose, remembering her dream of biting off her tongue.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne remembers her dream, waiting in her father's hall for the boy she was to marry. In the dream she had bitten off her tongue, and her mouth was full of blood. She takes a ragged breath and says she will not make that choice.

paragraphs.context: the outlaws slipped a noose about her neck
paragraphs.mainIdea: They noose Brienne under a crooked willow, Podrick and Hyle at elms, as the Hound dons his helm again.
paragraphs.simple: And so they do hang them. Beneath a crooked willow, the outlaws slip a noose about Brienne's neck, jerk it tight, and toss the other end of the rope over a limb. Hyle Hunt and Podrick Payne are given elms. Ser Hyle shouts that he will kill Jaime Lannister, but the Hound cuffs him across the face and shuts him up. The Hound has put the helm back on. He tells them that if they have crimes to confess to their gods, now is the time to say them.

paragraphs.context: All she could see was Podrick, the noose around his thin neck
paragraphs.mainIdea: As the rope strangles her, Brienne can only watch Podrick kicking and choking beside her in agony.
paragraphs.simple: Brienne feels the hemp constricting, digging into her skin, jerking her chin upward. Ser Hyle curses them eloquently, but not the boy. Podrick never lifts his eyes, not even when his feet are jerked up off the ground. Brienne thinks that if this is another dream, it is time to awaken, and if it is real, it is time to die. All she can see is Podrick, the noose around his thin neck, his legs twitching. Her mouth opens. Pod is kicking, choking, dying. She sucks the air in desperately even as the rope strangles her. Nothing has ever hurt so much.

paragraphs.context: But first we must dance the dance and never miss a step
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei performs outrage before the council, demanding the High Septon release Margaery and her cousins.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei sits beneath the Iron Throne, dressed in green silk and golden lace, with emeralds glittering on her fingers and in her golden hair. The eyes of court and city are upon her, and she means them to see Lord Tywin's daughter. By the time this mummer's farce is done, they will know they have but one true queen. But first they must dance the dance and never miss a step. She calls Margaery her son's true and gentle wife, his helpmate and consort. She says the High Septon had no cause to lay hands upon her or to confine her and her young cousins, who are so dear to all of them. She demands that he release them.

paragraphs.context: Megga Tyrell and Elinor Tyrell stand accused of lewdness
paragraphs.mainIdea: The septa lays out the charges: lewdness, fornication, and conspiracy to high treason against Margaery and her cousins.
paragraphs.simple: The septa says Megga Tyrell and Elinor Tyrell stand accused of lewdness, fornication, and conspiracy to commit high treason. Alla Tyrell has been charged with witnessing their shame and helping them conceal it. Queen Margaery has been accused of all this as well, plus adultery and high treason.

paragraphs.context: Ser Osney Kettleblack has confessed his carnal knowledge of the queen
paragraphs.mainIdea: The accuser is revealed: Osney Kettleblack has confessed to the High Septon himself, before the Father's altar.
paragraphs.simple: The septa says the accuser is a knight of Cersei's own household. Ser Osney Kettleblack has confessed his carnal knowledge of the queen to the High Septon himself, before the altar of the Father.

paragraphs.context: I examined her myself, at the behest of His High Holiness
paragraphs.mainIdea: The septa testifies she examined Margaery herself: her maidenhead is broken, and so are Megga's and Elinor's.
paragraphs.simple: The septa says Margaery is not a maiden. She examined her herself, at the bidding of His High Holiness. Margaery's maidenhead is not intact. Septa Aglantine and Septa Melicent will say the same, as will Queen Margaery's own septa Nysterica, who has been confined to a penitent's cell for her part in the queen's shame. Lady Megga and Lady Elinor were examined as well. Both were found to have been broken.

paragraphs.context: this High Septon may want to try the queen himself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Merryweather warns that the High Septon may try Cersei herself, as the Faith tried great men of old.
paragraphs.simple: Merryweather agrees, but warns that this High Septon may want to try the queen herself, as the Faith once tried men of old.

paragraphs.context: You have six thousand gold cloaks. Sufficient for ten, I would think
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei orders ten arrests, coldly noting the Redwyne twins must be found innocent to prove the trials fair.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says ten men are to be taken. Osfryd has six thousand gold cloaks, which should be sufficient for ten. Some of the clever ones may have fled, if the rumors reached their ears in time. If so, it makes no matter; their absence only makes them look that much more guilty. Ser Tallad is a bit of an oaf and may try to resist. Cersei orders that he must not die before confessing, and that no harm come to any of the others. A few may well be innocent. It is important that the Redwyne twins be found falsely accused. That will demonstrate the fairness of the judgments against the others.

paragraphs.context: all of the accused traitors were in custody
paragraphs.mainIdea: By sundown all the accused are seized; Tallad wounds three gold cloaks, and the Redwynes get comfortable chambers.
paragraphs.simple: By the time the sun went down that day, all of the accused traitors were in custody. Hamish the Harper had collapsed when they came for him, and Ser Tallad the Tall had wounded three gold cloaks before the others overwhelmed him. Cersei ordered that the Redwyne twins be given comfortable chambers in a tower. The rest went down to the dungeons.

paragraphs.context: her honor must be defended by a knight of the Kingsguard
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei muses that Margaery's champion must be a Kingsguard, then lists why each brother is unavailable.
paragraphs.simple: A smile brushes Cersei's lips. She says that as queen, Margaery's honor must be defended by a knight of the Kingsguard. Every child in Westeros knows how Prince Aemon the Dragonknight championed his sister Queen Naerys against Ser Morghil's accusations. With Ser Loras so gravely wounded, though, she fears Prince Aemon's part must fall to one of his Sworn Brothers. She shrugs and asks who it could be. Ser Arys and Ser Balon are far away in Dorne, Jaime is off at Riverrun, and Ser Osmund is the brother of the man accusing her, which leaves only one other.

paragraphs.context: Her cell was eight feet long and six feet wide
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery is confined in a tiny tower cell with only a pallet, water, a holy book, and a candle.
paragraphs.simple: The little queen has been confined atop one of the Great Sept's slender towers. Her cell is eight feet long and six feet wide, with no furnishings but a straw-stuffed pallet and a bench for prayer, a ewer of water, a copy of The Seven-Pointed Star, and a candle to read it by. The only window is hardly wider than an arrow slit.

paragraphs.context: They will not even let me sleep
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery describes her torment: kept from her cousins, woken hourly to demand confessions of fornication.
paragraphs.simple: Margaery fumes that the High Septon will not even let her see her cousins. He keeps each of them apart from the others. Until Cersei came, Margaery was allowed no visitors but septas. One comes every hour to ask if she wishes to confess her fornications. They will not even let her sleep. They wake her to demand confessions. Last night she confessed to Septa Unella that she wished to scratch her eyes out.

paragraphs.context: How else will you prove your innocence
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei urges Margaery to choose trial by battle, with the Kingsguard sworn to defend her.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei asks how else Margaery will prove her innocence. She gives Margaery's hand a reassuring squeeze. She says it is Margaery's right to decide the manner of the trial, to be sure. Margaery is the queen. The knights of the Kingsguard are sworn to defend her.

paragraphs.context: Loras has two brothers, not six
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery rejects the Kingsguard as champions, craven, old, maimed, absent, or Kettleblack, and demands Garlan.
paragraphs.simple: Margaery stares at Cersei, then pulls her hand away. She asks if this is a joke. Boros is a craven, Meryn is old and slow, Cersei's brother is maimed, the other two are off in Dorne, and Osmund is a bloody Kettleblack. Loras has two brothers, not six. If there is to be a trial by battle, she wants Garlan as her champion.

paragraphs.context: I am not your daughter, thank the gods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Margaery accuses Cersei of wanting Tommen all to herself and hating every wife he might have.
paragraphs.simple: Margaery says Tommen is Cersei's son, all for herself. He will never have a wife that Cersei does not hate. And Margaery is not her daughter, thank the gods. She tells Cersei to leave.

paragraphs.context: to murder the fruit of her fornications in her womb
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow lays out the full case: broken maidenhead, moon tea, and a knight's sworn testimony naming many lovers.
paragraphs.simple: The High Sparrow says Margaery is not a maiden. Holy septas have examined her and testify that her maidenhead is broken. She has drunk moon tea, to murder the fruit of her fornications in her womb. An anointed knight has sworn upon his sword to having carnal knowledge of her and two of her three cousins. Others have lain with her as well, he says, and he names many names of men both great and humble.

paragraphs.context: A sacred court of seven judges shall sit upon this case
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Sparrow decrees a holy court of seven, including a maiden, a mother, and a crone, to judge the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The High Sparrow steeples his thin hands. He says he has had the selfsame thought. Just as Maegor the Cruel once took the swords from the Faith, so Jaehaerys the Conciliator deprived them of the scales of judgment. Yet who is truly fit to judge a queen, save the Seven Above and the godsworn below? A sacred court of seven judges shall sit upon this case. Three shall be of Margaery's female sex: a maiden, a mother, and a crone. Who could be more suited to judge the wickedness of women?

paragraphs.context: I will take Ser Osney Kettleblack back with me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei asks to take Osney back to the castle for questioning, and the Sparrow answers with one icy word.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei says she must return to the castle. With his leave, she will take Ser Osney Kettleblack back with her. The small council will want to question him and hear his accusations for themselves.

paragraphs.context: it felt like a splash of icy water in the face
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Septon's single word, No, chills Cersei; her certainty flickers.
paragraphs.simple: It was only a word, one little word, but to Cersei it felt like a splash of icy water in the face. She blinks, and her certainty flickers, just a little. The High Septon promises that Ser Osney will be held securely.

paragraphs.context: Osney Kettleblack hung naked from the ceiling
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei finds Osney whipped and hanging in chains, his back laid bare with cuts and welts.
