paragraphs.simple: Within the chamber, Osney Kettleblack hangs naked from the ceiling, swinging from a pair of heavy iron chains. He has been whipped. His back and shoulders have been laid almost bare, and cuts and welts crisscross his legs and arse as well.

paragraphs.context: did you have carnal knowledge of the queen
paragraphs.mainIdea: The High Septon asks Osney directly whether he lay with the queen.
paragraphs.simple: The High Septon asks in a firm, clear voice whether Ser Osney had carnal knowledge of the queen.

paragraphs.context: The chains rattled softly as Osney twisted in his shackles
paragraphs.mainIdea: Osney says aye, and adds that Cersei sent him to smother the old High Septon with a pillow.
paragraphs.simple: Osney says aye. The chains rattle softly as he twists in his shackles. He points at Cersei, saying she is the queen he lay with, the one who sent him to kill the old High Septon. The old man never had any guards. Osney says he just came in while the old man was sleeping and pushed a pillow down across his face.

paragraphs.context: she was a lioness of the Rock
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei tries to flee, dreaming of sending gold cloaks to free Osney, but the septas block her; Taena knows everything.
paragraphs.simple: The High Septon tries to seize her, but he is some old sparrow and she is a lioness of the Rock. She pushes him aside and bursts through the door, slamming it behind her with a clang. She thinks she needs the Kettleblacks: she will send in Osfryd with the gold cloaks and Osmund with the Kingsguard, Osney will deny it all once they cut him free, and she will rid herself of this High Septon just as she did the other. But the four old septas block her way and clutch at her with wrinkled hands. She knocks one to the floor and claws another across the face, and gains the steps. Halfway up she remembers Taena Merryweather. It makes her stumble, panting. She prays the Seven save her. Taena knows it all. If they take Taena too, and whip her . . .

paragraphs.context: dragged her kicking up the tower steps
paragraphs.mainIdea: Septas and silent sisters seize the screaming queen, strip her bare, and lock her in a cell in a roughspun shift.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei runs as far as the sept, but no farther. Women are waiting for her there, more septas and silent sisters too, younger than the four old crones below. She shouts that she is the queen and will have their heads, and orders them to let her pass. Instead they lay hands upon her. She runs to the altar of the Mother, but they catch her there, a score of them, and drag her kicking up the tower steps. Inside the cell three silent sisters hold her down as a septa named Scolera strips her bare. She even takes her smallclothes. Another septa tosses a roughspun shift at her. The queen keeps screaming that they cannot do this, that she is a Lannister, that her brother Jaime will kill them all.

paragraphs.context: I will teach them what it means to put a lion in a cage
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei rages in her cell, tearing the shift and smashing the ewer, expecting her guards to free her.
paragraphs.simple: She is not meek Margaery Tyrell, to don her little shift and submit to such captivity. She will teach them what it means to put a lion in a cage, Cersei thinks. She tears the shift into a hundred pieces, finds a ewer of water and smashes it against the wall, then does the same with the chamber pot. When no one comes, she begins to pound on the door with her fists. Her escort is below on the plaza: ten Lannister guardsmen and Ser Boros Blount. Once they hear, they will come free her, and they will drag the bloody High Sparrow back to the Red Keep in chains.

paragraphs.context: You are to be tried before a holy court of seven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei learns she will be tried by a holy court of seven for murder, treason, and fornication.
paragraphs.simple: The septa tells her that will not be allowed. She is to be tried before a holy court of seven, for murder, treason, and fornication.

paragraphs.context: Osfryd Kettleblack no longer commands the City Watch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn reports the Kettleblacks are finished: Osfryd stripped of command of the City Watch.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn tells her that Osfryd Kettleblack no longer commands the City Watch. The king has removed him from office and raised the captain of the Dragon Gate in his place, a certain Humfrey Waters.

paragraphs.context: The realm is being ruled by Ser Harys Swyft and Grand Maester Pycelle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn reports Cersei's fall is complete: dismissed from council, her uncle summoned, Tyrell and Tarly marching on the city.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn tells her he has been dismissed from the council, though for now they allow him to continue his work with the eunuch's whisperers. The realm is being ruled by Ser Harys Swyft and Grand Maester Pycelle. They have sent a raven to Casterly Rock, inviting her uncle to return to court and assume the regency. If he means to accept, he had best make haste. Mace Tyrell has abandoned his siege of Storm's End and is marching back to the city with his army, and Randyll Tarly is reported on his way down from Maidenpool as well.

paragraphs.context: Lord Waters raised sail, unshipped his oars, and took his fleet to sea
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aurane Waters has fled with the royal fleet, perhaps to join Stannis or to turn pirate.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn says that as soon as word of her troubles reached the river, Lord Waters raised sail, unshipped his oars, and took his fleet to sea. Ser Harys fears he means to join Lord Stannis. Pycelle believes he is sailing to the Stepstones, to set himself up as a pirate.

paragraphs.context: Your Grace has the right to prove your innocence by battle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn offers hope: trial by battle, with an unbeatable champion waiting for her command.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn says no, and takes her hand. Hope remains. She has the right to prove her innocence by battle. Her champion stands ready. There is no man in all the Seven Kingdoms who can hope to stand against him. If she will only give the command . . .

paragraphs.context: I need you now as I have never needed you before
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei writes to Jaime begging him to come at once: she loves him, she needs him as never before.
paragraphs.simple: She licks her lips, shivering, as she dictates the letter. He must come at once. He must help her and save her. She needs him now as she has never needed him before. She loves him. She loves him. She loves him. He must come at once.

paragraphs.context: Ser Jaime has no sword hand
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qyburn reminds her of the cold fact: Jaime has no sword hand, and if he loses as her champion she dies.
paragraphs.simple: Qyburn asks if she has forgotten. Ser Jaime has no sword hand. If he should champion her and lose . . .

paragraphs.context: He will not lose. Not Jaime. Not with my life at stake
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei refuses to doubt: Jaime will not lose, not with her life at stake.
paragraphs.simple: Cersei thinks they will leave this world together, as they once came into it. She says he will not lose. Not Jaime. Not with her life at stake.

paragraphs.context: Am I to blame if your men let him slip through their siege lines
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmure points out Jaime only demanded the castle, not his uncle; the Blackfish's escape is the besiegers' failure.
paragraphs.simple: Edmure tells Jaime that he was required to surrender his castle, not his uncle. He asks if he is to blame because Jaime's men let the Blackfish slip through their siege lines.

paragraphs.context: We raised the portcullis on the Water Gate
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmure explains the escape: the portcullis raised three feet left an underwater gap, and the strong-swimming Blackfish slipped beneath the spikes.
paragraphs.simple: Edmure says sullenly that the Blackfish did swim. He has the same blue eyes as his sister Catelyn, and Jaime sees the same loathing in them that he once saw in hers. Edmure says they raised the portcullis on the Water Gate, not all the way, just three feet or so. That left a gap under the water, though the gate still appeared closed. His uncle is a strong swimmer. After dark, he pulled himself beneath the spikes.

paragraphs.context: You will never know how much I despise you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmure shows Jaime his father's solar and pours out his hatred for the Kingslayer sitting in his father's chair.
paragraphs.simple: Edmure says this was his father's solar. His father ruled the riverlands from here, wisely and well. He liked to sit beside that window. The light was good there, and whenever he looked up from his work he could see the river. When his eyes were tired he would have Cat read to him. Littlefinger and Edmure once built a castle out of wooden blocks beside the door. Edmure says Jaime will never know how sick it makes him to see the Kingslayer in this room, and will never know how much he despises him.

paragraphs.context: Robb had it made for me. I loved him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jeyne sobs that the crown was hers, made for her by Robb, whom she loved.
paragraphs.simple: Jeyne sobs that the crown was hers. Her mother had no right to take it. Robb had it made for her. She loved him.

paragraphs.context: Tywin Lannister was not a man to overlook such details
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime reflects that his father overlooked nothing, pardons the Westerlings, and makes Rolph Lord of Castamere.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime nods. Tywin Lannister was not a man to overlook such details. He orders Jeyne's mother to unhand the girl, saying he is done with her for now. As Jeyne flees sobbing down the stairs, he turns to her mother. House Westerling has its pardon, and her brother Rolph has been made Lord of Castamere. He asks what else she would have of them.

paragraphs.context: A betrothal can be arranged, if that is your wish
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime reflects that Tywin's dead hand still moves them all, and offers Joy, Gerion's natural daughter, as a bride.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks that even from the grave, Lord Tywin's dead hand moves them all. He says Joy is his late uncle Gerion's natural daughter. A betrothal can be arranged, if Lady Westerling wishes it, but any marriage will need to wait. Joy was nine or ten when Jaime last saw her.

paragraphs.context: twice as dangerous as Edmure if she were ever to escape us
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime deems the Young Wolf's widow twice as dangerous as Edmure should she ever escape them.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime finishes the thought: she is the Young Wolf's widow, and twice as dangerous as Edmure if she were ever to escape them.

paragraphs.context: Ryman Frey had been a fool, a craven, and a sot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime notes Ryman Frey's murder shows the outlaws growing bold, hanging Walder's heir near the Twins.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime frowns. Ryman Frey had been a fool, a craven, and a sot, and no one is likely to miss him much, least of all his fellow Freys. If Edwyn's dry eyes are any clue, even his own sons will not mourn him long. Still, these outlaws are growing bold, if they dare hang Lord Walder's heir not a day's ride from the Twins. Jaime asks how many men Ryman had with him.

paragraphs.context: He allowed the outlaws to escape after they murdered Merrett and Petyr
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edwyn suspects Black Walder arranged Ryman's murder to clear his own path to the Twins.
paragraphs.simple: Edwyn's mouth twists. He says his brother had a hand in this, he will wager. Black Walder allowed the outlaws to escape after they murdered Merrett and Petyr, and this is why. With their father dead, only Edwyn is left between Black Walder and the Twins.

paragraphs.context: when the crossbowmen began feathering the wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: Walder Rivers tells how a prisoner freed Grey Wind from the net, took two quarrels, and threw himself into the river.
paragraphs.simple: Walder Rivers says the man was in the yard when their men came to put the direwolf down. Whalen demanded his sword and he gave it over meekly enough, but when the crossbowmen began feathering the wolf with bolts, he seized Whalen's axe and cut the monster loose of the net they had thrown over him. Whalen says the man took a quarrel in his shoulder and another in the gut, but still managed to reach the wallwalk and throw himself into the river.

paragraphs.context: What I need to do is geld him and send him to the Wall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime muses on punishing Osmund like Lucamore the Lusty, but the White Book has no guidance on what to do with Cersei.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks it would not be proper for him to slay his own Sworn Brother. What he needs to do is geld Osmund and send him to the Wall. That is what they did with Lucamore the Lusty. Ser Osmund may not take kindly to the gelding, to be sure. And there are his brothers to consider. Brothers can be dangerous. After Aegon the Unworthy put Ser Terrence Toyne to death for sleeping with his mistress, Toyne's brothers did their best to kill him. Their best was not quite good enough, thanks to the Dragonknight, but it was not for want of trying. It is all written down in the White Book, save what to do with Cersei.

paragraphs.context: the pack was led by a she-wolf of monstrous size
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Dermot returns empty-handed: hundreds of wolves, led by a monstrous she-wolf, killed two sentries.
paragraphs.simple: The next day Ser Dermot of the Rainwood returns to the castle empty-handed. Asked what he found, he answers: wolves, hundreds of the bloody beggars. He lost two sentries to them. The wolves came out of the dark to savage them. They were armed men in mail and boiled leather, yet the beasts had no fear of them. Before he died, Jate said the pack was led by a she-wolf of monstrous size. A direwolf, to hear him tell it. The wolves got in amongst the horse lines too. The bloody bastards killed Dermot's favorite bay horse.

paragraphs.context: He would need to find some way to winkle Tommen from her clutches
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime resolves to return to King's Landing, pry Tommen from Cersei's grip before he becomes another Joffrey, and find a new Hand.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime reflects that he took Riverrun without ever raising arms against the Starks or Tullys. Once he finds the Blackfish, he will be free to return to King's Landing, where he belongs. His place is with his king. With his son. He wonders whether Tommen would want to know the truth; it could cost the boy his throne. Would the boy sooner have a father or a chair? Jaime wishes he knew. The boy does like stamping papers with his seal. The boy might not even believe him. Cersei would say it was a lie. His sweet sister, the deceiver. He will need to find some way to winkle Tommen from her clutches before the boy becomes another Joffrey. And he should find the lad a new small council too. If Cersei can be put aside, Ser Kevan may agree to serve as Tommen's Hand. If not, the Seven Kingdoms do not lack able men. Forley Prester would make a good choice, or Roland Crakehall. If someone other than a westerman is needed to appease the Tyrells, there is always Mathis Rowan, or even Petyr Baelish. Littlefinger is as amiable as he is clever, but too lowborn to threaten any of the great lords, with no swords of his own. The perfect Hand.

paragraphs.context: Tom of Sevenstreams, if it please my lord
paragraphs.mainIdea: The singer introduces himself as Tom of Sevenstreams, called Tom o' Sevens.
paragraphs.simple: The singer tells Jaime his name is Tom of Sevenstreams, if it please his lordship. He doffs his hat. Most call him Tom o' Sevens, though.

paragraphs.context: a woman emerged from the shadows and walked slowly to the bier
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime dreams he keeps vigil over Tywin's corpse when a woman emerges from the shadows toward the bier.
paragraphs.simple: That night Jaime dreams he is back in the Great Sept of Baelor, still standing vigil over his father's corpse. The sept is still and dark, until a woman emerges from the shadows and walks slowly to the bier. He calls her sister.

paragraphs.context: the candles burning in the green pools of her eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: The grey-clad silent sister approaches, candles burning in the green pools of her eyes.
paragraphs.simple: But it is not Cersei. She is all in grey, a silent sister. A hood and veil conceal her features, but Jaime can see the candles burning in the green pools of her eyes. He asks what she would have of him. His last word echoes up and down the sept.

paragraphs.context: I am not your sister, Jaime
paragraphs.mainIdea: The woman denies being Cersei and asks if he has forgotten her: his mother Joanna.
paragraphs.simple: The woman says she is not his sister Jaime. She raises a pale soft hand and pushes her hood back. She asks if he has forgotten her.

paragraphs.context: He could never abide being laughed at
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joanna says Tywin could never abide being laughed at; Jaime wonders if he ever truly knew his father.
paragraphs.simple: The woman asks if Jaime will forget his own lord father too, and wonders if he ever knew Tywin truly. Her eyes are green, her hair spun gold. Jaime cannot tell how old she is. Fifteen, he thinks, or fifty. She climbs the steps to stand above the bier. She says Tywin could never abide being laughed at. That was the thing he hated most.

paragraphs.context: In my dreams I always have two hands
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dreaming, Jaime stares at his stump: in dreams he always has two hands.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime counts: one. One hand, clasped tight around the sword hilt. Only one. He says that in his dreams he always has two hands. He raises his right arm and stares uncomprehending at the ugliness of his stump.

paragraphs.context: We all dream of things we cannot have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joanna tells him all dream of what they cannot have, as Tywin dreamed his children would be beyond mockery.
paragraphs.simple: Joanna says they all dream of things they cannot have. Tywin dreamed that his son would be a great knight and his daughter a queen. He dreamed they would be so strong and brave and beautiful that no one would ever laugh at them.

paragraphs.context: Winter is marching south, and half our granaries are empty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Snow in the riverlands: winter marches south with empty granaries, and Jaime wonders what his dead father would do.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime thinks of snow in the riverlands. If it is snowing here, it could well be snowing on Lannisport and King's Landing too. Winter is marching south, and half their granaries are empty. Any crops still in the fields are doomed. There will be no more plantings, no more hopes of one last harvest. He finds himself wondering what his father would do to feed the realm, before he remembers that Tywin Lannister is dead.

paragraphs.context: I need you now as I have never needed you before
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime reads Cersei's fevered letter begging him to come at once: she loves him, she needs him.
paragraphs.simple: Jaime reads the letter in the window seat, bathed in the light of that cold white morning. Qyburn's words are terse and to the point; Cersei's are fevered and fervent. Come at once, she says. Help me. Save me. She needs him now as she has never needed him before. She loves him. She loves him. She loves him. Come at once.

paragraphs.context: Jaime rolled the parchment up again, as tight as one hand would allow
paragraphs.mainIdea: As a snowflake blurs the ink, Jaime rolls the letter tight and orders it burned: No.
paragraphs.simple: A snowflake lands on the letter. As it melts, the ink begins to blur. Jaime rolls the parchment up again, as tight as one hand allows, and hands it to Peck. He says no. He tells Peck to put it in the fire.

paragraphs.context: she began to bump up against corpses drifting down to the sea
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ironmen have ravaged Whispering Sound: drifting corpses, burned villages, and shattered ships.
paragraphs.simple: The ironmen have penetrated even to the sheltered waters of Whispering Sound. Come morning, as the Cinnamon Wind sails on toward Oldtown, she begins to bump up against corpses drifting down to the sea. Some of the bodies carry complements of crows, who rise into the air complaining noisily when the swan ship disturbs their grotesquely swollen rafts. Scorched fields and burned villages appear on the banks, and the shallows and sandbars are strewn with shattered ships. Merchant ships and fishing boats are the most common, but they see abandoned longships too, and the wreckage of two big dromonds. One has been burned down to the waterline, while the other has a gaping splintered hole in her side where her hull was rammed.

paragraphs.context: Hundreds of their ships afflict us now
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain explains this is no mere raiding: hundreds of iron ships hold the Shield Islands and Arbor rocks.
paragraphs.simple: The captain of the Huntress gives Sam a curious look. He says these are no mere reavers. The ironmen have always raided where they could. They would strike sudden from the sea, carry off some gold and girls, and sail away, but there were seldom more than one or two longships, and never more than half a dozen. Hundreds of their ships afflict Oldtown now, sailing out of the Shield Islands and some of the rocks around the Arbor. They have taken Stonecrab Cay, the Isle of Pigs, and the Mermaid's Palace, and there are other nests on Horseshoe Rock and Bastard's Cradle. Without Lord Redwyne's fleet, the defenders lack the ships to come to grips with them.

paragraphs.context: the best we can do is guard the sound and wait
paragraphs.mainIdea: Oldtown's defense: Leyton locked in his tower with spell books, galleys building, Humfrey gone to hire sellsails.
paragraphs.simple: The captain agrees. Lord Leyton is locked atop his tower with the Mad Maid, consulting books of spells. Perhaps he will raise an army from the deeps. Or not. Baelor is building galleys, Gunthor has charge of the harbor, Garth is training new recruits, and Humfrey has gone to Lys to hire sellsails. If he can winkle a proper fleet out of his sister, they can start paying back the ironmen with some of their own coin. Till then, the best they can do is guard the sound and wait for the queen in King's Landing to let Lord Paxter off his leash.

paragraphs.context: only to abandon them in the midst of war
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam fears he has brought Gilly all this way only to abandon her in a war zone; even Horn Hill may not be safe.
paragraphs.simple: It makes Sam wonder if even Horn Hill is truly safe. The Tarly lands lie inland amidst thickly wooded foothills, a hundred leagues northeast of Oldtown and a long way from any coast. They should be well beyond the reach of ironmen and longships, even with his lord father off fighting in the riverlands and the castle lightly held. The Young Wolf had no doubt thought the same of Winterfell until the night Theon Turncloak scaled his walls. Sam cannot bear the thought that he might have brought Gilly and her babe all this long way to keep them out of harm, only to abandon them in the midst of war.

paragraphs.context: It has to be Horn Hill, Sam finally decided
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam decides he will hire a wagon and take Gilly to Horn Hill himself, turning back if anything seems wrong.
paragraphs.simple: It has to be Horn Hill, Sam finally decides. Once they reach Oldtown he will hire a wagon and some horses and take her there himself. That way he can make certain of the castle and its garrison, and if any part of what he sees or hears gives him pause, he can just turn around and bring Gilly back to Oldtown.

paragraphs.context: the beacon of the Hightower was the only part of the city
paragraphs.mainIdea: They reach fog-bound Oldtown: harbor boom, warships, and inspection by Gunthor Hightower.
paragraphs.simple: They reach Oldtown on a cold damp morning, when the fog is so thick that the beacon of the Hightower is the only part of the city to be seen. A boom stretches across the harbor, linking two dozen rotted hulks. Just behind it stands a line of warships, anchored by three big dromonds and Lord Hightower's towering four-decked banner ship, the Honor of Oldtown. Once again the Cinnamon Wind has to submit to inspection. This time it is Lord Leyton's son Gunthor who comes aboard, in a cloth-of-silver cloak and a suit of grey enameled scales. Ser Gunthor studied at the Citadel for several years and speaks the Summer Tongue, so he and the captain adjourn to the cabin for a privy conference.

paragraphs.context: He could feel eyes on him, peering down from balconies and windows
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam walks Oldtown's river road feeling watched, fearing recognition as Randyll Tarly's son.
paragraphs.simple: The day is damp, so the cobblestones are wet and slippery underfoot, and the alleys are shrouded in mist and mystery. Sam avoids them as best he can and stays on the river road that winds along beside the Honeywine through the heart of the old city. It feels good to have solid ground beneath his feet again instead of a rolling deck, but the walk makes him uncomfortable all the same. He can feel eyes on him, peering down from balconies and windows, watching him from the darkened doorways. On the Cinnamon Wind he had known every face. Here, everywhere he turns he sees another stranger. Even worse is the thought of being seen by someone who knows him. Lord Randyll Tarly is known in Oldtown, but little loved. Sam does not know which would be worse: to be recognized by one of his lord father's enemies or by one of his friends. He pulls his cloak up and quickens his pace.

paragraphs.context: a pair of towering green sphinxes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam reaches the Citadel gates, flanked by sphinxes, and stops at Scribe's Hearth for a map.
paragraphs.simple: The gates of the Citadel are flanked by a pair of towering green sphinxes with the bodies of lions, the wings of eagles, and the tails of serpents. One has a man's face, one a woman's. Just beyond stands Scribe's Hearth, where Oldtowners come in search of acolytes to write their wills and read their letters. Half a dozen bored scribes sit in open stalls, waiting for custom. At other stalls books are being bought and sold. Sam stops at one that offers maps, and looks over a hand-drawn map of the Citadel to ascertain the shortest way to the Seneschal's Court.

paragraphs.context: You need to slip Lorcas a penny
paragraphs.mainIdea: A voice advises Sam to bribe the clerk Lorcas with a penny, and asks what brings the Night's Watch.
paragraphs.simple: A voice beside Sam says he needs to slip Lorcas a penny, or he will be waiting there three days. The speaker asks what brings the Night's Watch to the Citadel.

paragraphs.context: a cap of tight black curls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam meets the slim, comely, half-Dornish youth Alleras, and explains the Watch needs more maesters.
paragraphs.simple: The speaker is a slim, slight, comely youth, clad in doeskin breeches and a snug green brigandine with iron studs. He has skin the color of a light brown ale and a cap of tight black curls that comes to a widow's peak above his big black eyes. Sam explains that the Lord Commander is restoring the abandoned castles. They need more maesters, for the ravens. Then he asks about the penny.

paragraphs.context: The sphinx is the riddle, not the riddler
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam blurts Aemon's riddle about the sphinx, startled by the name Alleras.
paragraphs.simple: The name gives Sam a jolt. He blurts out that the sphinx is the riddle, not the riddler, and asks Alleras if he knows what that means.

paragraphs.context: He died during our voyage south
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam tells Alleras that Maester Aemon died on the voyage south.
paragraphs.simple: Sam says he met Aemon once. Most just called him Maester Aemon. He died during their voyage south. Sam asks how Alleras knows of him.

paragraphs.context: You must tell them, Sam, Maester Aemon had said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Remembering Aemon's command to tell the archmaesters, Sam agrees to go with Alleras.
paragraphs.simple: Sam remembers Maester Aemon's words: he must tell them, Sam. He must tell the archmaesters. Sam agrees to go. He can always return to the Seneschal on the morrow, with a penny in his hand. He asks how far they have to go.

paragraphs.context: He has good days and bad ones
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alleras warns Walgrave has good and bad days, but Sam will not be seeing him; they climb past complaining ravens.
paragraphs.simple: Alleras says Walgrave has good days and bad ones, but it is not Walgrave that Sam is going to see. He opens the door to the north tower and begins to climb. Sam clambers up the steps behind him. There are flutterings and mutterings from above, and here and there an angry scream, as the ravens complain of being woken.

paragraphs.context: made him feel as if he were still a boy of seven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam recognizes Leo Tyrell and feels seven years old again, terrified.
paragraphs.simple: Sam knows him. He says the name Leo Tyrell. Saying the name makes him feel as if he were still a boy of seven, about to wet his smallclothes. He introduces himself as Sam, from Horn Hill, Lord Randyll Tarly's son.

paragraphs.context: he looked more like a dockside thug than a maester
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam meets Archmaester Marwyn: bull-necked, scarred, sourleaf-stained, with the biggest hands Sam has ever seen.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn wears a chain of many metals around his bull's neck. Save for that, he looks more like a dockside thug than a maester. His head is too big for his body, and the way it thrusts forward from his shoulders, together with that slab of jaw, makes him look as if he is about to tear off someone's head. Though short and squat, he is heavy in the chest and shoulders, with a round, rock-hard ale belly straining at the laces of the leather jerkin he wears in place of robes. Bristly white hair sprouts from his ears and nostrils. His brow beetles, his nose has been broken more than once, and sourleaf has stained his teeth a mottled red. He has the biggest hands Sam has ever seen.

paragraphs.context: The candle itself was three feet tall and slender as a sword
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam stares at the glass candle: unnatural flame, strange colors, shadows like holes in the world.
paragraphs.simple: The candle is unpleasantly bright. There is something queer about it. The flame does not flicker, even when Archmaester Marwyn closes the door so hard that papers blow off a nearby table. The light does something strange to colors too. Whites are bright as fresh-fallen snow, yellow shines like gold, reds turn to flame, but the shadows are so black they look like holes in the world. Sam finds himself staring. The candle itself is three feet tall and slender as a sword, ridged and twisted, glittering black. Sam starts to ask if that is what he thinks it is.

paragraphs.context: It burns but is not consumed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn names it dragonglass: it burns but is not consumed.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn tells him to call it dragonglass. He glances at the candle for a moment. It burns but is not consumed.

paragraphs.context: All Valyrian sorcery was rooted in blood or fire
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn explains the glass candles let Valyrian sorcerers see far, enter dreams, and speak across the world.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn asks what feeds a dragon's fire, and seats himself upon a stool. He says all Valyrian sorcery was rooted in blood or fire. The sorcerers of the Freehold could see across mountains, seas, and deserts with one of these glass candles. They could enter a man's dreams and give him visions, and speak to one another half a world apart, seated before their candles. He asks Sam if he thinks that might be useful, calling him Slayer.

paragraphs.context: Born amidst salt and smoke, beneath a bleeding star
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn knows the prophecy but distrusts it, quoting Gorghan: prophecy is treacherous and will bite you.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn recites the prophecy: born amidst salt and smoke, beneath a bleeding star. He says he knows the prophecy, then spits a gob of red phlegm onto the floor. Not that he would trust it. He quotes Gorghan of Old Ghis, who once wrote that a prophecy is like a treacherous woman: she pleasures you and you think how sweet and fine it is, and then her teeth snap shut. That is the nature of prophecy, said Gorghan. Prophecy will bite you every time. Marwyn chews a bit, then says still . . .

paragraphs.context: Aemon would have gone to her if he had the strength
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alleras says Aemon wanted a maester sent to Daenerys, to counsel, protect, and bring her home.
paragraphs.simple: Alleras steps up next to Sam. He says Aemon would have gone to her if he had the strength. Aemon wanted them to send a maester to her, to counsel her and protect her and fetch her safely home.

paragraphs.context: The world the Citadel is building has no place in it for sorcery
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn warns the Citadel is killing magic: they sidelined Aemon for his blood, and Sam must stay silent.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn warns Sam that if he tells the others, they may need to kill Sam too. He smiles a ghastly smile, the juice of the sourleaf running red between his teeth. He asks who Sam thinks killed all the dragons the last time around. Not gallant dragonslayers armed with swords. The world the Citadel is building has no place in it for sorcery or prophecy or glass candles, much less for dragons. Sam should ask himself why Aemon Targaryen was allowed to waste his life upon the Wall, when by rights he should have been raised to archmaester. His blood was why. Aemon could not be trusted. No more than Marwyn can.

paragraphs.context: Get myself to Slaver’s Bay, in Aemon’s place
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn will sail to Slaver's Bay in Aemon's place, racing the Citadel's man, and tells Sam to forge his chain quickly.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn says he will get himself to Slaver's Bay, in Aemon's place. The swan ship that delivered Sam should serve his needs well enough. The grey sheep will send their man on a galley, he does not doubt. With fair winds he should reach her first. Marwyn glances at Sam again and frowns. Sam should stay and forge his chain. If Marwyn were Sam, he would do it quickly. A time will come when Sam is needed on the Wall. He turns to the pasty-faced novice and orders him to find Sam a dry cell. Sam will sleep here and help tend the ravens.

paragraphs.context: say nothing of prophecies or dragons, unless you fancy poison in your porridge
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marwyn instructs Sam to flatter the archmaesters and say nothing of dragons or prophecy.
paragraphs.simple: Marwyn tells Sam to tell the archmaesters how wise and good they are. He should tell them that Aemon commanded him to put himself into their hands. He should tell them he has always dreamed that one day he might be allowed to wear the chain and serve the greater good, that service is the highest honor, and obedience the highest virtue. But he must say nothing of prophecies or dragons, unless he fancies poison in his porridge. Marwyn snatches a stained leather cloak off a peg near the door and ties it tight. He tells the Sphinx to look after Sam.

paragraphs.context: Ours was no chance encounter, Sam
paragraphs.mainIdea: Alleras confesses the meeting was arranged: the Mage sent him to snatch Sam up, knowing he was coming.
paragraphs.simple: Alleras says they are going to the docks. The Mage is not a man who believes in wasting time. He smiles and confesses that theirs was no chance encounter, Sam. The Mage sent him to snatch Sam up before he spoke to the Seneschal's man. Marwyn knew that Sam was coming.

paragraphs.context: the book had become too big to publish in a single volume
paragraphs.mainIdea: Martin explains he split the book in two because it grew too big for a single volume.
paragraphs.simple: Martin says he did not forget to write about the other characters. Far from it. He wrote lots about them, pages and pages, chapters and more chapters. He was still writing when it dawned on him that the book had become too big to publish in a single volume, and he was not close to finished yet. To tell all of the story he wanted to tell, he was going to have to cut the book in two.

paragraphs.context: in A Dance with Dragons, which will focus on events along the Wall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion, Jon, Dany, and the rest return in A Dance with Dragons, covering the Wall and the lands across the sea.
paragraphs.simple: Martin says Tyrion, Jon, Dany, Stannis and Melisandre, Davos Seaworth, and all the rest of the characters readers love or love to hate will be along next year, he devoutly hopes, in A Dance with Dragons. That book will focus on events along the Wall and across the sea, just as the present book focused on King's Landing.

paragraphs.context: shows the crowned stag of Baratheon, black on gold
paragraphs.mainIdea: This paragraph describes the design of King Tommen's banner, which combines the Baratheon stag and the Lannister lion.
paragraphs.simple: Tommen's flag shows the Baratheon sign, a crowned stag, in black on a gold background. Next to it is the Lannister lion in gold on crimson, a deep red. The two animals face each other as if fighting.

paragraphs.context: the fiery heart of the Lord of Light; a red heart
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis has changed his banner to the burning-heart symbol of his new god, R'hllor the Lord of Light.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis now flies a new flag: a red heart ringed by orange fire on a yellow background. The heart is the sign of the Lord of Light. Inside the heart sits the black crowned stag of House Baratheon.

paragraphs.context: the Grey King ruled the sea itself and took a mermaid to wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: This paragraph gives the legendary history and symbols of House Greyjoy of Pyke.
paragraphs.simple: The Greyjoys say they come from the Grey King, a hero of long ago. Old stories say he ruled the sea itself and married a mermaid. After Aegon the Dragon killed the last King of the Iron Islands, the ironborn were allowed to bring back their old custom and choose who should rule over them. They chose Lord Vickon Greyjoy of Pyke. The Greyjoy sign is a golden kraken, a great sea monster, on a black field. Their house words are We Do Not Sow.

paragraphs.context: first rebellion against the Iron Throne was put down
paragraphs.mainIdea: Balon Greyjoy rebelled once before, was beaten by Robert and Ned Stark, and crowned himself king again after Robert died.
paragraphs.simple: Balon's first uprising against the Iron Throne was crushed by King Robert and Eddard Stark of Winterfell. But after Robert's death threw everything into chaos, Balon named himself king a second time and sent his ships to attack the north.

paragraphs.context: descended from the Kings of Mountain and Vale
paragraphs.mainIdea: This paragraph gives the history and symbols of House Arryn.
paragraphs.simple: The Arryns come from the old Kings of Mountain and Vale. Their sign is a white moon and falcon on a sky-blue field. House Arryn took no part in the War of the Five Kings. Their house words are As High as Honor.

paragraphs.context: gave command of his fleet to Ser Imry Florent
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Alester Florent backed Stannis, lost everything at the Blackwater, and was burned alive by Melisandre for trying to make peace.
paragraphs.simple: The Florents serve Highgarden. When the war began, Lord Alester followed his lord in backing Renly, while his brother Ser Axell chose Stannis. After Renly died, Alester went over to Stannis too, bringing all the strength of Brightwater. Stannis made Alester his Hand and gave his ships to Ser Imry, Stannis's brother-in-law. The ships and Ser Imry were both lost at the Battle of Blackwater. After the defeat, Alester tried to arrange peace, which Stannis called treason. Alester was handed to the red priestess Melisandre, who burned him as an offering to her god R'hllor.

paragraphs.context: named the Florents traitors for their support of Stannis
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Iron Throne declared the Florents traitors, stripped them of their lands, and gave Brightwater to Garlan Tyrell.
paragraphs.simple: The Iron Throne also called the Florents traitors for backing Stannis and his uprising. They were stripped of their rank and lands, and Brightwater Keep and its lands were awarded, given, to Ser Garlan Tyrell.

paragraphs.context: conspired with Roose Bolton and murdered the Young Wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Freys broke faith with Robb Stark and murdered him and his followers at the Red Wedding.
paragraphs.simple: The Freys serve House Tully but have not always been loyal in their duty. When the war began, Robb Stark won Lord Walder's support by promising to marry one of Walder's daughters or granddaughters. When Robb married Jeyne Westerling instead, the Freys plotted with Roose Bolton and killed the Young Wolf and his followers at what became known as the Red Wedding.

paragraphs.context: welcoming the Andals rather than resisting them, and later bending
paragraphs.mainIdea: House Hightower is an ancient, rich, learned house that prefers trade and study to war.
paragraphs.simple: The Hightowers are among the oldest and proudest of the great houses, going back to the First Men. Once kings, they have ruled Oldtown and its lands since the earliest days. They welcomed the Andals instead of fighting them, and later bowed to the Kings of the Reach, giving up their crowns but keeping all their ancient rights. Though strong and very rich, the Lords of the High Tower have always liked trade more than battle and have rarely taken part in the wars of Westeros. They helped found the Citadel and guard it to this day. They are clever and refined, great friends of learning and the Faith, and it is said that some of them have meddled in alchemy, dark magic, and other sorcery.

paragraphs.context: a stepped white tower crowned with fire on a smoke-grey field
paragraphs.mainIdea: This paragraph describes the Hightower banner and house words.
paragraphs.simple: The Hightower sign shows a white tower built in steps, with fire on its top, on a smoke-grey field, a grey background like smoke. The house words are We Light the Way.

paragraphs.context: has made them the wealthiest of the Great Houses
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lannisters are the richest great house and the chief backers of Tommen's claim to the throne.
paragraphs.simple: The Lannisters of Casterly Rock are the chief support of King Tommen's claim to the Iron Throne. They boast of descent from Lann the Clever, a legendary trickster of the Age of Heroes. The gold of Casterly Rock and the Golden Tooth has made them the richest of the great houses. Their sign is a golden lion on crimson, a deep red field. Their words are Hear Me Roar!

paragraphs.context: murdered by his dwarf son in his privy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin Lannister, Lord of Casterly Rock, Shield of Lannisport, Warden of the West, and Hand of the King, was murdered by his son Tyrion in his privy.
paragraphs.simple: Tywin Lannister held the titles Lord of Casterly Rock, Shield of Lannisport, Warden of the West, and Hand of the King. He was murdered by his dwarf son in his privy, the small room with a toilet.

paragraphs.context: Dorne was the last of the Seven Kingdoms to swear fealty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorne stayed out of the war at first, then backed Joffrey after Myrcella's betrothal to Trystane.
paragraphs.simple: Dorne was the last of the Seven Kingdoms to swear loyalty to the Iron Throne. Its blood, customs, land, and history all set the Dornish apart from the other kingdoms. When the war began Dorne took no part, but when Myrcella Baratheon was promised in marriage to Prince Trystane, Sunspear declared its support for King Joffrey. The Martell banner is a red sun pierced by a golden spear. Their words are Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken.

paragraphs.context: he won every battle, but was betrayed and murdered
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb Stark won every battle of the war but was betrayed and murdered by the Freys and Boltons at the Red Wedding.
paragraphs.simple: The Starks come from Brandon the Builder and the old Kings in the North. For thousands of years they ruled from Winterfell as Kings in the North, until Torrhen Stark chose to kneel to Aegon the Dragon rather than fight. When Lord Eddard Stark was executed by King Joffrey, the northmen broke their loyalty to the Iron Throne and named Eddard's son Robb King in the North. Robb won every battle of the war, but the Freys and Boltons betrayed and murdered him at the Twins during his uncle's wedding.

paragraphs.context: rewarded him by raising House Tully to dominion over
paragraphs.mainIdea: House Tully was raised to rule the riverlands by Aegon the Conqueror.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Edmyn Tully of Riverrun was among the first river lords to bow to Aegon the Conqueror. Aegon rewarded him by raising House Tully to rule over all the lands of the Trident. The Tully sign is a leaping trout, a silver fish, on a field of blue and red rippling water. The Tully words are Family, Duty, Honor.

paragraphs.context: Mace Tyrell declared his support for Renly Baratheon at the onset
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tyrells rose from stewards to rulers of the Reach, backed Renly, then allied with the Lannisters.
paragraphs.simple: The Tyrells grew powerful as stewards, managers, to the Kings of the Reach, though they claim descent from Garth Greenhand, an old gardener king of the First Men. When the last Gardener king was killed on the Field of Fire, his steward Harlen Tyrell gave Highgarden to Aegon the Conqueror. Aegon granted him the castle and rule over the Reach. Mace Tyrell backed Renly Baratheon when the war began and gave him his daughter Margaery's hand in marriage. After Renly died, Highgarden allied with House Lannister, and Margaery was promised to King Joffrey.

paragraphs.context: oft wed brother to sister, cousin to cousin, uncle to niece
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Targaryens are of old Valyrian dragon-blood, wed close kin to keep it pure, and fly the three-headed dragon banner.
paragraphs.simple: The Targaryens are the blood of the dragon, descended from the high lords of the ancient Freehold of Valyria. Their heritage shows in lilac, indigo, and violet eyes and hair of silver-gold. To keep their blood pure, House Targaryen has often wed brother to sister, cousin to cousin, uncle to niece. Aegon the Conqueror, who founded their rule, took both his sisters as wives and fathered sons on each. The Targaryen banner is a three-headed dragon, red on black, the three heads standing for Aegon and his sisters. The Targaryen words are Fire and Blood.

paragraphs.context: He spent ten years in Hollywood as a writer-producer
paragraphs.mainIdea: George R. R. Martin sold his first story in 1971, worked ten years in Hollywood television, and has written A Song of Ice and Fire since the mid-1990s.
paragraphs.simple: George R. R. Martin sold his first story in 1971 and has been writing for a living ever since. He spent ten years in Hollywood as a writer and producer, working on The Twilight Zone, Beauty and the Beast, and various films and television pilots that were never made. In the mid-1990s he went back to writing stories, his first love, and began work on his epic fantasy series A Song of Ice and Fire. He has been in its world ever since. When he is allowed to leave, he goes home to Santa Fe, New Mexico, where he lives with his wife Parris, a big white dog called Mischa, and two cats named Augustus and Caligula, who think they run the place.

sentences.context: As great a maester as once he’d been, now his robes
sentences.simple: Walgrave had once been a great maester, but now he was old and helpless: his robes often hid dirty underclothes.
sentences.grammar: 'As great a maester as once he'd been' is a concessive opening meaning 'however great a maester he had once been'; the main clause that follows ('now his robes concealed...') gives the sharp contrast.

sentences.context: “If only it worked that way with apples, no one would ever need go
sentences.simple: If cutting things in two really made two of them, nobody would ever go hungry.
sentences.grammar: 'If only...' opens a wish about something impossible; 'need go hungry' uses the bare infinitive 'go' after 'need' (instead of 'to go'), an older pattern.

sentences.context: “You’d need to be down the belly yourself to swear they weren’t.
sentences.simple: You would have to be inside the fish's belly yourself to swear that the sailors were not telling the truth.
sentences.grammar: The ending leaves out the rest of the idea ('they weren't telling the truth'); the missing words must be filled in from the argument about the sailors' stories just before it (ellipsis of the predicate).

sentences.context: Whether this be Greydon or Gormond or Gran, the priest had
sentences.simple: It did not matter which of the three brothers this was; the priest had no time for him.
sentences.grammar: 'Whether this be' uses the subjunctive 'be' (not 'is') after 'whether' — an old formal pattern for an open question, meaning 'whichever one he may be'.

sentences.context: “He that does not die in truth cannot hope to rise from death.
sentences.simple: A person who does not truly die cannot hope to rise from death.
sentences.grammar: Archaic 'He that' stands in for 'whoever' or 'anyone who'; the sentence states a general rule with the old-fashioned relative 'that' after 'he'.

sentences.context: He is afraid to dismount, lest he get his boots wet.
sentences.simple: He is afraid to get off his horse, because he does not want his boots to get wet.
sentences.grammar: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' or 'so that... not'; it is followed by the bare subjunctive 'he get' (not 'he gets'), marking a feared outcome.

sentences.context: Four kings there were in Westeros, yet Aeron did not need
sentences.simple: There were four kings in Westeros, but Aeron did not need to ask which one the news was about.
sentences.grammar: Inversion for emphasis: 'Four kings there were' puts the number first instead of the normal order 'There were four kings'.

sentences.context: in the Drowned God’s watery halls, the four of us and Urri
sentences.simple: One day the four of them — Aeron and his brothers — will feast together in the Drowned God's watery halls, and Urri will be there too.
sentences.grammar: 'The four of us' packs the speaker plus three others into one phrase; 'and Urri too' is tacked on as an afterthought, adding one more person to the group.

sentences.context: “It has been twenty years, or near enough to make no matter.
sentences.simple: It has been twenty years, or close enough to twenty that the difference does not matter.
sentences.grammar: 'Near enough to make no matter' is an idiom meaning 'close enough that it makes no difference'; the 'to'-clause gives the result of being near enough.

sentences.context: Eyes, the captain thought, and steps he cannot climb.
sentences.simple: The palace is full of watching eyes, and it has steps the prince cannot climb.
sentences.grammar: Two bare noun phrases with no verb, in telegraphic style: 'Eyes' names the danger and 'steps he cannot climb' names the obstacle, with everything else left unsaid.

sentences.context: And so and so and so, as the bearded priests would say.
sentences.simple: And so on and so on, as the bearded priests would say.
sentences.grammar: Elliptical listing: 'and so' is repeated instead of naming each further thing, standing in for 'and so on' — and other things of the same kind.

sentences.context: The more she struggled the more the throne engulfed her, tearing chunks
sentences.simple: The harder she fought to get free, the deeper the throne swallowed her up, tearing pieces of flesh from her body.
sentences.grammar: Comparative correlative 'the more..., the more...': the two halves rise together — as the struggling increases, so does the throne's grip.

sentences.context: I have not woken, nor has my nightmare ended.
sentences.simple: I have not woken up, and my nightmare has not ended either.
sentences.grammar: Inversion after the negative 'nor': 'nor has my nightmare ended' flips to auxiliary-before-subject ('has' before 'my nightmare') instead of 'my nightmare has not ended'.

sentences.context: Her bedchamber was dark, but for the lantern one of the intruders held
sentences.simple: Her bedchamber was dark, except for the lantern that one of the intruders was holding up high.
sentences.grammar: 'But for' means 'except for' or 'if not for'; here 'but for the lantern' carves one exception out of the darkness.

sentences.context: hole in the world where Father stood, and holes want filling.
sentences.simple: Now there is an empty space in the world where Father stood, and empty spaces need to be filled.
sentences.grammar: 'Holes want filling' uses 'want' plus a gerund in the old sense of 'need': the holes need to be filled — not 'want' as in desire.

sentences.context: “But I’ll keep my eye out, that I will.”
sentences.simple: But I will watch for her, I certainly will.
sentences.grammar: The tag 'that I will' repeats the promise just made ('I'll keep my eye out') for emphasis — a folksy doubling common in speech.

sentences.context: “If she’s on the roads these days she won’t be no maid for
sentences.simple: If she is traveling the roads these days, she will not stay a maiden for long.
sentences.grammar: Double negative in dialect speech: 'won't be no maid' means 'won't be a maid' — the two negatives strengthen rather than cancel each other.

sentences.context: How better to conceal her murder than by sending some big stupid
sentences.simple: What better way to hide her murder than by sending some big stupid woman from Tarth to search for her?
sentences.grammar: Rhetorical question used as a statement: 'How better to X than by Y' means 'there is no better way to X than by Y'.

sentences.context: Illy, gods be good, the size of her.”
sentences.simple: Illy — may the gods be kind — look at how big she is!
sentences.grammar: 'Gods be good' is a subjunctive prayer ('may the gods be good'), and 'the size of her' is an exclamation built from a bare noun phrase instead of a full clause.

sentences.context: I had as well swap my longsword for a pair of knitting needles.
sentences.simple: I might as well trade my longsword for a pair of knitting needles.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned 'had as well' (meaning 'might as well'): 'I had as well swap' says it would make little difference if she did something so foolish as swapping.

sentences.context: Longclaw is Valyrian steel, but I’m not.
sentences.simple: Longclaw is Valyrian steel, but I am not as good as my sword.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis after 'but I'm not': the repeated part ('as good as my sword') is left out and must be supplied from the sentence just before it.

sentences.context: He wore so much padding he looked like a stuffed goose.
sentences.simple: He wore so much padding that he looked like a stuffed goose.
sentences.grammar: Result clause with 'that' dropped: 'so much padding (that) he looked like a stuffed goose' — 'so + much' sets up a result, and the 'that' is simply left out.

sentences.context: The more you give a king the more he wants.
sentences.simple: Giving a king more only makes him want still more.
sentences.grammar: Comparative correlative 'the more..., the more...': giving and wanting rise together, with each half of the sentence carrying its own 'the more'.

sentences.context: Faint and far away the light burned, low on the horizon, shining through
sentences.simple: The light burned faintly, far away and low on the horizon, shining through the sea mists.
sentences.grammar: Fronted adjectives: 'Faint and far away' are moved to the very front of the sentence for a poetic effect, instead of the normal order 'The light burned faint and far away'.

sentences.context: a terrible groaning and grinding, so loud it drowned out even the captain’s
sentences.simple: A terrible groaning and grinding, so loud that it drowned out even the captain's voice and the crash of the waves against the pine-covered ridges.
sentences.grammar: 'So loud (that) it drowned out...' is a result clause with 'that' omitted: the loudness is so great that it produces the drowning-out.

sentences.context: but if the captain had asked she would have told him she wanted
sentences.simple: She had crossed the narrow sea to get here, but if the captain had asked her, she would have told him she wanted to stay aboard the Titan's Daughter.
sentences.grammar: 'If the captain had asked' leaves out what he would have asked about (whether she wanted to stay aboard); the missing object is filled in from the sentence around it (ellipsis).

sentences.context: “I killed the boy who grabbed me last.”
sentences.simple: I killed the boy who was the last one to grab me.
sentences.grammar: 'Last' belongs to 'grabbed' (the grabbing), not to 'boy': it picks out the most recent grabber, not the last boy in some group.

sentences.context: cannot eat love, nor buy a horse with it, nor warm your halls
sentences.simple: You cannot eat love. You also cannot buy a horse with it, and you cannot warm your rooms with it on a cold night.
sentences.grammar: 'cannot' is said once but reaches over the whole list: 'nor buy' and 'nor warm' still mean 'cannot buy' and 'cannot warm', because 'nor' carries the negative forward through the parallel verbs.

sentences.context: No sooner had she eased off her shoes than Jocelyn entered timidly
sentences.simple: Jocelyn came in quietly just as she had finished taking off her shoes.
sentences.grammar: 'No sooner had she done X than Y' means Y happened right after X; the helping verb 'had' moves in front of the subject 'she', an old-style inversion for something happening at once.

sentences.context: I must needs equip myself with certain
sentences.simple: I really must get for myself the things I need.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned English: 'must needs' means 'must certainly' or 'have to'; 'needs' is not a verb here, it only strengthens 'must'.

sentences.context: not for nought do they speak of hands and knees.
sentences.simple: People say 'hands and knees' for a good reason; it is not for nothing.
sentences.grammar: A negative word at the front flips the word order: 'do they speak' instead of 'they do speak'. This old-style inversion adds emphasis.

sentences.context: if I may be so bold, I do not think them like to answer.
sentences.simple: If you will forgive me for saying so, I do not think they are likely to answer.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned word order: 'like' here means 'likely', and 'them' stands in for 'they are'; modern English would say 'I do not think they are likely to answer'.

sentences.context: Friend or foe, the crows care not.
sentences.simple: The crows do not care whether a dead man was friend or enemy.
sentences.grammar: Old-style negative word order: 'care not' instead of 'do not care'; the verb comes before 'not'.

sentences.context: The maester never knew her, no more than he knew Hollard.
sentences.simple: The maester had never known her, just as he had never known Hollard either.
sentences.grammar: 'no more than' here means 'just as little as': a negative comparison saying both things are equally untrue.

sentences.context: you need do is tell Lord Nestor the same tale
sentences.simple: All you have to do is tell Lord Nestor the same story.
sentences.grammar: Special grammar: 'need' takes the bare verb 'do' with no 'to'; 'need do' is a short form of 'need to do'.

sentences.context: I had eyes I should weep.”
sentences.simple: If I still had eyes, I would cry.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned use of 'should' where modern English uses 'would': 'I should weep' means 'I would weep'.

sentences.context: On the blades were writ the words Rodrik and Maron,
sentences.simple: The words Rodrik and Maron were written on the blades of the knives.
sentences.grammar: 'writ' is an old form of 'written'; 'were writ' means 'were written', a passive verb describing what was on the blades.

sentences.context: pluck the seaweed from out between his toes.”
sentences.simple: Pull the seaweed out from between his toes.
sentences.grammar: Three small words pile up into one direction: 'from' + 'out' + 'between', with 'out' sharpening the pulling action of 'pluck'.

sentences.context: Not so long as Stannis Baratheon held Dragonstone and Storm’s End,
sentences.simple: Tommen's hold on the throne would not be secure as long as Stannis held Dragonstone and Storm's End, as long as Riverrun kept defying them, and as long as ironmen roamed the seas.
sentences.grammar: Three 'so long as' clauses chain onto the sentence before it: all three reasons (Stannis, Riverrun, the ironmen) share the one thought 'not secure enough'.

sentences.context: The more we give these Tyrells, the more they demand of us.
sentences.simple: The more we give the Tyrells, the more they ask of us.
sentences.grammar: A comparative pair: 'the more X, the more Y' means that as X grows, Y grows with it; here, giving more only makes them demand more.

sentences.context: Past the candlemaker’s shop, she wrote, a gate and a short flight
sentences.simple: Go past the candlemaker's shop; then there is a gate and a short flight of steps outside.
sentences.grammar: 'she wrote' is tucked inside the directions like a label: the sentence is quoting written directions, so 'she wrote' sits in the middle telling you whose words these are.

sentences.context: it is not meet that you should make me beg.”
sentences.simple: It is not proper for you to make me beg.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned: 'meet' means 'proper' or 'fitting', and 'should make' is a formal older form where modern English would simply say 'to make me beg'.

sentences.context: It’s home they want, as much as gold.
sentences.simple: It is home they want, just as much as they want gold.
sentences.grammar: A split sentence for emphasis: 'It's home they want' puts 'home' in the spotlight; 'as much as gold' then compares the two wishes.

sentences.context: it could only be because no one thought him worth the killing.
sentences.simple: It could only be because no one thought he was worth the trouble of killing.
sentences.grammar: Old-style pattern: 'thought him worth the killing' means 'thought he was worth killing'; 'worth the' + an action describes what someone deserves.

sentences.context: not seen no maids, fair nor foul.”
sentences.simple: I have not seen any maids, neither fair nor foul ones.
sentences.grammar: Country dialect with two negatives in one sentence: 'not seen no maids' still means 'seen none at all'; the double negative does not cancel here.

sentences.context: Ser Robar was twice the swordsman that you are
sentences.simple: Ser Robar was twice as good a swordsman as you are.
sentences.grammar: 'twice the X that' means 'twice as much of X as': 'twice the swordsman that you are' compares Robar's skill to yours by doubling.

sentences.context: the waves were like to smash him up against some stone
sentences.simple: The waves were likely to smash him against some rock.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned: 'like to' here means 'likely to'; 'were like to smash' means 'were likely to smash'.

sentences.context: Sometimes there is no happy choice, Sam, only one less grievous than the others.”
sentences.simple: Sometimes there is no happy choice, Sam; there is only a choice that is less painful than the others.
sentences.grammar: 'one' is short for 'one choice', and 'less grievous' describes it after the noun instead of before: the sentence means only a less painful choice exists.

sentences.context: more modest man might have answered ‘My lord is too kind,’
sentences.simple: A more modest man would have answered, 'My lord is too kind.'
sentences.grammar: A pretend past: 'might have answered' pictures what he would have said if he were more modest; the sentence criticizes him by imagining the humbler reply he did not give.

sentences.context: the more they laugh, the less he is a threat
sentences.grammar: Comparative correlative: 'the more X, the less Y' — the two halves rise and fall together, and both clauses share one meaning.
sentences.simple: The more these men laugh, the less dangerous he becomes.

sentences.context: the crown is content with whatever dispositions they might make
sentences.grammar: Tangled clause: 'Elsewise' means 'otherwise'; 'whatever dispositions they might make' is a noun clause where 'whatever' = 'anything that'.
sentences.simple: The crown will accept whatever decisions they make about the Vale while Robert Arryn is still a child.

sentences.context: None is to leave save at my command, neither man nor crow.
sentences.grammar: Double negative for emphasis: 'None' and 'neither man nor crow' both say no; 'save' means 'except'.
sentences.simple: No one is allowed to leave except on my orders — no man and no crow.

sentences.context: Only when his arms and legs were numb from the cold did Aeron Greyjoy
sentences.grammar: Inversion after 'Only when': the normal order 'Aeron struggled back' flips to 'did Aeron struggle back'.
sentences.simple: Aeron Greyjoy only came back to shore and put his robes on again after his arms and legs had gone numb with cold.

sentences.context: He had run before the Crow’s Eye as if he were still
sentences.grammar: Subjunctive 'as if he were' (not 'was') for something unreal; 'the weak thing he had been' = 'the weak thing that he had been', with 'that' left out.
sentences.simple: He had run away from the Crow's Eye as though he were still the weak person he had once been. But when the waves broke over his head, they reminded him again that that weak person was dead.

sentences.context: What the kraken grasps it does not lose, be it longship or leviathan.
sentences.grammar: Fronted object: 'What the kraken grasps' (= 'whatever the kraken takes') is the object moved to the front; 'be it' is old-style subjunctive meaning 'whether it is'.
sentences.simple: Whatever the kraken (the Greyjoy) takes hold of, it never lets go — whether it is a longship or a sea monster.

sentences.context: their sons couldn’t win with swords, their pretty daughters won with kisses
sentences.grammar: Fronted object: the clause 'Only what their sons couldn't win with swords' names what was won, then 'their pretty daughters won [it] with kisses' gives the rest — the object comes before the subject.
sentences.simple: Whatever their sons could not win with swords, their pretty daughters won with kisses.

sentences.context: It is one thing to train in the yard with a blunted sword
sentences.grammar: Parallel contrast 'It is one thing to X, and another to Y': the second half leaves out the repeated 'It is' and 'one thing', so the reader must supply it.
sentences.simple: Training in the yard with a dull practice sword is one thing, but driving a foot of sharpened steel into a man's stomach and watching the light leave his eyes is another.

sentences.context: The Mother in their songs is not our Mother, but Mother Rhoyne
sentences.grammar: Not-X-but-Y contrast where 'Mother' is a title: 'our Mother' (the goddess) vs 'Mother Rhoyne' (the river), so 'Mother' means two different things in one sentence.
sentences.simple: The 'Mother' in their songs is not the Mother of the Seven gods; it is Mother Rhoyne, the river goddess.

sentences.context: she did not leave the temple, nor descend to the third cellar
sentences.grammar: 'Nor' after a negative keeps the negative going without repeating 'not': 'nor descend' = 'and she did not descend'.
sentences.simple: She was free to wander, as long as she did not leave the temple and did not go down to the third cellar.

sentences.context: The slaves were not crying out to a hundred different gods
sentences.grammar: Not-X-but-Y with a parenthetical: 'as it seemed' (= 'as it looked') breaks the middle of the sentence, and the main point comes after 'but'.
sentences.simple: The slaves were not praying to a hundred different gods, as it looked like; they were praying to one god with a hundred different faces, and the first Faceless Man was that god's tool.

sentences.context: She gave Him all she was, all she ever might have been
sentences.grammar: Triple parallel list with the verb left out twice: 'all she was, [all she ever might have been], [all the lives...]' all depend on the one 'She gave Him'.
sentences.simple: She gave the god everything she was, everything she might ever have become, and every life that was inside her.

sentences.context: had not seen the body, no more than Robert had
sentences.grammar: 'No more than Robert had' means 'and Robert had not either': it adds a second person to the negative without repeating 'had not'.
sentences.simple: Alayne had not seen the body, and neither had Robert — but she did not doubt that the singer was dead.

sentences.context: Had she chosen any one of us, no man here would
sentences.grammar: Conditional inversion: 'Had she chosen' = 'If she had chosen'; the 'if' is dropped and the verb moves to the front.
sentences.simple: If Lysa had chosen any one of us as her husband, no man here would now question his right to be Lord Protector.

sentences.context: Misrule there has been, I will not deny it
sentences.grammar: Inversion for emphasis: 'Misrule there has been' puts the object ('misrule') before the verb, instead of the normal 'There has been misrule'.
sentences.simple: There has been bad rule, I will not deny it — but it was Lysa's doing, not mine.

sentences.context: neither my good wife nor her mother had any hand
sentences.grammar: 'Lest' means 'so that not': the whole sentence is a warning — 'you should know this, so that bad feeling does not grow between us'; 'neither...nor' shares one verb.
sentences.simple: Neither my good wife nor her mother had anything to do with naming this bastard child — Lollys is a simple creature, and her husband is given to dark moods.

sentences.context: I could have hired a Faceless Man to kill Bronn
sentences.grammar: Counterfactual 'could have': she did not hire one, but it would have been cheaper — the sentence judges a past action that cannot be changed.
sentences.simple: She thought: I could have hired a Faceless Man to kill Bronn for half of what I have spent on sweet wine tonight.

sentences.context: that no trap nor snare can hold her, that she fears
sentences.grammar: Chain of four 'that' clauses with the last two dropping 'that': 'slays any wolf...' and 'devours no other flesh...' still belong to 'they will tell you that'.
sentences.simple: People say she has brought down aurochs all by herself, that no trap or snare can hold her, that she fears neither steel nor fire, kills any wolf that tries to mate with her, and eats nothing but human flesh.

sentences.context: they are stealing from the living too, from the smallfolk
sentences.grammar: Stacked commas piling on detail: 'from the living too, from the smallfolk...' and the trailing 'men very like the men they used to be' is an appositive restating who they steal from.
sentences.simple: Soon they are stealing from the living as well — from the smallfolk whose lands they are fighting in, men much like the men they used to be.

sentences.context: there is no land of light and honey, only cold
sentences.grammar: 'What if X, only Y' with the verb left out: 'only cold and dark and pain' = 'there is only cold and dark and pain', a dark answer to the sweet song of the septons.
sentences.simple: But what if there is no land of light and honey after death — only cold and dark and pain beyond the wall called death?

sentences.context: been lost here even if she had not been grief-stricken, but Dareon
sentences.grammar: The sentence breaks off after 'but Dareon...' with no ending: the three dots mean the thought is left unfinished, and the reader must guess what Sam meant.
sentences.simple: Maester Aemon's strength was gone, and Gilly would have been lost here even if she had not been stricken with grief — but Dareon... (the thought trails off unfinished).

sentences.context: No sooner had he entered, flushed and out of breath
sentences.grammar: 'No sooner had he entered... than...' = 'as soon as he entered...': inversion ('had he entered' instead of 'he had entered') is required after 'No sooner'.
sentences.simple: The moment he entered, flushed and out of breath, a one-eyed woman threw her arms around his neck.

sentences.context: Had they encountered other travelers, he might have stopped
sentences.grammar: Had they encountered ... is an inverted conditional (= If they had encountered ...): the if is dropped and had moves before the subject; the sentence then piles relative clauses (a face that would curdle milk) onto the object.
sentences.simple: If they had met other travelers on the road, he might have stopped to ask whether any of them had seen a pretty maid with reddish-brown hair, or a big ugly one whose face was so sour it would curdle milk.

sentences.context: Should you capture him, hold him for my return
sentences.grammar: Should you capture him inverts subject and verb to make a condition (= If you should capture him, i.e. If you capture him); the order gives a command the shape of a condition.
sentences.simple: If you capture him, keep him prisoner until I come back.

sentences.context: Had that doddering old worm forsaken the lion for the rose?
sentences.grammar: Had ... forsaken ...? uses the inverted-conditional form (Had he forsaken = If he had forsaken) as a surprised rhetorical question, asked to express disbelief rather than to get an answer.
sentences.simple: Had that old, trembling worm really deserted the lion for the rose?

sentences.context: Did not Jaehaerys the Conciliator once swear upon the Iron Throne itself
sentences.grammar: Negative inversion in a rhetorical question: Did not ... once swear ...? puts did not before the subject (= Did he not swear ...?); it is asked to make a point, not to get an answer.
sentences.simple: Did Jaehaerys the Conciliator not once swear on the Iron Throne itself that the crown would always protect and defend the Faith?

sentences.context: Would that I could deal with the Crow’s Eye as simply.
sentences.grammar: Would that ... is an old-fashioned wish form (= If only ... / I wish ...): would here expresses a wish, not the future, and the that-clause states what is wished for.
sentences.simple: I wish I could deal with the Crow's Eye as easily as that.

sentences.context: Beyond wait the Stepstones, with their storms and their nests
sentences.grammar: Locative inversion: the place word (Beyond) comes first and the verb (wait) comes before the subject (the Stepstones), so the subject lands at the end for emphasis.
sentences.simple: Beyond them lay the Stepstones, with their storms and their nests of Lysene and Myrish pirates.

sentences.context: would have us believe that her face was torn and scarred
sentences.grammar: would have us believe is an idiom meaning want us to believe; and her eyes terrible to look upon drops the was (= and her eyes were terrible to look at).
sentences.simple: The peasants want us to believe that her face was torn and scarred, and that her eyes were terrible to look at.

sentences.context: whereas the brothers weeding in the garden had had the stooped shoulders
sentences.grammar: had had is the past perfect (had + had, the past participle of have): the brothers had possessed those bent backs; whereas sets the whole clause up as a sharp contrast with what follows.
sentences.simple: He could hardly be called old, for a start. The brothers weeding in the garden had the bent shoulders and curved backs of old men, while he stood straight and tall, and moved with the strength of a man in the prime of his life.

sentences.context: Had he decided elsewise, I might have been on the other side
sentences.grammar: Had he decided elsewise inverts the conditional (= If he had decided otherwise): the if disappears and had moves in front of the subject.
sentences.simple: If he had decided differently, I might have fought on the other side of the river.

sentences.context: Come morning he remembered nothing, or so he would have had her believe
sentences.grammar: Come morning is a shortened time phrase (= When morning came); he would have had her believe is a tangled causative: he wanted her to believe it (he would have had her = he wished to make her).
sentences.simple: When morning came he remembered nothing -- or so he wanted her to believe.

sentences.context: and told me I had best be gone from Stokeworth before
sentences.grammar: I had best be gone = I should leave (had best gives strong advice); or I'd get the same clips the comparison short: or I would get the same [a dagger in my eye].
sentences.simple: Bronn put a dagger in his eye, and told me I should leave Stokeworth before the sun went down, or I would get the same treatment.

sentences.context: Would that he’d remained, I could have used his counsel
sentences.grammar: Would that ... is the old wish form (= If only he had stayed); the second half (I could have used his counsel) gives the reason behind the wish.
sentences.simple: I wish he had stayed; I could have used his advice.

sentences.context: The longer the siege dragged on, the more it would hearten other
sentences.grammar: A comparative correlative: The longer ..., the more ... links two rising scales -- as the first grows, so does the second.
sentences.simple: The longer the siege went on, the more it would encourage other rebels, like Tytos Blackwood.

sentences.context: No sooner was he gone than his lady wife rolled her
sentences.grammar: No sooner ... than inverts subject and verb (was he gone instead of he was gone) to stress that the second thing followed the first at once.
sentences.simple: The moment he was gone, his lady wife rolled her eyes.

sentences.context: but a monster with a dog’s head would not let her go save her
sentences.grammar: Two bare infinitives, go and save, both hang on let: would not let her [go] [save her] = would not let her go in order to save her mother.
sentences.simple: It was always raining in that dream, and she could hear her mother screaming, but a monster with a dog's head would not let her go to save her mother.

sentences.context: But she had never thought warm milk.
sentences.grammar: The preposition is dropped: she had never thought warm milk = she had never thought of warm milk (the idea had never come into her mind).
sentences.simple: She had imagined this talk in her head fifty times, like an actor in a play. But warm milk had never occurred to her.

sentences.context: Would that I was even ten years younger.
sentences.grammar: Would that ... is the old-fashioned wish form (= If only I were even ten years younger); was stands in for were here.
sentences.simple: I wish I were even ten years younger.

sentences.context: Had it been that way in life as well?
sentences.grammar: Had it been ...? uses inverted-conditional word order (Had it been = If it had been) as a wondering question she asks herself.
sentences.simple: Had it been that way in life too?

sentences.context: Cersei liked that not at all. Nor was she pleased by the High
sentences.grammar: liked that not at all puts not after the verb in an old word order (= did not like that at all); Nor was she pleased then inverts subject and verb after the negative opener.
