sentences.simple: Cersei did not like that at all. Nor was she pleased by the High Sparrow's endless rudeness and lack of gratitude.

sentences.context: did not concern Brienne half so much as
sentences.simple: Brienne cared much less about who these dead men were than about who had hanged them.
sentences.grammar: Two 'who' clauses act as the things compared: 'Who they were' did not concern her 'half so much as' — much less than — 'who had hanged them'.

sentences.context: Would that I had some land hereabouts
sentences.simple: I wish that I owned some land around here.
sentences.grammar: 'Would that' is an old way to begin a wish; the sentence leaves out the 'I wish' part: he wishes he owned land in these parts.

sentences.context: Hundreds of mine. Thousands of yours.
sentences.simple: Hundreds of my men will die. Thousands of yours will die.
sentences.grammar: Two fragments borrow the verb from the sentence just before them — 'Hundreds will die' — and shorten it to 'Hundreds of mine' and 'Thousands of yours'.

sentences.context: as small a risk as that may be
sentences.simple: Even though the risk of that happening is small.
sentences.grammar: 'As small a risk as that may be' is a concession built as 'as + adjective + a + noun + as': however small the risk may be.

sentences.context: I do not believe that. Nor will he
sentences.simple: I do not believe we will lift the siege if he wins, and he will not believe it either.
sentences.grammar: 'Nor will he' flips the word order after 'nor': instead of 'and he will not believe that either', the verb comes first and 'believe that' is left out.

sentences.context: Should Roslin give you a daughter, I’ll see her
sentences.simple: If Roslin gives you a daughter, I will see that she is well provided with a dowry when she is old enough to marry.
sentences.grammar: 'Should Roslin give you a daughter' is an inverted if-clause: 'should' moves to the front and 'if' is dropped, meaning 'if Roslin should give you a daughter'.

sentences.context: it’s me saying how I never fucked them and
sentences.simple: Usually, when I lie about some woman, it is me saying that I never had sex with them and them saying that I did.
sentences.grammar: Two parallel clauses are squeezed after 'it's': 'it's me saying...' and '[it's] them saying...' — each with its own hidden 'that' clause and a dropped verb at the end ('how I never [did] ... how I did').

sentences.context: The more she thought about her cousins, the more the princess missed them
sentences.simple: The longer and harder she thought about her cousins, the more she missed them.
sentences.grammar: A comparative correlative: 'the more..., the more...' links two changes — as one grows, so does the other.

sentences.context: It is for my prince to command, for Hotah to obey
sentences.simple: Commanding is my prince's part; obeying is Hotah's part.
sentences.grammar: 'It is for X to Y' assigns each person his role: 'for my prince to command' means commanding belongs to the prince, and 'for Hotah to obey' means obeying belongs to Hotah.

sentences.context: Arianne decided that she must needs be more subtle
sentences.simple: Arianne decided that she must be more subtle.
sentences.grammar: 'Must needs' is an old form: 'needs' works as an adverb meaning 'necessarily', so 'must needs be' means 'must necessarily be'.

sentences.context: He shook his head. “Would that we had.
sentences.simple: He shook his head. 'I wish that we had' — caught Ser Gerold.
sentences.grammar: 'Would that we had' is an old wish with the rest left out: 'I wish that we had' — what was wished for is understood from the question just asked, 'Have you caught Ser Gerold?'

sentences.context: and let our foes think us more powerful than we are
sentences.simple: And we have let our enemies think that we are more powerful than we really are.
sentences.grammar: 'Let our foes think us more powerful' uses 'let' with an object and a bare complement: 'think us [to be] more powerful' — no 'that' and no 'to be' appears.

sentences.context: though he was already holding her so tightly that she
sentences.simple: 'Will my Sweetrobin hold me tight?' she asked — even though he was already holding her so tightly that she could scarcely breathe.
sentences.grammar: The 'though' clause turns the request into a joke: she asks him to do what he is already doing, and the clause after 'though' tells what is already true.

sentences.context: She’s half mule herself, that one
sentences.simple: She is half mule herself, that one — Mya is as stubborn as a mule.
sentences.grammar: Right dislocation: the name comes last — 'She's half mule herself, that one' — restating the subject 'she' as 'that one' after the claim.

sentences.context: like calling a puddle on a privy floor a lake
sentences.simple: It is like calling a puddle on a privy floor a lake — naming something small and dirty with a grand name.
sentences.grammar: 'Call X Y' takes two objects: calling 'this' 'a castle' is like calling 'a puddle' 'a lake' — the second noun renames the first.

sentences.context: they soon run out of pity, as they do of milk and honey
sentences.simple: They soon run out of pity, just as they run out of milk and honey.
sentences.grammar: The comparison 'as they do of milk and honey' drops the repeated verb: 'as they do [run out] of milk and honey'.

sentences.context: They don’t mean so much as they used to, neither one
sentences.simple: Neither death nor guest right means as much as it used to.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither one' points back to the two things just named — death and guest right — and 'so much as they used to' compares with how much they meant before.

sentences.context: If I had a silver stag for every time you said his name
sentences.simple: If I received a silver stag every time you said his name, I would be as rich as the Lannisters.
sentences.grammar: A counterfactual 'if I had X for every time...': an impossible bargain used to say that you have said his name so many times the coins would make me rich.

sentences.context: the crowd was neither as numerous nor as unruly
sentences.simple: The crowd was not as large and not as wild as the sparrows had been.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither as X nor as Y as Z' pairs two 'as...as' comparisons under one 'neither': not as numerous and not as unruly, compared with 'the sparrows'.

sentences.context: the more diligently we applied the scourge, the more Ser Osney’s
sentences.simple: The more carefully we whipped him, the more Ser Osney's story about his crimes seemed to change.
sentences.grammar: A comparative correlative: 'the more..., the more...' — as the whipping grew more diligent, his story changed more.

sentences.context: bastards are treacherous by nature. Would that I had listened
sentences.simple: Bastards are treacherous by nature. I wish that I had listened to my father.
sentences.grammar: 'Would that I had listened' is an old wish with the rest left out: 'I wish that I had listened' — to the warning just given.

sentences.context: Fish swim. Even black ones.” Edmure smiled.
sentences.simple: But fish swim — and even black ones swim.
sentences.grammar: 'Fish swim. Even black ones' borrows its verb from the sentence before: 'even black ones [swim]' — the Blackfish escaped by swimming, like a fish.

sentences.context: what Ser Gregor did to the Goat will seem a jolly lark
sentences.simple: What Ser Gregor did to the Goat will seem like a merry game compared with what I will do to you.
sentences.grammar: 'What Ser Gregor did' is a headless 'what' clause — 'the thing that Ser Gregor did' — set against 'what I'll do to you' in a threat built on comparison.

sentences.context: that would have made the poor old dears wring their wrinkled hands
sentences.simple: That would have made the poor old men wring their wrinkled hands in worry.
sentences.grammar: 'Made X wring' uses 'make' with an object and a bare infinitive: 'made the poor old dears wring [their hands]' — no 'to' appears.

sentences.context: when by rights he should have been raised to archmaester
sentences.simple: When, by what was right, he should have been made an archmaester.
sentences.grammar: 'By rights' means 'according to what is right'; the clause gives the proper outcome that did not happen: he should have been raised to archmaester.

sentences.context: all the story for half the characters, rather than half the story for all
sentences.simple: A book that tells the whole story for half the characters, instead of telling half the story for all the characters.
sentences.grammar: A mirror-image pair joined by 'rather than': 'all the story for half the characters' is flipped to 'half the story for all the characters'.

sentences.context: Within the heart is the crowned stag of House Baratheon
sentences.grammar: Locative inversion: the place phrase 'Within the heart' comes before the verb 'is', so the subject ('the crowned stag') comes after the verb — read it as 'The crowned stag of House Baratheon is within the heart.'
sentences.simple: Inside the heart there is a black crowned stag of House Baratheon.

sentences.context: the Grey King ruled the sea itself and took a mermaid to wife
sentences.grammar: Archaic verb phrase: 'take X to wife' is an old-fashioned way of saying 'marry X'; 'wife' here works like a result after 'to', not a possession.
sentences.simple: Legend says the Grey King ruled the sea and married a mermaid.

sentences.context: The Iron Throne has also named the Florents traitors
sentences.grammar: Object complement: 'named' takes two objects here — the people ('the Florents') and what they are declared to be ('traitors'); it means 'declared to be', not 'gave a name to'.
sentences.simple: The Iron Throne has also declared the Florents to be traitors because they supported Stannis and his rebellion.

sentences.context: welcoming the Andals rather than resisting them, and later bending the knee
sentences.grammar: Three -ing phrases ('welcoming...', 'bending...', 'retaining...') all describe the same subject 'they' (the Hightowers) and run together in one long chain, so the reader must hold the subject across the whole sentence.
sentences.simple: Once kings, the Hightowers have ruled Oldtown for a very long time. They welcomed the Andals instead of fighting them, and later they submitted to the Kings of the Reach and gave up their crowns while keeping all their old rights.

sentences.context: chose to swear fealty to Aegon the Dragon rather than give battle
sentences.grammar: After 'rather than', the verb stays in its base form ('give', not 'giving' or 'to give') to match the infinitive it is compared with ('to swear').
sentences.simple: Torrhen Stark decided to swear loyalty to Aegon the Dragon instead of fighting him.

sentences.context: House Targaryen has oft wed brother to sister, cousin to cousin
sentences.grammar: Archaic and compressed: 'oft' means 'often', and the three parallel 'X to Y' phrases are short for 'brothers wed sisters, cousins wed cousins, uncles wed nieces', with repeated words left out.
sentences.simple: To keep their bloodline pure, House Targaryen often married brother to sister, cousin to cousin, and uncle to niece.

sentences.context: took both his sisters to wife and fathered sons on each
sentences.grammar: Two old-fashioned uses: 'take X to wife' means 'marry X', and 'father sons on each' means 'be the father of sons by each of them' — 'on' here does the work of 'by' or 'with'.
sentences.simple: Aegon the Conquerer, who founded the dynasty, married both his sisters and had sons with each of them.
